Some records in Ilhan Omar case will be released, judge says

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (472 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a news conference at the Capitol last summer.
  • In a recent development, A judge stated he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep.
  • Recent findings suggest that judge James Boasberg for the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a news conference at the Capitol last summer. Few details have emerged so far about the government’s search of her home earlier this fall. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

In a recent development, A judge stated he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., which included a search of her Washington house last month.

Recent findings suggest that judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia made the statement Tuesday during a hearing brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking details about the search. Boasberg ordered the government to provide him by Friday what could be disclosed in the case. He pointed to how investigators are handling the “speech or debate” clause immunity that Omar has as a sitting member of Congress.

“This is purely legal questions, interesting questions, about the privilege, the extent of the privilege and how it would apply,” Boasberg remarked.

The Constitution includes an immunity for members of Congress for the “speech or debate” they engage in as part of their jobs.

Recent findings suggest that boasberg also directed the government to propose redactions to the as-yet secret docket. While he said next week’s expected disclosures would not include the 67-page document that investigators provided to justify the search, he left the door open to unsealing that down the road if the government closes the case or brings charges.

Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano argued against broad disclosures, calling it “very rare that a precharging, pre-indictment unsealing would happen.”.

The high-profile nature of the investigation leaked into the courtroom Tuesday, as Boasberg cited statements by President Donald Trump and others about the investigation into Omar.

“You have had administration officials, prominent ones, talking about the purpose of the investigation,” Boasberg mentioned.

Administration officials have accused Omar of committing immigration crimes for years, and Trump said last month the DOJ was looking into Omar “strongly.” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on a recent podcast that investigators had served multiple search warrants and were investigating possible immigration fraud tied to when Omar entered the United States as a child.

Separately, Boasberg mentioned he may issue rulings in the coming weeks unsealing portions of other court cases tied to the investigation, including one brought by Omar herself earlier this month seeking the return of the items seized in the search.

The administration executed the search warrant in October, just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The timing of the search drew accusations of political bias from Democrats who claimed that the administration brought the case to sway the midterm elections.

For years Trump has said he wanted criminal charges to be brought against his political foes, including Omar and others in Congress.

Latest Update: 'Dune: Part Three' Expands Its Universe, From the Liwa Desert to the Volcanic Shores of Iceland

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1064 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that on Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television reveals, and more.
  • The celestial saga that is Frank Herbert’s Dune was practically made for cinema.
  • Industry observers note that on December 18, 2026, Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three arrives, overcoming the hurdles that had tripped up its predecessors and capping off the decade-in-the-making trilogy in an explosive finale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that on Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television reveals, and more. This time, we take a look at Dune: Part Three.

The celestial saga that is Frank Herbert’s Dune was practically made for cinema. And yet, for so long, adapting the breathtakingly expansive space opera seemed like something of a curse. David Lynch called his turn at the franchise “a huge, gigantic sadness” in his life, and for Alejandro Jodorowsky, his psychedelically expensive vision for Dune never escaped development hell.

Industry observers note that on December 18, 2026, Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three arrives, overcoming the hurdles that had tripped up its predecessors and capping off the decade-in-the-making trilogy in an explosive finale. Key to the creation of the trilogy’s universe was keeping it as grounded as possible in ours, with otherworldly planets raised from the volcanic shores of Iceland’s beaches and the banded dunes of the United Arab Emirates’ Liwa Desert. By this point, fans of the first two installments are well-acquainted with settings like the desert planet of Arrakis, but Villeneuve's latest offering delves deeper than ever into their intricate textures. Condé Nast Traveler spoke with production designer Patrice Vermette, location manager Duncan Broadfoot, and director of photography Linus Sandgren to learn how this much-anticipated conclusion was crafted.

Sources indicate that dune: Part Three opens with Fremen forces landing on Enfeil, a wetland planet that stuns the soldiers—used to desert and drought—with its rain. After the battle concludes, the Fremen forces run to the black sand shores of the planet and wade into the sea. This sequence was filmed in Iceland, specifically at Ingólfshöfði Beach, a nearly 250-foot-tall cape and nature reserve. “Denis [Villeneuve] always envisioned a black surface going on for forever, a super flat surface with those low clouds and a band of light, just the sun piercing through the horizon," said Vermette, “Because of the black sand, we thought, obviously, Iceland. We also looked to see if it was possible to shoot in the Canary Islands.” At the end of the day, Iceland won the booking, leading the team to spearhead an unprecedented film shoot. “When we scouted Iceland, there were multiple options,” said Broadfoot, “but this particular beach that we ended up on is part of a nature reserve, and actually during the summer, you can book puffin tours, but it's never been shot on before, so that was also an appealing aspect.”.

Twenty different locations across the UAE's Liwa Desert were stitched together to comprise Arrakis. Across all three films, the Liwa Desert has been used as a stand-in for the desert planet at the center of it all. “There's a reward to travel to the Liwa Desert, which is close to the border of Saudi Arabia, and the dunes there are like the kind you've seen in Lawrence of Arabia,” said Sandgren, “it's magical just to be there; they're beautiful and contain copper sand and beige sand, and the mix of the two creates these incredible patterns of ripples from the wind each night, and every morning, you see new patterns.” While Sandgren arrived at the desert for the first time to film for Part Three, for Broadfoot and Vermette, returning to the region was like a homecoming for the crew. “Denis [Villenueve] and Patrice [Vermette] are always very keen to find something new that we haven't filmed on before, so that was always the challenge," said Broadfoot, “specifically for Part Three, we had to go deeper and further into the desert than we had done in Part Two.” Filming in the ever-shifting landscape with temperatures peaking at a boiling 120 degrees Fahrenheit posed significant challenges to the shoot, especially as the crew based themselves even deeper into the desert, but getting comfortable was almost counter to the brief. “We love making movies because we thrive on challenges, you know?," said Vermette, "If it was easy, I don't think we'd want to make them.”.

While nearly all of the Arrakis scenes were shot in the Liwa Desert, select sequences were set in Al Ain, the UAE's “Garden City.” Though scenes shot in Al Ain didn't take up as much screen time as those shot in the desert, they span a considerable range as the area served as the setting for Alia Atreides's personal Golgotha—the site where Paul's sadistic younger sister crucifies traitors to the regime—as well as where Chani plays with her young children. “It's an incredible area that is still very unknown,” said Vermette. “We shot on a mountain called Jebel Hafeet, the only real mountain in the area,” said Broadfoot, “we scouted the entire mountain and found a plateau up high, which gave you this sort of scale and rocky, craggy environment that's very different than the desert which we were filming in. It was a blank canvas for Patrice [Vermette] to take over and create his beautiful set.”.

To enhance all the footage that was shot on location, several landscapes from Part Three were recreated using a combination of practical and digital effects across four facilities in Budapest: NFI Studios, HungExpo Budapest Congress and Exhibition Centre, Korda Studios, and Waberer. Much of the battle scene on Enfeil was shot in Budapest. “Most of it was in the back lot of Waberer,” mentioned Vermette, “the amazingly technical thing achieved by Denis [Villeneuve] and Linus [Sandgren] was that they erected a 65-foot-tall by 470-something-foot-long LED screen wall, which was the biggest wall of that sort ever built." The sheer scale of the shoot even required the crew to break out cranes to navigate the airspace around production to move props and equipment around.

Atreides home planet Caladan has made an appearance in all three films of the trilogy. The visual opposite of Arrakis, Caladan was shot on the northwestern Kråkenes region of Norway. The agrestic shoreline is hugged by verdant cliffs and the frosty Norwegian Sea. Caladan's cameos in Part Three come as brief flashes, but Vermette also winks to the filming location in an Easter egg on Arrakis. “In the movie, in the interior courts of Alia's meditation room, there's a tree,” says Vermette, “I had the idea of putting a pine tree, a Norwegian pine tree there, because it's the roots of their family; it's something that anchors their family. The only pine tree in all of Arrakis is right there.”.

Breaking: Setting Sail With Kids? These Are the Best Cruise Lines for Families

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The best cruise lines for families with kids and teens are likely more diverse than you realize.
  • Recent findings suggest that I’ve sailed on more than 80 cruises, sometimes with my kids, often surrounded by everyone else’s.
  • A cruise line that devotes a day to all things LEGO and offers a special baby laundry service gets top marks in my list of the best cruises for kids and teens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best cruise lines for families with kids and teens are likely more diverse than you realize. Many are the big-ship brands you see in ads, tricked out with waterslides, dazzling shows, and an abundance of onboard restaurants to satisfy picky toddlers and ravenous teens alike. Yet other family-friendly cruise lines let mom and dad get the taste of luxury they crave or provide the entire crew with adventure and active pursuits around the globe.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve sailed on more than 80 cruises, sometimes with my kids, often surrounded by everyone else’s. I can tell you that the best family cruises won’t make bedtime any easier, but they will do their best to make sure no one in your crew ever feels the need to cry, “I’m so bored!”.

A cruise line that devotes a day to all things LEGO and offers a special baby laundry service gets top marks in my list of the best cruises for kids and teens. MSC Cruises is a European big-ship cruise line that’s making waves in the US with its family-friendly mega-ships.

According to recent reports, five kids clubs for babies, preschoolers, kids, tweens, and teens target activities to different age groups. MSC is constantly developing new family programs, including family discos, original game reveals, drone races for teens, MasterChef at Sea cooking challenges, and obstacle course competitions.

Industry observers note that world Class ships feature the top-deck Family Aventura District with an outdoor adventure area (including an overwater swing ride), water park, and an indoor space for rollerskating and bumper cars. Select ships offer arcades with a Formula 1 simulator and virtual reality attractions or the Robotron robotic-arm thrill ride. The line’s US–based ships also feature connecting cabins and family-friendly dining (the pizza and gelato are superb).

Families looking for an exclusive hideaway can book rooms in The Yacht Club, with access to a private restaurant, lounge, sun deck, and pool—all ages welcome.

Standout itinerary: 7-night Caribbean and Bahamas cruise on MSC World America sailing round-trip from Miami.

Royal Caribbean operates the world’s largest, most activity-laden ships, and its calling card is high-energy fun for all ages.

Families can rock climb, zip-line, ice skate, splash down waterslides, solve escape room challenges, and enjoy entertainment ranging from musical performances to acrobatic high-dive dance shows without leaving the ship. The enormous Icon Class ships even have a dedicated family deck called Surfside, where kid-friendly restaurants, splash playgrounds, and a carousel are surrounded by cabins and suites designed to accommodate families.

On all ships, parents can steal away for adults-only fun when they drop the littlest cruisers at onboard nurseries run by professional caregivers. Kids can make crafts, play games, and do science experiments at onboard camps operating morning until late in spacious, tech-enhanced multipurpose spaces. Teens have their own hip hangouts for foosball, video games, and evening parties with new friends. The whole family can later reunite to share the day’s fun over Johnny Rockets burgers and shakes or perhaps a teppanyaki dinner with showman chefs.

Standout itinerary: 7-night Perfect Day CocoCay and Caribbean cruise on Icon of the Seas sailing round-trip from Miami.

Sources indicate that disney’s rapidly expanding cruise ship segment isn’t just for preschoolers reveling in their Frozen era. Its itineraries across the Caribbean, Alaska, and Europe offer family fun for a wide range of ages, including adults. Plus, its short itineraries pair nicely with a theme park visit.

Sources indicate that entertainment is a highlight, from live on-stage productions of classics like Moana and Beauty and the Beast to mealtime demonstrates themed around the Marvel universe and Coco. The ships’ movie theaters screen first-run flicks across the Disney-owned studios (not just animated classics), and the once-a-cruise Pirate Night is the only time you’ll ever see fireworks released from a cruise ship.

Sources indicate that disney Cruise Line’s enormous youth facilities, also with nurseries and teen clubs, offer activities themed to Disney IP. Kids can design a superhero suit or theme park ride, pilot the Millennium Falcon, and join Olaf for virtual snowball fights. The line also treats adults very well with pools, sun decks, fine-dining restaurants (including ones by Michelin-starred chefs), bars themed around The Haunted Mansion and Star Wars, and cafés exclusive to travelers ages 18+.

Disney supports traveling families in less flashy ways, as well. Cabins feature extra berths for kids, split bathrooms with a toilet in one room and a sink in the other, and room-dividing curtains so grownups won’t distract would-be nappers. Waiters will purée baby food and cut up your kid’s dinner all while cracking silly jokes and performing magic tricks. When the travel logistics are handled, families can focus more on having fun.

Standout itinerary: 4-night Bahamas cruise on Disney Wish sailing round-trip from Port Canaveral.

Retirees rule the world of river cruising, but AmaWaterways has teamed up with Adventures by Disney (Disney’s escorted travel arm) to offer select Rhine and Danube cruises to families.

In a recent development, disney’s onboard Adventure Guides handle all the logistics in port, from escorting tours in every destination to managing dietary restrictions and directing guests to the best restaurants and local treats. On board, they host movie evenings and kids-only dinners so parents can enjoy a leisurely meal with adult conversation.

Adventures by Disney swaps the history- and culture-focused walking tours typical of river cruise excursions for alpine coasters, amusement parks, river kayaking, and visits to chocolate factories. A selection of winery visits and slower-paced tours appeal to multigenerational families willing to split up childcare responsibilities ashore.

Recent findings suggest that amaWaterways, in turn, has specially built ships with more third-berth and connecting cabins than the typical river ship. It supplements its regional cuisine with kid favorites, while introducing the whole family to specialties like French macarons and German sausages.

Standout itinerary: 7-night Rhine River cruise from Basel, Switzerland, to Amsterdam, Netherlands.

In a recent development, A family cruise can be a nature-filled adventure to places like Alaska, the Galápagos, Baja California, Iceland, Greenland, and even Antarctica. For active families with curious kids and teens (and parents!), National Geographic-Lindblad Expeditions is a top choice.

It has been revealed that the cruise line’s ships carry under 200 guests, so families can focus on each other without those major-ship distractions. Though small, the ships do offer connecting cabins to accommodate groups and casual dining with plentiful options to suit all tastes.

According to recent reports, on a National Geographic cruise, the destination is the draw, and family-friendly activities range from snorkeling and kayaking to hiking and biking. On select voyages, the cruise line offers its National Geographic Explorers-in-Training program for kids and teenagers, led by certified field instructors. The program focuses on nature, science, and storytelling, with activities like practicing smartphone photography in Alaska with a photo instructor, collecting and then observing plankton under a microscope in Baja California, and learning to drive a Zodiac.

Standout itinerary: 7-night Galápagos Escape cruise from Quito, Ecuador.

Luxury cruise ships aren’t built for kids, but select cruise lines make an effort to entertain junior cruisers during holiday and summer sailings in places like Alaska and the Caribbean. Regent Seven Seas Cruises’ ships might not offer a dedicated kids club on board, but the line’s longstanding Club Mariner Youth Program welcomes children ages 5 to 17 with a schedule of onboard activities.

Trained counselors make use of the ships’ public spaces to keep kids busy with mini-golf games, dessert decorating, karaoke parties, and movie nights. In Alaska, programming is destination-themed, and a youth-oriented enrichment speaker engages kids in learning about Alaska’s nature and wildlife.

Don’t underestimate your family’s ability to find fun on an adult-oriented ship. On Regent, kids can enjoy swimming in the onboard pool, joining a team for trivia, and playing board or card games in the library. Afternoon tea and evening shows may also become family attractions. You might find that complimentary room service from the main dining room menu coupled with movies on-demand in your suite is the perfect family activity to end your day.

Standout itinerary: 7-night Alaska cruise on Seven Seas Explorer from Vancouver, Canada, to Whittier, Alaska.

My favorite thing about San Juan? You can have a morning that feels plucked out of a history book, an afternoon that commits you entirely to the beach, and a night that’s topped off with a frosty Medalla, sweet rum cocktail, and flirty bachata dance. It’s glitzy yet lush, historic yet ever-evolving, a city delightfully full of contrasts, and one I will never run out of reasons to revisit.

Recent findings suggest that my father’s side of the family is from Puerto Rico, so I’ve been coming back to the island for years, and I love that there’s always another corner to get to know. There’s Old San Juan, with all its pastel-painted façades, galleries and shops, blue cobblestone streets, and tucked-away restaurants; Condado and Ocean Park for long, sea-salty afternoons by the ocean; and Santurce, where street murals, galleries, haute dining, and a lively bar scene bring a fresh, creative vibe to the city.

Of course, there’s no shortage of hotels in San Juan, but sometimes a vacation to the island’s capital calls for a little more room to sprawl, or a front door that opens onto a lush little neighborhood rather than a buzzy hotel lobby. The city’s best Airbnbs offer just that, along with wonderful amenities, whether it’s a private pool hidden behind swaying palms or a breezy courtyard for sipping on some local morning coffee.

Sources indicate that consider this your invitation to soak up the sun in Puerto Rico's capital for a few days. Read on for nine of the best Airbnbs in San Juan to consider for your next trip.

We've selected these listings based on Superhost status, ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews.

Number of guests: 5Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Unique design, proximity to the beach, city skyline views, fully equipped kitchen.

Seemingly an ode to the vibrant murals and culture found in Santurce, to describe this Airbnb as “colorful” is simply an understatement. You’ll never be bored at this retro-inspired haven, what with its groovy wallpaper in nearly every room, playful lava lamps, disco ball, and hanging plants. Conveniently, it's situated right in the heart of San Juan’s food and arts district and just a few steps from Ocean Park Beach. If you do decide to stay in for the night, rinse off the sand in your designer rain shower, throw a vinyl on the record player, and cook up some local produce in the fully stocked kitchen. This central Carolina base is for those seeking out an easy, breezy group trip, whether traveling with friends or family. I’m no stranger to below-zero temperatures, snow up to my shins, and slippery strolls to and from extra-curricular activities. And if there’s one brand we trust to keep us warm—and keep us moving—up in Canada, it’s The North Face.

I’ve been donning The North Face’s parkas, snow boots, and insulating layers to stay toasty for as long as I can remember, but I’ve also brought the brand with me throughout my many travels. I still think fondly of the turquoise backpack-duffel combo that I took across Europe when I studied abroad in 2016, and in recent years, I’ve taken to the website to search for fanny packs, hiking boots, rain jackets, and other accessories for outdoor adventures (as well as to peruse the North Face x Skims outerwear collab, because I just can’t help myself). Plus, the quality is just unmatched, so I know I’ll have all of my gear for years to come.

According to recent reports, of course, between flights, hotels, and all the activities in between, travel can be expensive, so if you’re looking to save on gear, you’ve come to the right place. Read on for easy ways to get discounts on popular items from The North Face, including promo codes, sale picks, coupons, and more. Even better, we’re sharing some of our editors’ top recommendations from The North Face that you can save big on now.

In a recent development, if you haven’t yet joined The North Face’s loyalty program, XPLR Pass, now's the time. You'll earn 1 point for every $1 spent—and you can redeem $10 after gaining 100 points. You’ll have to create an account with your email, DOB, and a password, then enter your phone number and opt into text messages to join the loyalty program.

Recent findings suggest that whether you’re about to head out on an all-weather adventure, are looking for something comfy to wear on your next staycation, or are prepping ahead for next winter, chances are you could benefit from a scroll through The North Face’s Black Friday sale section where you'll find up to 40% off some of the brand’s bestsellers. Some highlights? Save 30% off the women's Frost Fall hooded jacket, 30% off the Cragmont fleece jacket, and 40% off the men's Summit Series half-zip. Browse the sale section to find even more deals on winter jackets, zip-ups, vests, and more.

Industry observers note that in addition to the 10% off promo code at sign-up, XPLR Pass members get perks like free shipping on every order, access to exclusive products, a birthday treat, and points on all purchases. You earn 1 point for every $1 spent, and can trade in 100 points for a $10 reward, up to $50 off per cycle (rewards are converted into coupon codes in March, June, and October). But you don’t need to shop to earn points; you can also accrue them by bringing a reusable bag when you make an in-store purchase, sending a personal referral link to invite friends, using the app to check in at a The North Face store or a US National Park, and more.

The North Face rewards deserving individuals in demanding careers with 10% off products in-store and online. If you’re a student, teacher (including professors, faculty, and staff members), or military member, verify your status on the website using SheerID to receive your discount code.

The North Face takes sustainability seriously, and its Renewed and Remade programs allow customers to participate in the action. On Tour: Australian Indie Darling Radio Free Alice on Tour Life, Guerrilla Gigs, and American Motels

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This article is part of a latest series, On Tour, in which we talk to touring artists about life on the road.
  • On Halloween, a bouncing crowd of skateboarders, witches, ghosts, and ghouls slowly coalesced in New York City's Tompkins Square Park.
  • That’s what makes the album title so apt: The young Aussies are caught between cities and countries, trying to make sense of everyday life while the road itself starts to feel like home.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article is part of a latest series, On Tour, in which we talk to touring artists about life on the road.

On Halloween, a bouncing crowd of skateboarders, witches, ghosts, and ghouls slowly coalesced in New York City's Tompkins Square Park. They were there for a quintessentially East Village pop-up concert headlined by the Melbourne-based post-punk band Radio Free Alice (followed by an after party at Niagara). The band's debut album, What’s In Between, was just released the day prior, blending the high energy of ’80s new wave with biting social satire and a healthy dose of cheek. Having picked up a following in Australia and Europe, the four-piece group has built an underground reputation on guerrilla gigs like this one—held everywhere from beneath London railway bridges and Melbourne’s former Pentridge Prison to suburban backyards in Austin, Texas.

That’s what makes the album title so apt: The young Aussies are caught between cities and countries, trying to make sense of everyday life while the road itself starts to feel like home. They’re in the thick of their own coming-of-age story, and one that's unfolding on an international stage. Fresh off the first dates of a nearly sold-out European lineup, tickets are now on sale for their What's In Between North America tour, which will kick off in San Francisco on February 24, 2027.

According to recent reports, earlier this month, vocalist and guitarist Noah Learmonth picked up my call from a Sprinter van somewhere in Germany, on the road from Copenhagen to Berlin. With the wit, gumption, and on-stage vocals of a Gen-Z Morrissey, his devilish grin fills the screen as he tells me he spends 99% of his time in the window seat behind the van’s little table, facing forward. His preferred seat is right now occupied by guitarist Jules Paradiso. He gives me a 360-degree tour of their ecosystem, where everyone has settled into their own version of life on the road. Drummer Lochie Dowd has claimed a small sleeping nook near the back. Michael Phillips, bassist and resident reader, sits with his Kindle, having just finished Christos Tsiolkas’s The Slap. As for who’s running the show? “Fuck, no one,” the still-grinning Noah claims. “There’s a man up front called Ben, our tour manager, who’s a crazy man. He’s the one who leads the blind. We’d all be fucked otherwise.”.

Sources indicate that what’s everyone’s travel personality on tour? Who’s running the show?

Sources indicate that yeah, [I'm] type D. I’m sort of in my own world when I’m traveling—headphones on, that kind of vibe. Jules is really easy firm. He’s a valuable asset to have in the world. Michael’s pretty chill, too. He’s looking at me now as I summarize his personality. Lochie likes to sleep in this little nook. That’s a substantial part of his tour experience: finding that little nook.

Sources indicate that when we met Ben, we just fell in love with him and his crazy methods, his madness. The thing about Ben is he gets our sound right every time. It’s really annoying when someone else does the sound and you watch the videos back and go, ‘Oh my God, what the fuck? Why is there no bass in the synth? Why do we sound like Duran Duran? What’s going on? I sound like Sonic Youth.’ That’s not at all what we were going for. Two of my favorite bands, though. But Ben gets exactly the sound we’re going for, and he’s a real empath. We’ve spent so much time on the road together. He’s our guy.

Where do you stay while you're on the road?

Industry observers note that when we’re touring Europe, we’ll stay in budget hotels. Either an Ibis or a Travelodge. In America, it’s more motel-type places—Motel 6 kind of things. It’s very cliché, but kind of sick in a way. Each morning when you wake up, you set your alarm for half an hour before you have to leave, get up, have a shower, smash your clothes into your backpack, and run down to the lobby so you’re not late and Ben doesn’t give you a verbal spanking.

Terrible. I just had McDonald’s. I don’t even like McDonald’s. You literally don’t have an option. You pull into a service station and the only food there is McDonald’s. Jules is a Major Mac guy, though. I know that.

In a recent development, I’m personally notoriously light. I just have this yellow North Face backpack that I’ve had since I was about seven years old. My auntie gave it to me for my birthday. My trusty yellow backpack. Lochie has a big suitcase, Michael has a smaller suitcase, and Jules has a big, backpacker-style backpack.

Essentials you can’t tour without?

I’m wearing the same jeans I’ve been wearing every day for the past year. I got them from a thrift shop in Melbourne. So my essentials are my jeans. Lochie’s are his headphones—we all use Sony. Jules’s is…video games. He’d hate that I just noted that. Let’s say his laptop. Michael’s is his Kindle. He’s the best reader. Let’s see what he’s reading…ah, he just finished The Slap.

What's your favorite city that you've played in so far?

According to recent reports, upcoming York. I mean, the obvious answer is New York. New York’s the best city in the fucking world. It’s amazing.

According to recent reports, the first few times we were there, we partied a lot. We just stated, ‘This is a fucking adult amusement park.’ It’s ridiculous. We were staying with this band called Been Stellar, too, who are great. When we’re back we like going out on the Lower East Side, especially to this bar called Treasure Club. I personally also love the diners. I think the atmosphere in an old-school, family-run diner might be the best atmosphere of any place in the world.

Favorite venue you’ve ever played?

A gig is just people playing music, and it can happen literally anywhere. There are no rules. You can do it anywhere. Shaking up the gig setting—rethinking what a gig is and what it can feel like—is really fun, and it keeps it notable. The Melbourne set at Pentridge Prison [a former 19th century prison that's been transformed into a residential area] was sick. It was an incredible visual.

What about a city that surprised you?

Recent findings suggest that zurich. So random. I just remember having a strangely amazing time. I remember leaving that gig thinking, ‘Actually, there was something incredibly awesome and sweet about that.’ And it was the people. They were just these thoughtful, sweet people.

After a show like Zurich, we’ll be in the green room after. We’ll probably crack open a beer, and Lochie will be funny. If it went really, really well, we might go out somewhere nearby, to a pub or a bar or something. But generally, what happens is we go back to the green room, we’re really buzzed, we’ll have a beer and we’ll be pretty hyped up. Then Ben will come in and say, ‘All hands on deck. We need to load up the van. We’ve got to get to the next city.’ Zurich, though—I’d love to do it again.

What's your impression of the United States so far?

I mean, there’s one thing about America: the difference between, say, Latest York and LA, and then LA and Minneapolis or somewhere, is worlds apart. You could be in completely different countries.

Sources indicate that middle America can feel like an absolute time warp. When you’re on the road, there’s a sort of repetitiveness to the long stretches of road that all seem to look exactly the same. You arrive at a petrol station that’s identical to the last one you stopped at. There’s that stereotype that Americans are big talkers, but I’ve found that’s almost underrated. I can’t believe how chatty Americans are. They love just talking, going on and on. Coming from Australia, it’s the opposite. I love it.

Any memories you've made on the road that you’ll never forget?

The first time we played in LA, this very sweet girl called Alice randomly made us all these gifts. She gave us all these handmade things: embroidered bracelets with band-related names and glasses with our names on them. I find something quite American about that. It’s just so sweet. In Europe, people tend to be a little less expressive in that way. It’s still just amazing to me.

Industry observers note that glasgow had this sort of “rara”-ness to it, which was really fun and funny for us. It just felt so boisterous. We’d play a slower song, and they’d still find a way to just absolutely lose their minds. It was cute.

When you're not on tour, where’s home for you guys?

Nowhere, not really anywhere. I’m not exaggerating. I feel disingenuous calling anywhere our home at this point. But if there were one, it would be London. It’s making a big impression on us. What’s cool is that, a year before we moved to London, we played to maybe one person at one of our gigs there. Then, the following year, we played to this really big, sold-out room. It was an incredibly high-energy, adrenaline-fueled, amazing, crazy show. That was special. I’ll never forget it. It was probably my favorite show.

Industry observers note that there are so many young indie-rock bands coming up in London that I’m seeing, and they’re all ambitious and exciting. I’m really excited by London. It’s lived up to the hopes I had for it. Because of that we’ve found ourselves hanging out at venues like the Shacklewell Arms and the George Tavern, that sort of thing.

While you're on tour, what do you miss the most?

In a recent development, you know, this isn’t a very cool answer, and I kind of wish it were, but the truth is I really miss having an exercise routine. In Melbourne, I was really major on swimming every morning, doing laps or going to the gym. I find it puts me in a really good place for the day. I’m chill and focused, not neurotic, and I just find it’s really good for me.

What's a band touring right now that you are personally excited about?

Recent findings suggest that lime Garden. They’re an all female lineup. The English rock scene is a bit of a sausage fest, so they’re a breath of fresh air.

Tech Report: Zinke PAC gave to family foundation he was investigated for

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1236 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025.
  • Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.
  • It has been revealed that the gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, rep. Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Outgoing Montana GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.

It has been revealed that the gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug. 31 from Zinke’s leadership political action committee to the nonprofit Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation, campaign finance records show. The donation is more than the foundation has reported receiving in any year since it was founded nearly two decades ago.

Zinke’s wife, son, and sister at the moment serve on its board of directors, according to the foundation’s annual filing with the state of Montana.

Sources indicate that in a brief interview, Zinke denied that any portion of the money transferred to the foundation will directly benefit him or any of his family members who sit on the board of directors. “No, no, never," he noted when asked if any family members will draw a salary from the gift.

The money will instead go to building a storage barn and kid’s sledding park on the property controlled by the foundation, Zinke said.

None of the records indicate Zinke violated the law or directly benefited from the gift to his foundation.

“While it's not uncommon for a politician to transfer leftover money from a political war chest to charity, it is pretty rare for a politician to transfer leftover political funds to a charity that they or a relative controls,” said Michael Beckel, director of money in politics reform at Glitch One, a bipartisan group that seeks to reduce influence of money in politics.

Instead, outgoing members typically transfer remaining campaign cash to local party committees or candidates, Beckel added.

Ethics experts say Zinke’s move highlights ongoing concerns over the broad latitude campaign finance law gives leadership PACs in how they spend money.

“I definitely think it is something to be concerned about,” noted Stuart McPhail, director of campaign finance litigation at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit watchdog.

“Leadership PACs are really nothing more than personal slush funds under today's rules,” he stated, noting that unlike regular campaign committees, member leadership PACs are not prohibited from donating to charities or organizations that could directly benefit the member or relative.

In a recent development, zinke, a former Navy SEAL who commanded special forces during the Iraq War, converted his traditional campaign committee to a leadership PAC — Commander Zinke Leadership Fund — in March 2026, shortly after announcing he would not run for reelection. It last reported having $1.4 million cash on hand in October of this year.

It marks the second time one of Zinke’s political committees made a payment to the organization. In 2019, the committee Zinke ran during his earlier years in Congress — he served one term in the House before being tapped as Trump’s first-term Interior secretary — gave over $11,000 to the foundation before winding down operations.

The Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation was founded by Zinke and his wife in 2007 in his hometown of Whitefish, Mont., with intends to provide winter recreational activities for children. Its latest tax filing reports revenue of $15,000 and roughly equal expenses in 2024 for snow plowing and park maintenance.

Zinke’s dealings with the organization were the subject of an ongoing inspector general investigation when he resigned as Interior secretary in January 2019.

Investigators ultimately did not find that Zinke violated conflict-of-interest laws, but they concluded that he failed to comply with federal ethics obligations and “misused his official position in violation of federal regulations.” The Justice Department declined to prosecute Zinke.

Zinke stepped down from the foundation in 2017, shortly after his Senate confirmation. But investigators found that he continued to represent the organization in negotiations with the developers of a commercial project adjacent to the foundation’s land and lied to an ethics agent about his involvement in the project.

The project’s investors included David Lesar, then-chairman of oil services company Halliburton.

Another Zinke-tied leadership PAC has previously raised eyebrows in Washington.

Recent findings suggest that supporting Electing American Leaders PAC — known as SEAL PAC — where Zinke serves as chairman, has been marred by accusations that it funneled money to political consultants instead of candidates. A 2022 CQ Roll Call analysis found that 87 percent of the PAC’s spending went to operating expenses.

The PAC also made recurring monthly payments to a firm registered to Zinke’s son, Wolfgang Zinke, and based at a Zinke family-owned home in Whitefish.

According to recent reports, SEAL PAC’s executive director, Rob Catron, maintained that the payments constitute a consulting fee to Wolfgang Zinke for management of the PAC website, among other tasks. “He earns every penny of it,” Catron said.

In a recent development, since May 2022, the PAC has given roughly $270,000 to Wolfgang Zinke’s firm, FG Solutions, for mailing and printing, records show — more than any individual candidate or committee supported by the PAC. The company also received $5,000 from a related super PAC, SEAL PAC USA, which can solicit unlimited contributions for independent expenditures but can’t donate directly to candidates.

Montana corporate records show Wolfgang Zinke founded FG Solutions – which says it provides services including “personal assistant and any lawful purpose” – just 10 days before it received its first payment from the PAC in 2022.

Catron defended how the PAC spends money on veterans running for the House, arguing that it takes money to raise money.

“We raise a lion’s share of our funding through national direct mail fundraising, which is very expensive to do,” he said, citing the PAC’s use of a national text message fundraising campaign as a major expense.

SEAL PAC raised about $9.6 million this election cycle, distributing about $1.1 million to GOP lawmakers and candidates, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Most of the committee's funds went to operating expenses, including over $3 million paid to Direct Support Services, a Washington-based vendor, for direct mail postage.

Zinke’s not the only lawmaker to face scrutiny over how they spent surplus campaign cash in recent years.

In 2023, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., set off alarm bells for transferring $200,000 from his campaign committee to The Sanders Institute, a nonprofit founded by his wife and stepson, following a $350,000 donation from his 2020 presidential campaign coffers.

The organization briefly shut down during Sanders’ presidential run in 2019 to avoid the appearance of impropriety.

Sanders’ stepson, David Driscoll — a former executive at Nike and snowboard manufacturer Burton — is listed on the think tank’s website as its executive director, drawing a six-figure annual salary according to tax filings.

It’s unusual, though not unheard of, for campaign committees to pay family members of the candidate for bona fide work.

“If [Wolfgang Zinke] is actually performing this work, he’s qualified to do it, and this is his typical market rate for this kind of contract, then it would be permissible, even if this was a campaign account,” McPhail said about SEAL PAC's payments.

But the payments could present a legal “gray area” over whether personal-use restrictions apply to certain PACs, according to McPhail.

In a recent development, “We’re grateful for the way customers across South Florida continue to embrace JetBlue, and we’re committed to delivering even more of the destinations and travel options they’re looking for,” Daniel Shurz, JetBlue’s senior vice president of revenue, network, and enterprise planning, remarked in a news release. “With upcoming international service to Honduras and Grand Cayman, we’re strengthening Fort Lauderdale’s role as a key gateway to Latin America and the Caribbean, making it easier for customers to reconnect with loved ones, explore new places, and travel across our growing network.”.

It has been revealed that american has prioritized Latin America as demand from U.S. markets, especially Miami, grows. The carrier just recently introduced service to Barranquilla and Cali in Colombia and will add Barcelona, Venezuela, to its network in January.

#145616. I Walked Solo Along England’s Rugged South West Coast Path for Three Days

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1650 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

I Walked Solo Along England’s Rugged South West Coast Path for Three Days

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1650 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, I’m standing atop a spit of land jutting out into the English Channel, peering down at a beach accessible only by boat, where a small group of sunbathers lounge on the rocky sand.
  • I was nearing the end of the first day of a three-day solo walking trip along a slice of England’s South West Coast Path, a 630-mile trail through some of the country’s most beautiful land- and seascapes.
  • Recent findings suggest that since tackling an admittedly easier two-day walk from Dover to Sandwich the previous summer, I’d become totally enamored with England’s coastal paths.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I’m standing atop a spit of land jutting out into the English Channel, peering down at a beach accessible only by boat, where a small group of sunbathers lounge on the rocky sand. The view is a welcome excuse to catch my breath before continuing along five more rolling cliffs—400 steep feet up, 400 steep feet down, and repeat. And so, despite my exhausted legs and the blister that’s forming over my right major toe, I decide to imprint this impossibly peaceful scene into my brain to remind myself why I’m doing this trip.

Dorset's limestone Jurassic Coast.

I was nearing the end of the first day of a three-day solo walking trip along a slice of England’s South West Coast Path, a 630-mile trail through some of the country’s most beautiful land- and seascapes. Earlier this year, it became part of the newly created King Charles III England Coast Path, inaugurated with a brisk March walk by the king himself (wearing a suit, natch). The route now incorporates all of England’s preexisting regional coastal paths, adding new sections to create a wider network that stretches across nearly 2,700 miles, giving walkers a chance to access parts of the country far beyond the typical travel itinerary.

Recent findings suggest that since tackling an admittedly easier two-day walk from Dover to Sandwich the previous summer, I’d become totally enamored with England’s coastal paths. I realized I could experience so much more of the country’s most beautiful landscapes by foot than I ever could by train or car. For my second foray, I chose one of the more frequented set of trails: walking east from Weymouth to Bournemouth across Dorset. This stretch is known for its incredible rock formations, the result of millions of years of waves washing against the coast. That erosion has also led to the discovery of some of the world’s oldest fossils—giving the region the name of Jurassic Coast.

A view of the South West coast Path's rugged countryside, which is now more easily accessible to hikers thanks to the wider newly created King Charles III England Coast Path.

In a recent development, when I’d set off five hours earlier from the charming seaside town of Weymouth—a destination made popular by King George III’s multiple visits at the turn of the 19th century—the going had been easy. My only roadblock was a military parade that a British historical society couldn’t have arranged any better: an Army band marched in front of a stretch of beach-facing Georgian townhouses as Union Jack bunting fluttered in the sea breeze. An Anglican priest delivered a short prayer. There was a Spitfire flyover. If you ignored all the iPhones and mobility scooters, it was a scene that would have fit in comfortably 80 years ago.

Recent findings suggest that by setting out alone on a three-day walk, I was seeking solitude, and moments like that clifftop break, when I had the view all to myself, delivered. But the long way out of the Weymouth hubbub also clarified why walking England’s coastal paths is so approachable—especially for those of us who love the outdoors but want to sleep indoors. Since the country is quite densely populated, you can easily walk the trails from town to town, and hotel to hotel, without the weight (and stress) of camping equipment. For those same reasons, it’s also perfect as a solo walker; the risks feel more manageable when you know medical care is within reach; that you’re rarely without phone service; and that your hotel door locks at night.

Industry observers note that after 12 miles or so of walking, I arrived at West Lulworth, a town of centuries-old stone cottages that can best be described as “quaint.” I was greeted by the famous Durdle Door, a limestone arch that snakes out of a cliff and into the Channel, with clusters of beachgoers splashing underneath. It's a place worth lingering: After going down my final descent of the day, I snuck a peek at Lulworth Cove, a popular bay almost fully enclosed by limestone (and a UNESCO World Heritage Site), before checking into the Old Barn Inn, a B&B up the road for a gloriously hot shower.

A view of Durdle Door, a limestone arch that can be seen from the trail.

It has been revealed that my second day of walking presented a latest challenge: Part of my planned route was closed because it crossed a firing range in use by the Army for training. To avoid it, I rode the bus (the Jurassic Coast is very well served by public transit, at least in summer) part of the way to my next destination, then planned to take a shortcut through some fields to get back to the coast. Sarah, the owner of the Old Barn, had given me extremely specific verbal directions based on local landmarks, which were easy enough to follow until I’d reached the “horrible hill” she warned me of. It was then that I realized I was in the middle of a field with no obvious path out. I bushwhacked to a nearby road, the peace of solitude nowhere to be found as I muttered, “I’ve done this to myself.”.

Sources indicate that but thanks to my two puny bars of cell phone service, I navigated over another field, through a herd of sheep, along a ravine, and then emerged, alarmingly sweaty, into the absolutely charming limestone village of Worth Matravers. I made a beeline to the local pub (as recommended by Sarah), and enjoyed what was undoubtedly the best pint of my life looking out over a grassy field—and to the ocean beyond. As I sipped my lager at a picnic table, a forceful summer wind whipped off the water, knocking down the pub’s sandwich board advertising Cornish pasties, but it didn’t bother me or the handful of other pubgoers sitting out in the sun.

It has been revealed that perhaps there is something to the old saying about victory being sweetest after you’ve known defeat, because for all of the frustration I endured that day, the second half of my walk was absolutely breathtaking. After an easy, peaceful meander back down to the coastal path, I spent the next two hours walking through clifftop fields where I saw more deer and cows than humans, and past the famous Danding Ledge, a stone shelf jutting into a patch of sea popular with wild swimming enthusiasts. The wind that had teased me earlier died down closer to the water, and all I could hear was the crash of the waves against the rocks below. When I’ve needed a moment of peace in the few months since then, I’ve summoned the memory of that afternoon and the calm those clifftop fields offered.

A solo walker making their way along the South West Coast Path.

I woke up the following morning in the seaside town of Swanage with calves so sore that the thought of any incline made me nervous. To my dismay, I discovered right away that, to pick up the coastal path from the inn where I’d stayed (Rivendell Guest House), I first had to climb a steep staircase from the sandy beach, up the cliff to the bluff. Thankfully, shortly thereafter things flattened out. It was also the busiest section of the trail I encountered—though, even here, I saw only a dozen or so people, mostly locals in athletic gear out for a morning ramble.

When I reached the hilltop, I was greeted by a few hundred cows—and just beyond their enclosure, the Old Harry Rocks came into view. Millions of years’ worth of waves have chiseled away at this promontory, carving a series of chalk stacks that now sit away from the mainland. I watched two ambitious kayakers appear on the side of the rocks where the water was calmer and stare up at the feat of nature—enjoying a perspective that I’m sure is heavily advised against, and which only few have gotten to enjoy.

According to recent reports, the final part of my walk was along Studland Beach, a sandy four-mile stretch that backs up onto a nature preserve. I waded into the water, sat in the sun, and saw a boat selling ice cream delight children up and down the crowded beach, before reaching the last mile—which also happens to be home to the UK’s most popular naturist (or nudist) beach. The ice cream boat pulled up again, and it tickled me to see that the evenly tanned sexagenarians were just as pleased to have a midday treat as the energetic children I'd just passed.

Boats bob in the water near Old Harry Rocks in Studland, Dorset.

The final adventure of my trip also brought out childish delight in me: To get to Bournemouth, where I’d catch a train back to London, I had to take a four-minute ferry ride. Alongside me on the ferry was a double-decker bus with its upper deck open to the elements, letting passengers take full advantage of the beach breeze. The sheer logistics of this was a thrill to witness: a convertible bus driving onto a boat.

According to recent reports, on the other side of the strait, I got onto that very bus—aptly called The Breezer—and watched as the natural coastline was slowly enveloped by an urban milieu. It was a slightly rude awakening to reemerge into Bournemouth, a small university city where the asphalt had soaked up the sun, presaging the upcoming heatwave. But I realized as I walked through the train station that I was inadvertently grinning with pride. I assumed no one would ask me, a stinky and visibly sweaty woman, what I’d been up to, but if they had, I would have been all too happy to tell them about my solo walk along the South West Coast Path.

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An American Airlines frequent flyer complained about a $91 first class upgrade offer and received a response asking him to delete his post.
  • This hit my algorithm on X (and apparently VFTW too), but an AAdvantage Executive Platinum member took to the platform to express frustration that American was offering paid first class upgrades for $91 while his complimentary upgrade had not cleared (this was on a short 551-mile flight from Dallas to El Paso).
  • American acknowledged his frustration, then added:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An American Airlines frequent flyer complained about a $91 first class upgrade offer and received a response asking him to delete his post. That might sound like an airline trying to suppress criticism, but there is a much more sensible explanation: his screenshot exposed his reservation details. As for the inexpensive upgrade itself, I see a pragmatic opportunity rather than a scandal.

This hit my algorithm on X (and apparently VFTW too), but an AAdvantage Executive Platinum member took to the platform to express frustration that American was offering paid first class upgrades for $91 while his complimentary upgrade had not cleared (this was on a short 551-mile flight from Dallas to El Paso).

American acknowledged his frustration, then added:.

“Please delete this from public view and join us in DM.”.

The response attracted attention, but the screenshot included the passenger’s reservation confirmation number. That is a good reason to remove it and not a sign of AA trying to hide from its transactional upgrade policy!

We can understand why this feels frustrating. Your loyalty is genuinely appreciated, and we're sorry this experience left you feeling overlooked. Please delete this from public view and join us in DM.

— americanair (@AmericanAir) November 18, 2026.

It seems obvious to me that American was trying to protect the passenger here.

According to recent reports, A reservation confirmation number, often called a record locator or PNR, is something you should keep private. Combined with your last name, it can potentially allow someone to retrieve your booking. Depending on the airline and its security controls, that could expose information about your trip or allow someone to interfere with it. At least with AA you also need your birthdate in order to access the record online or on the AA app.

Posting a screenshot to make a point about upgrades should not mean giving strangers an opportunity to tamper with your reservation…and some losers have far too much on their hand (which I’ve found out the hard way and why even when I “live blog” I never truly live blog).

American could have explained this much better. A simple request to remove the screenshot because it contained private booking information would have avoided the ambiguity. The passenger could then have reposted his complaint with those details obscured.

Sources indicate that as to the underlying complaint, I understand why an Executive Platinum member would be frustrated. If you have directed substantial business to an airline and are waiting for an upgrade, watching the airline offer that seat for a relatively small payment can feel like your loyalty counts for very little.

But I am not going to attack American for selling inexpensive upgrades. This is the business model now, and I use it to my advantage when I fly AA. If the economy fare is attractive and American subsequently offers a reasonably priced upgrade, I can evaluate the total cost and decide whether first class is worth it. Sometimes it is. Sometimes I am perfectly happy staying where I am, like on a recent flight where I ended up with an entire row to myself. Oddly, sometimes the cost of the upgrade is more than buying the ticket outright…I have no explanation for that.

That is a much more straightforward transaction than spending more throughout the year in the hope that an airline will eventually reward me with a seat it would still prefer to sell.

It has been revealed that fundamentally, a complimentary upgrade that has not cleared, even at the gate, is not a seat that already belongs to the elite member. We can debate all day long about how prominently or aggressively airlines market upgrades when frequent flyers are waiting when upgrades are dangled like a carrot on a stick, but passengers can respond to that change by reconsidering how much they are willing to spend pursuing status.

Industry observers note that I am a free agent, and it is liberating. More people should try it. Two years in, I’m more happy than ever (and flying in first class more than ever on domestic flights). I  choose a flight because the schedule works or because the price makes sense, without worrying that I am depriving my preferred airline of another qualifying flight or dollar toward next year’s status.

If American offers a good fare and an inexpensive first class upgrade, great. I can take advantage of it. I do not need to be an Executive Platinum member to recognize a good deal (as much as I miss the oneworld emerald lounge access when traveling internationally).

According to recent reports, that does not mean status has become worthless. I still receive occasional complimentary upgrades as both an American Airlines Gold and United Airlines Gold member. I appreciate those upgrades very much, especially when I am not expecting them. But I do not build my travel aims around them. Hoping for a free upgrade seems futile in many cases even with top-tier status, particularly when the airline business model now centers on actively trying to sell the remaining seats.

Recent findings suggest that for me, an occasional upgrade is a pleasant bonus on a flight I was otherwise willing to fly in economy class on. But upgrades are not a compelling reason to keep spending more with one airline when another offers a better flight….sorry, but the value proposition is gone.

Industry observers note that american Airlines could have been clearer about why it wanted this passenger to delete his post. Still, the exposed reservation details provide a sensible explanation, and I would not characterize the request as an attempt to silence criticism.

As for the $91 upgrade, I am pragmatically happy those offers exist. They give me another way to sit up front without organizing my travel around the pursuit of top-tier status. I still enjoy the occasional complimentary upgrade, but choosing flights on my own terms, and paying for a better seat when the price is right, has been far more satisfying than chasing an upgrade that may never clear. Try it, you’ll like it.

Over Arepas and Cachitos, Venezuelans in Madrid Find a Sense of Home

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1514 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I stroll down the wide aisles of the sprawling Mercado de Las Maravillas, passing greengrocers with yuca and plantains piled high.
  • I make my way to the prepared-food stalls aisle, where the woman at Buda Bar Delicias Venezolanas draws me in by calling me amor and asking what I’d like to order, reina.
  • The Mercado de Las Maravillas is "where the Venezolanismo here in Madrid started,” restaurant owner Manuel Pérez Álvarez claims.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I stroll down the wide aisles of the sprawling Mercado de Las Maravillas, passing greengrocers with yuca and plantains piled high. A digital billboard flashes congratulations for the recent Venezuelan team’s World Baseball Classic win. Nearby, a vendor hawks yellow, blue, and red flags, while signs advertising remittance services to Latin America clutter my sightline. All around me, the Madrid market fills with the round, sing-song accent of Venezuelan Spanish.

I make my way to the prepared-food stalls aisle, where the woman at Buda Bar Delicias Venezolanas draws me in by calling me amor and asking what I’d like to order, reina. The familiar warmth of Latin America—I lived in Mexico before moving to Spain—tears open a pang of nostalgia in my chest. Guests seated at the stainless-steel bar munch on empanadas de carne mechada, continuously reaching for the green, herby salsa guasacaca. “How can it be that they are pumping a million barrels of oil out a day but they cannot fix a single hospital in Caracas?” I overhear another diner say to a friend, discussing the latest spate of frustrations back home.

The Mercado de Las Maravillas is "where the Venezolanismo here in Madrid started,” restaurant owner Manuel Pérez Álvarez claims.

Among Madrid’s 130,000-strong Venezuelan diaspora, these conversations are not uncommon. Spain’s Venezuelan population has swollen to almost 700,000 people, making it the largest community outside of the Americas, and a significant portion of the country’s nearly eight million citizens living abroad. Many have fled their homeland amid the economic and political instability that followed Hugo Chavez’s Bolivarian Revolution and continued under Nicolás Maduro’s rule. Ongoing uncertainty continues to drive migration. Unlike other diasporas, Madrid’s Venezuelan population isn’t concentrated in a single neighborhood. Instead, it stretches across the city and spans a broad socioeconomic spectrum, from delivery drivers and financiers to political exiles.

Its food institutions mirror a similar range.

In a recent development, manuel Pérez Álvarez and his wife Maira María Gómez can pinpoint the moment they decided to open a Venezuelan restaurant in Madrid. The two, who moved to Spain in 1997 after a lifetime in the coastal city of Puerto de La Cruz, had gone to meet friends for Venezuelan empanadas at one of the few spots in town at the time. After waiting 45 minutes for their order in a long line of people hankering for a taste of home, Pérez—a natural entrepreneur—saw opportunity.

Manuel Pérez Álvarez and his wife Maira María Gómez opened El Empanadazo in Madrid nearly a decade ago.

Venezuela's national dish, pabellon criollo—rice, beans, shredded beef, and plantains—is served alongside cachapas, arepas, fried fish, and more.

Industry observers note that when they opened El Empanadazo nearly a decade ago, the couple joined the ranks of just a handful of other Venezuelan food joints. They chose to set up shop in the Mercado de Las Maravillas. “It was really where the Venezolanismo here in Madrid started,” Pérez says of the market. In no time, they were serving hearty plates of Venezuela's national dish, pabellon criollo—rice, beans, shredded beef, and plantains—crispy fried whole fish, sweet corn griddled cachapas, arepas, and more.

“Our restaurant really became a gathering place for Venezuelans. I remember the early days when I was spending more time there, seeing people with tears in their eyes,” Pérez notes. “When you’re an immigrant, little things like the taste of home really get to you.”.

Maira María Gómez and her husband Manuel Pérez Álvarez opened El Empanadazo in Madrid nearly a decade ago, there were far fewer Venezuelan restaurants in the city.

At the time, Venezuelan food wasn’t as easy to find and people went out of their way for it. Today, a quick search for “arepa” on the delivery apps will turn up hundreds of options. “Now there are lots of spots, but we were really pioneers, and it wasn’t even all that long ago,” Pérez says.

Be it Arepa’s Coffee Shop nestled next to the hustle of the Moncloa train and bus station, or the four-location La Arepera, the Insta-famous El Chino Venezolano, or the fast-growing Guasacaca, the country’s gastronomic footprint continues to grow alongside its diaspora in Madrid. At the March 2026 Arepa Fest, a celebration of Venezuelan and Colombian food and culture, in the north edges of Madrid, more than 5,000 people gathered to snack on the region's signature split- and stuffed-cornmeal snack, while the sound system alternated between pumping Venezuelan Merengue and reggaeton.

At Panadería Torrerí, warm pastries like cachitos, a brioche-like crescent roll most typically filled with ham and cheese, and golfeados, spiral pastry dough filled with cheese, keep customers coming back.

Industry observers note that A similar fervor can be felt at Panadería Torrerí. By mid-morning, the team is already replenishing their glass case of cachitos, a brioche-like crescent roll most typically filled with ham and cheese, and golfeados, spiral pastry dough filled with cheese, and brushed with panela (unrefined cane sugar) and anise. Regulars grab a table and owner Mara Azuaje, always poised with a “¿Cómo está usted?” rapidly ferries over their order.

Sources indicate that azuaje opened her bakery in 2024 to bring traditional Venezuelan pastries to the neighborhood of Barrio de Salamanca. For years, there had been no Venezuelan bakery in the area, despite this upscale neighborhood being nicknamed “Little Caracas” for its substantial diaspora. Today, Panadería Torrerí attracts both affluent property owners alongside motorbike messengers, all looking for a taste of home.

Mara Azuaje opened Panadería Torrerí in the Barrio de Salamanca in 2024.

Recent findings suggest that azuaje, who came to Spain at 27, knows what they're after. She spent years working odd jobs to save the money needed to open her bakery. “I cleaned homes, worked as a delivery driver, took care of children. I did whatever, but I was always very ambitious,” Azuaje claims. “I wanted to have my own business.”.

It has been revealed that she didn’t understand the exact shape it would take, but her grandmother’s lessons to her as a child around the importance of learning an oficio, a craft, stayed with her. “I was always baking with my grandmother who told me I needed to know how to do something, so I opened a bakery,” she claims. Today, Azuaje is proud to be known across the neighborhood for her homemade bread and her hearty rolled-dough pastries.

Other Venezuelan restaurant owners transitioned into hospitality later in life. At Bea Castelló Castro and Luis Felipe Fossa’s Cafetín, the menu—arepas with chia seeds, shredded chicken, and avocado for breakfast, or creamed curry soup and sweet corn and hearty salads for lunch—carries traces of Venezuela while honoring the other places the couple has called home.

At Cafetín, the menu showcases Venezuelan flavors through a global lens.

Cafetín's arepas are stuffed with chia seeds, shredded chicken, and avocado.

Recent findings suggest that the married pair came to Madrid after a full life in Caracas. “By 2007 Chávez just kept winning and winning, and things were getting worse and worse. It really scared us,” Felipe states. That year was Chávez’s first attempt at constitutional reform to remove presidential term limits and expand state control of the economy. He lost his bid but remained in power and went on to secure reform in 2009. So, when the bank Fossa worked for offered him a job in Zurich, they didn’t hesitate. It was a decision that has led to many years of living abroad.

Bea Castelló Castro and Luis Felipe Fossa say that their Cafetín has become a hub for Venezuelans, who connect over coffee and arepas.

It has been revealed that their clientele reflects a similar worldliness, with Venezuelans who arrived directly from Caracas but also those who have made it here by way of a university in Boston, or lived for years in Miami, Newly introduced York, or London. Cafetín is a meeting point where these Venezuelans intersect, creating a community within a community. As Castelló Castro put it, “empiezas a hacer nexo”—you start to make connections.

Recently, I'm told, a couple in a sunlit corner of the cafe started chatting with a man standing at the long bar after hearing him mention Caracas. They began tracing the routes through Miami and Fresh York that had brought them to Madrid. Another day, a college sweatshirt prompted a conversation—and a new friendship. “It’s beautiful to see, especially in difficult moments in Venezuela,” says Castelló Castro.

Recent findings suggest that back at the Mercado de Las Maravillas, I sit at Buda Bar watching the lunch rush fade, as owner Rebeksa Mouzaber prepares me a sweet-corn crescent-shaped cachapa, its edges lacy from a bed of hot butter on the flattop griddle. A food courier accepts a freshly-made pocket-sized empanada while he scrolls and waits for his order.

Venezuelans like coming here because they feel at home—not just in the dishes that are served but also in the way they are asked for, Mouzaber tells me. “We know what it means when they ask for an ñapa (a top-up), just like we know how it feels to be so far away from home.”.
