A mother indicates Delta Air Lines separated her from her two-year-old daughter, then told her to ask other passengers to switch seats. She says she had purchased Comfort+ and originally selected seats together. If her account is accurate, this was a problem for Delta to resolve before boarding, not something to leave a parent negotiating in the aisle.

In a Reddit post, a passenger describes trying to resolve separate seat assignments on a flight from Orlando (MCO) to Atlanta (ATL). She was traveling with her husband, their 2½-year-old daughter, and their one-year-old son.

She notes she was directed to the gate for assistance, but received this response:.

In a recent development, “I explained that she’s two and cannot sit by herself. Their solution? Tell me it was my responsibility to ask other passengers to switch seats.”.

Recent findings suggest that when commenters questioned whether she had purchased basic economy or failed to select seats, she clarified that she had booked Comfort+. After checking her original confirmation, she added:.

According to recent reports, “I just looked and it was definitely Delta. I have 3 flight / time changes – I originally booked us in 15 D / 15 E / 15 F – we ended up in 15 F / 15 A / 16 A.”.

This remains her account and we don’t have a way to verify the booking history or the exchange with the gate staff. She also does not clearly state how the family ultimately sat onboard.

I have traveled extensively with my children, including when they were very young. There is a considerable difference between wanting the entire family together and needing a two-year-old beside a parent.

Sources indicate that it is unreasonable to ask an airline to rearrange a cabin so that every adult in a traveling party can sit together. Heidi and I can sit apart. One parent can sit with one child while the other sits elsewhere with the other child. We have done that many times.

In a recent development, but a toddler needs an adult who can help with the seatbelt, food, and everything else that comes with flying at that age. The stranger assigned to the adjacent seat cannot reasonably become the person expected to provide that help.

Recent findings suggest that I see no excuse for the Delta agent. Once an agent knows a toddler has been assigned a seat away from both parents, someone needs to take responsibility for finding a workable arrangement and it should be someone in a position of authority…like the gate agent.

I am also sympathetic to passengers who pre-select a seat and then find themselves pressured to move.

According to recent reports, A parent should not board, occupy someone else’s seat, and announce that the family needs to sit together and a passenger should not be shamed for declining an aisle-to-middle swap. There may be very good reasons that person selected that particular seat, and those reasons are not necessarily anyone else’s business.

That is precisely why the airline should handle this.

An agent can review the seat map, identify possible swaps, and ask for volunteers. If necessary, the airline can offer an incentive rather than expect a stranger to absorb the inconvenience for free. There may also be a solution involving a different cabin, provided the family agrees and any fare difference is addressed.

The ultimate solution to situations like these does not have to preserve every preference the family had when booking. It does need to put a young child beside a responsible adult.

The published Delta family seating policy states:.

“Delta strives to seat family members together upon request.”.

According to recent reports, it directs customers who cannot obtain seats together online or through the app to contact reservations to review the available options. That wording is less reassuring than a guarantee. Even so, I would expect the assistance to amount to more than telling a parent to start asking around once onboard.

Parents should understand fare restrictions and select seats when possible, but a two-year-old’s need to sit beside a parent does not disappear because the family purchased a cheaper ticket and it becomes legally dicey to not sell basic economy tickets to young children. However, in this case it was not a basic economy ticket but a Comfort+ seat.

Selecting seats months in advance does not mean you can stop checking them. Whenever I receive a schedule change, I review the flights and seat assignments and check again often in the week leading up to travel. Be sure to take a screenshot of your original seat assignments if they were not reflected on your ticket confirmation.

Industry observers note that if a young child becomes separated from a parent, contact the airline promptly and explain the child’s age. If reservations cannot resolve it, arrive early and ask an airport agent…don’t agree to negotiate onboard…it’s unreasonable, even for Frontier Airlines.

This is called “gardening” your reservation.

A mother says Delta assigned her toddler a separate seat and left her to ask other passengers to move, despite originally booking seats together in Comfort+. We have only her account, but the underlying expectation is reasonable: a two-year-old should sit beside a parent, and the airline should help arrange that.

In a recent development, other passengers deserve respect for their seat choices too. Resolving the issue before boarding protects everyone from an awkward confrontation that should never have been necessary….

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Located just 40 minutes from Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport, Disneyland Paris is the ideal place to begin a Parisian vacation or say au revoir before returning home. Disneyland Paris's two theme parks, Disneyland Park and Disney Adventure World, pair timeless charm with an ease you'll never find stateside. Here, you can sip Champagne in front of Sleeping Beauty's castle—or visit a dragon beneath it—while filling your days with delightful architecture, unprecedented thrills, and the wildest wilderness ride Disney's ever built (Big Thunder Mountain!).

Recent findings suggest that there's also never been a better time to visit. Walt Disney Studios Park's March 2026 transformation into the latest Disney Adventure World brought a drone-filled nighttime show, Avengers coaster, and even a Frozen-themed land featuring a lifelike Olaf robot to its once-faltering second gate. Now, between Fantasyland classics and futuristic favorites, there's something new and thrilling for the entire family to experience.

Sources indicate that of course, you'll need somewhere to rest your head at night, and that's where the best hotels near Disneyland Paris come into play. Staying at a Disney-branded property typically affords guests special amenities including ticket packages, exclusive character meet-and-greets, and Extra Magic Time, which provides bonus time in the parks prior to opening. These hotels are great options, but can also be pricey—luckily, there are also a few non-branded properties in the area that make for great alternatives. There's something here for everyone and every budget.

In a recent development, unsure of whether you want to add something so Américain to your Paris vacation? As a theme park journalist who has visited all Disney parks worldwide, trust me: It's worth the visit. Even with so many cultural monuments in Paris, nothing is more delightfully uncanny than witnessing the United States section of It's a Small World. So, whether you're looking for glamour or simply a good location, read on for the very best hotels near Disneyland Paris.

Distance from Disneyland Paris: Three-minute walk.

In a recent development, as the crown jewel of France's Disney resort, this 487-room property is Disney's best hotel overseas—and, quite possibly, in the entire world. After undergoing an extensive three-year overhaul, the iconic pink palace reopened in 2024 with princess suites and luxurious amenities worthy of its five-star ranking. Great for couples or families, guests can anticipate the ultimate royal treatment thanks to rooms with romantic castle views just steps from the park. With kids treatments at the Spa by Clarins and two complimentary hours of childcare each day, parents can unwind at the Fleur de Lys bar, enjoy a prix fixe meal at chef Jean Imbert's on-site restaurant, or perhaps even sneak back into the parks themselves. (We won't tell.).

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Distance from Disneyland Paris: Eight-minute drive.

Rustic-chic in the best of ways, Marriott's Village d'Île-de-France offers cozy abodes that sleep up to eight with full kitchens, washing machines, and plenty of space to stretch out, all a short shuttle ride from the theme parks. Designed to emulate the charms of a small Parisian village, these quaint studios and multi-bedroom town houses feel more like cottages than traditional vacation rentals. Surroundings like these may sound quotidien to someone like Princess Belle, but the resort is as sweet as the rooms are spacious, making it an ideal choice for a hotel near Disneyland Paris as well as extended trips to nearby towns.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Distance from Disneyland Paris: 10-minute walk, 10-minute drive.

Industry observers note that considering it's the only hotel in the world dedicated to Marvel's famed comic book characters, it's no surprise the Infinity Stone–colored beverages and slick, silver rooms at Disney Hotel Upcoming York - The Art of Marvel are somewhat out of this world. Family-friendly amenities like superhero meet-and-greets and a design studio with character drawing experiences make it the ultimate getaway for any comic book–obsessed fan in your family. Yet, even with hundreds of unique pieces of artwork, it won't feel like you're living through an Infinity War. Delicately executed details, like Manhattan Restaurant's Asgard-inspired chandelier and Spider-Man swinging across the panel screens at Skyline Bar, provide simple city elegance with the lightest touch of Marvel magic.

Distance from Disneyland Paris: 17-minute walk, 8-minute drive.

If this hotel reminds you of Walt Disney World's Yacht & Beach Club resorts, you're not mistaken—this 1,098-room Disneyland Paris hotel was inspired by its Florida counterpart. The nautical theming is strong, and it's that seaside charm that keeps parkgoers returning to this waterfront escape. Just a 15-minute walk from the park gates, guests can meet maritime Mickey & Minnie Mouse (who don delightful cruisewear) or indulge in a seafood buffet at the aptly named Cape Cod restaurant. It's modeled after a familiar location back in the States, sure, but after spending the day with princesses, dragons, and superheroes, you may find yourself overjoyed to return to those country club comforts.

Distance from Disneyland Paris: 13-minute walk, 8-minute drive.

Sources indicate that craving a bit more theming on your Disneyland Paris trip? Look no further than this national park–inspired escape. It offers lodge-style living perfect for a wintertime trip. Cozy up to the Redwood Bar & Lounge hearth, or in one of the newly renovated rooms with nods to Bambi and Pocahontas, and take in the charms of what Disney does best. Multiple on-site buffets allow you to feast like you've been on the move all day because, well, you likely have.

It has been revealed that note that this Disney-operated hotel is currently undergoing a phased refurbishment. For stays in late 2026 and early 2027, I recommend selecting a refurbished room in The Lodges. Starting in February 2027, construction will move to general hotel spaces, and certain facilities will be temporarily unavailable.

Distance from Disneyland Paris: 30-minute walk, 10-minute drive.

Rooms at the boutique Hôtel l’Elysée Val d’Europe are modern and minimal, offering the perfect escape from any theme park chaos. Though it's just a 30-minute walk or a short, free shuttle ride away from the gates, the real perk of being a bit removed is its proximity to the Val d’Europe shopping complex and the designer outlet mall La Vallée Village. With a bounty of discounted prices on luxury brands like Prada, Saint Laurent, and Gucci, you're sure to find a Parisian souvenir that'll rival the array of Mickey Mouse goods sold within the parks.

Distance from Disneyland Paris: Nine-minute drive.

It has been revealed that if the City of Lights appeals to you for its style and romance, consider this your ideal hotel. Design-forward rooms with concrete walls, sleek bathrooms, and an open, plant-walled lobby offer reliable value without sacrificing taste, making it a perfect choice for travelers seeking something a little less Disney. While families will benefit from select rooms offering full kitchens and stovetops, the upgraded amenities—which include a heated indoor pool, sauna, and hammam—offer a little something for everyone, just beyond the parks.

Distance from Disneyland Paris: 16-minute walk, 10-minute drive.

Industry observers note that step right up to this quirky hotel that feels like a Western film set and is jam-packed with Toy Story details. Small touches, like cowprint bedspreads and appearances by Woody and Jessie, make Disney Hotel Cheyenne a hidden gem that's nearly as themed as Disneyland Paris's own Frontierland. Given that it's significantly more affordable than the majority of its Disneyland-owned counterparts yet retains perks like Extra Magic Time, this property offers a best-of-both-worlds approach for those who want to live a full Disney-fied day from first rides to fireworks.

Distance from Disneyland Paris: 10-minute drive.

Multi-room cabins at this expansive, woodsy resort are the perfect way to experience a taste of the outdoors between trips on Major Thunder Mountain. Sadly, there are no theme park shuttle services, so parks must be reached by car, rideshare, or taxi. But that's not to say it's worth skipping—here, nature abounds in both form and function. There's an on-site aviary, comfort food at the Crockett's Tavern buffet, and plenty of rustic charm, so the comforts of home are never too far away. Consider this Disneyland Paris hotel as close as you can get to camping at Disneyland's theme parks—if camping also included unfettered access to Mickey waffles.

What area is the best to stay in when visiting Disneyland Paris?

Any hotel near Disney Village, the entertainment and dining district at the entrance to Disneyland Paris's two theme parks, is going to be the most convenient choice. This not only offers more ease and access, but affords you the option to shop and dine after the parks close each night. Still, booking nearly any Disney-operated hotel will give you benefits like Extra Magic Time and exclusive character encounters, which help get you even more out of your Disneyland Paris vacation.

Are there any hotels that are walking distance to Disneyland Paris?

In a recent development, yes—but you might want to bring your sneakers. Disneyland Hotel is located directly at the entrance to Disneyland Paris, while Disney Hotel Upcoming York - The Art of Marvel, Disney Newport Bay Club, and Disney Sequoia Lodge are all a 10- to 15-minute walk through Disney Village to reach both parks. Disney Hotel Cheyenne is a further trek, about 15 to 20 minutes away, but absolutely doable. Shuttle buses are available as well.

What is the 3-2-1 rule at Disneyland Paris?

According to recent reports, the 3-2-1 rule is essentially shorthand for how to streamline your Disneyland Paris experience. Experts recommend selecting three rides, two entertainment offerings, and one dining option for an easy, straightforward approach to planning a day at any Disney theme park. It works as well at Walt Disney World and Disneyland as it does here at Disneyland Paris, but I recommend you still do a little research before you go. Be sure you don't skip Phantom Manor, which can only be found in Paris, secure your dining reservations early, and don't miss the nighttime reveals offered at both parks—they're among the best in the world.

It is best to stay within the park at Disneyland Paris, or outside of it?

It goes without saying that the closer you are to the castle, the “better” your hotel will be, but it shouldn't be a deal-breaker. Convenience is always a factor, but Disney-operated hotels at Disneyland Paris tend to be much pricier than their American counterparts, so staying a bus ride away might be necessary. Still, the perks are plenty across most of Disneyland's own hotels, including extra time in the parks, which is why I recommended so many of them.

Jeffries puts immigration bill high on Democratic priority list

💡 Key Takeaways
  • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday.
  • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move promptly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.
  • Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move promptly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.

Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.

“One of the things that we need to do is to move the Dream and Promise Act for DACA recipients and TPS recipients,” Jeffries said, referring to a Democratic bill introduced last year. “We should actually move that bill immediately.”.

It has been revealed that the proposal aims to create a path to citizenship for certain Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipients and Temporary Protected Status holders. Similar legislation has been a top priority for Democrats in both chambers for more than a decade, with Democrats unable to advance this bill in the House while Republicans have held the majority.

Jeffries also reiterated his calls to rein in Immigration and Customs Enforcement and redirect funding allocated to the agency through Republicans' budget law known as the One Significant Beautiful Bill Act, while expressing a desire for bipartisan cooperation on immigration more broadly.

“We think the border should be safe and strong and secure, and we think our immigration system overall is broken,” Jeffries said. “We need to fix it in a comprehensive way, and certainly, it's our hope that a handful of Republicans will be willing to join us, so we can fix it in a bipartisan way.”.

On healthcare, however, Jeffries offered fewer specifics, suggesting Democrats still have decisions to make before taking control of the chamber. Democrats broadly agree on the need to restore subsidies for plans purchased through health insurance markets that expired at the end of 2025. But the question of what additional steps the party should pursue with the goal of expanding coverage and lowering prices is likely to be a major test of Democratic leadership’s ability to find consensus among its robust new majority.

When asked how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that's all part of an ongoing conversation.”.

The Latest York Democrat outlined several broader healthcare priorities, including reversing Medicaid cuts enacted under President Donald Trump, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, all of which Democrats have vowed to do over the last year.

“Out of the gate, what we clearly have to do is fix our broken healthcare system in terms of the damage that's been done by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists over the last two years, and that clearly involves reversing the Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits, and beginning to engage in supporting medical research, particularly things like research for pediatric cancer,” Jeffries added.

Recent findings suggest that democrats established a healthcare working group earlier this Congress, led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., to gather perspectives and develop policy proposals as the party works toward a broader agenda.

Recent findings suggest that without an declared challenger, Jeffries has expressed confidence that he’ll secure the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who have remarked they remain “undecided” ahead of Wednesday’s elections. Jeffries, who was introduced as “Speaker Jeffries” on election night, said last week he was “very confident we’ll get there” and confirmed that the caucus will hold a recorded vote in the contest.

According to recent reports, rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to go forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives, many aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

Jeffries said Tuesday the approach mirrors the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who is best positioned to lead based on “track record, experience and vision.”.

Industry observers note that this report was corrected to reflect Rep. Nancy Pelosi’s status as a current member.

#145587. A Guide to NYC’s Little Italy—and the Culinary Gems Hidden Among the Tourist Traps

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1407 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

A Guide to NYC’s Little Italy—and the Culinary Gems Hidden Among the Tourist Traps

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1407 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that contrary to other tourist-focused neighborhoods in Latest York (looking at you, Times Square), Little Italy boasts an innate charm that resonates with visitors and locals alike.
  • A note on how we’re defining the area: Over the years, Little Italy’s boundaries have shrunk to focus on the touristic area of Mulberry Street and its immediate surroundings.
  • It has been revealed that located in the heart of Little Italy, Umberto’s Clam House is best known for its—you guessed it, all things clams.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that contrary to other tourist-focused neighborhoods in Latest York (looking at you, Times Square), Little Italy boasts an innate charm that resonates with visitors and locals alike. Sandwiched between SoHo and the Lower East Side, this jewel box area is home to long-standing, family-owned restaurants and authentic Italian bakeries, the majority of which have been neighborhood staples for decades. Yet despite its touristy atmosphere, a unique feeling of old school New York magic hangs in the air; beyond the personality-less stands and souvenir shops, framed family photos on restaurant walls and structural imperfections of tenement buildings speak to a bygone area of the city’s past, evoking a sense of nostalgia that so many neighborhoods lack. Pop down to Mulberry Street and see for yourself—though be sure you know which spots are actually legit (that’s where we come in).

A note on how we’re defining the area: Over the years, Little Italy’s boundaries have shrunk to focus on the touristic area of Mulberry Street and its immediate surroundings. While the southern and western boundaries of Canal Street and Lafayette Streets remain unchanged, the historic easterly Bowery boundary has arguably shifted to Elizabeth Street; similarly, the northerly boundary of Kenmare has also condensed down, according to many, to Broome Street. For the sake of this piece, we’re using the boundaries of Lafayette Street, Canal Street, Elizabeth Street, and Broome Street as a happy medium.

It has been revealed that located in the heart of Little Italy, Umberto’s Clam House is best known for its—you guessed it, all things clams. The restaurant quickly garnered attention shortly after opening in 1972, when mobster Joe "Crazy Joe" Gallo was shot in the restaurant’s dining room. Like its mafia-related history, the food at Umberto’s is as Italian-American as it gets. Baked clams and fried calamari are the appetizer list’s biggest show-stoppers, while superbly chilled clams on the half-shell pair exquisitely with equally cold (and generously sized) cocktails from the bar. Seafood-focused mains are the name of the game here, including the garlicky linguini and clam sauce and recently resurfaced scungilli with pasta served with piping hot red sauce.

Address: 132 Mulberry Street, Fresh York, NY 10013.

For Italian-American eats in a less stereotypically Little Italy ambiance, Il Cortile is the way to go. Contrary to the old school Italian vibes found in the majority of the neighborhood’s restaurants, Il Cortile’s atrium-style glass ceiling and plant-filled room feel more like dining al fresco in Trastevere than the heart of Mulberry Street. The family-owned restaurant’s neighborhood roots date back to 1975, with a solid focus on Northern Italian cuisine. The homemade cheese ravioli and wood-fired pizzas are always a safe bet, though for meat lovers, springing for the Fettuccine di Parma made with sweet sausage and wild mushrooms won’t disappoint—and be sure to save room for the pillowy soft tiramisu made with creamy mascarpone and imported Italian ladyfingers drenched in espresso.

Address: 125 Mulberry St, Fresh York, NY 10013.

Original Vincent’s, often called The Original Vincent’s Clam Bar, is home to one of the richest restaurant success stories in Little Italy. Founded in 1904 by Giuseppe and Carmela Siano, the business began as a sidewalk street cart serving up fresh seafood and jars of homemade red sauce, available in mild, medium, and hot. Today, the restaurant sits on the corner of Mott and Hester Streets, and is still known for its signature gravies, baked clams, and linguini-based pasta dishes (don’t skip the frutti di mare). As in its earliest days, Original Vincent’s still sells jars of their red sauce to-go, making replicating the restaurant’s pasta dishes at home a breeze—simply grab a bottle of Chianti, cue up your Louis Primo playlist and voila.

Address: 119 Mott St, Latest York, NY 10013.

Paesano of Mulberry Street is home to one of the coziest interiors in Little Italy, offering a peaceful refuge from the neighborhood bustle. Rustic twig bunches and leafy plants strung with twinkle lights hang from the ceiling, while traditional Italian frescos and framed family photographs adorn the whitewashed brick walls. Originally opened in 1961, the restaurant remains owned by the same family and continues to be known for their Southern Italian recipes, including linguini with clam sauce, wood-fired pizzas, and savory chicken marsala drenched in sautéed mushrooms. Meat lovers, don’t skip the restaurant’s signature Veal A La Paesano, featuring a juicy and tender veal base layered with thin slices of prosciutto, steamed broccoli, and gooey mozzarella cheese finished with succulent brown gravy.

Address: 136 Mulberry St, Newly introduced York, NY 10013.

Recent findings suggest that for serious pizza lovers, a trip to Lombardi’s is a no-brainer. Tucked on the corner of Mott and Spring, this neighborhood institution is credited as America’s first pizzeria, originally founded by Gennaro Lombardi in 1905. Lombardi swiftly rose to fame for his large, heavily-topped pies, which he baked in an on-site, coal-and-gas oven. The result? Smoky crusts topped with perfectly balanced tomato sauce and gobs of whole milk mozzarella—along with sweet Italian sausage and various other accoutrements. The interior oozes with classic Newly introduced York charm, featuring tables clad in red-and-white checkered cloths and framed family photographs strung along the red-hued walls. Head’s up, the spot is cash only, and while there’s an ATM on site, we recommend coming prepared to avoid the withdrawal fee.

Address: 30 Spring St, New York, NY 10012.

Pasquale Jones-12_2. Brussels Sprout Pizza with Red Onion, Smoked Mozzarella & Lemon.

It has been revealed that in a sea of mediocre neighborhood wine lists, Pasqule Jones offers a breath of fresh air for Little Italy exploring wine lovers. Situated on the cusp of the neighborhood’s boundaries (and easily identifiable by its rainbow neon lights), this Italian-American pizzeria first opened its doors in 2016 and quickly became a staple for industry folks and visiting oenophiles alike. Beloved for its wood-fired Fresh York style pizzas (don’t miss the signature clam pie) and thick, homemade pastas, the restaurant’s warm-yet-casual ambiance is ideal for posting up with a pie and a bottle—especially if you’re after great Burgundy, Champagne, or Italian reds. Expect classic picks from Pierre-Yves Colin-Morey, Domaine de l’Arlot, and Vietti, as well ample fun and fresh selections from Sandlands, Chacra, and Domaine Gramenon.

Address: 187 Mulberry St, Latest York, NY 10012.

Address: 195 Grand St, New York, NY 10013.

Although less famous than nearby Ferrara, Caffé Palermo features the innate Italian charm one looks for when wandering the neighborhood. Owned and operated by Baby John DeLutro (the self-proclaimed “Cannoli King”) since 1973, the establishment lives up to its owner’s moniker, offering flavored iterations—including pistachio and hazelnut made with sweet ricotta cream, the former of which is one of the joint’s standouts—in perfectly crisp shells. What Palermo does have over Ferrara is a solid amount of outdoor seating, ideal for posting up with a cappuccino and people watching on Mulberry.

Address: 148 Mulberry St, Newly introduced York, NY 10013.

La Compagnie des Vins Surnaturels.

If you’re looking for a wine break between pizza and pastries, this is just the ticket. Located on Little Italy's western limits (Centre Street between Broome and Grand), this French-inspired wine bar offers extensive by-the-glass options and shareable bites, including cheese and charcuterie boards to larger main courses, including beef tartare and lemon spaghetti. The comprehensive wine list, which features anywhere from 750 to 1,000+ references at all times, leans unsurprisingly French, though ample selections from Italy, Spain, and the USA are also available. Our suggestion? Post up with a bottle of Grower Champagne and relish in the perfectly executed Parisian bar à vin ambiance.

Address: 249 Centre St, Newly introduced York, NY 10013.

Address: 409 Broome St, New York, NY 10013.

In a recent development, technically located on the cusp of Little Italy’s historic boundaries (Kenmare and Broome Streets), La Esquina offers a flavor-packed reprieve from the classic red-sauce joints synonymous with the neighborhood. Situated in a former counter deli, this multi-level Mexican hotspot is best known for its casual taqueria (located in ‘The Corner Deli’ space) serving tacos, tortas, and ceviche. However, for those looking for something a bit stronger, head through the secret door and down the stairs to find the restaurant’s underground speakeasy. Lit by candle and adorned with Lucha Libre posters, the bar’s high-energy ambiance is prime for enjoying queso fundido and smoky Mexican street corn (elotes callejeros) washed down with expertly crafted agave-based cocktails.

Address: 114 Kenmare St, Fresh York, NY 10012.

#145586. Latest Update: The Best Places to Go in Australia, New Zealand, and the South Pacific in 2027

Latest Update: The Best Places to Go in Australia, New Zealand, and the South Pacific in 2027

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4121 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when it comes to the best places to go in Australia, New Zealand, and the South Pacific for 2027, there is a prevailing theme: Familiar destinations are finding new ways to surprise us.
  • This is part of our global guide to the Best Places to Go in 2027—find more travel inspiration here.
  • Go for: ancient cultural sites, eco-tourism, dazzling island landscapes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when it comes to the best places to go in Australia, New Zealand, and the South Pacific for 2027, there is a prevailing theme: Familiar destinations are finding new ways to surprise us. In Queensland, old pubs have become home to some of the hottest tables. Just take a look at Noosa’s restored 100-year-old Kin Kin, which has a new lease on life thanks to the arrival of Michelin-trained chef Oscar Holgado. And there’s much more where that came from. Across the country in the East Kimberley, this is the year to dine on native bush foods in the shadow of ancient boabs and red cliffs, and rest your head at the area’s stalwart bush lodges, two of which have just reopened after major renovations. Then there’s Tasmania’s east coast, which is always deserving of a long road trip—and now Tasmanian malt whisky is being made in an oyster hatchery, not far from where little penguins (the world’s smallest penguin species) return to shore after feeding at sea. Across the Tasman, Wellington’s new Michelin guide reminds us that even those stars can’t capture the effortless excellence of this area’s food and wine culture. Plan your visit around a culinary festival, several of which come to life in winter, and you’ll see what we mean. Meanwhile, in the Cook Islands at Highland Paradise on Rarotonga, descendants of the original Tinomana community guide visitors through a 600-year-old ancestral mountain settlement, sharing its history and traditions as they optimistically await UNESCO’s answer on recognition. On our below list of the best places to travel in Oceania for 2027, there is a trip for every type. —Chloe Sachdev.

This is part of our global guide to the Best Places to Go in 2027—find more travel inspiration here.

Go for: ancient cultural sites, eco-tourism, dazzling island landscapes.

On the South Pacific, the 15 isles of Cook Islands are scattered across nearly 900,000 square miles.

The Cook Islands’ 15 isles stipple roughly 849,000 square miles of the South Pacific, but total less than 100 square miles of land. Most first trips center on a southern pair of islands: Rarotonga and Aitutaki. On the one-hour propeller flight between two, the entire country arrives in flashes: a volcanic ridge inside a white reef, miles of open Pacific, then a blue lagoon with motu gathered along its rim. Rarotonga’s 20-mile coast road threads between reef and pleated peaks, while Aitutaki is defined by its broad lagoon.

On the west side of the island Rarotonga, a narrow road climbs from the lagoon into Maungaroa Valley, where a canopy of multi-trunked mato trees covers the remains of a centuries-old settlement. Taken together, the surviving sites form a cultural landscape that will appear before UNESCO’s World Heritage Committee in 2027 as the Cook Islands’ first nomination. At Highland Paradise, a cultural site within the old settlement and managed by descendants of Chief Tinomana, the Tapu’ae Day Tour follows those paths past chiefly house sites and sacred ground as guides explain how the stonework organized life here.

On Aitutaki, customary stewardship extends well below the waterline. In 2025 three lagoon zones came under ra’ui, a traditional temporary closure that allows coral and fish populations to recover, with protections scheduled to rotate in 2027. Aitutaki Coral Restoration takes small groups beyond the usual motu-and-sandbar circuit to its underwater nursery and a planting site, where guests clean a dead coral base and secure a naturally broken fragment. Part of each tour fee supports the restoration work.

Tourism is growing alongside the conservation push. In March 2027 a new, locally owned hotel, Grand Resort, billing itself as the island’s first five-star hotel, is scheduled to open with 61 adults-only suites on Rarotonga’s west coast. The Destination Stewardship Plan 2026–2030, meanwhile, shifts the focus from mainly growing tourism to managing its impact with protections for culture and the environment with a greater share flowing to island communities. —Paul Jebara.

Go for: red dirt, remote lodges, and wilderness on an epic scale.

After a multimillion-dollar transformation, Bullo River Station will reopen in May 2027.

Bullo River Station guests will have the opportunity to watch the seasonal mustering of cattle.

It’s not just helicopter blades creating a hum in Australia’s East Kimberley. A wave of luxury investment is putting this remote frontier on the global-travel radar—without sanding down the wilderness that makes it so worth the journey.

After devastating cyclone damage, Berkeley River Lodge welcomes guests back to a revived 15-villa hideaway, accessible only by private air charter from Darwin. Individual decks overlook a croc-filled coastline, while open-air en suites allow galaxy gazing from the bathtub. Just across the border in the Northern Territory, Bullo River Station sits on the eastern fringe of the East Kimberley. Come May 2027, it will reopen after a multimillion-dollar transformation, pairing a newly introduced level of comfort with conservation across its 400,000 acres. The good news is that it remains a dusty working cattle station: Guests can watch seasonal musters, fish for barramundi in the river, or helicopter to watering holes for swims beneath waterfalls or to Aboriginal rock-art sites.

In a recent development, there is even more to come. Abercrombie & Kent, in conjunction with the Billingjul Aboriginal Corporation, is developing its first Australian property: an off-grid eco-retreat offering access to the UNESCO World Heritage–listed Purnululu National Park, which contains the Bungle Bungle Range, where countless tiger-striped domes rise from the earth like sculpted beehives. (Originally slated for 2027, the lodge has been delayed, with a new opening date yet to be unveiled.).

Sources indicate that connecting much of this wilderness is Kununurra, a proper Outback town on the banks of the Ord River and the main jumping-off point for the Bungle Bungles, Lake Argyle, and the wider East Kimberley. If your itinerary calls for a night in town before heading deeper into the region, don’t waste it: The surrounding Ord River irrigation area is a surprisingly fertile food bowl. The Gourmet Camp Oven Experience puts that produce to work over four courses, cooked by fire in a secret off-grid location outside town, with dinner served beneath the stars and swinging chandeliers illuminating ancient boabs. —Katrina Lodge.

Go for: heritage buildings, creative energy, and a fresh wave of boutique stays.

In Western Australia, Fremantle's distinct creative scene centers on new boutiques, galleries, and stays.

Poppy Lissiman’s High Street flagship shines among a cluster of indie boutiques and maker pop-ups.

In 1987 the America’s Cup turned an unvarnished Western Australia port town into a global stage overnight. Forty years on, Fremantle has forged an identity of its own. Just 12 miles southwest of central Perth, Freo, as it’s known to locals—and Walyalup, as it’s known to the Whadjuk Noongar people—is the big city’s grittier cousin and the epicenter of one of Australia’s most eclectic creative scenes. This is, after all, fertile ground for Aussie homegrown musicians from Bon Scott to Tame Impala and John Butler. Now, right here at the mouth of the Swan River, a upcoming generation of tastemakers are transforming warehouse skeletons and limestone heritage façades into galleries, natural wine bars, and boutique stays.

The energy will hit fever pitch in November 2027 with the return of the Fremantle Biennale, which will bring immersive art into the city’s forgotten spaces (dates are yet to be unveiled, but the 2025 event stretched over two full weeks). It crowns a year-round festival calendar of street performances, exhibitions, and community celebrations steeped in Fremantle’s multicultural roots. On the fashion front, a revitalization of the central piazza—just down the road from Aussie cool girl Poppy Lissiman’s High Street flagship—is helping spotlight indie makers and pop-up retailers. Fremantle’s historic West End has welcomed several hotly anticipated bars from beloved names in Western Australia hospitality, beginning with much-loved merchant Wise Child Wine Store, which expanded its bottle shop in September 2026 to include a 50-seat wine bar. Around the corner, Cafe Music, from the team behind Northbridge institution Wines of While, earned cult status with teaser weekends of mini martinis and vinyl DJs ahead of its permanent 2027 opening. At the heritage-listed P&O Hotel, listening bar and restaurant Ode to Sirens occupies the ground floor, while bartenders at Reuben’s Supper Club have been shaking cocktails since October 2026.

The West End’s newest stay follows the same past-meets-present script. The 11-room Owston Hotel (March 2026), inside the former Roma Restaurant, is a modern locanda honoring the Italian families who settled here in the 1950s. Breakfast comes from Common Bakery downstairs; later, slip next door for a pour at Vin Populi. —Jessie Stoelwinder.

Go for: fresh sailings, revived resorts, and a quadrennial sporting showcase.

Traveling by ship to French Polynesia has never been more accessible, thanks to newly introduced yachts and cruises.

Recent findings suggest that with 118 palm-studded islands and atolls scattered across retina-popping blue waters, French Polynesia hardly needs help making a case for itself. But 2027 brings latest ways to explore this far-flung corner of the South Pacific—especially by ship.

It has been revealed that the Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection’s French Polynesia sailings debut in December 2026, with 149-suite Evrima cruising the mountainous Society Islands, where volcanic peaks meet reef-ringed lagoons. In February, Windstar adds a second ship to sail these waters year-round, with the newly refurbished Wind Star joining Star Breeze throughout the Society Islands and the low-lying Tuamotus, a scattering of coral atolls and luminous lagoons. In March 2027, Aranui Cruises will launch Aranoa, a 91-cabin hybrid freighter-passenger ship bound for the remote Austral Islands, the Tuamotus, and Pitcairn. Wild, mountainous, and little visited, the Australs offer a different face of French Polynesia from the one seen in postcards showing overwater bungalows.

Though there are plenty of those accommodations on stilts, if that’s what you’re after, a wave of arrivals on land and lagoon add to the momentum. On mountainous Moorea, Sofitel Kia Ora Moorea Beach Resort has emerged from a major renovation in 2026, with revamped public spaces and refreshed overwater bungalows. In October, Bora Bora’s legendary Bloody Mary’s returned with a fresh 53-key hotel on Povai Bay and its sandy-floored restaurant restored alongside it. In early 2027, ELYT Charter Tahiti sets sail as a four-bedroom floating villa for private adventures around Bora Bora.

Sources indicate that but 2027’s biggest arrival isn’t a hotel. In July the XVIII Pacific Games—the largest sporting event ever held in French Polynesia—will bring more than 4,500 athletes to Tahiti, Moorea, and Raiatea for 24 sports and more than 350 events. Among the sports is va’a, traditional outrigger canoe racing that is deeply embedded in Polynesian culture, alongside surfing, sailing, and open-water swimming. —Sarah Reid.

Go for: Southland’s fresh cultural landmark, wild kiwi, and dark skies.

Known in Māori as Rakiura, or “glowing skies,” Stewart Island is an International Dark Sky Sanctuary.

It has been revealed that latest Zealand doesn’t end at South Island. Farther down the map is Stewart Island, where the roads run out and the forest takes over. Rakiura, its Māori name, means “glowing skies”—fitting for an island that affords fiery sunsets, a visible Milky Way, and appearances of the aurora australis (southern lights) and is an International Dark Sky Sanctuary.

Recent findings suggest that for many travelers heading to New Zealand’s deep south, the journey begins in Invercargill, where the Te Unua Museum of Southland will open in 2027, returning a major regional museum to the city for the first time since the Southland Museum and Art Gallery closed in 2018. Telling the stories of Murihiku Southland and its people, its collection includes rich holdings of Māori taoka, archaeology, photography, social history, and artifacts from the Subantarctic Islands.

Across Foveaux Strait, Stewart Island (Rakiura) comes into view. Oban, its only settlement, curls around horseshoe-shaped Halfmoon Bay. Wildlife vastly outnumbers humans here, where fewer than 500 people live. As many as 15,000 southern brown kiwi, or tokoeka, are thought to live on Stewart Island and, unusual for kiwi, can sometimes be spotted foraging in daylight. Just offshore, pest-free Ulva Island (Te Wharawhara) is a sanctuary for native birdlife like native kākā parrots and flightless weka birds.

Recent findings suggest that around 85% of the island is protected within Rakiura National Park, a wilderness of native forest, wetlands, dunes, and granite ranges. For a deeper look at its cultural history, take a boat from Oban to remote Oneke, or The Neck, an early Māori settlement and the tūrangawaewae—place of belonging—of Rakiura Māori. The three-hour guided experience begins with a whakatau, a traditional Māori welcome, and a visit to the Oneke whare (Māori meeting house) before guests follow coastal and native-bush trails as guides unpack the area’s Māori and European history, traditional plant use, and conservation. —Louise Goldsbury.

Go for: lo-fi beach towns, long sweeps of sand, and a fast-evolving food scene.

Elysium Noosa Resort joins Noosa's ever-improving food scene, serving an Italian-meets-Australian menu of local ingredients.

Elysium Noosa Resort is one of several new stays on Queensland’s low-rise, low-key Sunshine Coast.

An hour north of Brisbane, stretching along 62 miles of coastline and backed by rainforest-covered hills and volcanic peaks, Queensland’s Sunshine Coast is the antidote to both Brisbane’s significant-city buzz and the Gold Coast’s five-star flex: lower-rise, lower-key, but home to an increasingly sophisticated run of ambitious openings that is raising its profile at home and abroad.

In Noosa the newly opened Elysium Noosa Resort has kicked lively Hastings Street up another notch. Cibaria Noosa trattoria, helmed by acclaimed Sydney chef Alessandro Pavoni, raids the Sunshine Coast food bowl for an Italian-meets-Australian menu of Queensland spanner crab risotto, Mooloolaba king prawns sharpened with finger lime, and locally sourced bistecca. Fifteen minutes south in Peregian Beach, two-hatted (”hats” are Australia’s equivalent of Michelin stars) restaurant Bask similarly puts local seafood, meat, and peak-season vegetables front and center.

Industry observers note that farther south, Avani Mooloolaba Beach Hotel, which opened in May 2026, has brought the lo-fi coastal town Mooloolaba its first internationally branded resort, with dazzling views and passionfruit-and-melon vodka cocktails at Sully’s Rooftop. On the waterfront at the Mooloolaba Spit, Fish House Steak & Grill jazzes up lobster rolls with a sunshiny yuzu emulsion. The region is serious about beer too: More than 20 independent brewhouses make the Sunshine Coast Australia’s craft-beer capital.

According to recent reports, inland, Casa Renoir, one of Australia’s chicest stays, will be completed in summer 2027 with six solar-powered villas. Limestone, olive trees, faded market finds, and private pools give the place the air of a Puglian masseria. That same connection to the land is shaping the hinterland’s food scene. Ēthos at Alsahwa Estate serves farm-to-table meals inside a barn on a 30-acre regenerative farm, while, in a plot twist for the 112-year-old Kin Kin Hotel, Michelin-trained chef Oscar Holgado, who has worked in the kitchens of Angela Hartnett’s Murano and Marcus Wareing’s The Berkeley, whips up a daily tasting menu—driven by whatever he’s plucked from the garden—in a converted barn called The Woodshed.

Recent findings suggest that for all these developments, the Sunshine Coast hasn’t lost its low-key appeal; it has simply acquired better places to sleep, eat, and drink. Luckily, it is becoming considerably easier to reach with growing international connections and a $170 million expansion of Sunshine Coast Airport’s domestic terminal underway and due for completion in 2027. —Ute Junker.

Go for: Rugby World Cup fever, landmark hotels, and a reinvigorated country escape.

In 2027, the Men's Rugby World Cup returns to Australia for the first time since 2003, with the final Cup decider taking place in Sydney.

UNESCO-listed Greater Blue Mountains occupy more than a million acres of eucalyptus forest, sandstone escarpments, and deep-cut canyons.

In a recent development, sydney has never struggled for attention, but 2027 is shaping up as a blockbuster year. The momentum began in November 2026, when Powerhouse Parramatta, the largest museum ever built in New South Wales, opened, bringing cultural heft to the city’s west. Also in November, Chanel staged its cruise 2026–2027 collection in Sydney. First shown in Biarritz, the fashion show found a natural second home in a city where salty hair, ocean swims, and year-round resort dressing are not just an aspiration but a way of life.

According to recent reports, in 2027 sport takes over. The Men’s Rugby World Cup, expanded from 20 to 24 teams, returns to Australia for the first time since 2003, and Sydney lands the sharp end of the tournament. Over six weeks the city will host 13 matches, including major head-to-heads like Australia versus Upcoming Zealand, England versus Wales, two quarterfinals, both semifinals, and the bronze final, before 82,000 fans pack Stadium Australia for the final on November 13—the first rugby World Cup decider in Sydney in 24 years.

Recent findings suggest that australia’s first Waldorf Astoria opens in early 2027 on Circular Quay, with 220 rooms and serious architectural pedigree along with floor-to-ceiling views of the Opera House and Harbour Bridge. Kengo Kuma & Associates—behind Scotland’s V&A Dundee and Tokyo’s Olympic stadium—has designed a striking glass-fronted tower on the harbor. Inside, Melbourne-born Curtis Stone will lead the hotel’s culinary efforts, opening a bar and a restaurant—his first in Australia, in fact, after graduating from television chef to serious Los Angeles restaurateur with Maude and Gwen.

Industry observers note that two hours beyond Sydney, the UNESCO-listed Greater Blue Mountains stretch across over a million acres of eucalyptus forest, sandstone escarpments, and deep-cut canyons, promising the perfect side trip. Near Katoomba, the main hub for exploring the Blue Mountains, the historic Lilianfels hotel emerged from a multimillion-dollar overhaul in 2026 as Ardour Lilianfels Blue Mountains, its 89 renovated rooms and suites set on an 1889 country estate that is a well placed base for days on the trails. The bigger arrival comes in 2027, when Emirates’ long-shuttered Wolgan Valley returns from a $35 million-plus overhaul as the world’s first Ritz-Carlton Lodge, with 40 lodges scattered throughout a 7,000-acre conservation reserve roamed by kangaroos and wombats. —Chloe Sachdev.

Go for: wild beauty and newly introduced-wave stays.

Long-known for its quiet beaches, Bicheno welcomes new names to the food and drink scene.

Dolphin Sands is a rural locality in the local government area of Glamorgan–Spring Bay in Tasmania.

It has been revealed that this area has long been home to one of Australia’s great road trips, a coastline drive linking Hobart with Launceston via Freycinet and the Bay of Fires. It’s a route of contrasts: the Tasman Sea on one side, forested hills on the other, past beaches and granite headlands, and a succession of fishing towns where boats still pull up with the day’s catch. Lately, though, there are more reasons to pull over.

According to recent reports, bicheno, two to three hours north of Hobart, is a case in point. The former fishing town turned low-key surf haunt remains better known for little penguins and deserted beaches than sceney restaurants, but a clutch of openings is evening the equation. At homegrown Waubs Harbour Distillery, award-winning whisky is made mere feet from the ocean in a converted oyster hatchery, with fireside tastings overlooking the Tasman Sea. Nearby, Le Gulch pours Tasmanian wines against pastel sunsets, while Parisian expat Tristan Punelle’s Le Coq, serving produce-led dishes by candlelight to a mix of both salty-haired locals and vacationers, is a humble ode to French cuisine. And after days spent surfing with dolphins and walking serene shorelines, Selkie Wellness restores balance at its beach-shack-housed massage studio and contrast therapy garden.

In a recent development, farther south, beneath the pink-granite peaks of The Hazards, Saffire Freycinet enters a new chapter. In December 2026 the landmark wilderness lodge is unveiling The Saffire Jewel, an 8,600-square-foot, three-bedroom villa with a 59-foot-long infinity pool, a Jacuzzi, a private chef, and an excursion guide. Then, over Easter 2027, the Australian Three Peaks Race returns after a 14-year absence. The competition involves teams heading down Tasmania’s east coast in a nonstop combination of offshore sailing and mountain running. Spectators can watch the fleet depart from Beauty Point, catch the runners changing over at Coles Bay before tackling Mount Freycinet, or see the race finish in Hobart. —Alex Mitcheson.

Go for: independent restaurants, wineries, and creative energy.

In walkable harbor city Wellington, dining is defined by spots like Graze, Margot, The Ram, and Hillside.

For the best expression of Upcoming Zealand (Aotearoa) food, head to Wellington. Seriously. Michelin might have shone an international light on the country’s culinary scene in June 2026 but Wellington has been diligently perfecting its food culture long before the inspectors came to town.

In a recent development, this compact, walkable harbor city with a strong sense of community has been a go-to weekend escape for eating and drinking at some of the country’s best restaurants, bars, cafés, bakeries, and food festivals. A cohort of passionate chefs and owner-operators embody this sense of independent hospitality, taking advantage of local produce and the area’s abounding cultural diversity. In Wellington, you’ll find the kind of informal dining that the Michelin system often overlooks.

According to recent reports, so how to tap in? At Graze in Kelburn, chef Max Gordy and sommelier Stina Persen serve a daily-changing menu built around New Zealand–grown produce and sustainably caught seafood. Over in Newtown chef Tom Adam and Juno Miers’s intimate Margot pairs seasonal cooking with an excellent drinks list. Elsewhere, The Ram recasts the Cuba Street pub as a serious food destination, while tiny vegetarian restaurant Hillside follows a low-waste philosophy grounded in local produce. Another to watch is award-winning Rita, which, in early 2027, will relaunch inside its century-old workers’ cottage as Super Rita, a deli and urban pantry showcasing local growers. The waterfront at Oriental Bay gets a new draw in early 2027, when The Pavilion opens its doors as an all-in-one food and wellness destination in a former 1930s bathing pavilion and band rotunda, with an all-day restaurant, a rooftop bar, and a bathhouse with hot pools, a cold plunge, a sauna, and treatments.

Sources indicate that bringing more of the creative energy Wellington is known for back to its Civic Square, City Gallery Wellington, a significant hub for contemporary art, reopened in October 2026 with a major exhibition by artist Cornelia Parker. Wellington’s city center continues to emerge butterfly-like from a long period of construction, and 2027 is a compelling time to visit, as several major civic buildings reopen to the public. Hot on the heels of the revitalized Te Matapihi ki te Ao Nui Central Library, the 120-year-old, heritage-listed Town Hall opens in February 2027 after more than a decade behind construction fencing, housing a new, world-class National Music Centre. From April 9–11, the restored venue will stage a new production of Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Sunset Boulevard, starring Tony-nominated performer Keala Settle. —Johanna Thornton.

Go for: major resort openings, reimagined experiences, and fresh ways to explore beyond the beach.

The Whitsundays' reborn Le Méridien Lindeman Island Resort & Spa and Hook Island eco-lodge are much anticipated for 2027.

The Great Barrier Reef may be the Whitsundays’ headliner, with Whitehaven Beach its opening act. Now, though, there are fresh perspectives on the beloved archipelago. Explore Whitsunday Island beyond its coral reef by hiking the 20-mile, three-day Ngaro Track, which threads through subtropical forests and coastline. Along the way, you'll learn its stories through Traditional Ngaro Custodians. There’s also a new way to experience the Great Barrier Reef itself. Some 40 nautical miles offshore, at Hardy Reef on the outer Great Barrier Reef, Cruise Whitsundays has reimagined its floating Reefworld pontoon as an overnight-only experience: Sleep beneath the stars in one of 12 new glamping-style Reefbeds, or below the waterline in one of just two Reefsuites, Australia’s first underwater accommodations, offering floor-to-ceiling windows onto the reef and, if you’re lucky, a passing turtle. Next door the newly upgraded Heart Pontoon, a second floating platform, caters to day-trippers.

Sources indicate that but the biggest news for the Whitsundays is the 2027 rebirth of two long-dormant island resorts. The 209-key Le Méridien Lindeman Island Resort & Spa—the brand’s first Australian resort—will bring an Explore Spa and a raft of water sports to Lindeman Island. More remarkable is the revival of Hook Island, which has been without a resort for more than a decade. The Whitsundays’ rugged second-largest island will get a low-impact eco-lodge with 39 cabins, forest pools, and wellness spaces, making the largely undeveloped landscape of lush rainforest, secluded bays, and color-popping coral reefs available to overnight guests once again.

Sources indicate that on the mainland, don’t miss Sollos Estate, Australia’s first agave distillery, which has just opened north of Airlie Beach. The Whitsunday Skyway sightseeing cable car and a latest five-star resort in development for Airlie add more reasons to visit this Sunshine State paradise. —Sarah Reid.

    #145584. As a Solo Traveler, I’ve Booked Tours Around the World—But This Fjord Excursion in Latest Zealand Took My Breath Away

    As a Solo Traveler, I’ve Booked Tours Around the World—But This Fjord Excursion in Latest Zealand Took My Breath Away

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1342 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that after taking the 17-hour Air New Zealand flight from New York City to Auckland this May, I was determined to make the most of my first visit to New Zealand.
    • Sources indicate that I booked several day trips, from an Arthur’s Pass train tour starting in Christchurch to a Walter Peak farm tour in Queenstown.
    • Sources indicate that I was eager to see what “business class” would look like on a day trip, and the moment the doors to the Sprinter van opened, I was impressed.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that after taking the 17-hour Air New Zealand flight from New York City to Auckland this May, I was determined to make the most of my first visit to New Zealand. I hopped around the North Island, relishing Auckland’s food scene, checking into the innovative Hotel Britomart, and visiting Wellington’s Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa. But when it came to the South Island, I realized the points of interest are far more spread out, with the massive Southern Alps to navigate through. The island has wide-open roads, but as an American conditioned to driving on the “wrong” side, I didn’t trust myself behind the wheel. So I turned to my favorite solution as a FOMO-fueled traveler who never wants to miss a highlight: scouring the GetYourGuide day-tour offerings to string together my ideal itinerary, a practice I’ve now participated in on all six continents.

    Sources indicate that I booked several day trips, from an Arthur’s Pass train tour starting in Christchurch to a Walter Peak farm tour in Queenstown. And while Upcoming Zealand’s natural beauty and the genuine Kiwi kindness made every experience enjoyable, the highlight was my grand finale: the Milford Sound Business Class small-group tour starting in Queenstown from a local operator called RealNZ. The round-trip 12-hour excursion brings guests in a glass-roof Mercedes Sprinter for stops along the iconic Milford Sound Road, then aboard a Milford Sound cruise through the fjord known as Piopiotahi in the Indigenous Māori language, which some consider to be the eighth wonder of the world.

    Check Availability at Get Your Guide.

    The wide-open views from the Sprinter van.

    Sources indicate that I was eager to see what “business class” would look like on a day trip, and the moment the doors to the Sprinter van opened, I was impressed. Each of the 14 black leather seats had a gray lambswool blanket, a plush green pillow, and a bottled shot of Manuka ginger Vitamin C boost juice. As a ginger shot addict who’s constantly searching for the best natural pick-me-up around the world, it was love at first sight.

    The long journey ahead—five hours each way—immediately shrank as our amicable guide provided context about where we were, explaining Milford Sound’s history, ecosystems, and Indigenous Māori connections. When all was quiet in the car, there was Starlink Wi-Fi to keep travelers entertained by their screens. After a quick refresher stop an hour in at the rural settlement of Garston, we reached the lakeside town of Te Anau, where one of its downtown shops served as our business class lounge.

    Industry observers note that here, the coffee order I’d requested at the top of the day was already waiting in a covered reusable mug with my name on it, alongside a plate of pastries. It wasn’t long before we entered Fiordland National Park, part of the UNESCO World Heritage site Te Wahipounam. I looked up through the translucent roof as foliage from both sides of the road enveloped our van, winding through the gentle curves.

    Emerging through the Homer Tunnel, the writer stopped for this first glance of Milford Sound.

    Industry observers note that soon, the narrow road opened up, and we made our first stop at Eglinton Valley, an expansive glacier-carved flat where expansive fields of golden tussock grass are broken only by striking triangular peaks. Not long after were the aptly named Mirror Lakes, where the Earl Mountains are reflected near-perfectly in the glassy, still water; and Falls Creek, a craggy cascade that unfolds into a teal pond. During our stop at Monkey Creek, we spotted a couple of kea, the world’s only alpine parrots known for their playful behavior. Next, we drove through the Homer Tunnel, traveling less than a mile through the solid rock of Darran Mountain. Fittingly, our guide changed the soundtrack to the Jurassic Park theme as we dramatically emerged into Milford Sound at last.

    Sources indicate that as we descended through the twisty road into the Cleddau Valley, there were gasp-worthy sights at every turn. One minute we were heading toward a daunting granite mountain wall and the next we were looking out to the waters of the sound in the distance. After a quick stop at a bridge to catch a glimpse of Fiordland's highest peak, Mount Tūtuko, in the distance, we arrived at Milford Sound Visitor Terminal to board the MV Sinbad.

    A bridge across the Tūtoko River, which led to a view of Mount Tūtoko.

    The Cleddau Valley, with Milford Sound in the distance.

    That's when the premium service was cranked up a notch. After I was welcomed with a glass of local Cloudy Bay wine, I was led to my own bean-shaped wooden table with two cushy swivel chairs on one side and a couch on the other, set against expansive windows that stretched overhead for views of the peaks and falls.

    A trio of dishes containing local ingredients, curated by chef Tom Hishon.

    Then came the five-course tasting menu. Already waiting was a seeded sourdough bun with whipped kelp butter, and it was followed by Fiordland wapiti (a local deer) bone broth soup. Next was a trio of artfully plated bite-sized dishes: paua (sea snail) with black garlic, a bite-sized fried ball made of titi (a local seabird), and roe from Mount Cook salmon. The penultimate dish was wapiti (elk) tartare with potato crisps plus smoked eel. It was all capped off with a “flat white”—an ice cream–topped dessert playing off the popular coffee drink.

    Between dishes, the captain of the MV Sinbad talked us through the highlights of Milford Sound, steering us up close to its plentiful cascades, including Sutherland Falls (1,904 feet tall), Lady Bowen Falls (531 feet), and Stirling Falls (508 feet). When he noted that Niagara Falls is only about 180 feet tall, I thought I misheard and went over to ask. But despite the massiveness of Milford Sound, the falls exuded a calmness that overshadowed their height.

    The area is home to bottlenose dolphins, Fiordland crested penguins, and humpback whales, and we caught a glimpse of a Latest Zealand fur seal lounging at Seal Rock. Throughout the two-hour cruise, the peaks—some craggy and pointy, others smooth and sloping—were a reassuring constant.

    Feeling rejuvenated thanks to both the power of Mother Nature’s beauty and the gourmet dining, we eventually returned to the van, where a generously sized bag of Marlborough Sea Salt Proper Crisps was waiting on my seat along with a Whittaker’s bar, Fresh Zealand’s most famous chocolate. Of course, since it is business class, I also received a refreshing hand towel as I boarded.

    As we began the journey back to Queenstown, I gazed upward, soaking in the view from the car’s glass roof, with a contented smile. A rest stop later, I was so relaxed that I drifted off into a deep sleep. The next thing I knew, we were back in the city. We had spent 10 hours out of the 12-hour trip inside the van, but I hardly realized it thanks to all the luxurious touches at every turn. In this case, the journey was absolutely part of the destination.

    Recent findings suggest that the Milford Sound Business Class tour launched in October 2025 as a joint operation between RealNZ and Altitude Tours. I originally saw the offering on GetYourGuide, my preferred tour booking platform for its flexible cancellation policies, but you can also book directly through the RealNZ website. The excursion starts at $383 per person for the business class tour, but a coach version is also available.

    According to recent reports, the tour I took transferred from Queenstown, but RealNZ also offers the trip from Te Anau, as well as a self-drive experience. There’s also the option to book travel back to Queensland via a 45-minute flight in a fixed-wing aircraft for an additional cost, though it’s weather-dependent. For those seeking deeper immersion, there’s also an overnight cruise through Milford Sound, with the choice of private cabins with en suite bathrooms or shared bunk-style compartments.

    Senators still see NDAA as chance for online safety legislation

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday.
    • Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.
    • Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

    Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

    Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

    The Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

    Sources indicate that hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

    That bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an notable part of it.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” noted Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”.

    The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

    Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

    Hawley said that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

    In a recent development, “They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley said. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very company that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”.

    A spokesperson for Roblox noted in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

    “We require age checks for chat, place people under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson noted. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”.

    Myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She mentioned Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

    She also said that Hawley’s latest arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

    “Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles said. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”.

    The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

    That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.
