    #145582. The Boeing 737 NG Fuel Saver That Was First Introduced As A Retrofit, But Became A Factory Option On Later Builds

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1509 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    The Boeing 737 NG Fuel Saver That Was First Introduced As A Retrofit, But Became A Factory Option On Later Builds

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1509 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age.
    • Sources indicate that the tall blended winglets on the 737 Next Generation became one of the narrowbody’s most recognizable features, but the design did not originate at Boeing.
    • It has been revealed that the retrofit version reached certification first, however, and the first airline to fly a winglet-equipped 737-800 did so with a retrofit installation.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age. He became involved in the flight simulator and VATSIM communities, which sparked his interest in aviation and eventually led him to earn his private pilot license. Outside of work, he continues to build flight hours, explore latest airports, and stay involved in the aviation community.

    Sources indicate that the tall blended winglets on the 737 Next Generation became one of the narrowbody’s most recognizable features, but the design did not originate at Boeing. Aviation Partners developed it for business jets, and the two companies formed a joint venture to bring it to Boeing aircraft. Boeing then unveiled it as a factory option for the 737-800 in early 2000.

    It has been revealed that the retrofit version reached certification first, however, and the first airline to fly a winglet-equipped 737-800 did so with a retrofit installation. Factory production approval followed weeks later, and the winglets went on to appear across most of the 737 NG family and on many older 737s already in service. The split scimitar that succeeded it took a different path and remained largely an aftermarket upgrade.

    According to recent reports, winglets were not a fresh idea when the 737 NG entered service. They reduce the drag created by the vortex at each wingtip, where high-pressure air from under the wing spills over to the low-pressure surface above. The 737 Technical Site credits NASA’s Richard Whitcomb with the winglet concept during the 1973 oil crisis, and Boeing began studying blended winglets in the mid-1980s. The version that eventually reached the 737 came from Seattle-based Aviation Partners, which developed blended winglets in the early 1990s and first fitted them to the Gulfstream II.

    In a recent development, the Boeing Business Jet opened the route to the 737. That aircraft combines a 737-700 fuselage with 737-800 wings, and a 737-800 flew with winglets in June 1998 as a testbed for the BBJ, with the first BBJ flight with winglets following on February 22, 1999. That same year, Aviation Partners Boeing (APB) was formed as a joint venture to offer Blended Winglets for Boeing aircraft, and the winglets became standard on the BBJ.

    Recent findings suggest that ownership of the design explains how one part could serve as both a factory option and a retrofit. Boeing stated in 2000 that Aviation Partners Boeing owns the design, which allowed the joint venture to supply winglets for the production line and to sell them directly to airlines for aircraft already flying. The BBJ installation was approved through that aftermarket route. APB received the Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) for 737-BBJ Blended Winglets on September 5, 2000, the type of FAA approval used for modifications to an existing aircraft design.

    It has been revealed that boeing declared the winglet for airline customers on February 18, 2000. It was available initially as an option on the 162-passenger 737-800, with availability on the 737-700C and 737-900 planned and the 737-600 and 737-700 under review. At that point, Aviation Partners Boeing was still developing a version for aircraft already in service. To prepare for it, Boeing stated all subsequent 737-800s would be equipped with structurally enhanced wings, which made later retrofits easier.

    Industry observers note that the retrofit reached approval first. The FAA granted the retrofit STC on March 23, 2001, and Germany’s LBA followed on May 4, 2001, while Boeing’s production approval came on May 9, 2001. Hapag-Lloyd had already flown the first 737-800 with blended winglets on a test flight in Seattle on September 26, 2000, and it became the first airline to operate a 737-800 with retrofit Blended Winglets. Air Berlin was the first to fly a 737-800 with factory-installed Blended Winglets later in 2001.

    Factory deliveries spread across the family rapidly after that. Production deliveries began in May 2001 for the -700, -800, -900, and BBJ, and Kenya Airways received the first 737-700 with blended winglets in September 2001. According to the 737 Technical Site, the winglet eventually became a production option for all NG models except the -600.

    Boeing introduces blended winglets as a factory option for the 737-800.

    Hapag-Lloyd 737-800 makes a winglet test flight in Seattle.

    FAA approves the 737-800 retrofit.

    Boeing receives production approval.

    Hapag-Lloyd enters service with retrofit winglets, and factory deliveries begin.

    FAA approves the 737-700 retrofit.

    Kenya Airways receives the first winglet-equipped 737-700.

    Boeing’s case for the winglet came down to three options for an airline. At its 2000 launch, the organization mentioned a winglet-equipped 737-800 could burn 3 % to 5 % less fuel, fly farther, or carry up to 6,000 pounds more payload, about 2,720 kg. Each winglet weighs about 120 pounds, or 54 kg, and is made of high-tech carbon graphite, an advanced aluminum alloy, and titanium. Boeing described each unit as eight feet (2.4 meters) long, and the 737 Technical Site indicates the pair adds about 5 feet of span, from 112 feet, 7 inches to 117 feet, 2 inches, or about 34.3 to 35.7 meters.

    The effects extend beyond cruise. The 737 Technical Site puts the drag reduction in the 5–7% range and says the winglets allow up to a 3% thrust derate on takeoff. It also credits them with a 6.5% reduction in noise footprint and a 5% reduction in NOx. Claimed fuel savings rose over time as airlines gathered operating data. The site lists figures of up to 4% in 2002, up to 5% in 2004, and up to 6% cruise fuel mileage in a later article, with the largest gains on longer sectors where the aircraft spends more time at cruise.

    The upgrade was expensive, but airlines could earn it back through fuel savings. The 737 Technical Site gives a price of about $725,000 per set, with installation adding $25,000–80,000. That cost helps explain why operators flying shorter, lower-utilization routes were slower to adopt the winglets than carriers with high-utilization fleets.

    Approvals for in-service aircraft followed the 737-800 within months and kept coming for years. The STC for 737-700 Blended Winglets came on August 27, 2001, and the 737-900 STC followed on October 10, 2007. The retrofit also reached the previous generation. APB received the STC for 737-300 Blended Winglets on May 29, 2003, and the 737-500 approval followed on May 24, 2007, so airlines could fit 737 Classics that Boeing never offered winglets on from the factory. Air Plus Comet became the first operator of a 737-300 with winglets in July 2003.

    Industry observers note that large North American operators drove the early retrofit orders. WestJet ordered up to 94 shipsets of 737-NG Blended Winglets on June 2, 2003, and 10 days later, Southwest ordered 169 shipsets of 737-700 retrofit Blended Winglets. Southwest extended the program to its older aircraft with an order for up to 90 shipsets of 737-300 Blended Winglets on June 20, 2006. On July 24, 2012, it placed the largest single order in APB history, for 268 additional 737-700/-800 Blended Winglet systems.

    In a recent development, A retrofit involved more than bolting a winglet onto the wingtip. The 737 Technical Site notes that the aircraft required a strengthened wing centre section and internal wing structure, along with systems changes to accommodate the winglet. Installation volume grew rapidly. Aviation Partners Boeing reached its 500th shipset on a Continental 737-800 on October 16, 2004, and its 2,000th on a Continental 737-900 on December 6, 2007, by which time the program had also spread to the 757.

    Sources indicate that the next step for the 737 NG was rolled out in late 2012. APB’s board approved the launch of the 737-800 Split Scimitar program on December 20, 2012, and United followed with the launch order for 53 737-800 Split Scimitar systems on January 14, 2013. The first test flight took place on July 16, 2013, from Paine Field, and the FAA granted approval on February 6, 2014. The first revenue flight came on February 18, 2014, from Houston George Bush Intercontinental (IAH) to Los Angeles (LAX).

    Industry observers note that the modification replaces the winglet’s tip with a sharply curved cap and adds a downward-pointing ventral strake below it. The full package also includes a trailing-edge wedge, strengthened stringers, and ballast, adding 294 pounds (133 kg) per aircraft. Aviation Partners notes it delivers at least 2% drag reduction and a corresponding range increase on longer flights, while the 737 Technical Site puts fuel savings at 1.6% on 1,000 nautical miles (1,852 km) sectors, rising to 2.2% on 3,000 nautical miles (5,556 km). Southwest became a major customer, ordering 85 firm and 600 optional 737-NG Split Scimitar systems on December 27, 2013.

    Unlike its predecessor, the split scimitar stayed mainly a retrofit. Delta’s final 737-900ERs were delivered with them, and they are standard on all newly introduced Boeing Business Jets, but most installations went onto aircraft already flying. Boeing took a different approach for the 737 MAX. It announced the Advanced Technology winglet on May 2, 2012, a split-tip design that adds up to 1.5% fuel-burn improvement over current winglets.

    American’s Longtime Chief Operating Officer to Retire

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (285 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Airlinegeeks

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • American Airlines is making another change to its senior leadership team, with Chief Operating Officer David Seymour set to retire at the end of the year.
    • Industry observers note that seymour will step down on Dec.
    • Industry observers note that seymour has served as American’s chief operating officer since 2020.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Airlines is making another change to its senior leadership team, with Chief Operating Officer David Seymour set to retire at the end of the year.

    Industry observers note that seymour will step down on Dec. 31 and remain with the Fort Worth, Texas-based carrier in an advisory capacity through the first quarter of 2027, CEO Robert Isom declared Friday.

    Industry observers note that seymour has served as American’s chief operating officer since 2020. He joined the airline in 1999 and held various leadership positions overseeing technical operations, crew scheduling, and flight operations.

    “He’s the guy you want in the room when the stakes are high,” Isom wrote in a letter to employees.

    In a recent development, jonCarlo “JC” Gulbranson, American’s current senior vice president of operations, will succeed Seymour on Jan. 1. He will report directly to Isom and assume oversight of the carrier’s technical operations, safety, and regulatory compliance teams.

    Gulbranson began his airline career at Northwest Airlines in 2000 before joining US Airways in 2008. He helped oversee the integration of flight operations systems following the merger with American.

    American will also move its corporate security team under its government affairs division. A fresh reporting structure for the airline’s regional operations will be confirmed in December.

    “For nearly three decades, jet fuel hasn’t just been in my veins. It’s been part of my DNA. To this day, I wake up excited to get to work — which is just about all you can ask for in a job,” Seymour wrote in a LinkedIn post.

    The changes follow a broader management reshuffle confirmed in August as the carrier works to narrow its profitability gap with competitors Delta and United.

    #145580. The Right Tote Bag Is the Ultimate Travel Companion—These Are Our Editors’ Favorites

    📅 06 Apr 2020 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2069 w)

    The Right Tote Bag Is the Ultimate Travel Companion—These Are Our Editors’ Favorites

    📅 06 Apr 2020 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2069 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you’re looking for a bag so versatile it can be your go-to personal item one day and your grocery shopping companion the next, the renowned tote bag is the only option.
    • Though the design of a tote bag is inherently simple, our favorite brands have curated precise variations to suit every kind of traveler.
    • Sources indicate that coach has been a favorite brand of mine ever since I got my first little black bag as a teenager.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you’re looking for a bag so versatile it can be your go-to personal item one day and your grocery shopping companion the next, the renowned tote bag is the only option. From early morning flights to daily office commutes, or even a packed Saturday afternoon at the farmers market, our editors are always relying on their favorite tote. The best tote bags hold everything from our laptops, headphones, and water bottles to sleep masks and our most-used beauty products. Whether you reach for a structured leather version to pack your essential items in or an oversized, canvas carryall for a day at the park, the functions of the right tote are infinite.

    Though the design of a tote bag is inherently simple, our favorite brands have curated precise variations to suit every kind of traveler. My favorite tote has been my everyday work bag for years, but it has also accompanied me on countless flights, weekend getaways, and last-minute happy hours. A reliable tote bag really can do it all. Keep reading to discover 15 of our editors' favorite tote bags and why we can’t live without them.

    Sources indicate that coach has been a favorite brand of mine ever since I got my first little black bag as a teenager. Though I still cherish that tiny bag, my most used Coach item is my leather tote. For years, the Nina Tote bag has been my reliable sidekick. I’ve had it for so long that Coach no longer produces it. On the bright side, the Maggie Tote bag is almost identical to mine and is just as practical. I have put my bag through anything and everything over the years, and there is very little wear and tear. The leather is structured and durable, yet flexible enough to fit everything I need without toppling over. With plenty of interior pockets, my necessities all have a place, so I never have to go digging through the bottom of my bag to find the right lip gloss. Not only do I love traveling with this tote, but it’s also my everyday work bag and my go-to for almost every kind of activity.

    I've never really had a work bag that I truly loved until I tried this one from Cuyana. What I appreciate about the System Tote are the additional organizational accessories that you can purchase to add a bit more structure to the interior. Aside from lugging it to and from the office each day, I use this tote as a personal item on the plane and brought it with me on a road trip to Acadia National Park, and have found it to be the ultimate travel companion. The built-in interior pocket is perfect for storing essentials you need to reach easily, like your passport, earbuds, or some petty cash, and since the bag can be snapped closed, you don't have to worry about anything flying out. —Jamie Spain, travel bookings editor.

    This bag is all about the pockets. No tote has ever kept me quite as organized as this one from MZ Wallace, a brand known for its signature quilted bags. It offers six interior pockets, five exterior pockets, and a detachable pouch, offering me a dedicated space for all of my essentials plus a whole lot more. I’m always impressed at how much this thing fits; an umbrella, my 13-inch laptop, a full change of clothes, and my lunch. The Medium Metro tote features ultra-soft shoulder straps, making it a go-to for commutes to the office. My favorite thing about this bag is how lightweight it feels even when full—it never digs into my shoulders or hurts my arms. More features that make this roomy tote a smart choice for travelers: a luggage sleeve, protective feet, and a detachable and adjustable crossbody strap. —Meaghan Kenny, commerce editor.

    Sources indicate that monos’s Metro Tote has been with me longer than most Fresh Yorkers are in relationships. I’ve had this faux-leather cutie for nearly five years now, and it’s traveled with me through new jobs, new apartments, and plenty of new adventures. I actually bring it to work with me every day—the laptop sleeve and spacious interior keep me organized on my way to and from the office. —Hannah Chubb, senior commerce editor.

    According to recent reports, I've received so many compliments on this gorgeous structured bag from Cuyana—it's been a great work bag, with plenty of space for my laptop, planner, Kindle, chargers, and other day-to-day essentials. I wasn't sure how well it would function as a personal item as there's not a zipper to fully close the bag, but on a flight to Aruba, I made use of the leather ties to keep items contained, and found it well-sized to slip under the seat in front of me, even with my toiletry bag and a sweatshirt stuffed inside. I'm also a substantial fan of the snap-to-close key leash, and the interior slips pockets and zipper pocket. —Madison Flager, commerce director.

    The bag is perfect in the way a red apple sitting on a teacher’s desk is perfect. It’s classic, without ornament, the kind of thing that expresses its utility in its design. It’s both ubiquitous and aspirational, stirring up images of a dreamy East Coast: a white-sand, Nantucket beach; a shabby, wood-planked boathouse on the coast of Maine; a Gothic-inspired Ivy League campus. I've used it as a carry-on item, a beach tote, and as a weekender. Simply having it out on display in your home has the power to imbue your space with a charming, outdoorsy vibe. —Jessica Sulima, commerce writer.

    Baggu’s Nylon shoulder bag is more durable than its canvas tote bags but equally as stylish. It’s slightly slouchy, slightly structured, and comes in the signature Baggu colors and patterns. The adjustable quilted shoulder strap allows for a crossbody fit, a must-have for me when I’m commuting into the office or walking longer distances (nobody needs their laptop sliding off their shoulder onto the sidewalk). The zip closure and interior pockets are handy for organizing miscellaneous goodies and preventing spillage. Plus, the lightweight material can easily be flattened to fit into my suitcase. I find myself continuously reaching for this multipurpose tote on my way to the gym, office, farmers market, and airport. —Hannah Towey, associate editor.

    Just when I think I’ve run out of room, I haven’t. The expandable bottom of this Calpak laptop tote adds an extra four inches, allowing me to add last-minute essentials or souvenirs mid-trip. Like all products in the brand’s Luka collection, it’s made of a lightweight, ultra-soft, puffy exterior that makes carrying its handle easy. The material is also easy to clean—simply wipe away dirt or spills without a worry. Inside, there’s a padded 15" laptop sleeve, multiple side pockets, and a zippered section to keep smaller items organized. Another feature I love: There’s a zippered pocket on the outside that keeps my phone or passport secure, while still being easy to access. It’s a great tote for commuters and thanks to its luggage trolley sleeve, an ideal carry-on bag for travelers. —M.K.

    According to recent reports, as a shopping writer who is constantly running between the office, press previews, catch ups with friends and, of course, the airport, I need a bag with space for all the day’s exploits and then some. July’s Juliette Soft Work Tote is my perfect do-it-all companion. It’s beautiful—I’ve received multiple compliments on this bag as I’ve been whizzing around with it, and the divided interior is really clever. There’s a 14" laptop sleeve to keep tech protected—all the more important when you’re headed on a flight— and there’s also a dedicated water bottle holder too. It has a wide bottom so your lunchbox can go inside flat, plus a key leash to stop the rummage for your house keys. Brushed gold hardware and a buttery-soft faux leather exterior mean it looks effortlessly chic at after-work drinks, and when I'm off to the airport, the removable trolley sleeve slides over my suitcase handle so I can breeze through the terminal. It is my favorite desk-to-departure tote bag. —Charley Ward, commerce writer, Condé Nast Traveller UK.

    In a recent development, my Strathberry Kite is my most-used travel accessory. Not only do I use it for day-to-day tasks, it comes with me on almost every trip (the exception being adventure travel), and most recently carried me through trips to Lisbon and Istanbul, where I spent weekends catching up with friends and sightseeing. It's an ideal size for a laptop, should you wish to take it, but fits in plenty of other necessary items, too (like flip-flops or ballet flats after hours of strolling through cobbled streets). I love the walnut color and the soft, supple leather. I'm sure this will be a favorite of mine for years to come. —Abigail Malbon, global audience development manager.

    When I first saw Parker Thatch offers its Jack Tote bag in this unique zebra and burgundy color combo, I knew it had to be mine. I never travel without animal print, and there was something about this colorway that felt perfectly understated yet maximalist. I found it online about a year ago, and it sold like hot cakes—and has been (devastatingly) sold out since. I received it as a sweet gift from my partner a few months ago, who had pre-ordered it to arrive right when it was back in stock. I've been using it as my go-to work bag ever since. It has an incredible amount of space and strength to carry all of my everyday essentials and then some—from my laptop and a book to makeup and toiletries. Because of its exterior fabric as hair-on cowhide, she just needs to be shielded from the rain a bit more than your average bag. If the design is calling your name on this bad boy, it’s well worth the splurge. —Jessica Chapel, commerce writer.

    I love anything Longchamp, and this gorgeous beach tote from the brand is my cherry on top of any vacation outfit. It’s large enough to hold a full day’s worth of goodies (sunscreen! sweatshirt! beach read!), but fits on the shoulder with ease. Plus, the toggle on the front keeps things contained in the most Longchamp-esque way. —H.C.

    After passing the gauntlet of a last-minute trip to the British Virgin Islands, I always keep the Foldie Travel Bag on me, whether it’s riding in my backpack during my daily commute or stuffed into my suitcase on longer hauls. The front pocket easily held my thick reading list and two Moleskine classic notebooks; the full 40 liters of space in the main compartment (with the expansion unzipped) fit a week’s worth of clothes, chargers for four different devices, and another bag filled with toiletry bottles, plus room to spare for souvenirs. Another perk: the two inner pockets and wet pocket proved useful in sorting out the bag’s increasingly chaotic contents. The luggage sleeve was a relieving bonus that allowed me to transfer the hefty weight of my zealous packing to my suitcase. —Kat Chen, editorial assistant, destinations.

    It has been revealed that I absolutely love this tote. Whether I’m wearing it to the office or while traveling, it fits everything I need. Plus, it comes with a separate removable pouch that I use even when I’m not wearing the bag. This slouchy bag is super durable and matches any outfit. —Pooja Nayyar, associate social media manager.

    Sources indicate that sentimentality may cloud my vision, for the tote in my possession belongs to my late grandmother. And when I tell you I was complimented frequently for it while in Italy, I mean I felt I needed to use the bag to beat back admirers waxing: “Wow, is Vera Bradley back?”; “Is it reversible?!”; “The textiles are so beautiful.” I often caught myself fantasizing about dumping it upside down to perform a “What’s in my bag” for nobody in particular—so capacious is the tote that I was needlessly carrying multiple novels within and rarely remembered to leave my toiletry kit on the hotel bathroom counter where it belonged. Handy pockets ringing the interior are just icing, and would have kept my passport safely inside had I ever been moved to act on the aforementioned dumping. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor.

    #145578. 11 Warm-Weather Destinations to Flock to This Winter

    📅 26 Sep 2025 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2657 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    11 Warm-Weather Destinations to Flock to This Winter

    📅 26 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2657 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that arguably the best way to overcome winter is to pretend like it’s not happening—i.e., jetting off to a warm-weather destination, where seasons are not taken very seriously and an outdoor adventure is always on the table.
    • According to recent reports, whether you’re interested in hiking to the wild and wondrous waterfalls of Puerto Rico’s El Yunque National Rainforest, snorkeling through the kaleidoscopic waters of Belize’s barrier reef, or simply want to kick back and relax with a dip in Costa Rica’s hot springs, these sunny locations are bound to cure those cold-weather blues.
    • When to go: JanuaryAverage winter temperature: 80–85 degrees.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that arguably the best way to overcome winter is to pretend like it’s not happening—i.e., jetting off to a warm-weather destination, where seasons are not taken very seriously and an outdoor adventure is always on the table. The best winter vacation destinations offer comfortable temperatures, off-peak advantages, and festive happenings. On this list, you’ll find some of the usual suspects, from Punta Cana to the US Virgin Islands, as well as locales you might not have considered (far too often, travelers forget vibrant Marrakech is a shorter-haul Mediterranean option).

    According to recent reports, whether you’re interested in hiking to the wild and wondrous waterfalls of Puerto Rico’s El Yunque National Rainforest, snorkeling through the kaleidoscopic waters of Belize’s barrier reef, or simply want to kick back and relax with a dip in Costa Rica’s hot springs, these sunny locations are bound to cure those cold-weather blues. So, trade your snow boots for flip-flops and get to plotting your next escape.

    When to go: JanuaryAverage winter temperature: 80–85 degrees.

    According to recent reports, if you’ve been looking for an excuse to finally book that trip to Hawaii, shoot for after the holiday rush, when flights get significantly cheaper. January might be the start of rainy season in Maui, but the showers are often short and localized; for the most part, you’ll enjoy sunshiny days with temperatures that hover in the low-80s. Humpback whales make their way from Alaska around this time, and you can spot the giant beauties from Papawai Point on Honoapiilani Highway, an overlook facing the ʻAuʻau Channel. If you’re not afraid of massive waves, heavy north swells at this time of year make for excellent surfing, especially at Ho‘okipa Beach Park. The Road to Hana, a scenic and beautiful drive at any time of year, becomes especially lush in the winter after the rain has fallen, and you’ll likely avoid the crowds too. Along the way, hit up sites like the Twin Falls or the black sand beach at Waianapanapa State Park.

    Where to stay: A Condé Nast Traveler Triple Crown winner, Hāna-Maui Resort, a luxurious off-grid escape, is the pot of gold at the end of the Road to Hana, while Hotel Wailea offers an adults-only vibe on the southwestern coast. Though much humbler, Jimi Hendrix’s former gingerbread-style home, now available for rent on Airbnb, is also a fair contender for your home away from home, surrounded by all kinds of fruit trees and perfectly positioned for daily rainbows.

    When to go: December–JanuaryAverage winter temperature: 65 degrees.

    Recent findings suggest that while you won’t be breaking a sweat in San Diego come December, it’s an excellent place to escape to around the holidays for festive fun in mild, mid-60-degree temperatures. The Parade of Lights is a classic seasonal event, when over 100 private boats get decked out in twinkling lights and sail around San Diego Bay (watch from spots like Shelter Island or Seaport Village on select nights in December). Between November and January, you can also enjoy ice skating without the chill at the Hotel del Coronado, where you’ll glide alongside the Pacific. They say San Diego sunsets are best in the winter, when the sun cuts a path closer to the horizon and there’s not as much coastal marine fog—one of the best places to catch one is Sunset Cliffs Natural Park on the Point Loma peninsula.

    Industry observers note that where to stay: La Valencia, otherwise known as the “Pink Lady” of La Jolla, is one of San Diego’s most iconic stays, and you might hear a seal or two barking in the distance. For unparalleled mountain views, consider this glass house overlooking Sweetwater Regional Park.

    When to go: December–MarchAverage winter temperature: 70–85 degrees.

    Sources indicate that for a Caribbean escape with outdoor adventure, cultural festivals, and farm-to-table splendor, head to Puerto Rico. From December to March, you can take advantage of the dry season on the island, which means your days won’t be interrupted by sudden showers. Holiday festivities continue well beyond Christmas, from Three Kings Day on January 6—the oldest of these celebrations takes place in Juana Díaz, with a reenactment of the Magi on horseback—to the San Sebastian Street Festival, when the namesake street in Old San Juan is filled with art vendors, live music, and plenty of mofongo (January 21–24 this year). Winter is also a great time to explore El Yunque National Forest when it’s not shrouded in unbearable humidity—hike to La Coca Waterfall, take in the green canopy from Yokahú Tower, and keep an ear out for singing coquí frogs.

    Sources indicate that where to stay: For luxe accommodations just a 25-minute drive from El Yunque, look no further than Four Seasons Resort and Residences Puerto Rico, which coordinates guided treks with a strong emphasis on Indigenous history. Condado Ocean Club offers direct access to the beach, while this lakefront retreat near Cueva Ventana and Arecibo Observatory is ideal for couples seeking verdant views.

    When to go: December–MarchAverage winter temperature: 85 degrees.

    Sources indicate that another destination where US travelers can leave their passports at home, the US Virgin Islands are a quintessential Caribbean paradise. December through March is peak season, and there are plenty of reasons why—no rain, calm seas, and temperatures that hover between 77 and 85 degrees, to name a few. St. Croix, the largest of the USVI’s three main islands, is defined by the white sands of Rainbow Beach, as well as its Danish ancestry, which you can explore at colonial-era sites like Fort Frederik and Fort Christiansvaern. St. John is filled with all kinds of natural wonders; take the Underwater Snorkel Trail at Trunk Bay to peer at parrotfish, or set off on the three-mile Reef Bay Trail to hike among pre-Columbian petroglyphs painted by Taíno Indians. St. Thomas is a bustling port with cosmopolitan charm, and you’d be well advised to sample a few conch fritters at Gladys' Café. Whichever island you choose, clear skies and turquoise waters await.

    Sources indicate that where to stay: One of Traveler’s favorite private island resorts (and the only one in the US Virgin Islands), Lovango Resort and Beach Club is located across St. John’s Caneel Bay and offers all kinds of eco-chic accommodations, from wooden treehouses to explorer-style tents. The Westin St. Thomas is set right in front of the harbor, with a stellar spa worth traveling for. For something a bit more intimate, this light-filled, two-bedroom cottage is just a five-minute walk away from Cruz Beach.

    When to go: December–FebruaryAverage winter temperature: 65 degrees.

    It has been revealed that while temperatures do drop in Marrakech during the winter—the peaks of the Atlas Mountains will be blanketed in snow—you’ll see far more sun than in certain parts of the US; plus, it’s all the more reason to enjoy a steamy hammam. Winter is a great time to explore the city's popular sites with thinner crowds: comb through the medina’s bustling souks for fragrant spices and a pair of babouche slippers, take in the cobalt blue buildings at the Jardin Majorelle, or learn about one of France’s most legendary fashion designers at the Yves Saint Laurent Museum. Keep an eye out for the dates of the Marrakech International Film Festival, which takes place between the months of November and December—this year it falls from November 20 to 28, and features 76 films from 39 countries.

    Where to stay: Traveler contributor Jordan Lippe-McGraw is a significant fan of this family-friendly villa, with a heated pool, hammam, and cinema room. A Triple Crown winner, La Mamounia is the city’s grand dame. As global features director Erin Florio puts it, “Every inch of this palatial property has been hyper-considered to make the guest feel as though they have arrived in some regal estate of an Arabian kingdom.” At the Royal Mansour, all riads come with 24/7 access to a private butler.

    When to go: December–AprilAverage winter temperature: 80–90 degrees.

    The Arenal Volcano looms over Costa Rica’s La Fortuna region, heating its natural springs, and there’s a greater chance you’ll see it without cloud cover in the winter. For travelers seeking a combo of adventure and relaxation, La Fortuna (about a three-hour drive from San José) is well-suited for both. Hike through cooled lava fields at Arenal Volcano National Park or swim around La Fortuna Waterfall, then take advantage of nature’s healing powers at Tabacón Thermal Resort and Spa. For a truly memorable experience, book a tour with Arenal Horse Tours and ride your steed straight into the Arenal River for a refreshing dip.

    Where to stay: While Tabacón is perhaps the most iconic resort in the area, The Springs Resort & Spa is another great option, boasting two dozen hot springs, pools, and waterfalls spread across the 65-acre property. If you’re looking for something more intimate, this forest cabin features a private spring-fed pool, rain shower, and marked hiking trails—a one-of-a-kind off-grid retreat.

    When to go: December–AprilAverage winter temperature: 80–85 degrees.

    Sources indicate that though small, this Central American country offers a diversity of experiences, whether you want to take it slow in a charming fishing village or ascend upcoming heights in the jungle. Perhaps the most popular destination on Belize’s tourism map, Ambergris Caye is a departure point for the country’s barrier reef—though just south of Ambergris Caye, Caye Caulker provides a nice alternative. While on the car-free island, book a tour with Ragga Sail Adventures for a half-day snorkel through Hol Chan Marine Reserve, the oldest marine reserve in the country. Further south in Punta Gorda, you’ll find rugged adventures and a strong sense of Mayan culture. Here, you’ll have access to several offshore cayes (Belize has hundreds of these small islands, brimming with marine life), from Snake Cayes to Sapodilla Cayes Marine Reserve; if you prefer jungle, take a boat tour through the Monkey River, or hike to the waterfall at Rio Blanco National Park. And be sure to explore the surrounding Toledo District for Mayan ruins, like the Lubaantun, which dates back to 700–900 AD and is also an excellent site for birdwatching.

    Sources indicate that where to stay: Nestled within the Belizean rainforest, Copal Tree Lodge’s jungle suites will make you feel as though you’re suspended among the trees. Wake up to the sounds of monkeys every morning, then take a farm tour around the surrounding property, where you’ll discover how cacao, vanilla, and sugar cane grow. Over in San Pedro, Alaia Belize is your luxury option, just 600 yards away from the barrier reef, while this tiny home will make you feel as though you’re vacationing in a fairy tale.

    When to go: December–AprilAverage winter temperature: 80 degrees.

    December through April is peak vacation time in Punta Cana, when the rainy season has subsided and there’s not a cloud in the sky. With average highs in the 80s and average lows in the 70s, you’re likely to experience perfect weather during your stay. Come February, you’ve got a good chance of spotting some humpback whales if you cast your eyes off the coast of the Península de Samaná, where they typically pass through until April. The country also celebrates Independence Day in February—on the 27th, to be exact. Visit around that time, and you’re bound to run into a Carnaval parade or bachata dance circle. With the Cordillera Oriental mountain range looming in the background and a selection of cenotes around town—from Hoyo Azul to Hoyo Claro—mountain buggy excursions and diving adventures await even in the winter.

    Where to stay: The W Punta Cana redefines the all-inclusive resort as we know it with top-tier dining and some of the largest rooms in the country. Hyatt Vivid Punta Cana, which just opened its doors in August 2026, is another upscale all-inclusive in the area, boasting swim-out suites and a chic speakeasy. If you’ve got kids in tow but still want to experience the height of luxury, Eden Roc Cap Cana is a consistent Readers' Choice Awards winner. For a villa the whole family will enjoy, this eight-bedroom Airbnb in Tortuga Bay comes with a private pool.

    When to go: December–AprilAverage winter temperature: 70 degrees.

    In a recent development, another prime location for whale watching, Baja California’s southern tip sees the migration of humpback and gray whales between the months of December and April (you might even elect to swim with whale sharks, too, which roam around the nearby Bay of La Paz around this time). You’ll have just missed the rainy season in November, making way for sunny, 70-degree beach days and not-too-chilly evenings. The creative town of Todos Santos boasts a number of art galleries to pop into, like Galeria de Todos Santos and La Sonrisa de la Muerte, while the Sierra de la Laguna mountains are home to stunning trails and swimming holes. If you’re a surfer, Playa Los Cerritos and Playa San Pedro offer some of Mexico’s best waves.

    Industry observers note that where to stay: Todos Santos is home to a number of cutting-edge boutique hotels. Hotel San Cristobal, with its vibrant interiors and delectably fresh seafood, perfectly embodies the bohemian vibes of this tiny surf town. Paradero Todos Santos, located on a five-and-a-half-acre farm, is designed around outdoor adventure: Pick the “Unbound” option, and surfing, hiking, and biking experiences will all be included in the nightly fare. If you prefer to go the rental route, this little bungalow is set among farmland in Pescadero, with its own private rooftop.

    When to go: December–FebruaryAverage winter temperature: 75 degrees.

    Industry observers note that miami is a good idea any time of year, but December through February is considered the dry season, promising temperatures in the mid-70s. Two important events pop up this time of year: Art Basel Miami, in December (4–6, this year), and the South Beach Wine & Food Festival, in February (running the 25–28 in 2027). But there’s always something to do in the Magic City, whether that’s taking a peek into the Pérez Art Museum, spending money in the Design District, or having a stroll through the Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden.

    Where to stay: To embrace the happy-go-lucky spirit of the locals, check in to the Goodtime Hotel and sip on a Purple Reign cocktail (co-owner Pharrell’s favorite drink) at the rooftop pool club. If you’d like to tap into the city’s Art Deco architectural history, stay at The Moore, where you’ll be close to Wynwood and Downtown Miami. This dreamy loft in Collins Park, just a short walk to the beach, is a good bet too.

    When to go: December–FebruaryAverage winter temperature: 85 degrees.

    Depending on where you’re coming from, Cape Town might be a little out of the way. But the US's winter is their summer, and with that comes sunny days and a dry, Mediterranean-like climate. Around mid-January, tourists start to flee and kids return to school, making popular attractions more accessible. Take a cable car (or hike, if you’re feeling bold) up to the famous Table Mountain, or drive to Boulders Beach, which boasts one of the last colonies of African penguins in the world. There are plenty of opportunities to engage with some art, as well, from the contemporary galleries at Zeitz MOCAA to the rainbow houses of the Bo-Kaap Museum. And if you’re feeling especially adventurous, you can treat Cape Town as a jumping-off point for the famed Garden Route road trip.

    Where to stay: For views of both Table Mountain and the V&A Waterfront, stay at the Silo Hotel, housed in a former grain silo and famous for its maximalist interior design. For something a little more off-the-beaten-path, Ellerman House is an Edwardian mansion turned boutique hotel situated in the exclusive Bantry Bay area. And if it's privacy you're after, this three-bedroom bungalow in St. James features a private hot tub and covered deck with gorgeous sea views.

    #145576. Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1000 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1000 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday.
    • Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s newly introduced ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.
    • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s newly introduced ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

    Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

    The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., mentioned, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

    Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five new air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

    They justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

    But it swiftly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

    Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

    Recent findings suggest that “I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, remarked Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”.

    Still, Cruz remarked the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization strategy so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

    Senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz remarked that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”.

    Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., mentioned after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

    Industry observers note that for his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

    “I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott said, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not big on government running things.”.

    Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

    “This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he said. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”.

    He called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy said, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

    Industry observers note that “I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy mentioned. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”.

    Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he remarked that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

    A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create issues in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

    The telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

    Bedford said Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

    Bedford mentioned he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

    David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

    Industry News: Qatar Airways Adds 1st Ever Airbus A321LR Routes: See Map Now

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (685 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Qatar Airways has not received its first Airbus A321LR yet.
    • Each week, airlines from around the world submit schedule changes to OAG and Cirium Diio.
    • Recent findings suggest that while subject to the exact date on which the initial airframe arrives in Doha and entry into service procedures, the first passenger-carrying A321LR service is due to take place on January 4, 2027.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Qatar Airways has not received its first Airbus A321LR yet. The latest information is that it'll be delivered at the end of 2026, which is just a few weeks away. Given this, the oneworld member has disclosed its first two routes on the fresh variant.

    Each week, airlines from around the world submit schedule changes to OAG and Cirium Diio. In the latest enhancement, Qatar Airways disclosed that its first two A321LR routes are due to be from Doha to both Vienna and Zurich, but things could change.

    Recent findings suggest that while subject to the exact date on which the initial airframe arrives in Doha and entry into service procedures, the first passenger-carrying A321LR service is due to take place on January 4, 2027. Running daily, the Gulf giant initially intends to fly the 160-seat variant to Vienna.

    Industry observers note that on January 4, the A321LR will be on QR185 from Doha and QR186 back home. Thereafter, it is entirely scheduled on QR189 to Austria and QR190 back, as outlined below. It'll replace the 132-seat and far less fuel-efficient A320ceo on those specific flight numbers on the route, which covers 2,144 nautical miles (3,971 km).

    Flight (From January 5 Onwards).

    Daily Schedule In January; Local Times.

    Recent findings suggest that then there's Zurich. The fresh variant in the airline's fleet is due to debut in Switzerland on January 16, with a daily service. As such, the airline anticipates at least two aircraft deliveries by then. Replacing the 283-seat A350-900, it'll help the airline to right-size capacity with demand. This approach should improve fare, yield, and load factor performance. It'll be the first time Qatar Airways has flown a narrowbody to Zurich since 2013.

    Flight (From January 16 Onwards).

    Daily Schedule In January; Local Times.

    Industry observers note that after a long-drawn-out battle, Qatar Airways confirmed its order for 50 A321neos — including ten A321LRs — in 2019. The LR will be the carrier's first narrowbody equipment with the latest cabins and lie-flat beds (a so-called mini-QSuite). Etihad Airways' A321LRs, which have two seats in first class and 14 in business, entered service in August 2025.

    According to recent reports, all ten of Qatar Airways' examples will have 160 seats. There will be 16 seats in business (using the STELIA Aerospace OPERA platform, with a privacy door in a reverse herringbone layout) and 144 in economy. 10% of the aircraft will be premium, which is the same proportion as Etihad on its 160-seaters.

    Looking at the share of premium seats among different operators is a bit unfair as it is not a like-for-like comparison. Nonetheless, if premium economy is stripped out, Qatar Airways' 10% is similar to other full-service operators, such as Gulf Air (just under 10%), Aer Lingus (just under 9%) and TAP Air Portugal (just over 9%). It is a notable increase on ITA Airways (a bit over 7%), which uses the same platform as the Gulf giant.

    Sources indicate that let's narrow the focus to January to June 2027. In this period, many Gulf airlines will fly narrowbody equipment to Europe. There have been intriguing developments recently. For example, Saudia has applied for slots at Edinburgh, and seemingly intends to use the 110-seat A320ceo. Elsewhere, SalamAir just began Muscat-Baghdad-Copenhagen service on the A320neo, replacing Oman Air's Boeing 737 MAX 8s. Etihad started flying to Luxembourg last month.

    From Doha To These European Destinations (January-June 2027)*.

    Ankara, Antalya, Athens, Belgrade, Bodrum, Bucharest, Budapest, Istanbul Airport, Istanbul Sabiha Gökçen, Larnaca, Malta, Mykonos, Sarajevo, Trabzon, Vienna, Zagreb.

    * See comments below about Turkey.

    In the first half of 2027, Qatar Airways intends a total of 1,587 departures on narrowbody equipment from Doha to Europe (including Turkey, as IATA includes the nation within that region). Such aircraft will account for 11% of the carrier's offering to the continent, which is a substantially smaller proportion than Gulf Air (73%) and Etihad (35%). Qatar Airways flew the A321ceo to Europe until 2022, a year after the last A319 operation. Between 2014 and 2016, the A319 even flew to London Heathrow with all-business seats.

    #145574. Breaking: How to Spend 3 Perfect Days in Naples

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1594 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: How to Spend 3 Perfect Days in Naples

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1594 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that A fascinating, complex, and multi-layered city, Naples is brimming with contradictions.
    • In a recent development, I’ve been visiting for over 30 years and have seen huge changes, most of them positive.
    • You could easily spend two weeks in Naples and not see everything.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that A fascinating, complex, and multi-layered city, Naples is brimming with contradictions. Dilapidated, neglected neighborhoods share city space with splendid palaces and world-beating museums. The city’s origins go back to the ancient Greeks, yet the contemporary art scene here is buzzing. There is a state-of-the-art metro system designed by renowned artists and architects (no wonder, since the traffic is infamously heavy).

    In a recent development, I’ve been visiting for over 30 years and have seen huge changes, most of them positive. Naples today is safer, more tourist-friendly, and cleaner than ever before, yet it remains Italy’s most beguiling city. The eating and drinking scene has evolved, there is a much wider choice of places to stay (with Rocco Forte due to open a hotel here in 2027), and museums and monuments have been spruced up and reorganized. In 2027, the America’s Cup will arrive as well.

    You could easily spend two weeks in Naples and not see everything. But if you only have three days, start early and be prepared to pack in as much as possible; you can rest once you get home. Here is my advice for how to make the most of it.

    You coudl easily spend two weeks in Naples and not see everything—but three days are a delicious taste, too.

    Historic Gran Caffè Gambrinus is a perfect place to start your first day, shoulder to shoulder with the locals at the bar for a shot of espresso and a warm cornetto (only tourists sit on the terrace). Just across Piazza Trieste e Trento lies the imposing dark grey and red Palazzo Reale where you can visit the sumptuous Royal Apartments and ornate Teatrino, and on the other side is the Teatro San Carlo, one of Italy’s most prestigious opera houses; opera buffs can book a behind-the-scenes tour, or even better, tickets for a performance.

    From the Toledo metro station, you get full immersion in the Stazione d’Arte, a public art project involving some of the greatest contemporary artists and architects who have transformed Naples’ main underground stations into public galleries. Dominated by Oscar Tusquets Blanca’s jaw-dropping mosaic, Toledo is one of the most impressive—but for just the price of a metro ticket (just over $2), you can tour them all.

    A quick walk north on Via Toledo leads to Via della Pignasecca, where you can catch the end of the lively morning market with its troughs of slithering, glistening fish and seafood, piles of seasonal fruit and vegetables, and stalls selling everything from tripe to knock-off designer handbags.

    Lunch at no-nonsense Trattoria da Nenella near Piazza Carità is a noisy, fun experience; you’ll probably have to queue, but the deep-fried anchovies and meatballs in tomato sauce are worth it, and prices are rock-bottom.

    The Cappella Sansevero is home to Giuseppe Sammartino’s sublime 1753 marble Cristo Velato.

    After a shot of the best coffee in the city at Café Mexico in Piazza Dante, you can spend the afternoon exploring the grid of streets around the so-called Spaccanapoli, the heart of Roman Neapolis where ancient monuments rub shoulders with street food stalls, tiny grocers, once-grand palazzi, and shops selling tourist trinkets and religious memorabilia. Piazza del Gesù, at the western end, is dominated by the eponymous church and an ornate roccoco ‘guglia’. Just to the east is the Church and Convent of Santa Chiara with a beautiful Gothic interior and a cloister famous for its bright, 18th-century majolica tiles. Close by is Naples’ most celebrated (and most crowded) sight, the Cappella Sansevero, home to Giuseppe Sammartino’s sublime 1753 marble Cristo Velato.

    According to recent reports, back on the Spaccanapoli, nip into Gay-Odin (n. 61) for a chocolate gelato and then continue to the vast Duomo where you will be dazzled by the gilt-encrusted Cappella di San Gennaro and the subterranean church of Santa Restituita and its 4th-century baptistery.

    Close by are the chapel of Pio Monte della Misericordia with Caravaggio’s seminal Seven Acts of Mercy and crumbling Piazza San Girolamini where Banksy’s Madonna with a Pistol appeared on the back right-hand wall in 2004. San Lorenzo Maggiore is an essential visit if you want to understand multi-layered Naples; under the 13th-century church, ongoing excavations have revealed the astonishing remains of a Greco-Roman city dating back 2,000 years.

    Sources indicate that A detour down Via San Gregorio Armeno takes you past shops selling pastori or figurines for Christmas cribs. Much of what you see is mass-produced these days, so for the real deal, visit Marco Ferrigno’s workshop at number 10. Continue to leafy Piazza Bellini, a lively evening hub, and bag a terrace table at Café Intramoenia for a Campari spritz—you’ve earned it.

    For dinner, Europeo di Mattozzi is a personal favorite for its echoes of elegant old Naples; the classic food is fantastic (try the sublime melanzane alla parmigiana and the pasta with potatoes and provola cheese), the host Alfonso is charming, and your fellow diners are likely to be mostly locals.

    Use Castel dell'Ovoa as your launchpad for a classic Neapolitan passeggiata along the wide, traffic-free seafront drag.

    Industry observers note that day two starts where it all began. Parthenope—later Neapolis and later still Napoli—was founded more than 2,500 years ago on the tiny island of Megaris, now occupied by the Castel dell’Ovo and the picturesque fishing hamlet of Borgo Marinari. There’s nothing much to see in the castle, but it’s a good launch pad for the classic Neapolitan passeggiata along the wide, traffic-free seafront drag. It’s lined with restaurants and cafés offering tables in the sun for a cappuccino and magnificent views.

    In a recent development, the delightful neighbourhood of Chiaia is a criss-cross of pretty cobbled lanes peppered with independent boutiques, cool bars, and tiny restaurants; Via dei Mille and Via dei Filangeri are known for designer clothes and chic galleries. The handmade silk ties at tiny, old-fashioned Marinella make wonderful gifts, and a counter perch at tiny Pescheria Mattiucci is a good choice for a quick seafood lunch with a glass of something chilled and white.

    Depending on the weather (and energy levels), one option from here is to head west beyond Mergellina to the upmarket seaside suburb of Posillipo for an afternoon on the beach; sunbeds and umbrellas can be rented at Bagno Sirena.

    Or you can hop on the Funicolare di Chiaia and trundle up to leafy Vomero and the panoramic Certosa di San Martino, a Carthusian monastery complex with an ornate church, several museums, two cloisters, and the famous Monk’s Cemetery decorated with marble skulls. It also has knock-out views over the whole waterfront and the Bay of Naples to the Sorrentine Peninsula. The Friggitoria Vomero—one of the city’s few remaining authentic ‘frying shops’—doles out sizzling snacks from 6 p.m. and is conveniently close to the funicolare stop as you head back down the hill.

    Chiaia’s quiet lanes morph into a nightlife hub from aperitivo hour on, filling up with smartly dressed locals and visitors in search of a good night out. Cocktail spot per eccellenza is retro-glam Antiquario where the jacketed barmen mix a stonking Negroni. From here it’s a short stroll to tiny Ristorante Dora, open since 1973, for textbook versions of fish and seafood classics such as spaghetti alle vongole (with local clams). Head back to Chiaia for a nightcap; follow your nose and the party crowd.

    The atmospheric burial site of Cimitero delle Fontanelle is a respite from the buzzing streets above.

    In a recent development, A no-go area for tourists until relatively recently, the dilapidated, densely populated but intriguing Rione Sanità is Naples in the raw. Breakfast at Pasticceria Popella in Via Arena alla Sanità is a must for their sfogliatelle and cream-stuffed ‘fiocchi di neve’ before having a rummage among the market stalls and tiny shops on Via dei Vergini; at n. 19 is the grand entrance to the famous pale green and cream Palazzo dello Spagnuolo with its celebrated ‘flying staircase’ by local architect Ferdinando San Felice.

    These shambolic streets are filled with tooting cars, buzzing vespas, and bewildered tourists, but there are hidden artistic gems too: the 2,400 year-old recently restored Ipogeo dei Cristallini, the atmospheric burial site of the Cimitero delle Fontanelle with its piles of skulls and bones; and the labyrinthine Catacombs of San Gaudioso under the basilica of Santa Maria della Sanità.

    You can’t visit the Sanità without a meal at Ciro Oliva’s crazy-lively temple to pizza Concettina ai Tre Santi (booking is essential), where the tasting menus offer an endless succession of slices topped with whatever the pizzaiolo dreams up at the time.

    Naples’ Archaeological Museum (aka Mann) houses one of the world’s great collections of ancient art and artefacts, and if you only visit one museum, make it this. Must-sees include the monumental Roman sculptures on the ground floor, the collection of ancient erotica in the Gabinetto Segreto, and the dazzling mosaics, wall paintings, and bronzes from Pompeii and Herculaneum.

    Afterwards, check out the brilliant selection of exquisite handmade gloves at factory prices in the workshops of Omega, a family glove business that first opened in 1923, before winding up the day in the surprisingly peaceful oasis of the exotic Orto Botanico gardens on traffic-clogged Via Foria.

    Industry observers note that for a last blast, Grand Hotel Parker’s on the way up to Vomero is the smart place to go. Cocktails and light bites are served on the rooftop terrace while on the floor below, chef Domenico Candela whips up a storm with his two-Michelin-star take on local cuisine to a backdrop of unforgettable views.

    #145573. The Best Places to Go in Europe in 2027

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 22m • 📚 Deep Dive (4378 w)
