    #145560. How Much Does A Boeing 777-300ER Cost To Operate Per Hour?

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1532 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    How Much Does A Boeing 777-300ER Cost To Operate Per Hour?

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1532 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age.
    • According to recent reports, boeing’s 777-300ER entered service in 2004 and is still the backbone of many long-haul fleets, but the cost of flying one is harder to pin down than its age suggests.
    • Fuel became far more expensive in 2026.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age. He became involved in the flight simulator and VATSIM communities, which sparked his interest in aviation and eventually led him to earn his private pilot license. Outside of work, he continues to build flight hours, explore newly introduced airports, and stay involved in the aviation community.

    According to recent reports, boeing’s 777-300ER entered service in 2004 and is still the backbone of many long-haul fleets, but the cost of flying one is harder to pin down than its age suggests. Published estimates for a mid-life aircraft range from about $18,000 an hour to the mid-$20,000s. Most of that gap comes from two inputs: the jet fuel price each estimate assumes, and how much engine maintenance it counts.

    Fuel became far more expensive in 2026. Jet fuel prices roughly doubled after the war in Iran began, so any estimate built on pre-war prices now understates the highest cost of operating a widebody. Lease payments, crew, maintenance, airport charges and insurance make up the rest of the bill, and each one varies with the airline, the route and the age of the aircraft.

    Sources indicate that simple Flying’s April 2026 analysis puts the hourly cost of a mid-life 777-300ER at about $18,000 to $19,000, or roughly $5 million a month and $60 million a year. That estimate assumes jet fuel at about $2.50 a gallon, which puts fuel at $5,000 to $6,000 an hour. The analysis also points out that actual costs vary widely with fuel prices, region, maintenance, financing, and how the aircraft is used, and cites a lower Eurocontrol estimate of about $40 million a year at 2022 prices.

    It has been revealed that aircraft Investigation produces a higher figure. Its model gives the 777-300ER a direct operating cost of €24,804 an hour, which the site lists elsewhere as about $26,000. That total assumes the aircraft’s hourly cruise burn of about 2,833 gallons (10,722 liters) costs €6,433, which implies a price of roughly €0.60 a liter, well below 2026 levels. The site cautions that its calculations “must be regarded as indication not as facts.”.

    It has been revealed that side by side, the two estimates agree closely on fuel and crew. The split comes on maintenance, where Aircraft Investigation lists the engines separately and ends up at more than twice the April figure. Its model also does not itemize leasing, airport fees, or insurance, so the two totals cannot be reconciled line by line. Maintenance, unlike fuel, has no public market price, and each estimate has to decide how to spread the cost of major engine work, which can come years apart, across individual flight hours.

    $3,000–4,000 (includes engines).

    Industry observers note that at economical cruise speed, the 777-300ER burns about 2,833 gallons (10,722 liters) of fuel an hour, or roughly 18,560 lb (8,417 kg). Fuel burn is highest during takeoff and climb, so the cruise figure understates the average across a full flight. All of that fuel goes through two GE90-115B engines, the only engine ever offered on the type.

    The price of that fuel rose sharply in 2026. The Argus US Jet Fuel Index put the average US price at $3.99 a gallon in mid-March, up from $2.50 the day before the war began two weeks earlier. By June, IATA said the price had “roughly doubled since late February.” Using IATA’s late-September price of $4.415 a gallon, an October 2026 analysis put cruise fuel for the 777-300ER at about $12,500 an hour, more than double the April estimate. In the week ending October 9, IATA’s global average reached $190.18 a barrel, 111.2% higher than a year earlier.

    It has been revealed that prices have eased since then but remain well above pre-war levels. IATA’s most recent weekly figure put the global average at $169.82 a barrel, down 5.1% from the week before, or about $4.04 a gallon. At that price, the 777-300ER’s cruise burn would cost roughly $11,450 an hour. Across the industry, IATA forecasts fuel expenses of $351 billion in 2026, lifting fuel’s share of operating costs to 31.4%. Hedging softens the blow for some carriers. Airlines had hedged roughly one-third of their 2026 fuel needs, but many hedged against crude oil rather than jet fuel, which left them exposed to the widening gap between the two prices.

    Recent findings suggest that ownership is a smaller share of the hourly cost than fuel. Aircraft valuation firm IBA put the lease rate for a mid-life 777-300ER at about $450,000 a month, or about $15,000 a day, in September 2024. At 292 flight hours a month, that comes to about $1,540 per flight hour. IBA valued the same aircraft at about $80 million, compared with the 2023 list price of $150 million that Aircraft Investigation records. Airlines that own their aircraft outright carry depreciation and financing costs instead of a lease payment.

    Crew costs come to about $2,000 per flight hour, and more than half of that goes to the pilots. Long-haul 777 flights typically carry two active pilots and two relief pilots, and senior captains can earn up to $400 an hour. Aircraft Investigation’s estimate of €1,650 an hour falls in a similar range. The total rises with sector length, because longer flights require relief pilots in addition to the operating crew.

    Airport charges vary the most between routes. At Upcoming York JFK (JFK), for example, landing fees have been $7.43 per 1,000 lb of maximum takeoff weight since January 1, 2025. With a maximum takeoff weight of 775,000 lb, a 777-300ER pays roughly $5,760 to land there. More broadly, a large 777 may pay $5,000 to $7,000 per arrival, plus $2,000 to $5,000 for handling and parking, which averages about $1,500 per flight hour. Insurance is minor at about $86,000 a year, or roughly $25 per flight hour. Another $2,000 or so per flight hour covers en route fees, cleaning, catering, and other expenses.

    Maintenance accounts for most of the difference between published estimates. The April 2026 analysis puts it at more than $1 million a month, or $3,000 to $4,000 per flight hour, with the engines making up a major part of that total. On those figures, maintenance is the second-largest cost after fuel. It also climbs as an aircraft ages, since a 777-300ER reaching midlife needs costly heavy maintenance on top of routine line work.

    It has been revealed that aircraft Investigation separates the engines from the rest of the aircraft and reaches a much higher number. Its model puts airframe maintenance at €4,842 an hour and adds €4,414 an hour for the engines, about €9,256 combined. That is more than double the April estimate before any currency conversion. The site rates the confidence of its underlying data as medium and does not explain how it spreads the cost of major shop visits across flight hours, which is the biggest variable in any engine maintenance estimate.

    How an airline pays for engine work shapes its hourly cost as much as the work itself. Many 777 operators buy engine support from GE at a fixed rate per flight hour, which turns irregular shop visits into a steady monthly cost. Emirates, for example, extended its TrueChoice Flight Hour agreement with GE covering maintenance, repair and overhaul for the 54 GE90-115B engines on its 777-300ERs, a deal valued at more than $400 million over the life of the contract. An airline that covers its own shop visits instead faces large bills at irregular intervals, which each estimate spreads across flying hours in its own way. Because flight-hour rates are negotiated, two airlines flying identical aircraft can carry very different maintenance costs per hour.

    At September 2026 fuel prices, the 777-300ER sits between its newer and older rivals. The A350-1000 burns about 2,268 gallons (8,585 liters) an hour at cruise, costing roughly $10,000, against the 777-300ER’s 2,833 gallons and $12,500. The four-engine 747-8 burns 3,914 gallons (14,818 liters) an hour, for about $17,280. On those numbers, the A350-1000’s cruise fuel cost is 20% lower than the 777-300ER’s, while the 777-300ER’s is nearly 28% lower than the 747-8’s.

    Recent findings suggest that capacity narrows the gap with the Airbus on a per-seat basis. Two-class layouts range from 350 to 425 seats on the 777-300ER, against 369 on the A350-1000 and more than 500 on the 747-8. An airline with a dense 777-300ER cabin spreads its higher fuel bill across more passengers than an A350-1000 operator with a premium-heavy layout. Engine count matters too. The 747’s four engines mean more overhaul programs and greater repair risk than the twin-engine 777 or A350, which is one reason the older Boeing’s block-hour cost is well above $20,000 and sometimes approaches $30,000.

    Ownership costs pull in the opposite direction from fuel. IBA’s September 2024 rates put a new A350-900 at $1.15 million a month to lease, against about $450,000 for a mid-life 777-300ER. IBA did not publish a comparable A350-1000 figure in that set, but the A350-900 rate alone shows how far a new widebody’s lease payment can exceed an older 777’s. For an airline choosing between them, the 777-300ER’s lower ownership cost offsets part of its fuel disadvantage.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The next frontier for the Airbus A321XLR is South America.

    Recent findings suggest that after opening dozens of newly introduced transatlantic routes, the long-range narrow-body will make its debut with LATAM Airlines in March 2027. The airline has yet to say which routes the XLRs will fly, but executives have previously outlined opportunities to connect the U.S. and South America.

    LATAM, a close partner of Delta Air Lines, will outfit its fleet of XLRs with 174 seats. Business class will feature 12 lie-flat suites supplied by Thompson Aero Seating in a 1-1 layout with privacy doors.

    The suites include 19-inch personal entertainment screens, Bluetooth connectivity and in-seat charging options.

    Economy features 13-inch screens at each of the 126 seats, which are supplied by Recaro, plus Bluetooth connectivity and USB-C outlets. The cabin includes 36 extra-legroom seats.

    “The Airbus A321XLR allows us to take our value proposition to the next level and elevate the travel experience for our passengers,” remarked Paulo Miranda, the chief customer officer of LATAM, in a statement. He described the interior, which features red, orange and blue hues, as “inspired by South America.”.

    LATAM executives have noted it could fly the XLR on routes into the U.S. from its hub at Jorge Chavez International Airport (LIM) in Lima. However, those aims were called into question in May over the addition of a "connection fee" at LIM.

    According to recent reports, the airline and Delta serve six U.S. destinations from LIM: Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL), Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), Miami International Airport (MIA), John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), Orlando International Airport (MCO) and, since January 2026, Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC).

    LATAM did not comment on specific route plans for the XLR.

    The XLR is the second new airplane type for LATAM in as many years. The airline took delivery of its first Embraer E195-E2 in October. It will use the small jet to expand its feeder network in Brazil and support additional long-haul, intercontinental flying.

    According to FlightAware, Delta delayed over 2,100 flights Sunday and canceled 274.

    Atlanta Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport was the hardest hit, with about 700 flights delayed, though not all were Delta connections.

    Industry observers note that delta said in a statement that its employees were using manual workarounds for baggage processing. It also said it would rebook customers on the next available flight and provide meals and hotel rooms where needed.

    The FAA said on X that the problem was specific to Delta and had nothing to do with the agency’s air traffic control system, which crashed on Nov. 13.

    Recent findings suggest that delta is working to resolve concerns with the airline’s weight and balance automation system. These delays are not related to any FAA air traffic systems. Please check with Delta for the latest information. https://t.co/q4Fc59VMYg.

    The outage was resolved Sunday afternoon.

    As of Monday morning, Delta’s delay rate was down to 6%.

    Recent findings suggest that while resolved fairly quickly, the system failure could hardly have come at a worse time. Millions of Americans are flying this week ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday, and there are concerns that technology outages could again snarl air traffic during the busiest time of the year. The single busiest day for air travel is expected to be Sunday, Nov. 29, after Thanksgiving.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, powerful storms bringing high winds and the potential for flooding could seriously disrupt commercial air travel in the U.S. during the single busiest week of the year.

    Forecasters are warning that storm systems will likely strike parts of the South, Mid-Atlantic, and Northeast, as well as Northern California and the Pacific Northwest. These regions are home to some of the nation’s busiest airports, through which millions of American travelers will pass this week en route to visit family and friends for Thanksgiving on Thursday.

    It has been revealed that in the Northeast, the remnants of a weakened, disorganized system were still clearing out on Monday. A much stronger storm is expected to develop in the Gulf of Mexico between Monday and Tuesday, impact parts of the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic Wednesday, and slam into the New York metro area and New England on Thanksgiving Day.

    According to an advisory from the National Weather Service’s Weather Prediction Center, strong wind gusts up to 50 mph will be felt from the Carolinas to Maine. Flooding and beach erosion could be seen in coastal areas due to the already high tides.

    In a recent development, WPC has initiated Key Messages for a Thanksgiving Coastal Storm that is expected to impact the U.S. East Coast. pic.twitter.com/pdQuU4U4yG.

    Americans traveling from, through, or to these areas should prepare for the possibility of flooded roads, damage from high winds, and power outages, the agency stated.

    NYC Emergency Management said Sunday that the storm could bring gusts of 40 to 45 mph and about one to two inches of rain to the city.

    Recent findings suggest that for Newly introduced York and New England, the storm will be at its strongest Thursday evening. Parts of the Adirondacks and northern New England could see ice and snow mixed in with rain.

    Industry observers note that in California, Oregon, and Washington, residents still recovering from flooding last week could be hit again by rain and strong winds. A newly introduced system is expected to move in Tuesday and Wednesday; combined with the “king tides,” the storm could cause flooding up and down the West Coast.

    Recent findings suggest that the impact is expected to be most severe between Portland, Oregon, and San Francisco. San Francisco’s mayor said residents should take the forecasts seriously and consider not traveling for the holiday.

    The Sierra Nevada, meanwhile, will see fresh snow, meteorologists noted.

    Over six million people are expected to fly within the U.S. this week for Thanksgiving. The surge is already underway, with many carriers adding flights to accommodate the increased traffic. American Airlines earlier this month projected its busiest Thanksgiving week since before the COVID-19 pandemic; that prediction could hold true for other U.S. airlines as well.

    AirlineGeeks will continue to monitor weather conditions and provide updates as the week progresses.

    And here are my thoughts on the main pros and cons of the Blue Cash Preferred Card:.

    When applying for a credit card, obviously the welcome offer, the eligibility, and the fees, are major considerations, given that they can be the first factors that impact interest in a card. So along those lines, let’s take a look at those details for the Amex Blue Cash Preferred.

    Industry observers note that the Amex Blue Cash Preferred is currently offering the following welcome bonus: You may be eligible for as high as $300 cash back after spending $3,000 in purchases on your new Card in the first 6 months.     Recent findings suggest that that’s a solid bonus for a card at this price point, and the six month window gives you plenty of time to hit the spending requirement. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

    Sources indicate that amex cards tend to be fairly easy to get approved for if you have excellent credit. A few rules to know:.

The way this works, you can apply for the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card, and then find out your offer amount. Then you can decide whether you want to accept the offer or not. That’s an unconventional approach for a welcome offer. At least Amex has the “apply with confidence” feature, so there won’t be a hard pull unless you accept the offer.

    The Amex Blue Cash Preferred has a $0 intro annual fee for the first year, then $95. (Rates & Fees). That puts it in line with other mid-range cards.     Sources indicate that the Amex Blue Cash Preferred offers 3% cash back on transit purchases, including taxis, ridesharing, parking, tolls, trains, and buses. If you commute by public transit or use rideshare services regularly, this is a solid bonus category.

    It has been revealed that with the Amex Blue Cash Preferred, you also earn 3% cash back at eligible U.S. gas stations, with no caps. Note that this doesn’t include gas purchased at superstores, supermarkets, or warehouse clubs that sell fuel.

    Britt bill would launch national office to combat financial fraud

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (501 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority.
    • Recent findings suggest that A bill introduced by Sen.
    • The draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Recent findings suggest that A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

    The draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

    The latest office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

    Britt, R-Ala., remarked the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

    Industry observers note that “This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting latest technologies and gaps between sectors,” she said in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”.

    The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide noted.

    The office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

    In a recent development, britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

    The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

    The House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

    In a recent development, senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring.

    It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

    “If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide said.

    Here’s How Much A Business Class Ticket On Emirates' Boeing 777-300ER Actually Costs In 2026

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, the Boeing 777-300ER is by far the most numerous 777 variant in the Emirates fleet, with 116 aircraft of the type owned by the airline.
    • Emirates has one of the world's best business class products, ranking 11th in the Skytrax World Airline Awards business class category.
    • Before we can judge how much an Emirates 777-300ER ticket costs, it is essential to understand exactly where they fly, and the most frequent routes on which readers are most likely to consider purchasing a business class ticket.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the Boeing 777-300ER is by far the most numerous 777 variant in the Emirates fleet, with 116 aircraft of the type owned by the airline. As a result, the jet is used to fly to a vast number of destinations at an incredibly high frequency. It will achieve around 5.7 billion available seat miles in November 2026 alone. Emirates passengers have plenty of 777-300ER business class seats to choose from across much of the network.

    Emirates has one of the world's best business class products, ranking 11th in the Skytrax World Airline Awards business class category. Tickets for this elite class come in at a little over $1,000 to over $3,000 for the most frequent routes operated by the airline using the 777-300ER. Prices vary depending on availability, demand, and the exact route chosen.

    Before we can judge how much an Emirates 777-300ER ticket costs, it is essential to understand exactly where they fly, and the most frequent routes on which readers are most likely to consider purchasing a business class ticket. Emirates flies its 777-300ER aircraft to a host of different destinations, totaling 3,684 flights in November for over 1.3 million seats and 5.7 billion available seat miles.

    Industry observers note that the table below uses Cirium data procured by Simple Flying to reveal the ten most frequent routes served by Emirates' 777-300ERs in November 2026. All of these routes start at DXB:.

    Malé Velana International Airport (MLE).

    Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL).

    Amsterdam Airport Schiphol (AMS).

    Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport (BOM).

    Indira Gandhi International Airport (DEL).

    Rajiv Gandhi International Airport (HYD).

    Sources indicate that O. R. Tambo International Airport (JNB).

    Chennai International Airport (MAA).

    Prince Mohammad bin Abdulaziz International Airport (MED).

    Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport (DAC).

    According to recent reports, emirates has eight 777-300ER routes that will be operated 90 times or more in November 2026. The most frequent route is to MLE. The airline will operate the DXB to MLE route 115 times across the month, totaling almost 40,000 seats and over 73 million available seat miles. Meanwhile, the least frequent route operated by the carrier's 777-300ER aircraft is to Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA). The carrier will operate this route two times during the month for 652 available seats.

    There is no fixed price for an Emirates business class ticket. The carrier alters its specific pricing, as with any airline, based on the distance of the particular route involved and the level of demand. A route at the edge of a 777-300ER's range that has an almost sold-out business class cabin will demand the highest prices. Meanwhile, you'll be able to access discounts if you buy your ticket before most of them have been sold or are traveling on a short route.

    A unique feature of Emirates' business class ticketing structure is that there are multiple tiers to choose from, although each gives you access to the same seat, dining, and lounge access experiences. Firstly, the cheapest tier is Saver. You will get an 88 lb (40 kg) check-in bag, as with the more expensive tiers, but you'll get the highest fees if you want to change or cancel your ticket. Saver passengers also earn fewer miles.

    Recent findings suggest that the table below uses Seat Maps data to show the various configurations Emirates has for the 777-300ER and the number of business class seats available across each. The exact configuration you will fly in will depend on the route and fleet usage. The final row shows the average availability across each class across all of the configurations:.

    The Flex tier is more expensive. It brings lower change fees and better refund terms. Flex Plus is the most expensive tier. These passengers can enjoy completely flexible flights and maximum refund values. Flex Plus passengers earn the most miles, which can make the additional cost worth it if you frequently fly Emirates business class.

    Simple Flying has run simulated bookings on the Emirates website for five of the most frequent routes as they are in November, selecting from the 90 frequency options at random. For the purposes of this search, the travel dates are set to December 1 for the departure, and the search is for a one-way ticket.

    The table below reveals the data. The lowest price available was selected in each case:.

    For the reasons described in the previous section, there will be a great degree of variation depending on the exact characteristics of your booking. That is why it is challenging to draw a pattern between these prices beyond the fact that a longer flight is normally more expensive. Furthermore, the ticket price could be significantly higher if you choose the Emirates Flex or Flex Plus option.

    Sources indicate that this summer, Simple Flying conducted a similar investigation into how much a business class ticket for a flight from the US to Dubai costs for the August 2026 to January 2027 period. It revealed substantially higher costs than what has been shown in this article, which will be partly due to the removal of the legacy configuration for routes to the US.

    It has been revealed that firstly, a flight to Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) cost around $4,620. This was less than a flight to Latest York JFK Airport (JFK) and Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR), coming in at $5,070. A business class flight to Miami International Airport (MIA) cost slightly less at $4,965. The cheapest business class flight featured was to Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD), costing $4,540.

    According to recent reports, the higher costs are unsurprising, given that a flight to the country from the Middle East is a lengthy affair. For example, a flight from DXB to IAD takes around 15 hours and 10 minutes. Furthermore, the United Arab Emirates and the US have a tightening business relationship, which will contribute to increasing demand for such services. The impact of this is shown by the higher price for both flights to Fresh York, the US' financial hub.

    Emirates 777-300ER business class is a mixed experience. The aircraft has traditionally used a legacy and comparatively cramped 2-3-2 configuration. The layout, as pictured, means that passengers can spend thousands of dollars extra and still end up in the dreaded middle seat.

    To amend the concern, Emirates is undertaking a substantial retrofit program. It will cost $5 billion and involve 110 A380s and 109 777s. The main change is that the cabin will switch to a modern 1-2-1 layout, giving each passenger more space and ensuring that they all have direct aisle access. The retrofits also ensure consistency between the Boeing 777X and older 777 variants.

    The table below highlights the differences between the legacy 777-300ER business class and what is available on the refurbished 777s:.

    Deep seat shells & privacy wings.

    According to recent reports, simple Flying's Abid Habib reviewed the old 777 business class in 2024. The route was from London to Dubai.     #145548. Enterprise AI is pushing cloud infrastructure beyond the GPU

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1993 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

    Enterprise AI is pushing cloud infrastructure beyond the GPU

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1993 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that enterprise adoption of artificial intelligence is creating latest requirements for enterprise AI infrastructure.
    • Agentic AI systems need environments where they can execute code, access data, connect to enterprise applications and operate securely across distributed infrastructure.
    • Industry observers note that that shift is creating an opportunity for neocloud providers, but it is also changing what enterprises expect from them.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    UPDATED 16:07 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

    It has been revealed that enterprise adoption of artificial intelligence is creating latest requirements for enterprise AI infrastructure. While much of the early AI investment centered on access to powerful GPUs, organizations moving AI applications and agents into production are discovering that accelerators are only one part of the equation.

    Agentic AI systems need environments where they can execute code, access data, connect to enterprise applications and operate securely across distributed infrastructure. That requires more than bare-metal GPU capacity. It calls for a complete cloud platform that combines compute, networking, storage, security and the services needed to manage applications at scale.

    Industry observers note that that shift is creating an opportunity for neocloud providers, but it is also changing what enterprises expect from them. Infrastructure providers increasingly need to support the full application lifecycle rather than simply supply specialized hardware.

    During a live interview at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026, theCUBE Research’s Paul Nashawaty spoke with Kevin Cochrane, chief marketing officer at Vultr, about the changing requirements of enterprise AI infrastructure, the return of CPU-based computing, data sovereignty and the growing role of platform engineering.

    “They need a full cloud platform,” Cochrane noted. “They need cloud compute, specialized AI compute, networking, storage and an open ecosystem.”.

    According to recent reports, vultr entered the cloud market in 2014 with a developer-focused platform built around performance, cost efficiency and accessibility. Since then, the company has expanded into AI infrastructure, offering both traditional cloud services and specialized GPU resources.

    Cochrane mentioned Vultr took a deliberate approach to the AI infrastructure market, prioritizing enterprise workload and platform-engineering requirements rather than focusing exclusively on GPU availability.

    “We’ve always mentioned that we’re the tortoise in AI infrastructure,” he said.

    In a recent development, that approach reflects a broader change in how enterprises are approaching AI. Early infrastructure demand largely came from hyperscalers, AI research organizations and startups building large-scale models. Those customers needed access to GPU clusters, often through bare-metal infrastructure.

    The next phase is different. Enterprises are looking to use AI agents to streamline operations, improve customer experiences and create new revenue opportunities. Those applications must work alongside existing enterprise systems, comply with security requirements and integrate with established network and application architectures.

    Bare-metal GPU infrastructure alone does not address those needs. Cochrane identified complexity and a lack of specialized skills as major obstacles to enterprise AI adoption. Organizations may have access to powerful accelerators, but they still need the surrounding infrastructure and services to build, deploy and operate applications.

    Vultr’s strategy is to provide a more integrated environment, including traditional cloud compute, GPU infrastructure, networking, storage and access to cloud-native projects. Cochrane mentioned the platform supports more than 60 Cloud Native Computing Foundation projects that customers can deploy directly.

    Recent findings suggest that the goal is to reduce the work required to assemble an AI environment. Rather than making enterprises integrate every component themselves, providers can offer preconfigured services and composable infrastructure that developers can deploy as needed.

    That distinction is becoming vital as AI moves beyond experimentation. Enterprises need infrastructure that supports production applications, not just model training and inference.

    The growing focus on GPUs has sometimes obscured the role of traditional computing resources in AI architectures. But agentic AI is expanding the range of workloads that infrastructure providers must support.

    According to recent reports, an AI agent does more than send a prompt to a model and receive a response. It may execute scripts, interact with repositories, run builds, access databases and invoke external tools. Those activities require compute resources beyond the GPU.

    “Not all workloads need to be on a GPU,” Cochrane said.

    Industry observers note that CPUs remain essential for databases, application code and data pipelines. They can also support smaller, optimized open-source models and inference workloads that do not require dedicated accelerators.

    Industry observers note that another emerging requirement is the environment in which agents execute tasks. As agents gain the ability to run code and interact with systems, enterprises need secure sandboxes that isolate those activities from production environments and sensitive resources.

    Cochrane pointed to work underway in the cloud-native ecosystem around safe and secure agent sandboxes as an indication of how infrastructure requirements are changing.

    Industry observers note that this creates a more complex infrastructure model. GPUs may handle demanding model reasoning and inference, while CPUs support the applications, pipelines and execution environments surrounding those models.

    In a recent development, for organizations, the implication is that enterprise AI infrastructure decisions should account for the entire agentic workflow. Buying GPU capacity without considering the compute, storage, networking and isolation requirements around it can create another infrastructure silo. A full-stack approach gives platform teams more flexibility to match resources to individual workloads while maintaining a consistent operational environment.

    As enterprises expand AI deployments across regions, data sovereignty is becoming more than a question of where information is stored.

    Organizations operating in regulated industries or under national data requirements need to understand where data resides, which services can access it and what happens if infrastructure outside a particular region becomes unavailable.

    Industry observers note that cochrane described Vultr’s regional architecture as an isolation model in which each of its 34 global data center regions operates independently. According to him, data within a region remains resident there and is not accessed by Vultr services outside that region.

    Recent findings suggest that the distinction extends beyond data residency to application operations. Cochrane used France as an example. An application running in a French region should continue operating even if Vultr’s global control plane and its other regions become unavailable.

    Recent findings suggest that “If the rest of the world went dark, your production application in France? It just runs,” he said.

    That approach is intended to reduce dependencies on global services that could otherwise affect regional application availability. It also gives organizations a clearer boundary for managing sensitive workloads and maintaining operational continuity.

    For enterprises, this is an vital architectural consideration. A cloud provider may offer regional data storage, but that does not necessarily mean every service required to operate an application is isolated within the same geography.

    As AI applications become more deeply integrated into business operations, organizations will need to evaluate sovereignty across the full application stack, including data, compute, management services and operational dependencies.

    The cost of running AI applications is becoming another major consideration as organizations move from pilots to sustained production workloads.

    It has been revealed that inference costs can increase quickly when agents repeatedly call models, retrieve information and execute multi-step workflows. As usage grows, enterprises must balance model performance, throughput and infrastructure expense.

    According to recent reports, cochrane believes some organizations will increasingly turn to open-source models that can be adapted to their own data and operated on infrastructure they control. Rather than relying entirely on large commercial models for every task, enterprises can post-train specialized models using proprietary information and deploy them for operational workloads where that approach makes sense.

    He described an example involving a platform engineering organization that reduced inference costs by 80% by post-training an open-source model and running it on its own infrastructure. The example illustrates a potential economic advantage, although results will depend on the workload, model, infrastructure and operational requirements involved.

    Recent findings suggest that the broader point is that organizations are beginning to evaluate the economics of enterprise AI infrastructure across the entire stack. Model selection matters, but so do infrastructure utilization, throughput, data movement and the cost of operating agents over time.

    For some workloads, owning more of the infrastructure and model lifecycle may provide better cost control than depending entirely on external inference services.

    That does not mean every enterprise should build and operate its own models. It does suggest that organizations need more flexibility to choose where models run and how workloads are distributed.

    The changing infrastructure requirements of agentic AI are also expanding the responsibilities of platform engineering teams.

    Cochrane expects platform engineers to become central to enterprise AI adoption, working more closely with business units to understand which agents and preconfigured application environments are needed across the organization.

    That moves platform engineering beyond infrastructure provisioning and developer enablement. Teams will increasingly need to help define the building blocks that allow developers to deploy governed AI applications without having to assemble every component independently.

    Cochrane also sees an opportunity for the cloud-native community to evolve how it shares infrastructure patterns. The CNCF ecosystem has helped developers adopt individual open-source projects across networking, storage, observability and other infrastructure categories. But as architectures become more complex, organizations need guidance on how those components fit together.

    Cochrane predicted the emergence of marketplaces where developers can share opinionated, prebuilt stacks for specific workload types. Instead of selecting and configuring individual components, teams could start with a tested architecture and adapt it to their requirements. That could help reduce the complexity of building agentic applications while encouraging more consistent deployment practices.

    According to recent reports, he also expects consolidation in the neocloud market. Providers focused primarily on bare-metal GPU capacity may face pressure as enterprises demand broader cloud capabilities. Those able to expand into full public cloud platforms could be better positioned to serve production workloads.

    Vultr’s existing cloud platform gives it a foundation for that transition, Cochrane said, with its investments in both traditional compute and specialized AI infrastructure.

    Enterprise AI is changing the definition of cloud infrastructure. GPUs remain important, but agentic applications require a broader foundation that includes CPUs, secure execution environments, networking, storage, data sovereignty and integrated cloud-native services.

    It has been revealed that that creates an opportunity for providers that can deliver more than specialized accelerator capacity. It also puts platform engineering teams in a more strategic position as enterprises work to standardize how AI applications are built, deployed and governed.

    The next phase of the neocloud market may therefore be determined less by who can offer the most GPU capacity and more by who can provide the complete environment enterprises need to run AI in production.

    As Cochrane’s comments suggest, the infrastructure challenge is no longer simply making AI compute available. It is making the entire system around AI practical to operate at enterprise scale.

    Latest Update: Amex Blue Cash Everyday Review: A No Annual Fee Card With Solid Bonus Categories

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2415 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • American Express is best known for its points-earning cards, but the Blue Cash Everyday® Card from American Express proves that Amex can do cash back well too.
    • Recent findings suggest that if you’re looking for a simple card that earns a solid return at supermarkets, gas stations, and online retailers, this one is worth a look.
    • This post is my in-depth Blue Cash Everyday Card review, so I’ll cover the bonus categories, the credits and perks, and how this card compares to both the Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express and the Citi Double Cash® Card.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Express is best known for its points-earning cards, but the Blue Cash Everyday® Card from American Express proves that Amex can do cash back well too.

    Recent findings suggest that if you’re looking for a simple card that earns a solid return at supermarkets, gas stations, and online retailers, this one is worth a look. It has no annual fee (Rates & Fees), a decent welcome bonus, a great intro APR offer, and some useful bonus categories that cover a good chunk of everyday spending.

    This post is my in-depth Blue Cash Everyday Card review, so I’ll cover the bonus categories, the credits and perks, and how this card compares to both the Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express and the Citi Double Cash® Card.

    Review: Learn more about the Blue Cash Everyday® Card from American Express.

    First, here’s an overview of the Amex Blue Cash Everyday benefits and value proposition, from fees, to rewards, to the welcome bonus:.

    I also put together my list of pros and cons for the Blue Cash Everyday Card:.

    It has been revealed that when applying for a credit card, obviously the welcome offer, eligibility rules, and fees, are major considerations. So below I’ll cover the details of that for the Amex Blue Cash Everyday.

    The Amex Blue Cash Everyday is offering the following welcome bonus: You may be eligible for as high as $200 cash back after spending $2,000 in purchases on your new Card in the first 6 months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer. Cash back is received as Reward Dollars, redeemable for statement credit or for other select options. Terms Apply.

    That’s a reasonable bonus for a no annual fee card, and the spending requirement is low enough that most people should be able to hit it. However, it’s also not that much to get excited about, compared to some of the other welcome offers out there.

    Amex cards tend to be fairly easy to get approved for if you have excellent credit. Here are the main rules to be aware of:.

    Amex also has a pre-application eligibility tool that lets you check whether you’ll be approved for the card without any impact on your credit score. This is worth using if you’re not sure that you’ll qualify.

    It has been revealed that the Blue Cash Everyday Card has no annual fee. Not the first year, not ever. That alone makes it worth considering as a long-term card in your wallet, even if it’s not your primary spender.

    Industry observers note that holding no annual fee cards long term is also a great way to help your credit score. About 30% of your score comes from credit utilization (the more available credit you have but don’t use, the better), and 15% comes from credit history length (the older your average account age, the better). A no annual fee card you keep open for years helps on both fronts.

    The Blue Cash Everyday Card does have foreign transaction fees (2.7%) (Rates & Fees), so I wouldn’t use it for purchases in foreign currencies. Stick to domestic spending with this one, and find a card with no foreign transaction fees if you’ll be spending time abroad.

    The Amex Blue Cash Everyday has three main bonus categories, each earning 3% cash back on up to $6,000 per year in purchases (then 1%).

    It has been revealed that with the Blue Cash Everyday, you earn 3% back at U.S. supermarkets on up to $6,000 per year (then 1%). Earning 3% back at supermarkets with no annual fee is a solid deal, and this is one of the better no annual fee cards for U.S. supermarket spending.

    As with most grocery bonus categories, this generally won’t include warehouse clubs (like Costco), superstores (like Walmart or Target), convenience stores, or discount stores. Traditional supermarkets and grocery chains are what you’re looking for.

    It has been revealed that with the Blue Cash Everyday, you also earn 3% back at U.S. gas stations on up to $6,000 per year (then 1%). This is one of the better no annual fee cards for gas station spending.

    It has been revealed that this is the bonus category that makes the Blue Cash Everyday stand out from its siblings. You earn 3% back on U.S. online retail purchases on up to $6,000 per year (then 1%). This covers purchases made on a website or app from a U.S. retail merchant that sells physical goods directly to consumers.

    Given how much shopping happens online these days, this can be a really valuable category. You won’t find this bonus on many other cards.

    For purchases outside the bonus categories, you earn 1% cash back. This is where the card falls short. At just 1% on non-bonused spending, you’ll definitely want to pair this with a card that offers a better return on everyday purchases.

    With the Amex Blue Cash Everyday, you earn Reward Dollars that can be redeemed as statement credits at a rate of 1.0 cents per point, and there’s no minimum cash back balance required before you can redeem.

    It’s simple and straightforward, though it’s worth knowing that you can’t use cash back to pay your minimum payment due.

    Industry observers note that benefits and credits can certainly help with justifying holding onto credit cards. In the case of the Amex Blue Cash Everyday, you wouldn’t expect very valuable perks, given the card’s lack of an annual fee. However, it’s an area where I’d say the card actually exceeds expectations, and offers solid value.

    Sources indicate that the Blue Cash Everyday offers up to $7 back per month (up to $84 per year) as a statement credit when you use your enrolled Blue Cash Everyday to purchase a subscription, including a bundle subscription, on DisneyPlus.com, Hulu.com, or Stream.ESPN.com U.S. websites, with no minimum purchase requirement. Subscriptions are subject to auto-renewal. If you already pay for any of those services, this is an easy credit to use. (Enrollment required).

    Recent findings suggest that you can also earn up to $15 per month (up to $180 per year) in statement credits when you purchase Home Chef meal solutions online with your Blue Cash Everyday Card. If you use Home Chef, this is a significant benefit. If you don’t, it’s probably not worth signing up just for the credit. (Enrollment required).

    The Blue Cash Everyday Card also offers 0% intro APR on purchases and balance transfers for 15 months from the date of account opening. After that, the variable APR is currently between 19.74% - 28.74% (Rates & Fees).

    It has been revealed that I generally recommend avoiding financing purchases through credit cards. But if a short-term 0% APR opportunity can help you manage a large purchase and you can pay it off before the rate increases, it’s a nice option to have.

    Another card benefit is access to Amex Presale Tickets® and Amex Reserved Tickets®, which can come in handy if you’re trying to score tickets to an in-demand concert or sporting event.

    Every Amex card gives you access to the Amex Offers program, which provides targeted deals with a variety of retailers. Different cards get different offers, so having multiple Amex cards means more chances to save.

    According to recent reports, I try to have as many Amex cards as possible specifically to take advantage of this. Having a no annual fee card like this is ideal, since the card isn’t costing you anything, but you’re still getting access to potentially valuable offers.

    The Amex Blue Cash Everyday comes with coverage to protect your rental car when you charge the rental to this card. The coverage applies for eligible damage or theft, and it’s secondary, so it kicks in after your own car insurance. There are some exclusions, and it doesn’t include liability coverage, so check your card benefits guide for the full details.

    According to recent reports, car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Tech giant. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc.

    The Blue Cash Everyday Card also offers purchase protection of up to $1,000 per covered purchase for up to 90 days from the purchase date. You need to pay with the card in order to take advantage of this coverage.

    Sources indicate that the Amex Blue Cash Everyday Card is a solid no annual fee cash back card with useful bonus categories at supermarkets, gas stations, and online retailers. The 3% rate in those categories is strong for a no annual fee card, and the Disney streaming credits, Home Chef credits, and Amex Offers add extra value on top.

    While there are several reasons to consider the Blue Cash Everyday Card, there are also a couple of alternatives that I think are better for most people.

    According to recent reports, if you generally like the idea of the Blue Cash Everyday Card, there might still be a better play here. The Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express (learn more) is the premium version of the card, and it could be worth applying for it instead (Enrollment is required for select benefits).

    The major question is whether the Preferred’s $0 intro annual fee for the first year, then $95. annual fee (Rates & Fees) is worth the upgrade. If you spend at least $267 per month at U.S. supermarkets, the extra 3% (the Preferred earns 6% cash back at U.S. supermarkets on up to $6,000 per year in purchases, then 1%) on groceries alone will cover the fee. The Preferred also adds 6% cash back on select U.S. streaming and 3% on transit, which the Everyday doesn’t offer.

    On the flip side, the Everyday has two things the Preferred doesn’t: 3% on U.S. online retail purchases and a 0% intro APR offer. If you do a lot of online shopping and not as much grocery shopping, the Everyday could be the better card.

    One nice thing is that you could start with the Blue Cash Preferred (with a $0 intro annual fee for the first year, then $95.), and if the math doesn’t work out, downgrade to the Blue Cash Everyday after year one. That way you get the bigger welcome bonus and can test the higher earning rates.

    While there are lots to like about the Blue Cash Everyday, it’s also not particularly well-rounded if you’re looking for an all-in-one cash back credit card.

    The card offers 3% cash back at U.S. supermarkets, U.S. gas stations, and U.S. online retail purchases (up to certain limits), but on other purchases you’ll earn 1% cash back.

    Everyone will have to crunch the numbers for themselves, but 1% cash back is pretty uncompetitive nowadays for savvy consumers. For example, the no annual fee Citi Double Cash® Card (learn more) offers 1% cash back when you make a purchase, and 1% cash back when you pay for that purchase (in the form of ThankYou points).

    In a recent development, the Blue Cash Everyday wins in its bonus categories, earning 3% at supermarkets, gas stations, and online retailers compared to the Double Cash’s flat 2%. But the Double Cash wins everywhere else, earning 2% on all purchases versus just 1%.

    In a recent development, if your spending is heavily concentrated in supermarkets, gas, and online shopping, the Blue Cash Everyday will earn you more. If your spending is more spread out across lots of different categories, the Double Cash’s flat 2% on everything will likely come out ahead.

    The Double Cash also has a major advantage in flexibility. Its ThankYou points can be transferred to airline and hotel partners (in conjunction with a premium Citi card like the Citi Strata Premier® Card), giving those points the potential to be worth well more than 2 cents each. The Blue Cash Everyday’s rewards are purely cash back.

    Recent findings suggest that the ideal setup? Have both. Use the Blue Cash Everyday for supermarkets, gas, and online retail where it earns 3%, and the Double Cash for everything else at 2%.

    I think the Blue Cash Everyday is a very decent cash back card with bonus categories most spenders can take advantage of. The card’s main weakness is the 1% rate on everything outside the bonus categories — and even on those categories once you reach the annual cap. For that reason, I’d recommend pairing it with a flat-rate card like the Citi Double Cash (2% on everything) to fill in the gaps. Together, they make a simple, effective, no annual fee credit card cash back setup.

    If you find yourself spending more at supermarkets over time, you can always upgrade to the Blue Cash Preferred for that 6% supermarket rate. But for a no annual fee, low-maintenance starting point, the Blue Cash Everyday is a great choice.

    Medical AI startup Boltz raises $110M to speed up small molecule research

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (823 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Boltz PBC, a startup that develops artificial intelligence models for pharmaceutical researchers, has raised $110 million in funding.
    • Bessemer led the Series A investment.
    • It has been revealed that small molecules, the building blocks of many drugs, can only neutralize a pathogen after binding to it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    UPDATED 16:17 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

    Boltz PBC, a startup that develops artificial intelligence models for pharmaceutical researchers, has raised $110 million in funding.

    Bessemer led the Series A investment. Boltz stated on Wednesday that the fund was joined by a large group of newly introduced and returning backers. The consortium included Greycroft, Andreessen Horowitz, Amplify Partners, F-Prime Capital, Hummingbird and others.

    It has been revealed that small molecules, the building blocks of many drugs, can only neutralize a pathogen after binding to it. As a result, researchers start drug discovery projects by looking for molecules that have a high binding affinity with pathogens. They often review hundreds of thousands of candidate molecules per project. The process can take months and often costs millions of dollars.

    Boltz offers an AI model called BoltzMol-1 that speeds up the workflow. It generates binding affinity data by reviewing only a few dozen, particularly promising molecules instead of the hundreds of thousands usually needed. The fewer molecules need to be studied, the less time the analysis takes.

    Industry observers note that binding affinity evaluations don’t yield drug discoveries right away. Instead, they produce data points called small molecule hits. Those are essentially faint clues that help researchers pinpoint the area where they should focus their efforts.

    In a recent development, boltz staffers asked BoltzMol-1 to look for small molecule hits across 10 “challenging and therapeutically-relevant targets.” Targets are biological building blocks that play a role in disease processes. According to the company, the model found small molecule hits for six of the targets.

    Sources indicate that scientists can adapt BoltzMol-1 to project-specific constraints. If a research team has access to a relatively limited number of compounds, it could configure the model to only consider small molecules that can be made from those compounds. When material procurement is not an obstacle, BoltzMol-1 evaluates a much larger number of candidates.

    The company also offers a second model called BoltzProt-1. It can generate tens of thousands of protein designs based on data gleaned from small molecule hits. Additionally, BoltzProt-1 automatically reviews each protein to determine if it could be used to develop a latest drug.

    Usually, AI models evaluate protein designs based on rubrics that provide only an indirect view of their effectiveness. BoltzProt-1 uses more direct metrics. The company says that BoltzProt-1’s protein evaluation mechanism demonstrated “higher success” than several competing models during internal tests.

    Boltz sells its algorithms via an application programming interface that is billed based on token usage. According to the company, customers’ token consumption has grown by a factor of 50 since BoltzMol-1 and BoltzProt-1 rolled out in June. Boltz counts six of the world’s 20 largest pharmaceutical companies as clients.

    The company will use its new funding to grow its headcount and procure more computing infrastructure. The extra hardware should make it easier for Boltz to keep up with leading AI labs such as newly public Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group. Over the past year, both companies have introduced models that are highly adapted to biology research tasks.

    Boltz has already started training a fresh generation of molecule design algorithms. The organization indicates that they are “showing substantial improvements” over its current models.

    Lufthansa Management Threatens To Massively Shrink Airline, Lay Off Employees

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1819 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, lufthansa is the “flagship” airline of Lufthansa Group, yet somehow, is the least profitable airline in the whole organization.
    • Industry observers note that unfortunately things haven’t turned out so great.
    • According to recent reports, how is that working out?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, lufthansa is the “flagship” airline of Lufthansa Group, yet somehow, is the least profitable airline in the whole organization. 2026 was supposed to be an exciting turnaround year for Lufthansa, as it’s even the carrier’s 100th anniversary.

    Industry observers note that unfortunately things haven’t turned out so great. Earlier this year, the carrier dealt with massive labor issues, and back-to-back-to-back strikes. Just a few months ago, the organization’s senior management claimed it wanted to turn over a fresh leaf with labor relations, and stop fighting with employees, so that it could find long term solutions.

    According to recent reports, how is that working out? Well, Lufthansa pilots are just days from possibly being able to strike again, no agreement has been reached for long term peace with employees, and management is threatening to massively shrink its mainline operation. In other words, it’s just another day at Lufthansa!

    Recent findings suggest that lufthansa and its pilots have been in negotiations for quite some time over the future of the manufacturer. As you’d expect, broadly speaking, negotiations revolve around pay and future flying opportunities. As you’d expect at any airline, employees want as much flying as possible, and as big of a fleet as possible, since that’s what maximizes their compensation.

    The problem with Lufthansa Group management is that the organization’s solution to everything is to simply create fresh, low cost subsidiaries. And if Lufthansa Group management doesn’t like the terms with its subsidiaries, then it just shuts down the subsidiaries and creates new ones.

    Sources indicate that so that brings us to the current concern. Essentially, Lufthansa’s problem is that the airline doesn’t make money on short haul flights, given high costs and intense competition. So we’ve seen the carrier increasingly outsourcing this flying to Lufthansa City Airlines, a subsidiary with lower operating costs, operating the same kinds of planes as you’ll see in the mainline fleet.

    Recent findings suggest that lufthansa is asking its pilots to accept wage freezes, and is promising a certain level of career development opportunities. Pilots aren’t happy with what’s being proposed, so what’s Lufthansa’s solution?

    Management is reportedly proposing a new initiative to the supervisory board, which would see the core Lufthansa brand massively reduce its regional flying, and largely outsource this to lower cost operations, like Lufthansa City Airlines. The idea would be to make Lufthansa primarily a long haul airline, and then have much of the short haul flying be operated by a subsidiary.

    Sources indicate that lufthansa’s mainline fleet presently consists of 260+ planes, with another 120+ planes on order. One proposal would see the mainline fleet reduced to 100 long haul aircraft and 100 short haul aircraft, with other planes being assigned to Lufthansa City Airlines.

    One radical proposal could even see Lufthansa exclusively have a long haul fleet and ditch short haul flying, though it’s noted that this isn’t the most likely scenario, and it could take several years for something like that to be implemented.

    Keep in mind that going back to 2017, Lufthansa had guaranteed pilots a minimum fleet size of 325 aircraft, but it terminated that agreement at the end of 2021. So it’s really hard for employees to trust any promises by management, when they can just be terminated.

    In a recent development, there’s no denying that labor relations can be incredibly challenging, and that the economics of intra-Europe flying are also tough, when you have competitors like Ryanair, though Lufthansa doesn’t face nearly as much competition on that front as other carriers. Then again, Frankfurt (FRA) and Munich (MUC) aren’t exactly massively leisure destinations either.

    Most airline employees want their firm to succeed, and just want to be compensated fairly. Admittedly economics don’t always align. But what I find incredibly toxic is the approach taken by Lufthansa management. Let’s compare it to a marriage (which I think is a fair way to view the relationship between management and employees, since they’re “stuck” with one another).

    Lufthansa’s approach is to constantly threaten employees by saying that “if you don’t do what we want, we’ll just get rid of you.” That’s simply not a good faith way to approach things. Why would Lufthansa employees trust management, when they’ve repeatedly torn up contracts, and shown employees they simply don’t care? It would be like threatening to leave your spouse every time you have an problem, rather than trying to find a solution.

    In a recent development, nothing against Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr personally, but I don’t understand how the board thinks he’s the best person for the job. Where’s the accountability for the endless management mistakes that have horribly impacted Lufthansa’s bottom line? Lufthansa’s employees are paying the price for the lack of success that comes as a result of all of Lufthansa’s errors, from the botched Allegris rollout, to Lufthansa’s very bad luck with upcoming aircraft orders.

    And before anyone says “oh, but the unions,” contrast what has happened at Lufthansa Group to what has happened at Air France-KLM, under the leadership of Ben Smith. Smith has now been CEO at Air France for over eight years, and there hasn’t been a single strike under his leadership. Under the previous Air France-KLM CEO, there were endless strikes, and the situation got so bad that senior executives were being chased up a fence and having their clothes ripped off.

    This shows that good labor relations absolutely can happen, balancing the needs of employees and the company. But it requires showing employees that you actually care about the company and their future. What was one of Smith’s first orders of business when he took the job at Air France-KLM? He eliminated Joon, the low cost carrier at the airline that was supposed to basically be a labor arbitrage opportunity. That was a way to show employees how much he respected them, and that he wanted a fair agreement, rather than one that would undermine them.

    It has been revealed that meanwhile Spohr’s solution to literally everything is to just threaten to start upcoming subsidiaries or shut down existing subsidiaries. The irony is that Spohr started his career as a pilot, so you’d think he’d have respect for employees, having been on the other side. But clearly once he became senior management, his love for aviation turned into disdain for employees.

    Sources indicate that A few months ago, Lufthansa management claimed it wanted to turn over a new leaf when it comes to labor relations. That didn’t last long, because now the airline is back to its “do what we say or we’ll create a new subsidiary” approach.

    I don’t have a strong opinion on the exact negotiations as such. Obviously it’s a tough time for aviation, and intra-Europe flying is challenging. But if you ask me, the toxicity that has been created by Lufthansa management due to the lack of good faith negotiations just can’t be undone.

    In a recent development, if your only solution to everything is “oh, we’ll create a newly introduced subsidiary,” and if that doesn’t work, maybe it’s time for a new strategy. The fact that American CEO Robert Isom and Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr still have their jobs are two of the industry’s greatest mysteries.

    The Bilt Palladium Card is one of my favorite credit cards, and it’s the card that gets the most of my spending. Just to cover some of the very basics, the card has a $495 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and offers the following value proposition at the moment:.

    For me, the logic of picking up this card is pretty straightforward, and I’ve shared that in much more detail. In other words, this card earns me 3x points on up to $25,000 of spending per year, plus I’m being rewarded on my housing spending.

    According to recent reports, points with Bilt rack up really swiftly, so if you spend quite a bit on credit cards, I do think this is tough to beat. And this doesn’t even account for the value of the hotel credit, as you can stack the credit card’s hotel credit with some Bilt Cash to get an even bigger discount on a hotel stay.

    Industry observers note that as I’ve covered, changes are coming to Bilt as of 2027. While the changes are being made in the name of “simplifying” things, I’d argue that it only creates even more complexity, at least for existing members. Essentially, starting in 2027, Bilt members will earn points for their housing payment as a percentage of their card spending, in lieu of earning 4% back in Bilt Cash on all their spending.

    In a recent development, the good news is that through December 31, 2026, you can still opt into the old system for being rewarded, and that will then be honored in 2027 and beyond. This applies both to existing cardmembers, and those who pick up the card before then, and select this as their earnings preference.

    I think the Bilt Palladium can still absolutely be worth it under the new system, where you’d be rewarded on housing payments per the below, and would also earn $600 in Bilt Cash annually (starting in 2027), but without the 4% back in the form of Bilt Cash on spending.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that included in this year's Cyber Week drop for AAdvantage® members is the Alpha Industries MA-1 Flight Jacket.
    • Industry observers note that the MA-1 Flight Jacket is available exclusively for purchase with AAdvantage® miles on the AAdvantage Exchange℠ marketplace.
    • American Airlines provided the clothing brand MA-1 with 650 used airline seats from across its historic fleet.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that included in this year's Cyber Week drop for AAdvantage® members is the Alpha Industries MA-1 Flight Jacket. This garment is made from reclaimed leather from the airline's most iconic aircraft, celebrating its 100th anniversary of flight. One of the jets included is American Airlines' McDonnell Douglas MD-80s.

    Industry observers note that the MA-1 Flight Jacket is available exclusively for purchase with AAdvantage® miles on the AAdvantage Exchange℠ marketplace. The jacket is available from November 30 to December 4 and costs 200,000 miles each.

    American Airlines provided the clothing brand MA-1 with 650 used airline seats from across its historic fleet. The brand, famous in music, streetwear, and fashion, decided to strip the seats of their leather and use them to create a patchwork material for the jacket's exterior. The effect is a traditional bomber jacket with a unique texture and weight. The garment includes a ribbon stating "remove before flight" on the left sleeve.

    In a promotional video for American Airlines, a representative from Alpha Industries said:.

    "This was really the most complicated product we've ever made. Each jacket required 10 to 12 seats... [For] each jacket, there's hours of labor. Understanding the logistics process behind this was crazy.".

    This Cyber Week, Black Friday, and Travel Tuesday, American Airlines has put together several exclusive offers for AAdvantage members, including the ability to purchase a bomber jacket built from reclaimed aircraft seats. For example, you can purchase 500,000 or more miles at a 50% discount.

    The Instagram post highlights exciting AAdvantage developments debuted by American Airlines in recent months, including the ability to combine miles and dollars to access rewards. However, it doesn't seem that AAdvantage members will be able to do this when purchasing the limited-edition bomber if they don't have the required 200,000 miles. The ability to purchase more miles at a discounted rate could be the right pathway to jacket ownership for some members.

    Sources indicate that american Airlines has also made a range of gifts available for travelers and aviation enthusiasts. This includes heritage-inspired suitcases designed in collaboration with July and limited-edition American Airlines x Volair pickleball paddles. It goes to show that miles can mean merchandise, not just an upgrade or a ticket.

    The jacket celebrates American Airlines heritage by reusing leather from 650 seats from the airline's retired fleet. The most iconic aircraft involved is the MD-80, which the airline stopped flying in 2019. This jet can carry 150 passengers up to 2,550 nautical miles (4,720 km). The carrier originally leased 20 of these jets in 1982, using them to replace its Boeing 727-100 fleet. The MD-80 was also American Airlines' first jet that could fly with just two pilots, rendering the flight engineer role obsolete.

    Air Fleets data indicates that American Airlines had a total of 384 MD-80s in its fleet at different times. The airline used the jet as a cross-country regional workhorse. It facilitated this type of traffic outside its main networks.

    Sources indicate that age was the main reason that American Airlines retired its MD-80s. The series was approaching 40 years old, and some of American Airlines' active MD-80s were approaching 20 years old. As with any airliner, the aging jet was no longer fuel-efficient, reliable, or suited to its role, with modern alternatives like the Airbus A320 series and the Boeing 737 MAX. Retiring the aircraft also allowed American Airlines to achieve a greater degree of fleet commonality, reducing pilot training, maintenance, and certification costs.

    Intuit sells Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68B, less than a third of what it paid
