    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that there’s something I really love about staying in a hotel room on a really high floor, where you’re so high up that you almost feel like you’re in an airplane.
    • In a recent development, the question of which hotel is the tallest and highest isn’t as straightforward as you might assume.
    • It has been revealed that generally speaking, the tallest hotel would be defined as the tallest building where a large percent of the structure is made up of the hotel.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that there’s something I really love about staying in a hotel room on a really high floor, where you’re so high up that you almost feel like you’re in an airplane. So, what are the tallest and highest hotels in the world? I want to talk about that in this post, and also discuss why the answer isn’t that straightforward.

    In a recent development, the question of which hotel is the tallest and highest isn’t as straightforward as you might assume. And even once we do define it, there’s the question of the extent to which the answer is actually useful. First let’s cover the distinction between the tallest hotel and the highest hotel.

    It has been revealed that generally speaking, the tallest hotel would be defined as the tallest building where a large percent of the structure is made up of the hotel. Most commonly, I see people suggest that this would include situations where at least 80% of the building is the hotel.

    This is different than the highest hotel, which would be the hotel that is highest above the ground, even if it only takes up a small percentage of a mixed-use building, where there might be apartments, residences, etc.

    In other words, a 50-story building that consists exclusively of a hotel would fall into the former category, while a 110-story building where the top 10 floors are a hotel would fall into the latter category.

    With that out of the way, let’s talk about the properties that are remarkable in these categories….

    First, let’s cover some of the world’s tallest hotels. We’ll define this as hotels where at least 80% of the building consists of the hotel facility.

    Sources indicate that let me of course mention one downside of very tall standalone hotels — you could end up being on a very low floor. After all, if a high-rise consists exclusively (or almost exclusively) of hotel facilities, some people will end up on very low floors. The other downside, of course, is that these hotels are necessarily huge. If you prefer boutique hotels, you won’t find any on this list.

    Presently, the tallest hotel in the world is Ciel Tower Dubai. The 1,042-room hotel opened in 2024, rises to a height of 1,227 feet (374 meters), and has 82 floors.

    To go over the list of the top five tallest hotels in the world:.

    As you can see, it’s interesting (but perhaps not surprising) that all four of the world’s tallest hotels are in Dubai.

    Industry observers note that the Conrad Shanghai, meanwhile, is located in the Shimao International Plaza, and this is the perfect example of how it’s tough to define what is technically the tallest. While the building it’s in rises to such a high height, roughly 25% of that height is the spire. So technically it’s a very tall building, but the usable space isn’t as high as you’d assume.

    In a recent development, if you ask me, the world’s highest hotels are much more interesting than the world’s tallest hotels. That’s because the world’s highest hotels typically take up the top floors of some gravity-defying skyscrapers, and therefore, they can also be boutique properties.

    When defining the world’s tallest hotels, there are some general challenges:.

    Because of the above, there are some minor disagreements as to which hotel wins the title, but I’ll share my take (while acknowledging that I don’t have the ability to scale buildings with a measuring tape).

    In a recent development, at the moment, the highest hotel is the Rosewood Guangzhou. The 251-room hotel opened in 2019, and it’s located at the top of the CTF Finance Centre Guangzhou, which reaches a height of 1,739 feet (530 meters).

    To go over the list of the top five highest hotels in the world:.

    As you can see, those last two properties are kind of hard to judge, and particularly J Hotel Shanghai is tricky, given that the property is split between different parts of the building.

    As the inverse of the above, I should mention that the Armani Hotel Dubai is located within the Burj Khalifa, which is the world’s tallest building. However, it’s located at the very bottom of the building, so that’s hardly that useful, for these purposes, since the hotel only goes as high as 39 floors.

    Lastly, in the interest of being thorough, if we’re going to define a hotel as being “highest” based on the altitude above sea level, then we’d of course end up with a completely different list. Hotel Tayka del Desierto is located near the Salar de Uyuni salt flats in Bolivia. It’s at an altitude of 14,800 feet (4,500 meters), so it’s generally considered to be the highest up hotel in the world.

    I suppose depending on how we want to define “hotel,” there would probably be some simple guest houses at Everest Base Camp that go even higher, but I don’t think that’s within the spirit of what I’m trying to cover here.

    Recent findings suggest that if you ask me, it’s always fun to stay in a hotel room that’s really high up. There’s an important distinction between the tallest hotels and the highest hotels, though sometimes, the exact rankings are a bit blurred.

    While I’ve long been interested in this, I enjoyed researching this a bit more closely, and actually having a (sort of) definitive list. Ciel Tower Dubai is the world’s tallest hotel, while the Rosewood Guangzhou is the world’s highest hotel (unless you want to consider the 120th floor of the J Hotel Shanghai separately from the rest of the property).

    Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of concerns even as he appears politically weakened at home.

    It has been revealed that trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal. But before he left, Trump signaled the three-way talks also likely would include the artificial intelligence race, Moscow’s bloody war with Ukraine, global trade and his standoff with Iran.

    The U.S. commander in chief’s tendency to sound deferential to Putin and habit of referring to Xi as a personal “friend” concerns many congressional Democrats. But Trump’s GOP allies on Capitol Hill, despite this month’s midterm election losses, still describe him as a dealmaker who has a chance to use his final years to bend Putin and Xi toward U.S. interests.

    Rick Scott, a Florida Republican who sits on the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, mentioned Tuesday he was hopeful that Trump could make some progress on at least one problem with the Russian and Chinese leaders.

    It has been revealed that “As we all know, China and Russia want to destroy our way of life,” he said. “But it would be great to reduce … nuclear stockpiles and make sure we're not going to ever get attacked.

    Still, Scott sounded skeptical about two world leaders Trump has tried to keep close during his two terms. “But do I trust Xi or Putin? No, they're a bunch of liars.” Asked if he worries Trump might trust them too much, Scott replied: “I don't think he trusts him any more than I do. … I'm glad the president's trying. Hope springs eternal. But do I actually really believe something good's going to come out of it? I don't.”.

    Outgoing House Armed Services Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., remarked part of Trump’s talks on Thursday “should be to make sure the world is a safer place, to make sure we don't have aggressive behavior like Russia in an unprovoked attack against Ukraine.

    “They ought to be talking about how they don't do those sorts of things, how they don't threaten their neighbors, how they don't try to intimidate through the assertion of force that they ought to be able to work together to make sure we assure a safe globe,” remarked Wittman, who lost his reelection race earlier this month.

    That comment came one day after Trump told reporters as he left the White House for Asia that he sees Putin “backing down a little bit” in his conduct of the war with Ukraine.

    “I think he could be tougher. I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” Trump remarked Monday. “I think he's backing down.”.

    Those kinds of deferential remarks about the Russian leader are a significant reason why some Democrats have heartburn about Thursday’s meeting.

    Recent findings suggest that senate Armed Services member Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, noted Tuesday that she’s concerned about the Shenzhen summit because “I’m not sure what’s going to pop out of [Trump’s] mouth next — especially for a meeting with two guys he clearly likes.”.

    According to recent reports, sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., also a member of the Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, remarked he has “high hopes” for the trilateral meeting — but “maybe not high expectations.”.

    “I have some points of anxiety. I'm nervous about any discussion about Ukraine that doesn't involve the Ukrainians. And, so, some of the advance to this is like, ‘We're going to talk about ending the Ukraine war.’ You can't do that without Ukraine at the table,” Kaine mentioned. “So the desire to bring about more peace and stability, that's a good thing to talk about. But no conditions about Ukraine and ending that war without them at the table? Not so sure about that.”.

    During remarks Tuesday on the Senate floor, Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer criticized what he described as Trump’s misplaced priorities.

    Industry observers note that “Enforcement of the new rules restricting China’s access to our most sensitive AI chips should start today,” the New York Democrat stated, adding that Trump should focus more of his Asia swing on securing commitments from U.S. allies to block China from gaining an upper hand in the AI technology race.

    Trump touted just that on Tuesday during remarks in Manila at a U.S.-Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in the Philippines.

    Recent findings suggest that “Since I returned to office, we've made major trade deals with Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia, as well as Japan, South Korea, and almost everybody, frankly, at the table,” he mentioned. “And we've made many other vital agreements across the region spanning energy, critical minerals and technology.”.

    But on Wednesday, Trump appeared to have pivoted to the trip’s main event.

    According to recent reports, he stood beside Xi at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen and smiled as Putin approached. Trump extended his hand and shook Putin’s as the Chinese leader looked on.

    Scott, a Trump ally in the Senate, said Tuesday he sees the president “trying to build relationships to try to make sure we don't end up at war [because] he doesn't like war.”.

    In a recent development, trump signaled Monday that he might press Xi for details on an alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, costing the AI mogul his job as the organization’s president and CEO. He also remarked he could bring up Nvidia’s sales of sophisticated microchips that many lawmakers — Republican and Democrat — want to ensure remain in the U.S. for domestic AI development.

    It has been revealed that the administration’s response to the turmoil at Nvidia, with Trump even suggesting he'd support Huang returning as CEO, is a rare area where Republicans have expressed concern publicly. House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie, R-Kent., wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Wednesday seeking information about “the implementation of federal laws governing technology exports, in particular the application of export controls relating to semiconductor chips, the effect of which has a broad impact on America’s race with China to artificial intelligence (AI) dominance and the ability of U.S. companies to set global technology standards.”.

    Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Issues at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote this week that for the three leaders, the “path is fraught with challenges.”.

    Sources indicate that “Putin could diplomatically outmaneuver the Trump administration and make any progress on nuclear concerns dependent on undermining Western support to Ukraine,” she wrote in an analysis for the Washington, D.C.-based think tank. “Even the optics of Trump and Putin negotiating while the war continues and as Russia ramps up missile strikes on Ukrainian civilian targets could be interpreted as undermining U.S. values.”.

    UPDATED 07:16 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

    Industry observers note that data center backlash is pushing builders to show communities what they get in return, and public-private partnerships are becoming one answer. As the race for sovereign AI heats up, the question is shifting from where intellectual property lives to where compute runs and who profits from it.

    Canada offers a sharp test case. A modern data hall employs few people, but its profits can fund the startups and jobs a region needs, according to Sharif Virani (pictured), chief executive officer of SPUR Innovation Center.

    According to recent reports, “There’s a major misnomer right now in the world that’s kind of landing from previous tech, where people think where your IP is where the wealth creation is going to be,” he said. “It’s not the case anymore. You have to make sure your inference happens in your country or in your region.”.

    Recent findings suggest that virani spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and host Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed sovereign AI, reinvesting data center profits in local entrepreneurs and winning over residents through public-private partnerships. (* Disclosure below.).

    It has been revealed that SPUR treats its Waterloo, Ontario, site as an innovation campus with an attached data hall rather than a pure data center. The firm reinvests about 10 percent of the campus’s data center profits in local entrepreneurs through a venture studio and takes first right of refusal on their office space and compute, Virani explained. Canada’s Dominion List counts more than 500 founders who have left for San Francisco, he noted.

    According to recent reports, “We have entrepreneurship at an all-time low, productivity at an all-time low [and] GDP in freefall,” he said. “That’s really the result. We’ve got to reverse that.”.

    Sources indicate that one of SPUR’s early investments went to two international students who had full scholarships to the University of Toronto and internships lined up in San Francisco. Instead, they introduced a startup called Auditorium AI and hired staff, according to Virani. The model also reaches Main Street, where on-campus hackathons helped a former long-haul trucker build AI software for logistics.

    “AI allows these people who know the problem, who have earned the right to solve the problem, to mobilize technology to do it and make the lives of their friends, families and neighbors better,” Virani said.

    Delta Air Lines Cancels 3-Hour Route After 15 Months: See Map Now

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (654 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Airlines routinely churn through routes, particularly those with lower load factors or poor yields, and Delta Air Lines is no exception.
    • Sources indicate that in its latest weekend schedule upgrade, the SkyTeam member confirmed that it is ending its service between Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC) and Clinton National Airport (LIT) in Little Rock, Arkansas.
    • It has been revealed that the route was indeed an interesting addition to Delta’s network when it launched.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Airlines routinely churn through routes, particularly those with lower load factors or poor yields, and Delta Air Lines is no exception. The carrier has withdrawn from several markets this year, including some underperforming international routes.

    Sources indicate that in its latest weekend schedule upgrade, the SkyTeam member confirmed that it is ending its service between Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC) and Clinton National Airport (LIT) in Little Rock, Arkansas. Delta launched the route in September last year only. Interestingly, it was among several routes the airline temporarily suspended earlier this summer amid rising jet fuel prices.

    It has been revealed that the route was indeed an interesting addition to Delta’s network when it launched. It has been serving Little Rock for decades, but primarily from its main hub at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL), where it currently offers six to seven daily flights. For passengers traveling from Salt Lake City, which is Delta's fourth-largest hub, by scheduled departures, this meant flying east to Atlanta before connecting to Little Rock.

    Delta Air Lines last SLC–LIT flight schedule.

    Salt Lake City – Little Rock (local time).

    Little Rock – Salt Lake City (local time).

    Industry observers note that so, the introduction of a nonstop service provided a more convenient option. Presently, the route is served by SkyWest Airlines, which operates a daily flight on behalf of Delta using Embraer E175 aircraft. The service was also scheduled to operate daily next summer using the same aircraft type. However, according to data from aviation analytics provider Cirium, the last scheduled flight on the route will take place on December 31, 2026.

    Looking at data from the US Department of Transportation (DOT), it is perhaps unsurprising that the SkyTeam member has decided to axe the route. The latest available figures, which cover the period from September 2025 to August 2026, show that the service carried 27,538 passengers, with an average load factor of 71.6%. However, this is just one factor.

    Airlines do not necessarily remove routes simply because of lower load factors, especially if they generate good yields or bring connecting passengers into their hubs. In this case, Delta may have hoped that the route would bring more connecting traffic through Salt Lake City. But despite the size of its hub, around 57% of passengers traveled only between Little Rock and Salt Lake City, rather than connecting onwards to other destinations.

    In addition, the route also performed poorly in terms of revenue. After adjusting for flight distance, it ranked fifth-lowest for total revenue per available seat mile (TRASM) among more than 90 markets served by Delta from Salt Lake City. Nevertheless, the airline will continue to serve Little Rock from its Atlanta hub, with six to seven daily flights, as well as from Newly introduced York LaGuardia Airport (LGA), with six weekly services.

    Industry observers note that while the Atlanta-based airline is saying goodbye to one destination from Salt Lake City, it is also adding newly introduced routes from the hub. Starting June 7, 2027, it will launch twice-daily, year-round nonstop flights to Flagstaff, Arizona, operated by SkyWest Airlines on its behalf. Another addition to its network is Monterey Peninsula Airport (MRY), which the carrier is scheduled to begin serving on December 19, 2026. Notably, this will mark its return to Monterey after nearly two decades.

    Recent findings suggest that overall, according to Cirium data, Delta has scheduled around 56,400 flights from Salt Lake City for summer 2027, compared to 52,859 during the previous summer season (approximately 6.7% more). The airline will offer more than 200 daily departures and over 250 on peak days.

    Unsurprisingly, Atlanta will remain its busiest destination from Salt Lake City next summer, with eight daily flights, followed by Los Angeles with seven daily services and Seattle with five to six. Among international destinations, Vancouver will see the most flights, with up to three daily departures on peak summer days.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, american Airlines offers a small business rewards program, known as the AAdvantage Business program. This is a great way to earn extra rewards for your travel on American, including qualifying for bonus Loyalty Points and miles.

    Best of all, eligibility for the program is surprisingly simple, assuming you have the Citi® / AAdvantage Business™ World Elite Mastercard® (learn more). There’s often even a bonus for upcoming AAdvantage Business members, making it even more rewarding.

    Industry observers note that in this post, I’d like to take a look at all of the details of the AAdvantage Business program, as many people find it to be quite complicated. Note that AAdvantage Business was launched in 2023, replacing the previous American Business Extra program, which no longer exists.

    AAdvantage Business is the name of American Airlines’ business rewards program. This allows you to earn extra rewards in a business account, in addition to the rewards you can earn through your own AAdvantage account. Best of all, you have quite a bit of flexibility in terms of distributing the rewards. Let’s go over the details of how this works.

    The AAdvantage Business program has a pretty straightforward rewards structure, as it rewards members with both Loyalty Points and AAdvantage miles. With the AAdvantage Business program, you earn the following rewards, which will post within 72 hours of an eligible flight:.

    Let me emphasize that business travelers only earn Loyalty Points through AAdvantage Business when the business is presently eligible to transfer miles, and that requires either having the Citi AAdvantage Business Card, or having at least five unique travelers who have credited flights to the AAdvantage Business account, totaling at least $5,000 in flight revenue, over the course of a year (the credit card method is obviously easier).

    Just to clarify a few additional points about AAdvantage Business rewards:.

    These rewards are all in addition to the standard rewards that AAdvantage members receive:.

    Just to be crystal clear, an Executive Platinum member ordinarily earns 11 Loyalty Points per dollar spent on airfare, while if enrolled in the AAdvantage Business program, they’d earn 12 Loyalty Points per dollar spent. There’s no reason to leave those bonus rewards on the table!

    In order to be eligible to participate in the AAdvantage Business program, you need to have a business in the United States or Canada with a Federal Employer Identification Number (FEIN) or Business Number. Even small businesses are eligible for this program.

    Industry observers note that the exceptions are that travel agencies, consolidators, wholesalers, and other sellers of travel, aren’t eligible to participate in AAdvantage Business. On top of that, AAdvantage Business technically can’t be used for leisure travel.

    You accrue rewards in the AAdvantage Business program without any minimums, and then you can transfer the rewards to individual members, so that they can then redeem them out of their own accounts. In order to transfer the miles in the AAdvantage Business account to an individual AAdvantage account, you need to meet one of two requirements:.

    Industry observers note that the AAdvantage Business program creates a huge incentive to get the Citi AAdvantage Business Card. That’s because just having the card allows many people to unlock the value of the AAdvantage Business program — there’s no need to actually use the card for your spending, but just having it is all that’s needed to redeem AAdvantage Business program rewards with no minimum on the number of travelers or revenue.

    There are several potentially useful perks to this card, and on top of that, the card is offering a great welcome bonus, which is the reason that I applied for the card (and got approved), as that’s a nice incentive, beyond the value of access to the AAdvantage Business program.

    It’s worth understanding how closely this card is actually integrated into the AAdvantage Business program:.

    For American frequent flyers with a small business, this creates a strong incentive to get the card. The card has a reasonable annual fee that’s waived the first year, and just having the card will allow many people to earn a sizable number of bonus miles.

    Recent findings suggest that if you’re curious about how the AAdvantage Business program works in practice, let me share some screenshots, for those who are more visual. Once you have an AAdvantage Business account, you’ll automatically become the travel manager for the account, and that means you can invite others to join your account (these should be people who work for your company, but there’s no verification process, as far as I know).

    According to recent reports, I should also mention that you can designate others to be travel managers as well, so that they can also invite others, transfer miles to people, etc. Travel managers must also be AAdvantage members who are adults and are residents of the United States or Canada.

    To go through the process of inviting others to join your account, you’ll want to click “Invite people,” and then once they accept your invitation, they’ll show up on your account.

    If someone’s AAdvantage account is linked to an AAdvantage Business program account, you’ll see that when you go to make a booking on aa.com, you’ll be asked for your “Travel type,” and can select “Business” or “Personal.” If you select “Business,” you’ll see that the company name populates, and you can select the name of the traveler.

    Note that AAdvantage Business bookings are limited to one passenger, so if you have multiple people traveling, you’ll need to book as separate reservations. Also, to state the obvious, AAdvantage award tickets don’t qualify.

    Industry observers note that while the Loyalty Points from flights will post directly to the AAdvantage account of the member, the redeemable miles will post to the AAdvantage Business program account (the same is true for miles earned on the Citi AAdvantage Business Card). If you want to redeem miles, the only option is to transfer them to individual members, as you can’t redeem the miles directly out of the AAdvantage Business account.

    Recent findings suggest that if you’re eligible to transfer those miles, you’ll see the mileage balance listed, plus a “Transfer miles” button. There’s also a dashboard that shows your eligible number of travelers and eligible spending. However, as you can see above, I’ve met the transfer conditions even though I haven’t met the required threshold, since I have the Citi AAdvantage Business Card.

    It has been revealed that the process of transferring miles is super easy. You’ll just enter how many miles you want to transfer, and who you want to transfer them to, and then they should post to the AAdvantage account instantly.

    My general take on the AAdvantage Business program is as follows:.

    In a recent development, the program basically offers an incremental 1.5% return on your American spending, since you earn one extra AAdvantage mile per dollar spent, and based on my miles & points valuations, those are worth 1.5 cents each. On top of that, the program offers an incremental Loyalty Point per dollar spent — that will have no value to some, while it will have significant value to others, depending on the extent to which you’re pursuing status in the coming year.

    Sources indicate that it is interesting the extent to which American has basically given up on corporate travel. American’s priority is getting people to book direct and keeping distribution costs as low as possible. So this program is intended as the major incentive for most small businesses.

    Sources indicate that american Airlines offers the AAdvantage Business program. With this program, the business earns one AAdvantage mile per dollar spent on eligible airfare, while the individual traveler earns one Loyalty Point per dollar spent. In order to participate and be able to redeem miles, you need a business with at least five registered employees who have each taken at least one eligible flight, along with $5,000 in annual spending, or you need to have the Citi AAdvantage Business Card.

    What do you make of the AAdvantage Business program?

    In a recent development, membership is free and takes no more information than commenting as a guest. Earn status points for good contributions, and see fewer ads as your status grows.

    In a recent development, dozens of passengers across two separate transatlantic Condor flights became ill, causing a mass casualty incident response at Frankfurt Airport (FRA), as reported by aeroTELEGRAPH. While this is still being investigated, there’s a theory as to what happened, given what all passengers had in common….

    On Saturday, November 21, 2026, Condor operated two flights from La Romana, Dominican Republic (LRM), to Frankfurt, Germany (FRA). Both flights were operated by the Airbus A330-900neo, with as many as 620 passengers onboard.

    Flight DE3705 took off at 8:03PM on Saturday and landed at 9:23AM on Sunday, while DE3845 took off at 9:14PM on Saturday and landed at 10:35AM on Sunday. The flights had one thing in common, which is that between them, dozens of passengers became ill.

    Industry observers note that the illnesses onboard were so bad that a “MANV 25” response was triggered at Frankfurt Airport. That’s a German emergency response alert for a mass casualty incident — “Massenanfall von Verletzten” (though fortunately there were no fatalities here).

    Passengers onboard were screened by medical teams, and one person on each flight was taken to a local hospital, while others are being monitored.

    Industry observers note that it’s not uncommon to hear stories of multiple people becoming sick on flights. Sometimes it’s a fume event, sometimes it could be a case of food poisoning (though it doesn’t usually happen that fast), etc. So what’s going on here, that people on two separate Condor flights became ill?

    Well, the passengers on these two flights had one thing in common — they all came off the AidaBella cruise ship in La Romana, and then these flights were sold as part of the cruise package.

    It has been revealed that so while this is still being investigated, a norovirus outbreak on the cruise ship is believed to be the likely culprit. I’ve gotta say, an airplane seems like a pretty unpleasant place to come down with a gastrointestinal illness, so I imagine the lavatory situation onboard probably wasn’t great.

    Dozens of passengers on two separate Condor flights between the Dominican Republic and Germany around the same time became ill, triggering an emergency response at Frankfurt Airport, which included a couple of people being hospitalized.

    Sources indicate that while it remains to be seen what caused this, the belief is that it could be some sort of a norovirus outbreak, based on the symptoms, as well as the fact that the passengers had all come off the same cruise ship. I hope everyone makes a quick recovery.

    Enterprise AI hits a wall of power and cooling, not GPU supply

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (901 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that enterprises racing to build AI factories and push edge inference into the field are learning that buying graphics processing units is the easy part.
    • Those physical limits shaped much of the high-performance computing and AI conversation at SC26, where commercial AI infrastructure increasingly shares the floor with scientific computing.
    • “When we look at the full stack, we recognize that customers are getting tripped up.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    UPDATED 07:55 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

    Industry observers note that enterprises racing to build AI factories and push edge inference into the field are learning that buying graphics processing units is the easy part. Power, cooling and network throughput now decide whether those costly systems produce intelligence or sit idle.

    Those physical limits shaped much of the high-performance computing and AI conversation at SC26, where commercial AI infrastructure increasingly shares the floor with scientific computing. Rack densities that once topped out at about 10 kilowatts are now on a path toward a megawatt, a step change that forces enterprises to look both above and below the traditional network, storage and compute layers, according to Jack Hogan (pictured), senior vice president of advanced growth technologies at SHI International Corp.

    “When we look at the full stack, we recognize that customers are getting tripped up. They can go get the GPUs, but they can’t power them. They can’t cool them,” Hogan stated. “These are not cheap systems either. Procuring the infrastructure is just the start.”.

    Industry observers note that hogan spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed edge inference and how power, networking, model choice and business outcomes are reshaping the way enterprises build and run AI infrastructure. (* Disclosure below.).

    According to recent reports, the economics of AI infrastructure are shifting along with the hardware. Enterprises once sized deployments by the rack unit or the rack, but entire data centers now operate as a single system with shared memory, and every GPU must be kept fed to justify its cost. That change has altered how SHI measures success, Hogan explained.

    In a recent development, “Now we’re talking about row and now data center scale. … We’re measuring that now in megawatts,” Hogan remarked. “So the megawatt now starts to become a measurement that people start to grasp and understand. How many flops can you get through that megawatt? How fast can you process your tokens?”.

    Recent findings suggest that SHI’s role spans the full life cycle of these systems. Drawing on 37 years in the industry, the tech giant builds customized racks in its integration facilities around the globe and runs pre-site assessments so systems can be powered on as soon as they arrive. In a recent Newly introduced Jersey project, SHI is hosting and operating the customer’s system in its own data center. Location matters at the edge, too, where workloads such as video input generate data that must be processed in place, Hogan noted.

    “You can’t backhaul that. The networks are not necessarily the right way to move that,” Hogan noted. “We’re creating the scenario of both the mega hyperscaler as well as the edge inference and be able to tie those two things together.”.

    Busy GPUs are not necessarily productive ones. SHI starts every engagement by asking customers what they are trying to achieve, then works backward to the right model, whether that means frontier intelligence or a small language model running on an edge device. Silicon follows the same logic, with GPUs, newer CPUs, inference-specific chips and neural processing units validated in the company’s AI and Cyber Lab.

    Industry observers note that “It’s not about the cost of the token or reducing the number of tokens or even finding cheaper tokens. It’s about optimizing and ensuring that those tokens are turning into business value,” Hogan noted.

    Qatar Airways Airbus A321LRs With Flat Bed Business Class Launching Soon

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (982 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In the coming weeks, Qatar Airways is expected to take delivery of its first Airbus A321LR, which will be the carrier’s first narrow body aircraft featuring latest generation interiors, including flat beds.
    • Qatar Airways presently has a total of 50 factory fresh Airbus A321-family aircraft on order.
    • Industry observers note that the expectation is that the first A321LR will be delivered in the coming weeks, before the end of 2026.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In the coming weeks, Qatar Airways is expected to take delivery of its first Airbus A321LR, which will be the carrier’s first narrow body aircraft featuring latest generation interiors, including flat beds. The airline will be introducing a “mini-Qsuite” type product on these planes, and we’ve now learned exactly when this new premium narrow body jet will enter service.

    Qatar Airways presently has a total of 50 factory fresh Airbus A321-family aircraft on order. This includes 10 A321LRs and 40 A321neos — both of those are latest generation aircraft, with the A321LR featuring additional range.

    Industry observers note that the expectation is that the first A321LR will be delivered in the coming weeks, before the end of 2026. The 10 A321LRs should join the fleet pretty rapidly, and will then be followed by the A321neos. The A321LRs will be configured with 160 seats, including 16 business class seats and 144 economy class seats.

    According to recent reports, the A321LR has a maximum range of 4,000 nautical miles, so it can be used for many destinations in Europe, Africa, and Asia. Below is a map showing the rough range from Doha (though in reality it won’t be quite as far, accounting for winds, fuel reserves, etc.).

    Now, for those paying close attention, I should acknowledge that Qatar Airways briefly flew six leased, all-economy A321neos, but those were just intended as a temporary solution, and are now flying for Sun PhuQuoc Airways, which is running an interesting operation.

    Qatar Airways’ A321neo-family aircraft order goes back a long time, and involved a lot of drama. The order was first announced in 2011, then the airline reconfirmed and upsized it in 2017. However, then former Qatar Airways CEO Akbar Al Baker got into a fight with Airbus over A350 production quality, and refused to take delivery of any Airbus planes.

    That turned into a massive court battle, which was eventually resolved. But in the process, Qatar Airways lost all of its Airbus delivery slots, which is why these planes are coming way later than initially expected.

    Qatar Airways has been promising all along that it would introduce some sort of a next generation flat bed business class product on its Airbus A321LRs. As you’d expect, business class seats on narrow bodies sometimes differ from those on wide bodies, due to differing cabin constraints.

    What can we expect onboard these Qatar Airways A321LRs in business class? Executive Traveller quotes Qatar Airways CEO Hamad Ali Al-Khater as saying that the newly introduced business class product will be based on the STELIA Aerospace OPERA platform.

    According to recent reports, these planes will boast 16 business class seats, in a 1-1 configuration. This product offers reverse herringbone seats, and Qatar Airways prepares to have doors at each seat as well, of course with its customized finishes.

    Sources indicate that the launch customer for the STELIA Aerospace OPERA platform was Air France on its A350s. However, that’s the wide body version of the seat, which is modified from the narrow body version.

    When it comes to the narrow body version of the STELIA Aerospace OPERA platform, ITA Airways was the launch customer, on its A321neos.

    This is also the product that Etihad is installing on its A321LRs. ITA Airways and Etihad don’t have doors in business class, but Qatar Airways does plan to offer it. Etihad also markets the first row of the cabin as first class (and that has doors), but I wouldn’t expect Qatar Airways to do something similar.

    This is about as good as narrow body business class seats get, as it’s generally preferred to the herringbone seats you’ll find on other carriers, like JetBlue A321LRs, American A321XLRs, etc.

    Qatar Airways now seems pretty certain about the delivery of its upcoming Airbus A321LRs, as the airline has officially put the first routes on sale, as flagged by AeroRoutes:.

    When you pull up the above flights, you’ll now see the seat map for the A321LR, which confirms the 16-seat business class cabin.

    In a recent development, in the coming weeks, Qatar Airways is expected to take delivery of its first of 10 Airbus A321LRs. This will be the first custom designed next generation narrow body that the airline takes delivery of. We knew the airline would offer flat bed seats on these planes, and now we have the details of that.

    According to recent reports, the airline has gone with the STELIA Aerospace OPERA platform, the same product you’ll find on similar planes of Etihad and ITA Airways. However, unlike those airlines, Qatar Airways will have doors in business class. The planes will enter service by very early 2027, flying from Doha to both Vienna and Zurich.

    What do you make of Qatar Airways’ upcoming A321LRs, and the planned interiors?

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In May 2026, we saw American introduce a major fresh restriction for award travel, which had the biggest implications for those redeeming on American through partner programs, like Alaska Atmos Rewards or British Airways Club (in other words, anyone redeeming through a program other than American AAdvantage).
    • With this, American started to restrict its own saver level award availability close to departure.
    • Historically, American has been by far the best of the “massive three” US carriers when it comes to making award seats on its own flights available, especially on domestic and short haul international flights.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In May 2026, we saw American introduce a major fresh restriction for award travel, which had the biggest implications for those redeeming on American through partner programs, like Alaska Atmos Rewards or British Airways Club (in other words, anyone redeeming through a program other than American AAdvantage).

    With this, American started to restrict its own saver level award availability close to departure. Initially, all domestic nonstop saver awards within six days of departure were pulled. In recent days, it looks like American has expanded this to all domestic connecting itineraries as well, so I’d like to cover those details (thanks to azbobcat for flagging this).

    Historically, American has been by far the best of the “massive three” US carriers when it comes to making award seats on its own flights available, especially on domestic and short haul international flights. American actually releases a good amount of saver award seats across cabins, and it’s one of the things that makes AAdvantage better than the competition.

    However, in May 2026, we saw American introduce a major change to how it releases award space to partner frequent flyer programs. Long story short, American started blocking all nonstop, domestic saver award availability, for flights within six days (exactly 144 hours) of departure.

    As soon as a flight gets to the point where it’s 144 hours until departure, you’ll see that the airline “turns off” its saver fare classes — I’m referring specifically to the “U” (saver business class award) and “T” (saver economy award) fare classes, which show up when searching on ExpertFlyer, for example.

    Initially, this applied exclusively to nonstop, domestic award tickets, as connecting itineraries and all international itineraries (including short haul international ones) weren’t impacted by this. However, this seems to have now expanded to domestic connecting itineraries as well.

    So any wholly domestic itinerary exclusively on American is no longer bookable at the saver level within six days of departure. International itineraries continue to be bookable within six days of departure, whether traveling nonstop or with a connection.

    What would cause American to suddenly “shut off” saver awards for domestic routes within days of departure?

    It has been revealed that what’s interesting here is that the implications for AAdvantage members are limited. Yes, American has shut off awards in the saver fare classes, but that’s not to say that American isn’t making reasonably priced awards available within days of departure. American has long used some kind of dynamic award pricing concept for its own flights, regardless of whether or not there’s saver availability.

    It’s just that any awards in the official saver fare buckets aren’t available, and therefore aren’t bookable with points belonging to partner programs.

    It has been revealed that so it sure seems to me that the intent here is to block award availability for those booking through partner programs, like Alaska Atmos Rewards or British Airways Club. It goes without saying that I absolutely hate this restriction, as someone who “funds” a vast majority of my domestic American travel using Atmos Rewards points. At the same time, I also have to say that I can’t blame American for this change, as the airline has just made it too easy.

    Recent findings suggest that I’ve been booking basically all my travel directly into American first class using Atmos Rewards points — I just set ExpertFlyer availability alerts for “U” class, it opens up a vast majority of the time, and then I book. It’s not surprising that American finally got a bit savvier.

    American is now blocking all saver awards within exactly six days of departure for all domestic itineraries. This means within that timeframe, there’s no “U” or “T” availability, which corresponds to the saver business and economy award fare buckets, respectively. Initially this only applied to nonstop flights, while now it also applies to connecting itineraries.

    Recent findings suggest that for American AAdvantage members, the implications are limited, since American can still make reasonably priced awards available, just not formally in those fare buckets. The practical implications here are that partner programs just don’t have access to these award seats close to departure anymore.

    What do you make of American’s six day rule on award tickets?

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    UPDATED 10:00 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

    THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof.

    Anthropic came through with its initial public offering Thursday, but did it just signal a top in the AI trade?

    Recent findings suggest that the artificial intelligence model maker’s IPO went almost picture-perfectly, really, producing a 17% pop that wasn’t so high that it left an excessive amount of money on the table but high enough to call it a success. But it seemed to take some of the air out of AI stocks. Continued worries over AI spending and prospects, as well as factors such as a likely interest-rate hike, dragged down the entire market, including other AI names from Google, Microsoft and Meta to AMD, Broadcom and Nvidia. Asian stocks too.

    In a recent development, and on Friday it got even worse, as the Nasdaq crashed 5.6%. Bye-bye, $4 trillion. No doubt Anthropic stock will be at least as volatile as other AI stocks — today it fell 9% — but it can live with that alongside the more than $90 billion now in its bank account. Now all eyes turn to OpenAI, which finds itself chasing after Anthropic in more ways than one, with plans to go public sometime in next year.

    Nvidia posted its usual better-than-expected earnings this week, which didn’t help its stock much but indicates, along with interim CEO Colette Kress’ bullish comments during the earnings call, that it’s going to be fine for some time to come in disgraced former CEO Jensen Huang’s absence.

    Meantime, Huang remarked he’s open to returning — but that’s not only appallingly premature at best, the board appears adamant it’s not going to happen. The supposed friends clamoring for his return are just reinforcing their selfish, clueless nature, the attitude that has plunged tech into such low esteem that auto salespeople and journalists have more manufacturer now. Maybe those guys on X (always guys) approve of behavior like this.

    What’s with all the outages all over the place? That’s what everyone’s asking, and we looked into what’s behind them all. It doesn’t seem to be the obvious thing — cybersecurity attacks — or really any single cause. Perhaps it’s a lot of 20th century technologies that just aren’t ready for the AI-driven speed of the 21st century, making everything less reliable. Or: All those AI-driven fixes to vulnerabilities are getting done so fast they’re breaking things along the way. Still, is it only a coincidence that the U.S. cyber director just got canned this week?

    Sources indicate that palo Alto Networks remains one of the most acquisitive cybersecurity companies out there, once again laying out a tidy sum this week, buying AI startup Applied Compute $4.5 billion. It’s a sure bet consolidation will accelerate as AI enables more and much faster attacks. Indeed, late Friday came a report that an equally acquisitive CrowdStrike is looking to buy Zscaler, which has been a consistent acquirer itself.

    Next week’s significant earnings reports include Dell, HP, Nutanix, Workday and Zoom. And then we can all take a brief respite for Thanksgiving before gearing up for AWS re:Invent the following week in Las Vegas, with its blizzard of news. SiliconANGLE, theCUBE and theCUBE Research will be onsite with news, analysis and interviews.

    Here’s all of this week’s enterprise and emerging tech news, analysis and commentary from SiliconANGLE and beyond:.

    #145507. FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

    FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (898 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday.
    • The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.
    • Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

    Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.

    The fate of the nominations and bills could ultimately be decided via a challenge on the Senate floor, according to a Democratic committee staffer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

    In a statement Wednesday morning, committee Democrats, led by ranking member  Maria Cantwell of Washington, said they objected to Thumann Severs’ nomination without a Democratic “pair” nomination and referenced a letter they sent to Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Monday requesting the nomination be removed from the agenda.

    In a recent development, “Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times,” the group wrote. “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”.

    Thumann Severs, if confirmed, would give the FCC three Republican members and one Democrat, Gomez. The three Republicans could then constitute a quorum on the commission, allowing President Donald Trump to potentially fire Gomez. The commission generally has five members, three of the president’s party and two in the minority.

    Cruz remarked at the markup that there is nothing in the law that requires moving nominees in pairs, and that committee Republicans would continue their work on what he called a nomination that followed a “typical process.”.

    In a recent development, “Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January,” Cruz said. “But today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent, for our full terms.”.

    Related: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing.

    The Democratic staffer told reporters that because the committee did not adopt rules at the beginning of the 119th Congress, it has been operating under rules from the 118th, which required the attendance of at least one member of the minority party to constitute a quorum for reporting bills or nominations.

    Recent findings suggest that “The remaining recourse is to basically go to the floor and . . . make an inquiry in terms of what took place today, and then there would have to be a formal ruling by the chair,” they remarked.

    They added that in determining whether the committee had a quorum to advance the nomination, “It would depend on how they view our committee rules from the 118th that we practice under for the 119th versus what the Senate rules are.” The staffer noted they have not yet spoken with committee Democrats or Democratic leadership about plans for such an inquiry.

    Democrats also previously boycotted a committee markup in March over an aviation safety bill left off the committee’s agenda, after which action was deferred. The committee later came to agreement and rescheduled the markup.

    In their letter Monday, Democrats quoted Cruz from a 2014 statement about the nomination of Loretta Lynch to be attorney general.

    “As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the letter said.

    On Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee.

    In a recent development, “While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related challenges,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,” Luján wrote.

    Democrats have criticized the FCC and Carr for allowing media consolidation, including by Skydance. There has also been bipartisan criticism of Carr’s threats against broadcasters for speech he disagrees with.

    Luján told reporters Wednesday prior to the markup that he expects, under Democratic control next year, Carr and potentially Thumann Severs would be called to testify.

    It has been revealed that “I have questions. I certainly hope that Brendan Carr will voluntarily show up to this committee when invited, and that other rules and tools do not need to be used,” Luján remarked, responding to a question about possibly subpoenaing Carr. “But . . . everything should be on the table.”.

    Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., stated at the markup that he spoke with Thumann Severs about her role at the FCC and her “lack of engagement” as the commission has made decisions regarding broadcasters. He also said he found her testimony at last week’s nomination hearing “comforting.”.

    “I have concerns with FCC action in regard to political speech, broadcasters, and she indicated in her answers . . . in a way that provided me with a level of comfort about her nomination in regard to that issue,” Moran said.

    Moran also remarked he hopes to meet with Thumann Severs before her nomination is brought to the floor.

    Southwest Airlines Plus Card Review: Modest Benefits For A Low Annual Fee

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2146 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Southwest Airlines and Chase have a great portfolio of co-branded credit cards at a variety of “price points” (and by that I mean annual fees).
    • According to recent reports, in my Southwest Plus Card review, I’ll cover the benefits and explain why now is a good time to consider this card if you want to use credit card spending to earn the Companion Pass.
    • Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Southwest Airlines and Chase have a great portfolio of co-branded credit cards at a variety of “price points” (and by that I mean annual fees). In this post, I’d like to take a closer look at the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card, which is Southwest Airlines’ lowest annual fee credit card.

    According to recent reports, in my Southwest Plus Card review, I’ll cover the benefits and explain why now is a good time to consider this card if you want to use credit card spending to earn the Companion Pass. I’ll also explain why other Southwest cards can be better, and share a great alternative to earning Southwest Rapid Rewards points altogether.

    Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card.

    Before I get into my Southwest Plus Card review, here are some of the key card details:.

    Here are my thoughts on the Southwest Plus Card’s pros and cons:.

    Let’s take a look at the Southwest Plus Card‘s welcome bonus, annual fee, and eligibility rules, as these are some of the most key factors to take into account if you’re considering applying.

    The Southwest Plus Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus: Earn 80,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. This is one of the higher bonuses I’ve seen on this card recently, making now a particularly good time to apply.

    It has been revealed that rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Rapid Rewards points to be worth 1.2 cents each. So to me, the points from this welcome offer are worth $960.

    In terms of Southwest credit card eligibility, the card isn’t available to anyone who right now has a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card, or anyone who has received a welcome bonus on a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card in the past 24 months. However, you are eligible if you have a Southwest business credit card.

    Sources indicate that beyond the restrictions related to which Southwest cards you have, keep in mind the general restrictions for Chase card approvals, including the 5/24 rule. However, there are increasing data points of this no longer being consistently enforced.

    Another rule worth mentioning here involves how Southwest credit card welcome bonuses help you earn the Companion Pass, which lets you bring a companion with you on flights (both cash and award tickets) and pay just taxes and fees.

    It has been revealed that for a long time now, the points earned as part of Southwest credit card welcome bonuses have counted towards the 135,000 qualifying points needed to earn the Companion Pass. But starting soon, credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward qualification.

    Recent findings suggest that you’ll need to apply for a card by December 2, 2026, for your welcome bonus to count toward the Companion Pass for a final time. So apply for this card now if you’re hoping to earn that perk with the help of credit card spending.

    In a recent development, now is also your last chance to get an annual boost of 10,000 Companion Pass qualifying points as a Southwest credit card holder. Starting next year, instead of a boost of 10,000 TQPs for having a Southwest card, you’ll get 10,000 TQPs if your TQP balance is 130,000 by December 31, 2027. That would be enough to get you to Platinum status, which will include unlimited Companion Pass trips as a benefit.

    Sources indicate that this change eliminates the easiest way to earn this valuable benefit, and it’s not the only newly introduced rule: referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending, and partner spending won’t count toward the Companion Pass either. In fact, Southwest’s rolling the Companion Pass into its highest elite tier, Platinum, and requiring either 140,000 TQPs or 100 qualifying flights to earn it.

    The Southwest Plus Card has a $99 annual fee, and you can add authorized users to the card at no extra cost.

    Sources indicate that $99 is the lowest annual fee of any Southwest Airlines credit card. Looking at the high end, Southwest’s personal cards have annual fees of up to $229, and Southwest’s business cards have annual fees of up to $299.

    The Southwest Plus Card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s a solid card to use for purchases abroad.

    As far as the Southwest Plus Card‘s rewards structure goes, the card offers the following:.

    Since I value Southwest Rapid Rewards points at 1.2 cents each, I think you get an effective return of 2.4% on purchases that qualify for 2x points, and a 1.2% return on everything else.

    In a recent development, it’s nice that the card has some bonus categories, though there are ultimately more rewarding cards out there for everyday spending. Plus, a few of the non-Southwest bonus categories have an annual cap, which limits how useful this card is for maximizing your return on gas station and grocery store purchases.

    I have a dedicated post that covers how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but let’s briefly look at how you can use the points you earn from the Southwest Plus Card.

    In a recent development, rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, meaning that the value you get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. There are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares, so the exact value can vary a bit.

    It has been revealed that basic award fares tend to offer the best redemption value. You’ll also usually get the best value on international Southwest routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. I’ve been able to get about 2.0 cents per point on these redemptions.

    Starting in spring 2027, Southwest will add points earning and redemption opportunities with select airline partners, which should make your Rapid Rewards points more valuable for international travel. The planned partners include Icelandair, China Airlines, and Etihad Airways — I look forward to seeing how these add value to the program.

    Sources indicate that one great thing about the Southwest Rapid Rewards program is that there are no change or cancellation fees, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d cancel and rebook rather than change.

    Sources indicate that the Southwest Plus Card offers some benefits that could make the card worth keeping long term. However, this is also Southwest’s lowest annual fee card, so it doesn’t have the most benefits. What are the ongoing perks of having this card?

    Industry observers note that the Southwest Plus Card gets the primary cardholder and up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation a first checked bag at no additional cost. Checked bags on Southwest cost $45 each way, so this can save you up to $90 roundtrip on checked bag fees per person. So with just one roundtrip flight per year, this benefit can almost offset the annual fee.

    Southwest now charges for seat selection, so it’s helpful that the Southwest Plus Card includes complimentary standard seat selection starting 48 hours out from departure. This perk is based on availability, and it could save you around $20 to $40 per flight.

    Sources indicate that another Southwest benefit is early boarding. You’ll be able to board with Group 5, or earlier if you have elite status or a fare or seat type that qualifies you for an earlier boarding group. Southwest has eight total boarding groups, so while there are several ahead of Group 5, it’s better than boarding last.

    Each year on your Southwest Plus Card cardmember anniversary, you’ll get a 10% promo code that applies to Southwest flights. Just note that this discount excludes Basic fares.

    On your Southwest Plus Card cardmember anniversary every year, you’ll receive 3,000 bonus points. Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and you’ll typically need 83 Rapid Rewards points for every dollar of airfare you book. In other words, those 3,000 Rapid Rewards points should get you around $36 worth of airfare on Southwest annually.

    As part of an overhaul of the Rapid Rewards program, Southwest is simplifying TQP earning on credit cards. Starting in 2027, every dollar spent on a co-branded Southwest credit card will earn you one TQP. In other words, $35K in spending would earn you Silver, $65K in spending would earn you Gold, and $140K in spending would earn you Platinum.

    This earning rate is the same across cards, so this isn’t specific to the Southwest Plus Card.

    The Southwest Plus Card offers 25% savings on inflight purchases of Wi-Fi and drinks. Simply pay with your card, and you’ll automatically receive a statement credit for that amount.

    The Southwest Plus Card offers a variety of travel & purchase protection benefits, including:.

    You’ll want to check the cardmember agreement for the full terms & conditions associated with these benefits.

    One of the great features of Chase cards is access to Chase Offers, which provides savings on purchases with all kinds of retailers. This program has saved me a significant amount of money.

    In a recent development, the Southwest Plus Card is a solid entry-level airline credit card. If you want a credit card from Southwest and want an annual fee as low as possible, then this card could make sense to you.

    According to recent reports, you’ll receive a 3,000-point bonus on your cardmember anniversary every year, and 25% savings on inflight purchases. The free checked bag benefit can save you $90 on a roundtrip and the complimentary standard seat selection benefit can add up quickly after a few flights. These perks can more than justify the annual fee, and that’s not even accounting for the massive welcome bonus.

    However, there are other options that I think can make more sense.

    If your main reason for considering the Southwest Rapid Rewards Plus Card is to earn points for Southwest award flights, you might be better off skipping a Southwest co-branded credit card altogether and just earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points. You can transfer Chase points to Southwest to book flights, and cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) have stronger earning categories and benefits overall.

    You can also redeem Ultimate Rewards points with other travel partners, not just Southwest, so this option gives you more flexibility.

    According to recent reports, the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Premier Credit Card (learn more) is one step up from the Southwest Plus Card, with a $149 annual fee. Here’s a look at its key perks:.

    Industry observers note that there’s also the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card (learn more), the most premium personal Southwest card with a $229 annual fee. If you want as many Southwest perks as possible, this is a better pick.

    The Southwest Priority Card’s main perks include:.

    So you’re getting a higher return of 4.8% on Southwest spending on the Priority Card, based on my valuations, and better complimentary seat selection and upgrade options.

    Recent findings suggest that if you want a Southwest Rapid Rewards business credit card in place of or in addition to a personal card, I highly recommend considering the Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card (learn more). The Southwest Performance Business Card offers the following benefits, which make it the best Southwest credit card, in my opinion:.

    The Southwest Performance Business Card offers a lot of points, and more perks overall than other Southwest cards.

    Recent findings suggest that the Southwest Plus Card is a good entry-level credit card for someone who wants to earn Rapid Rewards points without paying a high annual fee. It’s not the most valuable Southwest credit card in the lineup, but its benefits and strong welcome bonus make it a good option at this price point.

    #145505. Own, don’t rent: Why agentic AI is pulling cloud computing back on-prem

    Own, don’t rent: Why agentic AI is pulling cloud computing back on-prem

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (806 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that agentic AI is reviving an argument over renting versus owning compute, and the model plane — the layer that decides where AI models run — sits at the center of it.
    • According to recent reports, that shift favors companies that built early for on-premises cloud infrastructure.
    • According to recent reports, “Cloud computing is great, but the model shouldn’t be exclusively to rent it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    UPDATED 12:46 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

    It has been revealed that agentic AI is reviving an argument over renting versus owning compute, and the model plane — the layer that decides where AI models run — sits at the center of it. Open-source efforts such as Upbound Inc.’s Modelplane route inference across clouds, but many enterprises want the models on hardware they control.

    According to recent reports, that shift favors companies that built early for on-premises cloud infrastructure. Oxide Computer Co., which raised $445 million in October to expand rack production, built its business on the idea that enterprises at scale will want to own their computers, according to Bryan Cantrill (pictured), co-founder and chief technology officer at Oxide.

    According to recent reports, “Cloud computing is great, but the model shouldn’t be exclusively to rent it. You get to a certain scale, as it turns out, you want to own your own computer,” Cantrill noted.

    Cantrill spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed renting versus owning compute, why agentic workloads are moving on-prem and multi-tenancy for isolating those workloads.

    According to recent reports, agentic workloads are driving an explosion in compute demand, and much of it is CPU-heavy work that enterprises would rather own than rent. Economics remains the main reason to bring it in-house, but where models live is a close second, Cantrill explained. That makes the model plane as much a data governance decision as an infrastructure one.

    “There is a real enterprise drive towards open-weight models, and I think you’re going to see more and more of that as people want to run the models on-prem and allow their data to not actually leave,” Cantrill stated.

    Sources indicate that security is the other half. Oxide stripped the UEFI BIOS and baseboard management controller out of its rack to shrink the attack surface, and built public cloud-grade multi-tenancy in from the start. Those early design choices give enterprises a perimeter for isolating agentic workloads, according to Cantrill.

    It has been revealed that “I think multi-tenancy means you’ve got potentially adversarial tenants that are going to be on the same resource,” Cantrill noted. “They’re going to be sharing the same computer, sharing the same network, and they need to do that … without violating the confidentiality, without breaching one another.”.

    In a recent development, the same racks can take on legacy virtualization workloads from customers unhappy with pricing changes at Broadcom Inc.’s VMware business. That lets enterprises run old and new applications on one general-purpose platform, Cantrill noted.

    “You want all that flexibility that you get from elastic compute, but you need it for economic reasons, security reasons, latency reasons,” Cantrill said of the case for on-premises cloud computing. “You need it in your own data center. You want to control your fate.”.

    Tech Report: Delta Is My Preferred Airline Of The “Big Three” US Carriers (Hear Me Out)

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2165 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I’ve never been one to take the easy road, so I thought I’d bite the bullet and talk about my love for Delta in what you might call a baptism of fire.
    • This year, Delta has nudged up to fourth most-flown of the 94 airlines I’ve tried out over the years, and I’d like to share a little bit about why.
    • Sources indicate that starting from the ground, I am a big fan of what Delta is doing with its lounges.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I’ve never been one to take the easy road, so I thought I’d bite the bullet and talk about my love for Delta in what you might call a baptism of fire. Before I jump in, I’m not here screaming that Delta is the best US airline. Far from it. Rather, I’m explaining why, as someone who is not based in the US, Delta is my go-to airline.

    This year, Delta has nudged up to fourth most-flown of the 94 airlines I’ve tried out over the years, and I’d like to share a little bit about why.

    Sources indicate that starting from the ground, I am a big fan of what Delta is doing with its lounges. Stepping inside one of Delta’s newer Sky Clubs, you feel like you’re in the lobby bar of a luxury hotel rather than the corporate canteen-style spaces offered by competitors.

    I know these newer lounges aren’t in every airport yet — Honolulu (HNL) is a notable exception — but lately I’ve found myself enjoying them before the majority of my latest Delta flights departing from a US airport.

    Don’t get me started on the Delta One Lounges: I’ve visited locations at LAX and JFK, and these are without a doubt my favorite airline lounges in the US.

    Sources indicate that stepping onboard, I actually like the planes. In recent times, I’ve flown mainly on its Airbus A320 family aircraft, a few Boeing 757s (which I love), and once on a Boeing 767-300 from Honolulu to LAX.

    I like how they’ve all had seatback screens, I’ve never had an concern using my SkyMiles account to access the fast free WiFi (it’s decent, even though it’s not Starlink), and I’ve never felt uncomfortable on one of Delta’s planes.

    I also have to say, I’ve always had pleasant, if not better-than-your-average service when flying Delta.

    I love a good redemption as much as the next frequent flyer. However, our credit cards in the UK earn us far fewer points than those in the US, so for me, redeeming points is the exception, not the norm.

    As such, I don’t hate on Delta’s SkyMiles for its mostly sky-high redemption rates. Even if finding a one-way in Delta One from Rio or São Paulo to New York for less than 470,000 miles is almost impossible.

    Besides, I credit my Delta flights to my Flying Blue account, which is therefore home to my SkyTeam elite status and miles earned on Delta and all other SkyTeam airlines.

    In a recent development, neither do I fly often enough nor have the funds to unlock top-tier status in all three alliances. Aside from the Virgin Atlantic Gold status I got from a status match and my BA Silver, which expires in April, Flying Blue is the only program whose status I’m actively chasing.

    According to recent reports, as a direct result of Air France and KLM’s membership in the SkyTeam alliance, I actively choose to fly other SkyTeam airlines, such as Delta. Also, thanks to the relationship between Delta and fellow SkyTeam member Aeroméxico, I’ve managed to find great-value cash fares on several occasions when planning travel between Mexico and Canada or the US.

    Sources indicate that I actually used to be a die-hard American boy until the BA Club was sabotaged. In terms of lounges, aircraft comfort, complimentary amenities (like seat back screens and Wi-Fi), and service, Delta has felt like an upgrade.

    For what it’s worth, if status had nothing to do with it, I’d still choose Delta.

    My experience with American, Delta, and United has mainly been on domestic flights around the US, including transcons. In fact, I’ve never flown Delta One, American Flagship, or United Polaris on long-haul international flights. Who knows, my top three could reshuffle once I’ve tried and tested each of those. Maybe I’ll have to have a word with Ben about this….

    I know Delta gets a bad rep, but honestly I have only had pleasant experiences when flying the airline over the years. As long as I’m being loyal to SkyTeam, it will remain my preference when traveling to or around the US (unless it’s from the UK; then I’m team Virgin).

    Sources indicate that I’m going to make it a priority to fly each of American, Delta, and United’s best international long-haul products over the coming months. Watch this space for my thoughts on flying those for the first time, and to see whether Delta remains my US number one.

    I’m curious, what do you love or hate about Delta?
