    #145488. Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of the Dell Technologies New York Symposium

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1424 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

    Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of the Dell Technologies New York Symposium

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1424 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • AI operational readiness requires more than selecting the right servers, storage and computing capacity.
    • Those considerations are particularly consequential for financial institutions, where reliability, regulatory obligations and the need to demonstrate returns on technology investments shape deployment decisions.
    • According to recent reports, “I think the pyramid still exists, but undoubtedly, the cost of entry and the barriers to entry have crumbled,” he told theCUBE.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    UPDATED 19:21 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

    AI operational readiness requires more than selecting the right servers, storage and computing capacity.

    Those considerations are particularly consequential for financial institutions, where reliability, regulatory obligations and the need to demonstrate returns on technology investments shape deployment decisions. Meanwhile, AI is changing the threat landscape, giving less sophisticated attackers access to capabilities that once required considerably greater resources, according to John Scimone, president and chief security officer of Dell Technologies Inc.

    According to recent reports, “I think the pyramid still exists, but undoubtedly, the cost of entry and the barriers to entry have crumbled,” he told theCUBE. “Said another way, the least sophisticated attack tomorrow is more sophisticated than the world will have ever seen a year ago.”.

    Sources indicate that scimone spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante during the Dell Technologies Newly introduced York Symposium, part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exclusive coverage on theCUBE. Across the event, Dell executives and cloud infrastructure providers examined the economics of enterprise AI, the operational challenges of scaling infrastructure and the decisions shaping AI adoption.

    Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with John Scimone:.

    Here are three insights you might have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of the Dell Technologies Fresh York Symposium:.

    It has been revealed that dell has spent nearly two years running fully autonomous agents internally, capturing institutional knowledge in machine-readable skill files that guide their behavior. The effort is part of a broader reorganization of work around AI agents, according to John Roese, global chief technology officer and chief AI officer of Dell.

    “It doesn’t mean you can’t use frontier models and open models,” he said during the event. “It just means that when you design your AI system, you need to realize that the thing that is your moat is not the actual tools. It’s not even the models. It’s the special knowledge that’s now manifesting in these new forms that really capture what you know and do differently than your competitors.”.

    Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with John Roese:.

    Sources indicate that the financial side of AI operational readiness presents a different challenge. As enterprises scale their deployments, finance teams are establishing dedicated budget lines for token consumption and evaluating which workloads can run more economically on-premises. Repetitive financial processes, for example, can use open-weight models to convert variable token expenses into more predictable fixed costs, according to David Kennedy, chief financial officer of Dell.

    Industry observers note that “It’s not necessarily about the amount and the cost of a token,” he told theCUBE. “It’s about the tokens you use. Can you be efficient with them? If you are, you’re going to see great outcomes.”.

    Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with David Kennedy:.

    In a recent development, the growth of AI inference is changing how enterprises distribute workloads across cloud environments, data centers and edge devices. Dell’s expanded agentic AI portfolio reflects that shift, with solutions spanning desktop systems and data center infrastructure. Organizations are evaluating where to run models based on performance, data control and cost, according to Kyle Dufresne, senior vice president of sales at Dell.

    It has been revealed that “We’re seeing the business owners saying, ‘Oh my gosh, these costs are getting really high for inferencing. How do we reduce those costs without curbing innovation?’” he said during the event. “We’re finding it’s happening across that continuum but more and more right out at the far edge.”.

    Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Kyle Dufresne:.

    Recent findings suggest that infrastructure availability presents another challenge. Demand for AI servers has strained supplies of components ranging from memory and processors to rack-level cooling, networking and power equipment, according to David Schmoock, senior vice president of global revenue operations at Dell.

    In a recent development, “We didn’t do that collaborative planning, and now your project may have been delayed 60, 90, 120 days, which has both the cost impact and a business impact,” he told theCUBE. “I would say bring us in earlier. Allow us to do that collaboration with you. I think, at the end of the day, you get the most optimal outcome.”.

    Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with David Schmoock:.

    According to recent reports, AI operational readiness is also becoming a consideration for smaller businesses that need access to GPU computing without the resources of large enterprises. Comet Cloud Inc. is targeting this underserved market, where access to AI infrastructure can be constrained by purchasing commitments and provider priorities, according to Thomas Kato, founder and chief executive officer of Comet Cloud.

    Recent findings suggest that “You go to [Amazon Web Services] now; they want a multiyear contract from you. They’re picking who they’re taking,” he said during the event. “To the small and medium businesses, they’re not even coming up on that scope at all to be able to have that AI. Really, that’s our focus.”.

    Comet Cloud is developing an alternative approach aimed at giving smaller organizations greater control over their computing environments, Kato noted.

    “What we do is we put together clusters, and we’re giving clusters to a whole organization. All their information, all their security, everything is within that cluster. There’s no one else tied or connected to it,” he told theCUBE.

    Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Thomas Kato:.

    It has been revealed that alpha Compute Corp. is also building its neocloud infrastructure around data sovereignty and confidential computing requirements. The company’s sovereign-by-design approach is intended to help customers maintain control over sensitive workloads and meet data residency obligations, including those associated with European regulations, according to Tom Richer, executive vice president of Alpha Compute.

    “We start with the hardware. Think of a stack. All the way down to the chip level, we are creating enclaves,” he told theCUBE. “We’re a Dell partner, so we use Dell technology as well as Intel technology.”.

    Sources indicate that keeping GPU infrastructure operational presents a different challenge for neocloud providers. Alpha Compute provides integrated infrastructure support and ongoing managed services to address those demands, Richer noted.

    “You can cobble together a lot of different providers, but then when stuff goes wrong, the finger-pointing starts,” he said during the event. “You just want that integrated solution provider who can ensure success, help you with all of the build-out, then all of the … managed services to keep it going healthy and to keep everything performing in line with [service-level agreements].”.

    Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Tom Richer:.

    #145486. Latest Update: CrowdStrike reportedly in talks to acquire cybersecurity provider Zscaler

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: CrowdStrike reportedly in talks to acquire cybersecurity provider Zscaler

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (744 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • is reportedly in talks to buy Zscaler Inc., a publicly traded provider of cybersecurity software.
    • Sources told Bloomberg today that the acquisition could “come together soon.” However, they cautioned that it’s still possible the talks will fall through.
    • According to recent reports, investors seem to be confident that the deal will materialize.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    UPDATED 20:50 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

    CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. is reportedly in talks to buy Zscaler Inc., a publicly traded provider of cybersecurity software.

    Sources told Bloomberg today that the acquisition could “come together soon.” However, they cautioned that it’s still possible the talks will fall through.

    According to recent reports, investors seem to be confident that the deal will materialize. Zscaler’s share price jumped more than 16% in after-hours trading, while CrowdStrike dropped about 4.8%.

    Software buyouts tend to value the acquired manufacturer at a premium to its last unaffected market capitalization. As a result, CrowdStrike is likely to pay more than the $32 billion Zscaler was worth at the end of today’s trading session. That means the deal could take CrowdStrike’s market capitalization above $250 billion.

    CrowdStrike sells one of the world’s most popular cybersecurity platforms. Falcon can detect and block malicious activity across cloud instances, on-premises servers, employee devices and other assets. It also automates certain related tasks, such as finding sensitive records that are stored in an insecure manner.

    In a recent development, zscaler competes in a different part of the cybersecurity market. It sells software that protects the network connections through which a company’s employees access its business applications.

    Enterprises historically used virtual private network, or VPN, tools for that task. Such programs tend to be quite slow. More significantly, they give employees access to the entire corporate network rather than to the specific applications they need for their work. That broad access can create cybersecurity risks.

    Zscaler sells a zero-trust network access, or ZTNA, platform designed to replace legacy VPN software. It limits the number of applications that workers can access within the corporate network. If Zscaler detects risky activity, it asks the affected user to complete additional authentication steps.

    According to recent reports, the company’s ZTNA software doubles as an observability tool. Administrators can monitor employees’ connections for technical concerns that may hinder productivity. A built-in artificial intelligence assistant, the ZDX Agent, generates troubleshooting advice.

    According to recent reports, zscaler also competes in other product categories where CrowdStrike has a limited presence. Notably, it offers a tool that deploys bogus applications, user passwords and files in customer networks. Those simulated assets act as sensors. When an attempt is made to access one of them, Zscaler Deception notifies the customer that a cyberattack is underway.

    According to recent reports, the potential deal would mark CrowdStrike’s largest acquisition by a wide margin. The organization’s biggest buyout to date is its $970 million purchase of startup SGNL Inc., which closed earlier this year. The deal bought CrowdStrike a platform that can automatically end owners’ application sessions when it detects cybersecurity issues.

    #145485. United Airlines Remembers Your Bad Flight—And May Upgrade You Next Time, Even Without Status

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3718 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    United Airlines Remembers Your Bad Flight—And May Upgrade You Next Time, Even Without Status

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3718 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • United Airlines is giving some passengers free extra legroom on an upcoming trip because an earlier one went badly.
    • It has been revealed that aviation watchdog JonNYC shares a report from a passenger who missed a connection about a month earlier.
    • We know your previous travel experience may have faced some challenges.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    United Airlines is giving some passengers free extra legroom on an upcoming trip because an earlier one went badly. These are passengers without elite status, and who haven’t even complained. The airline remembers the problem and offers something on its own. Aviation watchdog JonNYC shares a report from a passenger who missed a connection about a month earlier. Before their next flight, United sent a message saying they’d been moved to Economy Plus. The passenger claims they have no status and the upcoming flight had a light load. The message, also covered by Paddle Your Own Kanoo, connects the better seat to the earlier experience: We know your previous travel experience may have faced some challenges JonNYC’s report on United’s next-flight Economy Plus recovery gesture — JonNYC (@xJonNYC), November 22, 2026 I like this. Airlines know when they’ve inconvenienced you. Making you write a complaint explaining something already in their records adds work to a bad experience. But the timing limits what United can accomplish: the customer already has another ticket, or buys one. This doesn’t reach someone who has no further United trip booked and refuses to buy another. This isn’t really a pure ‘win back’ effort. But this isn’t something that just started. Passengers have been reporting it since at least August 2025. Several Passenger Reports Show How This Works There are several passenger reports of this on Reddit: August 26, 2025: A Silver member reported an eight hour-plus delay leaving Denver. United gave them a $75 travel certificate, then assigned Economy Plus two days before their next flight. The seat was an additional gesture after the certificate. December 3, 2025: Another passenger the gesture after a trip with delays and seating problems. They said they hadn’t even contacted United about the previous trip. January 5, 2026: A passenger said a solo flight three weeks earlier had been delayed two hours. On the subsequent trip, both the passenger and their fiancée received Economy Plus. Jon’s example adds a customer without status, which is especially useful – United may not be using a ‘customer value score’ and limiting whom they’re reaching. And the January example suggests a companion can benefit even when they weren’t on the disrupted flight. Recipients generally appreciated being remembered. The Silver member in the August thread liked the gesture even though they expected to get Economy Plus at check-in anyway. Economy Plus is extra legroom coach. This upgrade isn’t to first class or long haul business. American Had Eagle Scores Years Ago Back in 2018, I wrote about the long-standing American Airlines Helix system and customer Eagle ratings. Those scores combined how valuable a customer was with how badly American had treated them and their risk of leaving. The one-to-five rating was recalculated daily. A high spending customer whose flights went smoothly didn’t necessarily receive the highest score. Neither did someone with terrible experiences who brought little revenue. The system helped employees decide when to make exceptions and spend more to preserve a customer relationship. One practical consequence was that customers with sufficiently high Eagle ratings could get expiring systemwide upgrades extended. Other airlines have remembered past problems, too. British Airways’ 2012 Know Me announcement described telling crew about a regular customer’s earlier weather delay so they could acknowledge it and thank the passenger for returning. Delta’s 2017 onboard recognition tool included recent flight interruptions among the reasons to flag someone for attention. British Airways and Delta were recognizing the earlier problem. United is pairing that with a better seat. United Has Been Talking About Recovery At the Barclays investor conference in February, chief financial officer Mike Leskinen discussed using technology for getting displaced crews and disrupted customers where they needed to go. And United’s Sheryl Lee described presenting Flight Finder at this year’s Grounded in Iceland conference. That tool looks for open seats for disrupted passengers already on standby. This also fits Scott Kirby’s public argument for technology that anticipates customer needs, and a pattern I’ve covered at United: making customer milestones visible to employees and offering selected travelers Global Services treatment they weren’t expecting. Airlines collect enormous amounts of customer information. The hard and useful part is actually doing something with it. But Here The Next Booking Has Already Happened The economics of this can be very good. If an Economy Plus seat would otherwise go unsold, giving it to an inconvenienced passenger costs United very little. The passenger gets something the airline normally charges for, and the message tells them why. Waiting until close to departure gives them more information about which seats they’re likely to sell. But an unannounced benefit delivered after booking can’t persuade someone to make that booking in the first place. A credit or an advance offer of a better seat can give an angry customer a reason to try the airline again. This gesture reaches people who already have another United reservation. And that doesn’t mean they’ve forgiven the airline. Their next trip could have been purchased before the bad trip. United may have the only convenient nonstop. They may be flying because their employer booked it. I especially like, though, that this can reach someone without status. An empty extra legroom seat may do more to win that customer’s business than offering the same thing to a frequent flyer who already gets it regularly. And United has to get the seat choice right. I wouldn’t consider moving from an aisle to a middle seat an improvement just because it’s in Economy Plus, and by the way United doesn’t offer free drinks in their extra legroom coach seats like even American does. A credit or an advance offer of a better seat can give an angry customer a reason to try the airline again. This gesture reaches people who already have another United reservation.

    And that doesn’t mean they’ve forgiven the airline. Their next trip could have been purchased before the bad trip. United may have the only convenient nonstop. They may be flying because their employer booked it.

    I especially like, though, that this can reach someone without status. An empty extra legroom seat may do more to win that customer’s business than offering the same thing to a frequent flyer who already gets it regularly. And United has to get the seat choice right. I wouldn’t consider moving from an aisle to a middle seat an improvement just because it’s in Economy Plus, and by the way United doesn’t offer free drinks in their extra legroom coach seats like even American does.

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (298 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nationalreview ↗ Open Full Page

    Grand Theft Auto VI and How We Spend Our Time

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (298 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Donald Trump just met with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China for a tripartite global summit — and nobody has any real news to report, except for Trump, so desperate for media attention that he’s giving interviews to anyone holding a hot mic and a video camera.
    • Every periodical you might care to read — even the political or news-based ones — has brought forward its major-think “review” of the game, now available on PlayStation and Xbox.
    • Sources indicate that jeffrey Blehar is a National Review staff writer living in Chicago.

    Donald Trump just met with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China for a tripartite global summit — and nobody has any real news to report, except for Trump, so desperate for media attention that he’s giving interviews to anyone holding a hot mic and a video camera. The lack of news is not just because of a (predictable) blackout enforced by the Chinese Communist Party, but because the collective consciousness of America has shut down for the next few days. If you thought the traditional four-day Thanksgiving Day Weekend was typically slow, get ready for a one-and-a-half-week productivity dip in the economy as the video game Grand Theft Auto VI goes live across the nation. Even National Review, as sober-minded as it is, has more than a few fans of the series on its staff.

    Every periodical you might care to read — even the political or news-based ones — has brought forward its major-think “review” of the game, now available on PlayStation and Xbox. For all I know we’ll be publishing one too. But I am not a gamer — not in the modern sense of the word, although I did whip out my copy of Battletoads for the NES the other day to prove that I’ve still “got it” — and this will not be a review of GTA VI. Instead, I want to talk about time spent — and time wasted.

    Sources indicate that jeffrey Blehar is a National Review staff writer living in Chicago. He is also the co-host of National Review’s Political Beats podcast, which explores the great music of the modern era with guests from the political world happy to find something non-political to talk about.

    On “Grand Theft Auto VI and How We Spend Our Time”.

    #145483. Delta’s CEO Indicates It Flew To LaGuardia In The 1950s—It Didn’t, But His Predecessors Figured Out How To Win Fresh York

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 44m • 📚 Deep Dive (8735 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    Delta’s CEO Indicates It Flew To LaGuardia In The 1950s—It Didn’t, But His Predecessors Figured Out How To Win Fresh York

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 44 min read (8735 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~44 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Delta CEO Ed Bastian says flying from Atlanta to LaGuardia takes longer today than when Delta launched the route in the 1950s.
    • Sources indicate that delta’s New York service began at Newark.
    • Today it takes more time to fly from Atlanta to LaGuardia than it did in the 1950s when we first launched that flight, which is absurd.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Delta CEO Ed Bastian says flying from Atlanta to LaGuardia takes longer today than when Delta launched the route in the 1950s. Except Delta didn’t fly to LaGuardia in the 1950s. Delta’s Fresh York service began at Newark. It took another 13 years to start LaGuardia. And the distinction between serving New York and serving the airport a New Yorker actually wants has been costing airlines money ever since. Speaking with Fortune, Bastian mentioned: Today it takes more time to fly from Atlanta to LaGuardia than it did in the 1950s when we first launched that flight, which is absurd. Delta’s history gives its LaGuardia launch date as October 1, 1969. Northeast and Northwest Airlines, which Delta later absorbed, served LaGuardia in 1945. But there was no Delta Atlanta–LaGuardia service in the 1950s. The airline that became such a powerful force in New York was a late arrival, built through acquisitions, deals with competitors, and an understanding of what New Yorkers would put in their wallets. The Mayor Who Refused To Get Off His Plane In New Jersey On November 24, 1934, New York Mayor Fiorello La Guardia arrived from Chicago on TWA. The plane landed at Newark. The mayor refused to get off. His ticket said New York. This was New Jersey. After an argument, the aircraft took him onward to Floyd Bennett Field in Brooklyn. He told the New York Times, “my ticket says New York and that’s where they brought me.” He repeated the stunt the following month. He wasn’t demanding to be taken to what’s now New York LaGuardia. That airport wouldn’t open until 1939. He was promoting New York City’s existing airport in Brooklyn, trying to pull airline business across the state line. Ironically, Floyd Bennett Field was about the same distance from Times Square as Newark. Delta’s First New York Flights Landed At Newark Delta didn’t grow up as a New York airline. Its roots were in Southern crop dusting, and its headquarters moved to Atlanta in 1941. Eastern had a substantial head start in the New York–Atlanta market. Back then an airline couldn’t just decide to add a route. The federal government’s Civil Aeronautics Board decided who could fly where. Delta’s 1956 annual report says its new route award allowed three daily round trips between New York and Newark. The launch timetable shows flight 724 leaving Atlanta at 6:05 p.m. and arriving at Newark at 9:21 p.m., with a Washington stop. That’s 3 hours 16 minutes. Comparing that one-stop propeller service with today’s nonstop wouldn’t tell us much about air traffic control in any case… Delta was already selling New York from Manhattan ticket offices, including Rockefeller Plaza. It added Idlewild, today’s JFK, on May 15, 1957. The airline’s August 1957 timetable shows Delta’s four-engine Flying Scot daytime coach flights using Idlewild, while its other flights used Newark. Why Did LaGuardia Take Until 1969? Delta had arrived late in a regulated market, and LaGuardia was difficult to get into. Eastern and American each essentially had a concourse to themselves, while the other airlines shared the remaining two. Delta initially served the airport with relatively small DC-9s, while Eastern already had 727s. Delta began advertising LaGuardia in its August 1969 timetable, Flight 620 will begin operating upon completion of arrangements for terminal facilities at LaGuardia. The actual October 1969 launch schedule offered non-stop service, not available from Delta’s 1950s service. Flight Leaves Atlanta Arrives LaGuardia Scheduled time 168 6:15 a.m. 8:15 a.m. 2 hours 620 12:10 p.m. 2:08 p.m. 1 hour 58 minutes 622 6:15 p.m. 8:13 p.m. 1 hour 58 minutes The 1956 annual report advertised a future Atlanta–New York time of 1 hour 41 minutes aboard forthcoming DC-8 jets, which Delta hadn’t introduced yet. How Delta Bought Its Way Into Being A New York Airline A Civil Aeronautics Board examiner recommended giving Delta New York–Miami authority in 1956, but the board itself rejected that awarding the service to Northeast. Sixteen years later, Delta bought Northeast. That 1972 acquisition brought a much stronger position in New York, Boston and Florida. In 1991, Delta acquired Pan Am’s transatlantic operation and its Northeast shuttle. Then came the deal that changed the scale of LaGuardia. Proposed in 2009 and completed in 2011, the US Airways slot swap gave Delta 132 daily LaGuardia slot pairs. US Airways received 42 daily Washington National pairs, $66.5 million, and rights for additional São Paulo service. The Government Accountability Office measured Delta’s LaGuardia slot share rising from 24% in April 2011 to 44% in May 2012. Regulators required slots to go to smaller competitors as a condition of approval. At LaGuardia, JetBlue received eight daily pairs and WestJet another eight. JetBlue actually bid the most for both packages, but the auction rules wouldn’t let one airline win both. Then, as I reported in 2024, following Enilria’s examination of slot trades, Delta even managed to get back the eight round trips WestJet had received as a competition remedy. Slots handed to a rival to keep Delta’s expansion competitive wound up back with Delta. US Airways helped Delta grow at LaGuardia. United would help at JFK. When United pulled out in 2015, Delta took over its JFK slots under a long-term lease. Delta also spent money leveraging that access with its $4 billion LaGuardia terminal project. United Tried To Prove Newark Was New York Using Taxi Ads Newark is a New York metropolitan airport. Depending on where you’re going and the traffic, it can be the most convenient one. It also serves a large and wealthy New Jersey market in its own right. United’s digital taxi top campaign revealed real-time driving estimates to Newark and JFK. The advertising industry’s account reveals the best detail: when Newark wasn’t the quickest, the display switched to generic United branding. The comparison disappeared when United lost it. When United left JFK in 2015, that meant premium Los Angeles and San Francisco service to Newark. After Scott Kirby joined United, he called the decision a mistake. The airline had looked at the money its JFK flights made or lost. Kirby explained that leaving also helped American win corporate accounts such as Disney and Time Warner. Those customers bought travel beyond Los Angeles–New York, including Los Angeles–London. United returned to JFK in 2021, then left again in 2022 after failing to obtain the access it wanted to build a larger operation. Its Blue Sky partnership with JetBlue provides another way back: access for up to seven daily United round trips from JFK’s new Terminal 6 as early as 2027, alongside reciprocal loyalty benefits and the ability to sell each other’s flights. Winning New York Also Means Winning Credit Card Spending I’ve made the same argument about American’s retreat in major markets. An airline needs to be useful where high-spending customers live. Otherwise why would those customers choose its credit card? A New Yorker who wants LaGuardia for domestic trips and JFK for longer journeys is a candidate for a Delta Amex (even though those miles are worth less than competing currencies). Delta’s investor presentation connects large coastal metropolitan economies with its premium and loyalty growth. In 2023 Delta described its cobrand spending as approaching 1% of U.S. GDP. Using American Express’s disclosures for that year—Delta represented about 10% of $1.680 trillion in worldwide network volume—implies roughly $168 billion. Against the contemporary $27.36 trillion estimate of U.S. GDP, that’s about 0.61%. As I’ve argued, they’re rounding generously. And there’s a bigger problem with the growth story. When Delta renewed its American Express deal in 2019, it projected $7 billion annually by 2023. It delivered $6.8 billion. That sounds like nearly hitting the target, until you account for how much pandemic-era inflation had shrunk the value of each dollar – in a way that hadn’t been anticipated in 2019. Consumer prices rose about 19% between 2019 and 2023. Using annual consumer price indexes, the $6.8 billion payment had only about $5.7 billion of 2019 purchasing power. Delta nearly hit its 2019 goals in nominal terms due to inflation, but its actual performance was a real miss. Delta now expects more than $9 billion from American Express in 2026. It’s an enormous business, but it’s had a ceiling greater than what Delta had hoped in 2019 – which also explains the importance of free wifi, Uber and Starbucks – looking for new customers anywhere they can find them. The poor return on spending of a Delta credit card finally matters. Ultimately, though, Delta wasn’t born a New York airline. Ed Bastian’s predecessors assembled one, including airport access its competitors willingly gave up. United is still working to repair its decision to leave JFK. For customers who insist that their New York ticket take them to a particular New York airport, being told Newark is close enough still doesn’t close the sale. And Bastian’s 1950s comparison is typical Bastian – never let facts like connecting service and which airport the airline served get in the way of the story he wants to tell.     Sources indicate that delta was already selling New York from Manhattan ticket offices, including Rockefeller Plaza. It added Idlewild, today’s JFK, on May 15, 1957. The airline’s August 1957 timetable indicates Delta’s four-engine Flying Scot daytime coach flights using Idlewild, while its other flights used Newark.

    Delta had arrived late in a regulated market, and LaGuardia was difficult to get into. Eastern and American each essentially had a concourse to themselves, while the other airlines shared the remaining two. Delta initially served the airport with relatively small DC-9s, while Eastern already had 727s. Delta began advertising LaGuardia in its August 1969 timetable, Flight 620 will begin operating upon completion of arrangements for terminal facilities at LaGuardia. The actual October 1969 launch schedule offered non-stop service, not available from Delta’s 1950s service. Flight Leaves Atlanta Arrives LaGuardia Scheduled time 168 6:15 a.m. 8:15 a.m. 2 hours 620 12:10 p.m. 2:08 p.m. 1 hour 58 minutes 622 6:15 p.m. 8:13 p.m. 1 hour 58 minutes The 1956 annual report advertised a future Atlanta–Newly introduced York time of 1 hour 41 minutes aboard forthcoming DC-8 jets, which Delta hadn’t introduced yet. How Delta Bought Its Way Into Being A New York Airline A Civil Aeronautics Board examiner recommended giving Delta New York–Miami authority in 1956, but the board itself rejected that awarding the service to Northeast. Sixteen years later, Delta bought Northeast. That 1972 acquisition brought a much stronger position in New York, Boston and Florida. In 1991, Delta acquired Pan Am’s transatlantic operation and its Northeast shuttle. Then came the deal that changed the scale of LaGuardia. Proposed in 2009 and completed in 2011, the US Airways slot swap gave Delta 132 daily LaGuardia slot pairs. US Airways received 42 daily Washington National pairs, $66.5 million, and rights for additional São Paulo service. The Government Accountability Office measured Delta’s LaGuardia slot share rising from 24% in April 2011 to 44% in May 2012. Regulators required slots to go to smaller competitors as a condition of approval. At LaGuardia, JetBlue received eight daily pairs and WestJet another eight. JetBlue actually bid the most for both packages, but the auction rules wouldn’t let one airline win both. Then, as I reported in 2024, following Enilria’s examination of slot trades, Delta even managed to get back the eight round trips WestJet had received as a competition remedy. Slots handed to a rival to keep Delta’s expansion competitive wound up back with Delta. US Airways helped Delta grow at LaGuardia. United would help at JFK. When United pulled out in 2015, Delta took over its JFK slots under a long-term lease. Delta also spent money leveraging that access with its $4 billion LaGuardia terminal project. United Tried To Prove Newark Was New York Using Taxi Ads Newark is a New York metropolitan airport. Depending on where you’re going and the traffic, it can be the most convenient one. It also serves a large and wealthy New Jersey market in its own right. United’s digital taxi top campaign showed real-time driving estimates to Newark and JFK. The advertising industry’s account reveals the best detail: when Newark wasn’t the quickest, the display switched to generic United branding. The comparison disappeared when United lost it. When United left JFK in 2015, that meant premium Los Angeles and San Francisco service to Newark. After Scott Kirby joined United, he called the decision a mistake. The airline had looked at the money its JFK flights made or lost. Kirby explained that leaving also helped American win corporate accounts such as Disney and Time Warner. Those customers bought travel beyond Los Angeles–New York, including Los Angeles–London. United returned to JFK in 2021, then left again in 2022 after failing to obtain the access it wanted to build a larger operation. Its Blue Sky partnership with JetBlue provides another way back: access for up to seven daily United round trips from JFK’s new Terminal 6 as early as 2027, alongside reciprocal loyalty benefits and the ability to sell each other’s flights. Winning New York Also Means Winning Credit Card Spending I’ve made the same argument about American’s retreat in major markets. An airline needs to be useful where high-spending customers live. Otherwise why would those customers choose its credit card? A New Yorker who wants LaGuardia for domestic trips and JFK for longer journeys is a candidate for a Delta Amex (even though those miles are worth less than competing currencies). Delta’s investor presentation connects large coastal metropolitan economies with its premium and loyalty growth. In 2023 Delta described its cobrand spending as approaching 1% of U.S. GDP. Using American Express’s disclosures for that year—Delta represented about 10% of $1.680 trillion in worldwide network volume—implies roughly $168 billion. Against the contemporary $27.36 trillion estimate of U.S. GDP, that’s about 0.61%. As I’ve argued, they’re rounding generously. And there’s a bigger problem with the growth story. When Delta renewed its American Express deal in 2019, it projected $7 billion annually by 2023. It delivered $6.8 billion. That sounds like nearly hitting the target, until you account for how much pandemic-era inflation had shrunk the value of each dollar – in a way that hadn’t been anticipated in 2019. Consumer prices rose about 19% between 2019 and 2023. Using annual consumer price indexes, the $6.8 billion payment had only about $5.7 billion of 2019 purchasing power. Delta nearly hit its 2019 goals in nominal terms due to inflation, but its actual performance was a real miss. Delta now expects more than $9 billion from American Express in 2026. It’s an enormous business, but it’s had a ceiling greater than what Delta had hoped in 2019 – which also explains the importance of free wifi, Uber and Starbucks – looking for new customers anywhere they can find them. The poor return on spending of a Delta credit card finally matters. Ultimately, though, Delta wasn’t born a New York airline. Ed Bastian’s predecessors assembled one, including airport access its competitors willingly gave up. United is still working to repair its decision to leave JFK. For customers who insist that their New York ticket take them to a particular New York airport, being told Newark is close enough still doesn’t close the sale. And Bastian’s 1950s comparison is typical Bastian – never let facts like connecting service and which airport the airline served get in the way of the story he wants to tell.     #145482. Progressive advocates call on House Democrats to force Cuba vote

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (859 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Progressive advocates call on House Democrats to force Cuba vote

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (859 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May.
    • Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the issue is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.
    • “The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the issue is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.

    “The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday. “In the midterm elections, U.S. voters resoundingly rejected a foreign policy of war and domination, and made clear their desire for Congress to act forcefully to rein in the Trump administration.

    Holding a vote would demonstrate that Democrats recognize the urgency facing the Cuban people, and would help set the tone for an assertive agenda of peace, diplomacy and respect for international law in the 120th Congress, the letter added.

    In a recent development, at issue is a war powers resolution introduced in May by Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., and House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking member Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., that would call on the president “to remove the United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Cuba, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force.”.

    The letter was sent to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of Newly introduced York, Meeks and House Rules Committee ranking member Jim McGovern, D-Mass. It was signed by prominent anti-war groups such as Win Without War, Just Foreign Policy, the Friends Committee on National Legislation, Indivisible and Code Pink.

    Advocates are frustrated that House Democrats have not forced a vote on a Cuba war powers resolution even as they have forced multiple war powers votes on Iran and see it as an example of leadership that is at odds with the progressive wing of the party. One advocate who requested anonymity to speak candidly stated it’s their understanding Democratic leaders are hesitant to make potentially vulnerable Florida members of the caucus vote on the problem.

    Spokespeople for Jeffries and Meeks did not respond to requests for comment Wednesday on whether Democrats will force a vote before the end of the year, what their reasoning is if they don’t and whether they strategy to bring up a vote next year.

    Industry observers note that senate Democrats sought to force a vote on a similar resolution earlier this year, but Republicans in that chamber successfully derailed the effort. Senate Republicans raised a point of order that the resolution was not entitled to privileged status under the War Powers Resolution since U.S. troops aren't actively engaged in combat against Cuba. The point of order was sustained in a mostly party-line vote of 51-47.

    Senate Democrats later introduced another Cuba war powers resolution, which they have not tried to force a vote on and have not signaled they will do so before the end of the year.

    The resolutions have come amid several veiled threats from President Donald Trump suggesting eventual military action against Cuba.

    “I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt last week when asked if he would order the use of military force against Cuba.

    “Frankly, I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” Trump said, adding he would “certainly consider” taking military action.

    According to recent reports, trump’s comments are on top of a pressure campaign his administration has been waging against Cuba. Since January, the United States has imposed a blockade of oil shipments to the island, causing fuel shortages that have led to lengthy blackouts and aggravated an economic crisis.

    While the Senate vote in April did not go Democrats’ way, advocates still saw it as sending a strong message.

    “Despite falling short of the majority, this was among the strongest votes in congressional history against the use of blockades, and one of the most crucial stands Congress has taken against U.S. economic sanctions toward Cuba in over six decades,” the letter from progressive organizations remarked. “The House should take a similarly forceful action at this crucial moment.”.

    The House vote, even if successful, would be largely symbolic since the measure Democrats can force a vote on is a concurrent resolution. Concurrent resolutions are widely considered to be nonbinding even if cleared by both chambers of Congress since they do not get a presidential signature, though anti-war advocates dispute that applies to war powers.

    The progressive groups in their letter called for “decisive leadership” in forcing a vote on the glitch.

    “Across the political spectrum,” the letter noted, “Americans do not want another regime change war, nor an open-ended, nation-building project abroad based on false pretenses — especially not when escalation risks exposing the United States to newly introduced national security risks, placing US servicemembers in harm’s way, stoking regional instability, and becoming the latest chapter in a long history of harmful U.S. regional policies that have fueled mass migration to U.S. shores.”.

    #145481. Which restaurant reservation platform offers the best rewards: OpenTable, DoorDash, Seated or Resy?

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (226 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thepointsguy ↗ Open Full Page

    Which restaurant reservation platform offers the best rewards: OpenTable, DoorDash, Seated or Resy?

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (226 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thepointsguy

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
  • Dining reservation platforms like OpenTable, DoorDash, Seated and Resy now offer rewards for booking and completing restaurant reservations, each with distinct earning and redemption models.
  • OpenTable awards points redeemable for dining credits or experiences, DoorDash provides credits for future orders, Seated offers a percentage back as rewards for gift cards and Resy grants additional loyalty points at participating venues.
  • The value and structure of rewards vary: OpenTable is widely available but offers lower returns, DoorDash is best for smaller bills, Seated can be most lucrative for larger spends, and Resy delivers a strong return but is currently limited in scope.
  • All programs are free to join, but eligibility, reward expiration and redemption options differ, so choosing the best platform depends on your dining habits and location.
  • Some programs require app activations or enrollment steps, and certain benefits are only available in select cities or on specific devices.
  • Rewards may expire after periods of inactivity or have usage restrictions, such as not covering taxes and fees or being limited to certain brands for gift card redemption.
  • Stacking reservation rewards with eligible payment methods can further enhance overall value, but terms and availability vary by platform.

    #145480. Sovereign AI: Where control becomes an architectural requirement

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2145 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

    Sovereign AI: Where control becomes an architectural requirement

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2145 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • BREAKING ANALYSIS by David Vellante, Amit Eyal Govrin and John Furrier.
    • We believe sovereignty is becoming an architectural requirement for firms operating globally, especially in highly regulated industries.
    • companies supply most of the cloud and frontier artificial intelligence technology enterprises depend on.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    UPDATED 12:50 EST / NOVEMBER 21 2026.

    BREAKING ANALYSIS by David Vellante, Amit Eyal Govrin and John Furrier.

    We believe sovereignty is becoming an architectural requirement for firms operating globally, especially in highly regulated industries. The business question for buyers is how much control an organization needs over the systems that produce its intelligence, and what happens when that control is ceded to others.

    U.S. companies supply most of the cloud and frontier artificial intelligence technology enterprises depend on. Buyers need to understand the resulting jurisdictional, operating and commercial risks, and put in place compensating controls to mitigate them. This reality applies for U.S. firms operating abroad and even those in the US, especially for regulated firms.

    Welcome to Breaking Analysis #334: Sovereign AI: Where control becomes an architectural requirement.

    In this episode we examine the challenges around where data lives, who holds the keys, which model touches the data, who operates the system and who is exposed to the bill. Our premise is that sovereignty requires deliberate risk decisions, compensating controls and proof that those controls work. The appropriate architecture involves tradeoffs and will depend on the workload and the consequences of losing control.

    Today we draw on three sources of input as shown below:.

    First, Amit Govrin’s buyer’s guide, which evaluates the documented controls across hyperscaler offerings and buyer territories. Second, a study we commissioned with our partners at Qualitate that brings the experiences of eleven senior technology decision-makers in regulated and critical-infrastructure organizations. Third, John Furrier’s conversation with Amit at SC26, which explains the reasoning behind our framework.

    Industry observers note that the buyer’s guide independently measures vendors’ documented claims. The in-depth interviews show what buyers care about and what they’ve tested. theCUBE interview helps connect those findings to architecture and business risk. The survey sample is small but deep, so we use it to understand decisions and expose gaps.

    Let’s start by hearing from Amit with why he developed a practical and uniform framework to measure organizational control over AI, data and local risk:.

    It has been revealed that the first set of takeaways from our survey shows a gap between buyer priorities and operational reality. Legal exposures featured prominently in purchasing decisions within the sample. Yet seven of eleven respondents report no testing of disconnected systems, key-revocation or exit scenarios. So the hard evidence for practical operational control is somewhat shaky given the high levels of concern about losing that very control.

    As shown below, buyers also tend to add controls to the platforms they already use. Only four of eleven have deployed or piloted a distinct sovereign or dedicated offering. Cost and the burden of adding another environment was the primary reason that explained such behavior.

    Sources indicate that as seen in the quote above, a European information technology and telecom buyer notes deep support escalations “can still in some cases involve personnel or systems outside the EU, particularly for deep technical issues.” What’s the message there? Our take is that the support protocol must become a fundamental part of the architecture review; and that has to account for emergency and privileged access. The key point as Amit often stresses is sovereignty is not a purity test. Organizations can certainly live with such an exposure during an emergency. Our message is simply be aware of the condition, evaluate the risk and if necessary put in compensating controls or live with the exposure.

    It has been revealed that it’s early days, so some customers are waiting for clearer sovereign-specific mandates or enforcement guidelines from local governments before expanding deployment and testing sovereignty. In other words, they’re leaning on existing privacy and cybersecurity laws and practices. We’d caution, however, that this type of uncertainty only strengthens the case for preparing acceptance tests sooner rather than later.

    Costs heavily influence the scope of sovereignty investments. Buyers justify stronger controls for sensitive workloads while accepting different levels of exposure for lower-risk activity. Migration effort, retraining and the cost of exiting all affect that decision. At the very least, this means customers should assess their sovereign exposure, much in the same way they would do so for cybersecurity.

    AI inference introduces another gotcha. Nine of 11 respondents require inference inside the sovereign or regional boundary. Buyers report that model availability can lag inside those environments. As such, the architectural choice has to make a potential tradeoff between local jurisdiction risk and model capability for a specific workload. The question buyers are asking: Is it worth stepping outside the lines to get a business result? The answer depends on the degree of risk and the magnitude of the business value. Sometimes it’s worth just paying the parking fine.

    We’re not going to go deep into the buyer’s guide – we did that last week and we’d encourage you to read the full report.

    What we will share is one high-level comparison from the buyer’s guide as shown below.

    Google LLC leads all measured cloud vendors with a score of 3.45 across all regions and tests. Google is followed by Oracle Corp. at 3.25. IBM Corp. and Microsoft Corp.’s Azure score 3.0. AWS scores 2.7 – its score suffers from not having the ability to have a customer-run air-gapped stack without vendor management. Huawei Technologies Co. Ltd. and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. came in at 1.2.

    It has been revealed that now to be clear, this is a point-in-time index from the Nov. 14 revision. It averages each supplier’s best live offering across five buyer regions. The framework has five pillars (territorial, legal, operational, technical and financial), 17 yes-or-no tests across four nonlegal dimensions, plus a separate legal evaluation.

    As well, a low score at the highest level doesn’t mean a vendor won’t be chosen. We found many situations, for example, where Amazon Web Services Inc. was the choice despite its lower score because of its excellent quality and incumbent position. We found similar dynamics with Azure as a ubiquitous cloud and often a convenient option. Similar dynamics are in play within IBM and Oracle customer bases.

    It has been revealed that that noted, we’re assessing the architecture and the vendor claims to help buyers make better decisions. Customer-run deployments generally improve the scores because the methodology rewards controls the buyer can exercise independently. Missing documentation also affects the grades. We would use the previous chart to start an evaluation, then examine the actual offering available in the buyer’s jurisdiction against your specific workload requirements and local laws.

    These findings bring us back to five key questions:.

    Listen below to John and Amit connect operational controls and money flows to sovereignty. Those dependencies extend well beyond the physical location of the data center.

    Let’s dig into some more survey data.

    Seven of eleven buyers say a locally incorporated subsidiary does not completely clarify the local jurisdiction question. This is a buyer assessment, and it suggests the need for much deeper legal analysis beyond technical evaluations.

    Under the U.S. CLOUD Act, a vendor subject to U.S. jurisdiction can be required to produce data in its possession or control, regardless of storage location. Corporate relationships and actual control do matter here.

    According to recent reports, customer-held keys may limit outside access, but key ownership does not necessarily ensure legal immunity. Buyers also need to know what stops working if and when access is revoked.

    The fuzzy gap is captured by a South American bank’s executive director for AI, talking about the absence of testing: “That’s probably the weakest point in our whole sovereign story.” Our takeaway is that legal review and operational testing serve different purposes and both are critical.

    It has been revealed that coming back to the AI inference issue. As we revealed earlier, nine of 11 buyers require inference to take place inside their sovereign or regional boundary. One Latin American financial-services buyer said: “If it calls out to a U.S. endpoint, it doesn’t count no matter what the contract states.”.

    According to recent reports, this means you have to trace the end-to-end request cycle, from prompt, retrieval, model usage, outputs and even logs. An application that gets green lit can still depend on another service which lives in the execution sequence. The test is what happens to the data during its actual use.

    Recent findings suggest that for sensitive workflows, buyers should compare a self-hosted open-weight model architecture with an approved frontier service and evaluate the cost and quality of the outcome. Open weights create optionality but the frontier often produces superior results which may warrant easing up on sovereignty requirements.

    Industry observers note that sovereignty needs ongoing attention because the architecture changes continuously. A model endpoint can move, a new model ships, a service contract changes or a new capability goes into production. Every change can affect exposure and risk.

    It has been revealed that in this clip, Amit describes an AI-driven five-pillar framework for continuous assessment and management of data sovereignty and third-party risk. The approach brings vendor capabilities and claims, and the customer’s architecture, into an ongoing assessment. Let’s hear how he puts it:.

    Industry observers note that we see tremendous value in this framework. Our test for any assessment comes down to the evidence it produces. In other words, what’s the exposure, who has control, is there an accountable owner and ultimately, what’s the risk you’re absorbing? Our advice is that major changes to models, services or contracts should trigger a reassessment. Documented assurance from the vendor combined with technical tests should both be included in that process.

    Our recommendation is to make sovereignty evaluations at the workload level. Start with a core business process, identify the exposures and agree on the controls it requires based on the risk you’re willing to absorb. Importantly, for critical workloads, we suggest obtaining proof that those controls work in a safe sandbox environment and then push into production.

    In a recent development, this means you have to pay attention to privileged access. And you must test what happens when a key gets revoked and you have to recover. As we’ve talked about in previous episodes, verifying what the model did and the route of the execution path is something most organizations can’t observe today. Testing and telemetry are major gaps with most customers. Can you observe the route and exercise an exit or completely disconnected scenario if a workload requires it? Your financial assessment should include ongoing operation, migration, retraining, the cost of leaving and business disruption. And importantly, a business owner has to accept the risk, not an IT pro.

    Industry observers note that for vendors, we believe the opportunity is substantial to document controls, establish predictable operating economics and provide credible evidence that can support your proposed solution. In many cases we’ve seen public documentation and evidence lack marketing claims.

    Sovereignty is becoming part of enterprise architecture because intelligence now depends on these relationships. Buyers need the ability to make an informed choice and demonstrate that the resulting system behaves as intended.

    Check out the Hyperscaler Sovereign Buyers Guide – it’s the first of its kind and very comprehensive.

    And do let us know if you you have any questions – we’re here to help.

    Rove Gives You 1,500 Free Miles Just For Signing Up—Plus 5,000 More On Your First $500 Hotel Booking

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1733 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Rove is offering 1,500 free miles just for signing up.
    • Recent findings suggest that I’ve written quite a bit about Rove, and asked them to improve the offer available through my link.
    • They’ve also created a hotel booking code for readers:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rove is offering 1,500 free miles just for signing up. You don’t have to book a trip, buy anything, or complete any other transaction. I specifically asked about an activity requirement, and Rove confirmed that new members get the miles instantly. I’ve written quite a bit about Rove, and asked them to improve the offer available through my link. This is three times the standard 500-mile referral signup bonus. Just like normal referrals, I receive Rove Miles when someone signs up through this link. It doesn’t cost you anything. In fact it gets you much more than not using this link. They’ve also created a hotel booking code for readers: 1,500 miles for joining: Use this link to create your new account. There’s no purchase requirement. 5,000 additional miles on your first hotel booking of $500 or more: Enter promo code VFTW when booking through Rove. A new member who uses both offers would earn 6,500 bonus miles, on top of the normal miles from their qualifying hotel booking. You can also just take the signup miles. And 5,000 miles on a $500 booking is twice what Rove offered at that spending level during its May promotion. What You Can Do With These Miles Rove is a free rewards program that lets you earn miles from hotel and flight bookings, online shopping, dining and gift cards. You don’t have to apply for a credit card, and you can earn rewards from the card you use to pay as well. Their transfer partners include familiar programs like Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France KLM Flying Blue, Qatar Airways Privilege Club and Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. They also have programs that are harder to access through the major bank currencies, including Lufthansa Miles & More (for better availability of business and first class awards), Japan Airlines Mileage Bank (better availability of awards, lower prices on partner awards), Air India Maharaja Club (United awards starting at just 3,500 points) and Copa ConnectMiles (Emirates awards with no fuel surcharges). Rove has a 2,000-mile minimum for partner transfers. You don’t need a hotel stay to earn additional miles. I’ve covered Rove’s dining program and instant gift card rewards, and just wrote about its personalized shopping offers of up to 25 miles per dollar. When The Hotel Bonus Makes Sense You can also redeem Rove Miles directly for travel. As I wrote last month, I can usually get around 1.5 cents apiece redeeming them for hotel stays that still earn hotel points and elite status credit. Using that benchmark, the 5,000-mile hotel bonus is worth about $75 toward travel. On a qualifying $500 booking, that’s an extra 15% in value before the booking’s regular rewards. Expressed another way, the promo adds 10 miles per dollar at exactly $500 in qualifying spend. I’ve been particularly interested in Rove’s Loyalty Eligible hotel rates. There are two different kinds of bookings to compare: Loyalty Eligible rates generally earn 5 Rove miles per dollar, while preserving eligibility for the hotel’s own points, elite night credit and status benefits. The hotel charges your card, which can make paying with that chain’s credit card attractive. Rove Rates can offer more Rove miles, with the site advertising up to 25 per dollar, but generally give up the hotel loyalty program earnings and benefits. That tradeoff is easier at an independent hotel where you wouldn’t earn chain points anyway. I’d take the free signup miles. For the hotel offer, enter VFTW and consider the rate you’re selecting before booking for the 5,000-mile bonus.     #145478. Inference now drives two-thirds of AI workloads, changing where chips get deployed

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (810 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

    Inference now drives two-thirds of AI workloads, changing where chips get deployed

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (810 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • AI spending is shifting from giant training clusters toward smaller, promptly built sites, and modular data centers are becoming a natural home for inference workloads.
    • Inference-first chipmakers want to capture that shift.
    • Sources indicate that “We’re at a point where about two-thirds of the workloads being run through these AI infrastructures are inference versus one-third is training.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    UPDATED 13:28 EST / NOVEMBER 21 2026.

    AI spending is shifting from giant training clusters toward smaller, promptly built sites, and modular data centers are becoming a natural home for inference workloads. Power, cooling and memory supply now shape where tokens get generated as much as raw chip performance does.

    Inference-first chipmakers want to capture that shift. Positron AI Inc., which raised $875 million at a $5 billion valuation in September, builds inference appliances around commodity memory instead of scarce high-bandwidth memory. Inference has overtaken training as the force behind infrastructure buying decisions, according to Cameron McCaskill (pictured), head of sales and business development at Positron.

    Sources indicate that “We’re at a point where about two-thirds of the workloads being run through these AI infrastructures are inference versus one-third is training. And back in 2023, it was like 85% training, 15% inference,” McCaskill said. “So now you can see why inference is driving the economic decisions of how they’re going to build out their infrastructure.”.

    According to recent reports, mcCaskill spoke with theCUBE Research’s Rebecca Knight and John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed inference overtaking training, Positron’s commodity-memory chip design and why low-power modular data centers suit inference. (* Disclosure below.).

    Industry observers note that positron’s first-generation Atlas server ran on a programmable chip, and the company prepares to tape out its own silicon early next year for its Titan server. Oracle Corp. is bringing about 340 Atlas servers live in its cloud this quarter, McCaskill noted. A neocloud provider has also signed on for Atlas and committed to Titan. Positron’s central design choice was skipping high-bandwidth memory.

    “Everyone else pretty much in the industry is using what’s called HBM or high bandwidth memory. It’s very limited in supply, very expensive,” McCaskill stated. “We went with commodity memory.”.

    That choice also keeps power low enough for air-cooled rooms. A single Positron server draws about 4,500 watts, and a full rack of Titan servers fits within 40 kilowatts, McCaskill explained. That footprint suits sites where operators can find a few megawatts of cheap power without heavy regulatory hurdles. For inference providers monetizing latest capacity, deployment speed is a significant part of the appeal, according to McCaskill.

    “One of the groups of companies that we’re seeing a rise in right now and coming to us for product is these modular data centers, where they have a half megawatt or, 1 megawatt or 2.5 megawatt modular data center, and those can be deployed very swiftly,” McCaskill said. “And the goal of a lot of these inference players is I want to get from land and power to monetizable tokens within 90 to 120 days. And those modular data centers, coupled with our technology, can be a great solution.”.

    Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of SC26:.

    #145477. Breaking: Rove Rolls out Elite Status With Third Night Free Hotel Awards—Will This Turn Deal Chasers Into Loyal Customers?

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 29m • 📚 Deep Dive (5747 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Rove Rolls out Elite Status With Third Night Free Hotel Awards—Will This Turn Deal Chasers Into Loyal Customers?

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 29 min read (5747 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~29 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Rove is launching elite status with a third night free on eligible hotel awards, and top tier Diamond members get two free nights on a six night stay.
    • The benefits can make Rove more rewarding.
    • Rove Status launches November 23, 2026.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rove is launching elite status with a third night free on eligible hotel awards, and top tier Diamond members get two free nights on a six night stay. You can qualify through travel bookings, shopping and dining, without holding a particular credit card. The benefits can make Rove more rewarding. They may also bean attempt to address the problem I’ve had with the business from the beginning: when you attract customers by giving them the best deal, what keeps them around when somebody else offers more? How Rove’s Fresh Status Program Works Rove Status releases November 23, 2026. Everyone starts as a Member, and there are three earned tiers. You need both qualifying miles and qualifying transactions during a calendar year: Status Qualifying Miles Qualifying Transactions Gold 50,000 5 Platinum 125,000 10 Diamond 250,000 20 Qualifying activity from earlier in 2026 counts retroactively, and status earned in 2026 lasts through December 31, 2027. Rove clarified what counts: Transaction earnings count, including elevated rates and status bonuses. Miles associated with paid travel bookings, shopping, gift cards and dining qualify. That includes purchased Miles Boost earnings. Flat bonuses don’t count. An offer of 2,500 bonus miles for spending $500 won’t add those 2,500 miles to your status progress, although the qualifying purchase and its ordinary earnings still count. Referrals, transfers, customer support credits and other miles unrelated to a cash transaction don’t count. Pure award redemptions don’t earn qualifying miles or transactions either. Rove makes an exception for miles + cash bookings. Shopping, dining and gift cards count based on the purchase date. Travel counts when it’s completed: hotel checkout or the last flight of a multi-segment trip. Booking a hotel in December for a January checkout won’t help with 2026 status. Late posting doesn’t move activity into the wrong year. If a December purchase posts in January, it still counts toward 2026 qualification, and Rove can award the resulting status after the new year begins. The spending required depends on how quickly you earn qualifying miles. At an average of 10 qualifying miles per dollar, Gold takes $5,000, Platinum $12,500, and Diamond $25,000. At 25 qualifying miles per dollar, Diamond takes $10,000. At 5, it takes $50,000. You still need the required number of qualifying transactions. And once you earn status, the extra miles from eligible elite earning bonuses help you reach the next tier or requalify. Here are the announced benefits: Benefit Gold Platinum Diamond Free night on eligible Rove Rate awards Fifth night Fourth night Third night Discount on eligible paid hotel rates, excluding Loyalty Eligible 5% 8% 10% Additional shopping miles per dollar at select brands Up to 5 Up to 8 Up to 10 Paid Miles Boost limit Up to 12x Up to 15x Up to 20x Rove’s partner transfer minimum 1,500 miles 1,000 miles No minimum Extra transfer bonus during eligible promotions None listed 10 percentage points 15 percentage points Customer support Gold priority Platinum priority Diamond priority and Diamond Desk All three earned tiers also offer parental leave: new parents can extend their status expiration by 12 months. Rove indicates additional partner benefits are coming. The Free Hotel Night Is The Biggest Benefit — With An Crucial Limitation A third night free can be substantial, and Rove confirms a six night Diamond stay receives two free nights. The deduction uses the average nightly price, so a cheaper third night doesn’t shrink the benefit. On a three or six night Diamond award, the eligible award cost falls by a third. Platinum saves 25% on a four night award and Gold saves 20% on a five night award. Rove says the free night calculation excludes only fees due at the hotel, such as resort fees or locally collected taxes. (Those charges remain payable.) That also makes each mile worth more. A third off the miles required means 50% more value per mile. And I generally get about 1.5 cents per Rove Mile as it is. But both the free award nights and the paid hotel discounts exclude Loyalty Eligible bookings. Those have been my favorite use of Rove miles. The free nights apply to Rove Rate awards, which are going to be third party bookings (may not earn points, status credit or receive status benefits). With Loyalty Eligible stays, you can redeem Rove miles and still earn hotel points and elite night credit, while receiving your hotel status benefits. Rove Rate bookings don’t earn those hotel points or nights, and don’t guarantee your hotel elite benefits. I’d be most interested in the free night benefit at independent hotels, or on stays where I don’t have valuable hotel status to give up. A discounted three or six night award could be a much better use of miles than the same stay was before. Rove explains that it can’t offer the paid hotel discount on Loyalty Eligible rates because the hotel is the merchant of record and Rove doesn’t control the pricing. I’d note that commissions are lower, too, so it would also be costlier to offer. Extra Transfer Bonuses And Shopping Bonuses The extra transfer bonuses apply on top of eligible existing promotions, and Rove confirms they’re additive. A 40% promotion becomes 50% for Platinum and 55% for Diamond. At a partner with a normal 1:1 ratio, transferring 10,000 Rove miles during that offer would yield 14,000 partner miles ordinarily, 15,000 for Platinum, or 15,500 for Diamond. There’s no standing 15% Diamond bonus on every transfer. The shopping bonuses mean additional miles per dollar. Diamond’s maximum is 10 extra miles per dollar at select brands, rather than multiplying the ordinary earning rate by ten. These bonuses aren’t available on everything you buy, but where offered they improve both your redeemable points-earn and status progress. Lower transfer minimums are useful for topping off an airline account. Rove’s ordinary minimum is 2,000 miles, though individual partners can have their own minimums or increments. Removing Rove’s minimum is a nice convenience. Rove Needs Customers Who Come Back I’ve written about Rove’s customer challenge. An airline starts with passengers who need its flights. A hotel tech giant starts with guests who need rooms in its locations. Rove has to persuade people to use its platform for purchases they were already making. They’ve done that by frequently being more rewarding than competitors. That’s attracted attention and business, but it also attracts the loyalty equivalent of hot money. Customers compare offers, take the richest one, and potentially. Status gives the next transaction value beyond the miles it earns immediately. Someone approaching Gold might choose Rove even when another portal offers a little more. Someone who already has Diamond may keep earning because they want enough miles for another discounted three night stay. And even without doing the math, people like reaching a tier and dislike losing it. The transaction requirements push customers beyond one big purchase. Rove’s expansion into dining, shopping and an app gives customers more reasons to return between trips. Status gives those activities a common target. And while a rich acquisition offer pays someone who might never come back, a status discount generally requires another booking before Rove incurs the cost. Some members won’t use it. Rove can direct more of its rewards spending toward customers who return, instead of having to offer the biggest public bonus to everyone. The hotel award benefit also encourages members to redeem within Rove instead of transferring their miles to an airline. That may be cheaper where Rove has favorable hotel inventory costs. I’d Like To See More Than Bigger Rebates What’s largely missing is the experience of being treated differently. An airline can give you a better seat that would otherwise go empty. A hotel can upgrade you to an unsold suite. The customer may value that far more than it costs to deliver. Rove doesn’t control those seats and rooms, so promising similar treatment would require agreements with partners. Rove is giving better customer service with status – I asked what the Diamond Desk actually does, and they shared it provides maximum customer support priority and a dedicated email address. Rove is doing the rewarding part well, but they haven’t quite yet figured out recognition which is just as much a part of loyalty.
