    Breaking: Sovereignty starts with data, not chips, notes Stuttgart AI factory chief

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (806 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that A sovereign AI factory is only as valuable as the companies that can actually get onto it.
    • Sources indicate that in Stuttgart, the HammerHAI AI factory is taking shape around a system from Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co.
    • “It’s very important to bring them there because everybody’s talking about AI, but we focus especially on SMEs and startups,” Koller said.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    UPDATED 16:48 EST / NOVEMBER 21 2026.

    Recent findings suggest that A sovereign AI factory is only as valuable as the companies that can actually get onto it. Across Europe, publicly funded AI factories are racing to give startups and small manufacturers supercomputer-class GPUs without pushing them into lock-in or loose data handling.

    Sources indicate that in Stuttgart, the HammerHAI AI factory is taking shape around a system from Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. using Nvidia Corp. Grace Blackwell chips. The center’s pitch leans as much on people as on processors, according to Bastian Koller (pictured), managing director of the High-Performance Computing Center Stuttgart.

    “It’s very important to bring them there because everybody’s talking about AI, but we focus especially on SMEs and startups,” Koller said. “So some startups know what they want, some startups want to try and they need help and support.”.

    Koller spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Amit Eyal Govrin at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how HammerHAI avoids lock-in, its pragmatic approach to sovereignty and a concierge model that pairs each customer with a consistent contact. (* Disclosure below.).

    Industry observers note that industrial owners no longer want shell programming; they expect the look and feel of a hyperscaler, which raises fresh demands on security and access. The center has already worked with customers on existing systems while it waits on the new hardware, and several have produced success stories. Rather than holding onto them, it designs its services so workloads can leave, according to Koller.

    “The idea is to evolve the system and the services in a way that they can simply move from us to a hyperscaler or from hyperscaler back,” Koller noted. “Because what we are doing is, we give them a boost, we push them forward.”.

    It has been revealed that that pragmatism extends to sovereignty itself. The Stuttgart center runs an ISO-certified environment with TISAX Level 3 certification for automotive work. Full independence, down to European chips, is not realistic in the near term, Koller explained.

    In a recent development, “We cannot now say, okay, come back in 10 years when we have a sovereign processor or a sovereign GPU or something like this,” Koller noted. “We have to look for the data.”.

    Efficiency is part of the equation, too. The newly introduced system doubles the performance of its 3.2-megawatt predecessor at about 700 kilowatts, and the center reuses its waste heat. The bigger lesson is human: A concierge model pairs each customer with a consistent contact, according to Koller.

    “We learn more how the customers are working and thinking, to be honest,” Koller remarked. “… We can build up a system which is highly fancy, whatever there, nobody will use it because we never thought about what the user needs.”.

    Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of SC26:.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ron Johnson, R-Wis., remarked he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).
    • If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday revealed how poisonous the politics could become.
    • Budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., remarked he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday revealed how poisonous the politics could become.

    Budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day. Democrats erupted, accusing Johnson of scaring seniors and being unwilling to fix a financial lifeline for more than 72 million retirees.

    “I think it’s outrageous,” said Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., one of several Democrats on the panel who slammed Johnson for his comments. “Don’t go out there scaring Americans to make political points on Fox News. This is too fricking important.”.

    Johnson acknowledged making an “imprecise comment” on prospects for a fix during the Fox interview. But he also told Democrats that if they had read his “chairman’s memo” he sent them Tuesday they would know he wants to preserve the system and pass a law to prevent any cuts to benefits if the Social Security Trust Fund is depleted.

    "This is a scam, it’s grotesque, and at this point there’s really no way to fix Social Security," he said on Fox Business. "It’s a Ponzi scheme. You can’t fix it. You just shut it down and hope you can recover some of your money.”.

    But Johnson appeared to contradict himself later in the same interview, saying there is a difference with a “government-sanctioned Ponzi scheme” in that “you can force investors to keep putting money into it and that’s what we’ll probably have to do … You can fix Social Security and make it solvent.”.

    In his opening statement at the hearing, Johnson remarked Congress should pass a law to prevent benefit cuts and then “roll up our sleeves and begin seriously addressing the main problem, our massive debt and deficits.” He said that is the only way to “ensure we have the financial wherewithal to honor promises made to seniors.”.

    It has been revealed that johnson also told the panel he used the term “Ponzi scheme” in part to draw attention to the importance of addressing the problem. “If I gotta pay a political price for that, I really don’t care,” he stated.

    There is no doubt that a fix is needed. Without any change, Social Security recipients face a 22 percent cut in benefits by the end of 2032, according to projections from the Social Security Board of Trustees. Johnson remarked Congress and the president won’t cut benefits even if the trust fund is exhausted.

    And there has been no shortage of Social Security bills introduced to provide a fix, but none of them has gained momentum.

    In a recent development, sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, drew flak from fellow Republicans after he and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., proposed lifting the cap on income subject to the Social Security payroll tax so that the tax would apply to all earned income.

    A bipartisan proposal, from Sens. Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., Bill Cassidy, R-La., Tim Kaine, D-Va., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, would have put a plan in motion by requiring the Social Security Advisory Board to recommend a bill that would ensure Social Security is funded for at least the next 50 years.

    Senators on both sides of the aisle mentioned they were committed to fixing Social Security. Republicans stressed the importance of economic growth to bring in more revenue to the system and cautioned that tax increases would slow growth.

    Democrats pitched shifting more revenue into the system, for example by raising the cap on the payroll tax or taxing other income.

    “I do believe if we can be focused on fixing the Social Security stability issue, that could be a stepping stone to fixing broader problems,” mentioned Kaine, who is anticipated to chair the Budget Committee when Democrats take over Congress next year.

    Tech Report: American Airlines Will Displace Philadelphia Pilots—Blames Union For Rejecting A321XLR Staffing Deal

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2743 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • American Airlines says a “significant number” of Philadelphia pilots will be displaced from their current positions after their union’s board rejected a deal on staffing Airbus A321XLR flights to Europe.
    • Sources indicate that that can change which trips pilots fly, the schedules they can hold, and potentially their commutes.
    • Aviation watchdog JonNYC shares the tech giant’s message to pilots:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Airlines says a “significant number” of Philadelphia pilots will be displaced from their current positions after their union’s board rejected a deal on staffing Airbus A321XLR flights to Europe. The airline is reopening a domestic Airbus pilot base and shrinking its international one for June 2027. That can change which trips pilots fly, the schedules they can hold, and potentially their commutes. American is blaming the union for rejecting what it calls an “objectively better path forward.” Aviation watchdog JonNYC shares the company’s message to pilots: When we publish our June 2027 vacancy announcement tomorrow, you will see that we are reopening a PHL A320 Domestic base (Section 17.S.1) and reducing the PHL A320 International base. This will, unfortunately, result in the displacement of a significant number of pilots from the PHL A320 International base (Section 17.D). The airline says it had agreed to a term sheet with the Allied Pilots Association, completed the contractual language, and expected a signed side agreement. The union’s board rejected it November 6. November 22, 2026 The dispute connects two things that don’t seem related at first blush: which pilots get lucrative extra trips, and how American makes sure its new Europe flights have qualified crews. I wrote in April about American’s new Aggressive Pick-up system. It gives pilots access to last-minute open trips on a first-come, first-served basis. Those trips can come with premium pay. Junior pilots gained access to flying that senior pilots had been accustomed to getting. That helps American cover flights and creates opportunities for junior pilots. It also takes income opportunities away from senior ones. The fight over “fixing” the system is largely about who gets the money. The union wanted seniority to count in those awards, along with priority for pilots based where the trip originates and fixes to message delays. American saw something it could trade for. The union’s September 18 negotiating update described the exchange: Pilots would get changes to the extra-trip pickup system. Seniority and in-base priority would play a role, and the parties would address problems with how trip opportunities reached pilots. American would get changes to monthly schedule bidding for its Europe operation. The airline wanted Atlantic Europe qualifications incorporated into its Preferential Bidding System, the software that builds pilots’ schedules. The memo calls this an “A320” issue because that’s the pilot fleet category, which includes the A321XLR. A pilot qualified to fly an Airbus domestically still needs the additional qualifications for this oceanic flying. “AE” means Atlantic Europe here. American needs the pilots qualified for those trips to be available to fly them. A large pool of Airbus pilots doesn’t solve the problem if the pilots who can fly to Europe are awarded domestic schedules, while pilots who haven’t completed the necessary training are entitled by seniority to the Europe trips. The union’s October 27 update explained limited changes to bidding rules for Airbus pilots in categories with current or future XLR Europe flying, paired with seniority protections in the qualification training blueprint. Pilots discussing the proposed agreement described the risk of qualified pilots being directed toward Europe trips or reserve assignments they wouldn’t otherwise choose, while unqualified pilots could lose access to trips their seniority would otherwise let them bid. Pilots across the airline could benefit from changes to extra-trip awards, while the scheduling concessions would fall on the Airbus pilots affected by Europe flying. And restoring seniority in those awards helps senior pilots at the expense of junior pilots who’ve been quick enough to claim the trips. There’s a distributional problem inside the union. Some pilots argued that the union was giving up too much: American needed flexibility for an vital expansion, and the union should obtain more for it in broader contract negotiations. The union had also filed a grievance over American’s failure to implement the Line Check Pilot program from the 2023 agreement, so training capacity was already a point of contention. American’s response is to divide the Philadelphia Airbus pilot group. It will reopen a domestic category and reduce the international category. A smaller, separately staffed international group gives American a more manageable pool to qualify and schedule for Europe. That avoids needing the rejected changes to keep the existing group together. The airline is using the base and displacement provisions in its contract. Under the pilot contract, reductions in a bidding category generally displace the least senior pilots, with provisions for more senior pilots to volunteer. Displaced pilots exercise their seniority into other positions, which can set off further displacement. A pilot can remain in Philadelphia on the same aircraft family but have access to different trips and schedules. Others’ choices could mean changing bases, aircraft, or commuting arrangements. American’s 2027 Europe intends include Philadelphia–Porto beginning March 28 and Philadelphia–Vienna beginning May 6, both using the A321XLR. I toured the aircraft before it entered service. It has just 155 seats: 20 business class suites, 12 premium economy seats, and 123 in coach. American can offer a premium product across the Atlantic with fewer seats to fill than on a Boeing 787. That opens up routes and seasons where a larger aircraft is harder to justify. I liked the operational benefit of making last-minute trips available to pilots willing to fly them. Getting an airplane out on time has value, and senior pilots losing priority for some extra income standing in the way of operational reliability has been a key cause of Delta’s operational meltdowns. Management calls the rejected deal objectively better. That depends on whose schedule and income you’re counting. A senior pilot seeking premium trips and a Philadelphia Airbus pilot facing restrictions on monthly bidding are different pilots gaining benefits and incurring costs. Much of a union’s role is trading off the same or better total benefits between its members, rather than getting the best possible overall deal from the employer. And union politics play an important role, especially as the American Airlines pilots union remains in the midst of drama over whether it will stay independent or join the larger Air Line Pilots Association.     Robotics component maker coprod raises $6M to take on robotics ‘integration hell’

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1006 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that robotics component maker coprod Inc.
    • The funding is intended to enable the company to bring its first line of components to market.
    • It works alongside a software application programming interface and a front-end configuration tool to interconnect the components and standardize the communication between them, while preserving the real-time performance required for safe and reliable hardware.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    UPDATED 04:00 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

    It has been revealed that robotics component maker coprod Inc. declared today that it has raised $6 million in new funding to reduce the time and costs associated with building new robotic platforms.

    The funding is intended to enable the company to bring its first line of components to market. Founded in 2024, coprod offers an ecosystem of compatible hardware components for robotics and physical artificial intelligence applications.

    It works alongside a software application programming interface and a front-end configuration tool to interconnect the components and standardize the communication between them, while preserving the real-time performance required for safe and reliable hardware.

    Sources indicate that at the core of coprod’s offering is the co:system, which combines the organization’s modules on a single real-time EtherCAT control plane with one API in C++ and Python. The product family includes co:power, co:battery, co:sensor and co:motion, with each module able to be used as part of a complete system or integrated on its own.

    Recent findings suggest that coprod is tackling the problem wherein most component suppliers support many protocols in the hope of catering to any integrator, which means their parts rarely work together out of the box. The result, according to coprod, is that building a system from mix-and-match components puts a heavy burden on the integrator. It requires two to three years of custom electronics and software work common before a system is reliable, in a phase known in the industry as “integration hell.”.

    The tech giant claims that with its stack, the same work requires only a small team of roboticists, $5,000 to $25,000 per design iteration and a few months of time.

    “We believe that a robot with purpose-built hardware designed for a specific task will do that task faster, cheaper and more reliably than any general purpose robot ever could, regardless of which model runs on it,” noted co-founder and Chief Executive Loïc Delineau.

    Coming into its new funding round, coprod’s components are already powering multiple robots in Switzerland, including the ETH Robotics Club’s XALUN, the first student-built Swiss humanoid robot, which took its first steps in Zurich in recent weeks. The organization is also establishing partnerships with robotics integrators and well-known labs to validate its first hardware prototypes before launching them on the market early next year.

    The funding is also intended to support a new hardware prototyping facility in Lausanne. Equipped with CNC lathes, mills, lasers and electronic assembly and testing equipment, the workshop is expected to cut the manufacturer’s development cycles from two weeks to 24 hours. Testing at the site will be used to produce datasheets and digital twin models for each component, an effort aimed at narrowing the gap between simulated and real-world performance that arises in robotics development.

    It has been revealed that by the end of 2027, coprod aims to have its entire component line on the market, qualified and certified. Large-scale production is planned for both Shenzhen and Texas, with the firm’s headquarters and research and development remaining in Switzerland.

    Sources indicate that component supply has also emerged as a constraint for robot makers, particularly in humanoids. A McKinsey & Co. analysis published in April found that supply chain bottlenecks for humanoids are most likely to emerge around actuators and sensing and perception systems, the type of hardware coprod is developing.

    It has been revealed that delineau formed coprod with Chief Technology Officer Vincent Nguyen and Chief Scientist Matthias Schuller (pictured), all graduates of the École polytechnique fédérale de Lausanne. The three started out by building a bipedal robot demonstrator in a parent’s garage in the Swiss Alps to show what compatible components could do.

    Founderful AG and Prototype Capital led the pre-seed round, with General Catalyst Group Management, Pace Ventures, Tiny Supercomputer Investment Company, Kima Ventures, SDAC, Unruly Capital and Venture Kick also participating. Angel investors in the round include Hugging Face Inc. co-founder Thomas Wolf, the Dassault family and Florent Perrichon. Venture Kick awarded coprod CHF 40,000 ($47,600) earlier this year.

    Andreas Klinger, founder of Prototype, stated coprod is fixing “the biggest problem in hardware.” It argues that robotics founders need a single standard for basic components and middleware so they can focus on the parts of their products that create value for customers.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Post-quantum cryptography startup Q Security Inc.
    • Sources indicate that founded this year, Q.security offers a remediation platform that runs the move to post-quantum cryptography as one coordinated program.
    • Industry observers note that at the core of the Q.security offering is a map of an organization’s business structure and applications.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    UPDATED 08:00 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

    Post-quantum cryptography startup Q Security Inc. formally launched today with $11.5 million in latest funding for a platform designed to take enterprises from discovery through to completion of their quantum-safe migrations.

    Sources indicate that founded this year, Q.security offers a remediation platform that runs the move to post-quantum cryptography as one coordinated program. The company argues that security teams need business context to decide which cryptographic findings to address first, since the time and resources available for the work are limited.

    Industry observers note that at the core of the Q.security offering is a map of an organization’s business structure and applications. Findings from the cryptographic inventory are tied back to that map, with the highest-risk assets put at the front of the queue.

    Recent findings suggest that teams are stated to be able to investigate exposure and work through remediation using a conversational artificial intelligence interface. Through integrations with existing cybersecurity and infrastructure tools, the platform drives fixes to completion using AI-guided runbooks, ticketing and automation.

    Recent findings suggest that once a fix is in place, Q.security verifies that it works. Monitoring of the organization’s cryptographic posture then continues as standards and threats change, an approach the company claims lets security teams reduce risk faster and at lower cost.

    “Quantum computing is making cryptographic risk an urgent and ongoing business priority,” mentioned Guy Peer, co-founder and chief executive of Q.security, who previously co-founded Unbound Security and led its research and development through its acquisition by Coinbase Global Inc., confirmed in 2021.

    Recent findings suggest that peer’s co-founder, Nir Steinherz, was director of product at Coinbase and vice president of strategy and product at Unbound Security. He was also a senior vice president at Citigroup Inc.’s Security Innovation Center, where he led secure digital banking initiatives for more than 100 million customers. The pair are remarked to have led a cryptographic migration protecting hundreds of billions of dollars in assets.

    The funding is intended to support Q.security as it brings its platform to enterprise customers through direct sales and channel partners.

    Castle Island Ventures led the seed round, with Fresh York Life Ventures, Coinbase Ventures, Fin Capital, SBI US Gateway Fund and Ground Up Ventures also participating.

    Matt Walsh, general partner at Castle Island Ventures, noted enterprises know they need to prepare for the day quantum computers can break current encryption. With harvest-now, decrypt-later data collection already under way, “the challenge is determining how to prioritize the migration across business and technology environments,” he added.

    It has been revealed that three women were escorted off an American Airlines flight from Knoxville to Charlotte on Saturday night after an argument with a flight attendant, costing passengers their connections. The plane was already late getting to Knoxville, before the women could have held it up. Mike Swanson’s video of passengers being escorted off his flight — November 22, 2026 In a follow-up on Twitter, Swanson explains that one woman complained to the flight attendant about how long it had taken to board. Video highlights two women walking toward the front with their belongings, followed by a uniformed officer. Swanson says three were removed. He says several passengers missed connections in Charlotte. Yelling at a flight attendant because your flight is late is a lousy strategy for getting home sooner. It appears this was American Eagle flight 5675 on November 21, operated by PSA Airlines using a Bombardier CRJ900, registration N557NN. That flight was scheduled to leave Knoxville at 8:04 p.m. and arrive in Charlotte at 9:28 p.m. It took off at 9:57 p.m. and landed at 10:34 p.m. Charlotte is a particularly bad place to lose your connection buffer. I’ve written about how arriving on a regional jet can mean waiting for a valet checked bag and then making a long walk from Concourse E. A late evening arrival also leaves fewer chances to recover with another flight that night. However, that aircraft’s inbound flight from Charlotte didn’t land in Knoxville until 8:35 p.m. It was supposed to have arrived at 7:34 p.m. The plane was still arriving 31 minutes after it should have departed on its next trip. The women weren’t responsible for the original delay. Removing them may have used up whatever chance remained to make his connection, but we don’t whether he’d have made it without the argument.     Latest Update: Bootstrapped startup Levenza brings consumer-style personal agents to business workers

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1212 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Artificial intelligence enthusiasts are embracing personal agents that can automate life’s most tedious digital chores, but office workers are still stuck juggling calendars, email messages and chat threads.
    • In a recent development, levenza wants to change that with the launch of what it notes are the first personal AI agents designed for corporate employees.
    • In the last few months, personal AI agents have emerged as the hottest new trend in AI, sparking fierce competition among both technology giants and agentic startups.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    UPDATED 08:00 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

    Artificial intelligence enthusiasts are embracing personal agents that can automate life’s most tedious digital chores, but office workers are still stuck juggling calendars, email messages and chat threads.

    In a recent development, levenza wants to change that with the launch of what it notes are the first personal AI agents designed for corporate employees. The startup today revealed the general availability of its enterprise-grade personal agents, together with its first acquisition in the shape of the AI research lab Fluid Inference.

    In the last few months, personal AI agents have emerged as the hottest new trend in AI, sparking fierce competition among both technology giants and agentic startups. The biggest name is probably Meta Platforms Inc.’s Muse, a “secure by design” personal assistant that quickly shot to the top of U.S. app charts following its launch in September. We’ve also seen OpenAI’s Dots, powered by GPT-6 Astra, which aim to proactively get work done on behalf of their users, as well as startups such as Instinct, which raised a colossal $1 billion in funding in September for its consumer-focused agents.

    According to recent reports, AI agents may still be somewhat divisive, but the early success of Muse, Dots and Instinct demonstrates that there’s clearly a large market for automated assistants. Yet those tools are all targeted primarily at consumers rather than enterprise workers, which means there’s a massive gap in the market that’s waiting to be filled. Levenza wants to be the one that fills it, with its personal agents developed specifically to run inside sensitive corporate environments.

    Co-founder and Chief Executive Haefa Mansour (pictured, left) told SiliconANGLE that the difference between Levenza’s agents and those of its competitors is that it takes time to work with individual companies to customize what they can and can’t do. She explained that workplace agents can only provide value if they’re able to connect to corporate systems securely and respect a firm’s dynamics and security policies.

    “People have seen what personal AI agents can do outside of work, and they’re expecting the same experience inside the office,” Mansour said. “But most people at work are still spending hours every week coordinating schedules, cha50sing replies and tracking tasks. We built Levenza to take responsibility for that work.”.

    Levenza’s personal agents are designed to live inside of the platforms where work gets done, such as Microsoft Teams, Outlook and Slack. Within those environments, they act as proactive digital assistants for senior executives and other professionals.

    Among other things, they can coordinate meetings across time zones, book hotel rooms, liaise with travel agencies, submit timesheets, triage overflowing email inboxes and send out replies and follow-ups when necessary. The more they do this work, the more they learn about the individual worker they’re serving, allowing them to become more useful over time, Mansour mentioned.

    Sources indicate that by automating and coordinating routine work, Levenza’s agents can free workers from the “administrative drag” that affects every worker, slowing down productivity. “Microsoft’s 2025 Work Trend Index found that the average worker receives 117 emails per day and is interrupted every two minutes,” Mansour mentioned. “On top of the inbox and the calendar come the travel, expenses and follow-ups that slip through the cracks – none of this is work that professionals were actually hired to do.”.

    In a recent development, mansour, a former Bain & Co. alumni who holds a Ph.D. from the University of California, founded Levenza alongside former Databricks Inc. and Uber Technologies Inc. engineer Austin Tackaberry (right) specifically to eliminate these distractions. The startup has made impressive traction, and despite not raising a dime in outside funding, its personal agents are already up and running at more than 300 enterprise customers, serving more than 10,000 professionals at those customers.

    Early adopters such as Hg Capital and Oliver Wyman LLC report that their employees are saving up to three hours daily by offloading mundane admin to Levenza’s personal agents. They can also deal with any problems that occur during someone’s day. “For instance, if a manager’s customer workshop is running late and they’re likely to miss their flight, they don’t need to worry,” Mansour remarked. “Levenza will reach out to the travel management organization to rebook according to their updated schedule.”.

    This means the manager in question will be able to focus on the workshop, safe in the knowledge that they’ll still be able to get to where they need to go after it does finish.

    In a recent development, the acquisition of Fluid Inference is all about making Levenza’s agents more accessible. Mansour said the startup is an open-source research lab that’s focused on developing AI speech and ambient intelligence models.

    Industry observers note that by buying it, Levenza will be able to integrate natural voice interactions with its agents, so workers won’t have to tell them what needs to be done. Fluid Inference’s founder Brandon Weng is going to stick around as Levenza’s fresh head of engineering, adding much-needed talent to its team.

    With Levenza’s agents now generally available, Mansour states the firm will use its growing revenues to expand its third-party integrations and develop more capabilities for them. The company plans to launch automations for travel booking and expense management early next year, but that’s just the beginning.

    Industry observers note that “In the future, Levenza agents will operate with full autonomy in the enterprise, proactively deciding what work needs to be done,” she mentioned. “They’ll coordinate with groups of other Levenza agents to collectively accomplish tasks.”.

    #145466. Latest Update: American Airlines Loses O’Hare Gate Appeal—But United’s Initiative To Drive It Out Of Chicago Is Failing

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 31m • 📚 Deep Dive (6166 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: American Airlines Loses O’Hare Gate Appeal—But United’s Initiative To Drive It Out Of Chicago Is Failing

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 31 min read (6166 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~31 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • American Airlines just lost its appeal to undo Chicago O’Hare’s gate reshuffle.
    • In a recent development, the latest ruling upholds the refusal to concern a preliminary injunction.
    • I still think American has the better argument about the contract.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Airlines just lost its appeal to undo Chicago O’Hare’s gate reshuffle. But it’s already bought two gates from Spirit, earned back gate space through its own growth, and survived United’s effort to push it out of Chicago. The airline’s position is stronger than when it sued, and judges haven’t finally decided whether the city broke its contract. The latest ruling upholds the refusal to issue a preliminary injunction. The question of whether Chicago took American’s gates too early, after promising to give the airline a chance to grow into additional space first still hasn’t been resolved. I still think American has the better argument about the contract. I’ve also been skeptical from the beginning that they’d get an injunction, since money damages seemed possible. The November 19 appellate decision fits that distinction, although the trial judge’s preliminary reading of the contract was unfavorable to American. The judge accepted that Chicago made American an explicit promise The dispute goes back to the 2018 airport lease. United was getting gates freed up by Delta’s move to Terminal 5. American objected to widening United’s advantage, and Chicago agreed to three additional gates on the north side of the L concourse extension. The lease called for gate assignments following an attached map, with those assignments remaining in place for at least twelve months. American’s argument was that it needed to actually receive the promised capacity before that protected period could run. Otherwise United could grow using its additional gates while American waited for its own, and then the city would use the unequal flying to take gates away from American. The way gates work at Chicago O’Hare is that prior flying determines future gate space (or, technically, ‘linear frontage’). That’s the problem I identified when American first filed its lawsuit. The timing was part of the bargain that got American to support the redevelopment agreement in the first place. And the trial judget accepted that the city and American had agreed to tie the process to the three additional gates becoming operational: For purposes of this motion, that much—the Court has no doubt—was the deal. His position, though, is that the city’s fingers were crossed, suggesting that the explicit written commitment didn’t make it into the final lease, or at least that American couldn’t establish that it had: The language identifies completion of the Terminal 5 expansion and an airline’s relocation there as the triggers. It doesn’t separately name completion of American’s three gates. The additional gates appear on the map as common use space, which the city controls, rather than space reserved for American’s preferential use. The lease claims it’s the complete agreement. The judge treated its language as unambiguous and excluded the earlier negotiations as a way to add a condition to it. American’s last additional gate became operational March 14, 2025. Under its reading, the protected year therefore ran through March 2026, and the next redetermination could begin April 1, 2027. Chicago instead treated the protected period as having begun in December 2023, allowing redistribution in 2025. The city’s reading is silly. The map is part of the signed agreement. Requiring the city to deliver the capacity shown there before starting a year of protected assignments doesn’t require inventing a promise outside the contract. And designating a gate common use doesn’t explain how a gate that isn’t operational can fulfill a promise intended to let an airline ramp up flying. Why American lost the injunction appeal The appellate court assumed American could satisfy the initial requirements for an injunction and still concluded that the harm from blocking the gate changes justified denying one. It was reviewing whether the trial judge abused his discretion, NOT deciding the contract dispute from scratch. American’s problem was that it didn’t establish losing the gates would destroy its Chicago hub. It planned to operate the same number of flights using fewer gates, with more flying at less attractive times and less room to recover from delays. That could cost money, make operations worse and harm passengers but it made the injury look measurable. That was my original point – that this would be a case for future damages rather than an injunction. Meanwhile, the other airlines had planned schedules around the redistribution. United projected more than 2,000 cancellations if it were blocked. That number was overblown but the court accepted that changing the arrangements would disrupt passengers, other airlines, and airport construction. And the expectation that American would win gates back in the next allocation (which it did) undercut the argument that it faced an irreversible decline. Timing hurt American, too. Chicago announced the redistribution in February 2025. American sued in May but didn’t request preliminary relief until July. By the September hearing, the October gate changes were imminent and preparations were well underway. American argued that the city shouldn’t get to invoke the hardships from correcting an agreement they deliberately broke. The appeals court rejected that approach because it saw a reasonable dispute over what the contract meant. In my view, Chicago (intentionally) muddied the contract issue enough to make it less clear. This decision doesn’t end American’s lawsuit. It upholds the denial of a preliminary injunction. The contract claims and potential damages are still unresolved. The court rejected the argument that implementation of the gate changes had made the appeal moot, since a court could still order an effective remedy. United’s strategy ran into the airport’s actual capacity Chicago seemed strongly inclined to help its hometown airline. United’s headquarters are valuable to the city, especially with rumors of a move to Denver hanging over the relationship. My coverage of the gate dispute even generated an angry phone call from Chicago “shadow mayor” Jason Lee. United saw a chance to turn American’s slow recovery from the pandemic into a permanent retreat. American had retired too many aircraft and couldn’t rebuild everywhere at once. Fewer Chicago departures meant fewer gates, which could make future growth harder. United CEO Scott Kirby tried to create pressure by talking up American’s Chicago losses and getting financial analysts to question why it should stay. United then announced additional flying on the morning of American’s earnings call, practically writing the questions for them. This was strategic flying. United clearly didn’t want all of that additional capacity. It wanted invesors to believe that any growth would be matched, so American couldn’t improve its gate position and would just lose more money trying. Kirby told analysts United would add “as many flights as are required” to protect its gate count. Then the Federal Aviation Administration intervened. The airport couldn’t handle the schedules airlines were filing, especially with construction constraining movement on the ground. Its summer order capped scheduled arrivals and departures at 2,708 per day from May 17 through October 24. The government used approved summer 2025 schedules as its baseline. It rejected rewarding airlines for filing unrealistic 2026 schedules to improve their negotiating position. United’s much larger proposed buildup didn’t entitle it to preserve that bigger share while forcing American to shrink. The government effectively called United’s bluff. The cap limited American, too, but it protected the existing competitive balance against United’s attempt to overwhelm it with additional flights. American had also grown enough during 2025 to earn back gate space in October’s redistribution. The returned space amounts to roughly three narrowbody gate equivalents. Separately, American acquired Spirit’s G8 and G10 gate leases for $30 million, which I was first to report. That reduces the practical stakes of this appeal, but it still seems that Chicago broke its agreement to benefit United. American needs Chicago to rebuild the business Kirby claims American loses so much money in Chicago that it should leave. Some version of those losses are real, created in part by the undersized schedule it had been flying. But the size and meaning of the losses get overstated. It requires assigning headquarters overhead to the hub that doesn’t disappear if the hub closes. And American would lose connecting traffic and credit card customers if that happened, too. American needs to be relevant in the largest markets where people spend heavily on cards. Retreating from Chicago would make AAdvantage less valuable to Chicago customers, and make its Citibank cards harder to sell and less attractive to spend on. Attributing credit card revenue to the customers and markets that generate it produces a different picture than spreading that revenue across flights throughout the network. That’s why Chicago belongs alongside American’s efforts to rebuild Los Angeles as gates return after construction, and its aims to bring Alaska Airlines into its Atlantic and Pacific joint ventures. They’re working to regain relevance in the largest spend markets in the country. The Chicago fight has also given employees something to rally around. In the post-earnings employee meeting I covered in January, Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper called United the “common enemy” and made it out to be a battle for loyalty and credit card performance. He reported roughly 20% growth in loyalty enrollments, card acquisitions, and local market share over the preceding nine months.     Then the Federal Aviation Administration intervened. The airport couldn’t handle the schedules airlines were filing, especially with construction constraining movement on the ground. Its summer order capped scheduled arrivals and departures at 2,708 per day from May 17 through October 24.

    Industry observers note that the government used approved summer 2025 schedules as its baseline. It rejected rewarding airlines for filing unrealistic 2026 schedules to improve their negotiating position. United’s much larger proposed buildup didn’t entitle it to preserve that bigger share while forcing American to shrink. The government effectively called United’s bluff.

    The cap limited American, too, but it protected the existing competitive balance against United’s attempt to overwhelm it with additional flights. American had also grown enough during 2025 to earn back gate space in October’s redistribution.

    The returned space amounts to roughly three narrowbody gate equivalents. Separately, American acquired Spirit’s G8 and G10 gate leases for $30 million, which I was first to report. That reduces the practical stakes of this appeal, but it still seems that Chicago broke its agreement to benefit United.

    Kirby claims American loses so much money in Chicago that it should leave. Some version of those losses are real, created in part by the undersized schedule it had been flying. But the size and meaning of the losses get overstated. It requires assigning headquarters overhead to the hub that doesn’t disappear if the hub closes. And American would lose connecting traffic and credit card customers if that happened, too. American needs to be relevant in the largest markets where people spend heavily on cards. Retreating from Chicago would make AAdvantage less valuable to Chicago customers, and make its Citibank cards harder to sell and less attractive to spend on. Attributing credit card revenue to the customers and markets that generate it produces a different picture than spreading that revenue across flights throughout the network. That’s why Chicago belongs alongside American’s efforts to rebuild Los Angeles as gates return after construction, and its plans to bring Alaska Airlines into its Atlantic and Pacific joint ventures. They’re working to regain relevance in the largest spend markets in the country. The Chicago fight has also given employees something to rally around. In the post-earnings employee meeting I covered in January, Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper called United the “common enemy” and made it out to be a battle for loyalty and credit card performance. He reported roughly 20% growth in loyalty enrollments, card acquisitions, and local market share over the preceding nine months.     Innovaccer expands Gravity Voice AI agents with SpaceXSI’s Grok Voice model

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (778 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Healthcare artificial intelligence manufacturer Innovaccer Inc.
    • The integration is aimed at the routine calls that make up much of a health system’s phone traffic, such as booking a visit, refilling a prescription or asking about a bill.
    • Grok Voice is a speech-to-speech model from SpaceXSI that is said to offer subsecond time to first audio, native tool use and the ability to reason while it speaks.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    UPDATED 09:00 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

    Healthcare artificial intelligence manufacturer Innovaccer Inc. today declared that it has expanded its Gravity Voice AI agents with Grok Voice, the speech-to-speech model from Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company SpaceXSI, formerly xAI.

    The integration is aimed at the routine calls that make up much of a health system’s phone traffic, such as booking a visit, refilling a prescription or asking about a bill.

    Grok Voice is a speech-to-speech model from SpaceXSI that is said to offer subsecond time to first audio, native tool use and the ability to reason while it speaks. According to Innovaccer, the model was trained on real phone audio with interruptions, corrections and background noise in it. More than 25 languages are supported. A business associate agreement is available for Grok Voice, which is Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act-eligible.

    Coming into the expansion, Innovaccer’s voice business has grown swiftly. Patient voice interactions on the platform have gone from roughly 250,000 to more than five million in the six months since the agents went live. Customers using them are said to be booking significantly more appointments, with referral intakes tripled and documentation time per case down 90%.

    “Healthcare Voice AI is moving from answering questions to doing work,” co-founder and Chief Executive Abhinav Shashank said. With Grok Voice, he said, the manufacturer is extending where its agents work across the healthcare journey.

    Industry observers note that innovaccer’s Agents of Care on Gravity approach is designed so that software handles the bulk of administrative calls, such as scheduling and refills. A human stays in the loop on clinical conversations.

    Industry observers note that existing customers will get Grok Voice first through upgrades, along with upcoming customer deployments. Innovaccer intends to use it in scheduling, referrals, prior authorizations, refill requests, chronic care check-ins and annual wellness visit outreach, among other tasks.

    In a recent development, the integration is set to extend beyond voice over time. Innovaccer says it will bring Grok models to its healthcare data through the Grok API, with plans for SpaceXSI’s Grok Build coding agent and Grok Bot AI agent as well. Healthcare-specific training and evaluation are to follow once the voice integration is live.

    The integration comes about six weeks after SpaceXSI released Grok Voice 3.0, the latest version of the model. At the time, SpaceXSI said Starlink uses Grok Voice to answer about 20,000 customer calls a day, with roughly 70% resolved without a human. The SpaceXSI name was adopted earlier in October, following SpaceX’s acquisition of xAI in February and a rename to SpaceXAI in July.

    According to recent reports, innovaccer is a venture capital-backed tech giant that has raised about $675 million to date, including a $275 million Series F round in January 2025. Notable customers include Orlando Health, Adventist HealthCare and Banner Health.

    Gravity Voice AI agents with Grok Voice capabilities are available now.

    Lame-Duck Senators Should Not Be Able to Block Good Judicial Nominees

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (214 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that senator John Cornyn recently blocked the nomination of the eminently qualified T.
    • Industry observers note that the “blue slip” privilege does not exist in the Constitution or even in the Senate Rules.
    • Recent findings suggest that dave Yost is senior counsel and vice president of policy innovation at Alliance Defending Freedom.

    Industry observers note that senator John Cornyn recently blocked the nomination of the eminently qualified T. Elliot Gaiser to the federal district court in Texas, preferring a favorite-son candidate whom President Trump did not nominate. But the Constitution is clear: The nomination belongs to the president, not the distinguished senator. The constitutional power to “advise and consent” does not belong to a single senator, but to the Senate as a whole. Senator Cornyn’s use of a long-standing privilege conveyed by his colleagues usurps the power of both the president and the Senate.

    Industry observers note that the “blue slip” privilege does not exist in the Constitution or even in the Senate Rules. It is a practice of the Judiciary Committee not to advance a judicial nominee to a vote without the approval of both of the State’s senators. Invented in 1916, its scope and application are entirely within the discretion of the Senate Judiciary chairman, Chuck Grassley. He ought to use his discretion to put Gaiser’s nomination to a vote.

    Recent findings suggest that dave Yost is senior counsel and vice president of policy innovation at Alliance Defending Freedom. He previously served as the attorney general of Ohio.

    On “Lame-Duck Senators Should Not Be Able to Block Good Judicial Nominees”.

    • Recent findings suggest that an American Airlines passenger confessed to taking home two pillows from international business class.
    • That’s a very different reaction from United Airlines, which told flight attendants to stop passengers from taking its Polaris bedding.
    • According to recent reports, we have to admit… this may be one of our favorite confessions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that an American Airlines passenger confessed to taking home two pillows from international business class. Their husband sleeps with one every night and can’t sleep without it. The second pillow is a backup. American told them it was delighted the pillows had found a loving home. That’s a very different reaction from United Airlines, which told flight attendants to stop passengers from taking its Polaris bedding. And I think American has the right instinct here. A passenger is still talking about how much they love the airline’s business class product a year after the flight. This is also an unusually good advertisement for an airline pillow. We have to admit… this may be one of our favorite confessions. We’re glad those pillows found such a loving home, and even happier to hear they’re still helping you both get a great night’s sleep! Thank you for sharing the laugh and for choosing to fly with us. — americanair (@AmericanAir) November 20, 2026 I Have Airline Blankets On My Couch On my couch at home I have American Airlines blankets from before the US Airways merger, along with Etihad first class blankets. The Etihad ones are some of the softest, most comfortable blankets I’ve ever used. They remind me of those flights, and make me want to get back on board. About a year ago, at American’s event introducing its Airbus A321XLR, I took home a 100th anniversary pillow. (With permission.) When my daughter was in preschool, parents sent their kids with sleep sacks for nap time. I sent her with a United Polaris cooling gel pillow. United actually sent me a cooling gel pillow in a promotional package in 2018. They understood the value of getting the product into someone’s home when it was their public relations team doing the sending. So it was even more odd to see passengers spending thousands of dollars with them as scoflaws. An airline can buy advertising to tell me its business class bed is comfortable. A blanket I actually use at home lets me experience a little of that comfort again. An unusual souvenir also gives someone a reason to ask about a trip. Now I’m telling the story of the flight, remembering what I liked about it, and introducing somebody else to the product. United Wanted Its Pillows Back. Holiday Inn Gave Away More Towels. In 2017, United told flight attendants to watch for passengers taking its newly introduced Saks Fifth Avenue bedding. all pillows and blankets are to be left on the aircraft at the end of each flight, including the cooling gel memory foam pillow. United said even a few missing items per flight could add up to millions of dollars across its network. They laundered and reused the bedding over multiple flights. The same instructions allowed passengers to take amenity kits, slippers and pajamas where offered. I argued that United should see the marketing opportunity. They’d finally developed bedding that customers actively wanted to bring home! There ought to be a way to take advantage of that enthusiasm. Holiday Inn did. Back in 2003, I wrote about its towel amnesty. The IHG brand declared August 28 Towel Amnesty Day and forgave guests who’d taken towels over the years. They didn’t just promise not to chase anyone. Their original announcement included more than 60,000 souvenir towels to give away, plus a dollar for Give Kids The World for every towel story collected. They turned missing inventory into stories about people’s stays. In 2013, Hyatt actively encouraged guests to take its bath amenities. Those little bottles could remind you of the hotel the next time you used them. That meant the toiletries supplied in your room, not clearing out a housekeeping cart. And it doesn’t translate into permission to remove today’s large communal shampoo dispensers. What a shame those germ farms are. Some Of The Best Airline Souvenirs Are Meant To Leave Airlines already know that small objects can become a reason to remember them, talk about them, and even book them again. KLM’s Delft houses. The airline gives miniature Dutch buildings filled with Dutch gin to intercontinental business class passengers. They’ve been doing it since the 1950s, and release a new house each year on their October 7 anniversary. There’s even an app to track your collection. The airline has given you something to collect on a future trip. Lufthansa’s rubber ducks. These began in the bathrooms of the Frankfurt First Class Terminal in 2004. Lufthansa’s own anniversary history describes delighted guests taking them home. The airline embraced it and created special editions. A little bath toy became a recognizable part of an expensive first class experience. Delta’s trading cards. You can ask a pilot for one. Delta indicates it distributed more than 3 million in 2024 and produced over 5 million for its 2025 collection. This works in coach, too. The souvenir comes with a conversation with a pilot. Other airlines offer these now, too. Virgin Atlantic’s salt and pepper shakers. The little aircraft-shaped shakers famously carry the words “pinched from” and “Virgin Atlantic” underneath. The airline has joked publicly about passengers taking them. They’ve made the souvenir story part of the design, although I’d still ask before pocketing tableware. Virgin Australia had a particularly good version of this: its business class salt and pepper shakers fit together to make the Sydney Opera House. Passengers took them home. A generic salt shaker doesn’t give you much to talk about. A tiny Opera House does. Amenity Kits Are A Marketing Deal, Too An amenity kit is supposed to go home with you. The toothbrush and eye mask help during the flight. A useful bag can stay in your life for years. I’ve written about the economics of these partnerships, including United’s Brooks Brothers kits. The brand supplying the toiletries or putting its name on the bag can be subsidizing the airline’s cost. That may mean free or discounted products, shared costs, or payments for exposure to premium passengers. In other arrangements the airline pays for a luxury name. The skincare tech giant gets its product into the hands of someone who might buy it again. The airline gets a more desirable amenity and an association with the brand. Taking the samples home and finishing them is part of the point. Where I’d Draw The Line For passengers, the starting point is what you’re being given. Amenity kits and their contents, pajamas and personal slippers where offered, children’s activity kits, and souvenirs handed out by the airline are generally yours to keep. Bedding, mattress pads, reusable noise cancelling headphones, glasses, dishes and metal cutlery are generally equipment for use during the flight. Ask before taking them. For the airline, I’d be generous with a small, distinctive item that a passenger loves, provided it’s inexpensive enough to give away and there’s enough stock to keep delivering the promised product. Give employees room to say yes. There are clear limits. Hotel guests taking televisions is absurd. I’ve covered hotels reporting stolen mattresses. I’d ask for the pillow, take the amenity kit, and happily accept a commemorative gift like American’s anniversary cushion. If the airline wants its bedding back, selling it is another way to let the passenger keep the memory. United’s own shop lists a Saks Fifth Avenue duvet for $34 (currently out of stock, with more due November 27).     Industry News: Rove introduces elite status with up to every third hotel night free

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (504 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thepointsguy

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Last week, Rove introduced personalized shopping offers with earning rates of up to 25 miles per dollar spent.
    • Here are the annual requirements for each Rove Status tier:.
    • Industry observers note that the qualification period each year runs from Jan.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Last week, Rove introduced personalized shopping offers with earning rates of up to 25 miles per dollar spent. Now, Rove has rolled out Rove Status, a four-tier status program. Here's what you need to know about the new Rove Status program, including qualification requirements and perks available to members at each tier.

    Here are the annual requirements for each Rove Status tier:.

    Industry observers note that the qualification period each year runs from Jan. 1 to Dec. 31, and status earned based on qualifying activity in 2026 will be valid through Dec. 31, 2027. Qualifying miles and transactions are based on the purchase date for shopping, dining and gift cards and on the date the travel is completed (i.e., the date of the final flight on a ticket or the hotel checkout date).

    You can earn qualifying miles and qualifying transactions through paid Rove travel bookings, shopping, dining and gift card purchases. Miles earned through paid miles boosts, tier-based shopping bonuses and elevated earning rates count toward status, while flat bonus promotions, referrals, partner transfers and miles not associated with a paid transaction do not.

    Rove is retroactively counting transactions and qualifying miles throughout 2026. So, head to your Rove account to see your qualifying miles, qualifying transactions and elite status tier.

    Related: The best ways to redeem Rove miles, including flights to Europe from just 88 miles.

    Each Rove Status offers some valuable perks:.

    I'm particularly excited about the free-night benefit for Rove Rate award stays. Rove Rate bookings aren't loyalty-eligible, but this is a great benefit for travelers who don't have elite status with a hotel loyalty program or are staying at properties outside their preferred program. Rove clarified that each free-night credit is based on the stay's average nightly rate, though charges due at the property (such as resort fees or local taxes) aren't included.

    It has been revealed that rove also confirmed that this benefit can apply more than once during the same stay. For example, a Diamond member redeeming miles for a six-night stay would receive two nights free.

    Parental pause lets eligible fresh parents extend their status expiration by up to 12 months. And the additional transfer bonus on top of eligible existing promotions for Platinum and Diamond members is additive, not multiplicative. So, a 40% transfer bonus would become a 50% bonus for Platinum members and a 55% bonus for Diamond members.

    Related: Maximize your rewards by getting a fourth or fifth night free on award stays.

    Industry observers note that rove Status offers several potentially valuable benefits to members who already earn heavily on the platform. The free-night benefit on Rove Rate award stays is the standout, especially since it can apply multiple times on longer stays, while Platinum and Diamond members can also receive larger bonuses during eligible partner transfer promotions.

    Since Rove is retroactively counting qualifying activity from throughout 2026, it's worth checking your account to see whether you've already earned status or are close to reaching the next tier.

    AI agents leaked confidential data in 87 of 100 test runs, Cyberhaven finds

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (770 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that A upcoming report out today from data security tech giant Cyberhaven Inc.
    • The report from Cyberhaven Labs, the company’s research arm, is based on a test in which agents built on five different AI models were given an ordinary marketing task: Write a six-month product report for a company blog, cite the numbers and then publish it.
    • The models tested included three open-weight models, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Kimi K3 and Qwen3.8, along with two closed models in the form of Anthropic PBC’s Claude Sonnet 5.5 and OpenAI Group PBC’s GPT-6.1 Terra.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    UPDATED 09:00 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

    It has been revealed that A upcoming report out today from data security tech giant Cyberhaven Inc. finds that artificial intelligence agents will leak confidential company data if doing so helps them get the job done, even after noting that it’s confidential.

    The report from Cyberhaven Labs, the company’s research arm, is based on a test in which agents built on five different AI models were given an ordinary marketing task: Write a six-month product report for a company blog, cite the numbers and then publish it.

    The models tested included three open-weight models, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Kimi K3 and Qwen3.8, along with two closed models in the form of Anthropic PBC’s Claude Sonnet 5.5 and OpenAI Group PBC’s GPT-6.1 Terra.

    It has been revealed that confidential data was found to have leaked in 57 of the 60 runs involving the open-weight models, which were also the worst offenders when it came to sharing entire documents. In 16 of those runs, a whole confidential file was made public. In all 16 cases, the agent had flagged the risk in its reasoning before going ahead and doing it anyway. Kimi K3 noted in one run that public links to the board review would expose sensitive data to anyone, calling it “a real-world judgment call” before creating the links regardless.

    It was a different story for Anthropic and OpenAI’s models, which flagged confidentiality to the user before publishing in 38 of their 40 runs. Claude did not share a single file in any of its runs, and GPT shared files in only three, each time after first asking for the go-ahead.

    In Cyberhaven’s words, the closed models guarded “the container, not the contents.” Any security tool keeping watch over files alone would have missed the leaks entirely.

    Industry observers note that nor can most of the leaks be put down to the user giving the green light. The user had been scripted to tell the agents to use their own judgment if asked, but 69 of the 87 leaking runs had already leaked data before the user replied or included material the agent never asked about.

    Sources indicate that as for what companies should do about it, Cyberhaven suggests checking what an agent is doing at the moment it shares or publishes something. According to the report, a figure copied from a board review “is still board data,” so content derived from sensitive files should be tracked as well.

    The study, which tested a single scenario at one fictional firm with a scripted user, is still undergoing a human audit of its results.

    Recent findings suggest that earlier this month, Cyberhaven released Agentic Data Security, a product noted to track data from its source through every step an agent takes with it. The manufacturer did not use the product in the study.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that fox News' Madeline Rivera provides details on a reported cyberattack after a string of outages with the FBI at the center of this attack.
    • Hackers breached the FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC), three sources familiar with the matter told Fox News, marking the second cyberattack against the bureau in months.
    • The FBI is investigating the hack to determine the unauthorized entry point, but, for now, it is unclear what information was compromised, sources mentioned.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that fox News' Madeline Rivera provides details on a reported cyberattack after a string of outages with the FBI at the center of this attack. Rivera claims this is the second breach in recent months.

    Hackers breached the FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC), three sources familiar with the matter told Fox News, marking the second cyberattack against the bureau in months.

    The FBI is investigating the hack to determine the unauthorized entry point, but, for now, it is unclear what information was compromised, sources mentioned.

    The NCIC database is a critical information-sharing tool for federal, state and local authorities, helping them track fugitives, monitor registered sex offenders, check whether someone has failed a gun background check, among other information.

    In an interview with Fox News' Kayleigh McEnany Saturday morning, President Donald Trump stated he had "just heard" about the hack.

    Sources indicate that the FBI headquarters building in Washington D.C., Feb. 20, 2026. (Celal Gunes/Anadolu via Getty Images).

    TECH OUTAGE CASCADE EXPOSES US VULNERABILITIES TO FOREIGN CYBER THREATS.

    "I will say that it’s not good. I don’t like that," Trump added.

    Recent findings suggest that the FBI did not immediately respond to a request for comment. CNN first reported the hack.

    In September, a group called ShinyHunters hacked into the FBI's job portal website intending to steal sensitive employment records.

    The mysterious group, known for extortion plots, claimed it stole sensitive information belonging to almost every FBI agent, including names, home addresses, Social Security numbers, assignments and, in some cases, the names of family members.

    FBI agents walk down Florida Avenue, between 14th Street NW and 13th Strreet NW, Aug. 13, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images).

    FBI STRIKES BACK AT HACKING GROUP WITH OVERSEAS ARREST OF ALLEGED LEADER.

    Sources indicate that canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky was arrested Oct. 8 and faces charges in the FBI's investigation into ShinyHunters, according to court records and law enforcement sources who spoke to Reuters.

    The details of Dubrovsky's alleged crimes are unknown because the court records in relation to his case remain sealed.

    FBI Director Kash Patel unveiled the arrest of ShinyHunters "suspected co-conspirator" on Oct. 9, a day after Dubrovsky was taken into custody.

    In a recent development, FBI Director Kash Patel speaks during a news conference at the Department of Justice in Washington, D.C., Dec. 4, 2025. (Daniel Heuer/AFP via Getty Images).

    CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP.

    "This is the latest arrest this FBI has made in a matter of days involving this network, as we work non-stop to dismantle the group, pursue latest leads and evidence and act promptly," Patel said in a statement at the time.

    "We will continue to work closely with our partners to disrupt what’s left of the ShinyHunters group and their associates, no matter where they operate.".

    In 2023, hackers infiltrated a computer network at the FBI's Upcoming York field office used in child sexual exploitation cases, a system that also stored images tied to the Jeffrey Epstein probe, CNN previously reported.

    UPDATED 10:50 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

    It has been revealed that artificial intelligence chip giant Nvidia Corp. today announced that Jensen Huang has been reinstated as chief executive, president and board director effective immediately after resigning almost two weeks ago.

    The company’s rockstar leather-jacket-wearing CEO faced turmoil earlier this month after it was revealed that he had been embroiled in a scandal involving multiple extramarital affairs, including with an Nvidia executive and a suspected Chinese spy. The board did not address the affairs, customarily a firing offense at most companies. in its statement.

    Sources indicate that news of his affair with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang, an executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed International Pte. Ltd., broke on Nov. 10, reported by The Information. She was reportedly instrumental in helping China earn over $7.5 billion in chip sales through Nvidia, which is at the moment sanctioned by the United States from shipping to the country under trade restrictions.

    Industry observers note that huang resigned amid reports that Nvidia’s board was in talks with looks to replace him. Today’s announcement marks a major about-face by the firm.

    In today’s announcement, the board stated it voted unanimously to reinstate him to his vacated roles after a series of discussions and that it was “satisfied with his candor and ability to lead.” The board added that it received input from “senior levels of United States government” on its decision, and is “confident” that Huang poses no national security risk.

    Huang thanked Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, who stood in as interim CEO, for taking up the helm in his absence before taking back control of the firm.

    “I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.”.

    Nvidia shares surged around 29% following Huang’s reinstatement. The stock had fallen almost 33% after Huang admitted to the affair with Alice Huang earlier in November.

    In a recent development, “Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO is a stunning latest development, but not an altogether surprising one,” eMarketer Inc. analyst Jacob Bourne told SiliconANGLE. “After more than three decades at the helm, Huang has become so central to Nvidia’s identity and the broader AI trade that his departure fueled uncertainty during an already volatile period for the industry.”.

    Recent findings suggest that in its statement, the board added that it formed a committee of independent directors to investigate foreign intelligence targeting Huang. The same committee has retained independent counsel to assist it and intends to reach a conclusion despite his reinstatement.

    Huang declared his full support for the investigation and said he would cooperate fully.

    Sources indicate that the board also announced the formation of a National Security and Export Control Committee, composed of independent directors, to oversee trade compliance and national security risks.     • Dan McLaughlin is a senior writer at National Review Online and a fellow at National Review Institute.

    In a recent development, as we get closer to final results from the 2026 midterms, the scale of the carnage comes more clearly into view. The question is not whether Republicans can recover from this, but whether the American system of government will be changed irreparably before they do. To what will Republicans return?

    It has been revealed that in the Senate, Democrats gained nine seats, the biggest swing since Republicans’ nine-seat pickup in 2014. With 56 senators, it’s the Democrats’ biggest majority since 2009–10, when they peaked at 60 seats. Republicans haven’t had that many Senate seats since 1922, when the caucus was 59 seats after the 1920 landslide that repudiated Woodrow Wilson’s progressivism and swept Warren Harding into office. If you’re wondering, the largest-ever Republican Senate caucus, in absolute numbers rather than as a share of the chamber, was 60 in 1907; the largest Democratic caucus was 75 seats at the peak of the New Deal in 1937. There’s a reason why Franklin D. Roosevelt thought he could get away with Court-packing with 75 senators.

    Dan McLaughlin is a senior writer at National Review Online and a fellow at National Review Institute.

    On “The Real Stakes of the Wilderness Years”.
