    Miren introduces flexible application deployment platform built for the agentic era

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1179 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Miren Inc., an agentic infrastructure company, rolled out its platform today to make it easier for developers to deploy applications anywhere they need, without requiring them to become a solutions expert or set up and configure the application.
    • Industry observers note that artificial intelligence coding agents have changed the playing field for developers by making it easier than ever to build applications, but getting that software into deployment has remained a challenge.
    • “[Our platform] transforms a computer anywhere you want into a place for your application to live,” Chief Executive Evan Phoenix told SiliconANGLE in an interview.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    UPDATED 12:00 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

    Miren Inc., an agentic infrastructure company, rolled out its platform today to make it easier for developers to deploy applications anywhere they need, without requiring them to become a solutions expert or set up and configure the application.

    Industry observers note that artificial intelligence coding agents have changed the playing field for developers by making it easier than ever to build applications, but getting that software into deployment has remained a challenge. Configuration of resources, storage and the actual end maintenance of infrastructure that keeps everything running can be a burden that requires constant attention.

    “[Our platform] transforms a computer anywhere you want into a place for your application to live,” Chief Executive Evan Phoenix told SiliconANGLE in an interview.

    Miren gives developers a way to turn virtually any computer, from a virtual machine or bare-metal server to a local system, into a platform for running applications. Developers write their code locally, or have an AI coding agent generate it, and then hand it over to Miren, which handles building, running and much of the configuration necessary to deploy it. Once deployed, the application is accessible through a URL, without the developer having to set up and manage the underlying infrastructure individually.

    The idea is to take much of the heavy lifting off the developer so they can do what they do best: designing, coding and strategizing.

    It has been revealed that “I was always interested in this, like the application development is sort of like the final boss of someone’s great idea, right? They’re working on this great idea, and they’re like, ‘Oh, now I need to share it with somebody,'” Phoenix explained.

    The deployment is easy. A developer logs into their virtual machine or bare-metal server and installs Merin server, which then acts like a technician on the other end, watching over maintenance and deployment. The developer can then code locally, sandbox and do all of their work on a laptop or local machine, and when they’re ready, deploy to production with a command.

    Critically, all of a developer’s data and application resources exist and run on their chosen infrastructure, virtual machines and servers. Phoenix stressed that this provides customers the flexibility to run wherever they choose and however they like. One customer in particular wanted to run software inside a German sovereign cloud environment, something that could be difficult with traditional platform-as-a-service providers that restrict people to their infrastructure. Miren lets the customer choose an appropriate environment while keeping the same development and deployment workflow.

    “We’ve really attempted to have people be able to control where it runs, but still have the ease and the flexibility of it just running on the internet at the same time,” Phoenix remarked.

    Industry observers note that miren also provides a third service that complements the developer client and the server: Miren Cloud, which is optional for a standalone deployment. However, it becomes particularly useful when multiple developers need to work with the same infrastructure.

    “Miren is addressing one of the biggest challenges in modern application development: giving developers the flexibility to run applications anywhere without adding another layer of operational complexity,” stated Paul Nashawaty, practice lead and principal analyst, application development at ECI Research. “As enterprises expand across hyperscalers, sovereign clouds and private infrastructure, managing distributed clusters becomes increasingly difficult.”.

    Nashawaty cited ECI internal research, noting that 61% of developers cite tool fragmentation as the biggest barrier, making more unified approaches to application delivery and operations a top need.

    Sources indicate that alongside the platform, Miren is also introducing Workbench, an AI-powered infrastructure operator built into Miren Cloud that can help developers manage and troubleshoot their applications. Unlike coding agents that primarily work with application code, Workbench has access to deployed clusters and specialized knowledge of Miren’s infrastructure. Developers can ask it to investigate performance problems, examine logs and analyze traffic without having to manually navigate the underlying systems.

    “Think of it as a teammate, a sysadmin teammate,” Phoenix said.

    Sources indicate that phoenix added that many customers were already bridging the gap between development and deployment using their own AI coding agents, allowing agents to generate application code, deploy it and then check results. With Workbench, they can extend this into the operational environment where the application runs in production, where the agentic operator can investigate problems and help navigate issues specific to the end infrastructure and relate them back to the coding agent.

    Sources indicate that miren is also introducing paid support packages, giving customers a direct line to the organization’s team, which has primarily provided community support until now. Phoenix remarked the company is expanding Miren Cloud with services that improve the reliability of customer-operated infrastructure, including automatic database backups.

    According to recent reports, phoenix also sees an opportunity to turn customer support into a continuously improving layer of automation. Rather than having engineers repeatedly diagnose the same problems for different customers, Miren wants to feed the knowledge gained from individual support interactions back into its AI operators.

    In theory, that would allow the platform to recognize and resolve familiar problems before other customers encounter them, shortening the cycle between discovering an issue and making its solution available across the platform. This follows a broader industry trend in which companies have begun building self-diagnosing, learning AI agents that improve themselves.

    Trump banks on personal relationships moving Putin, Xi toward U.S. interests

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1251 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S.
    • That was the greeting, complete with a lengthy handshake, President Donald Trump gave Vladimir Putin before two high-level meetings Thursday, including the first “trilateral” session with sitting U.S., Russian and Chinese heads of state.
    • “It’s nice to see you,” Trump told Putin before a private one-on-one meeting in China’s Shenzhen economic zone, before pulling the Russian strongman close and saying something into his ear too low for journalists’ microphones to pick up.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump arrive for a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. (Win McNamee/AFP via Getty Images).

    That was the greeting, complete with a lengthy handshake, President Donald Trump gave Vladimir Putin before two high-level meetings Thursday, including the first “trilateral” session with sitting U.S., Russian and Chinese heads of state.

    “It’s nice to see you,” Trump told Putin before a private one-on-one meeting in China’s Shenzhen economic zone, before pulling the Russian strongman close and saying something into his ear too low for journalists’ microphones to pick up.

    In a recent development, trump and Putin then posed for the cameras with wide grins, again underscoring the U.S. president’s closeness with a world leader who has been partially shunned by the West since he launched a war with Ukraine in February 2022. Trump on Thursday also appeared several times alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping, who like Putin has been scorned by Republican and Democratic lawmakers for years.

    According to recent reports, “We’ve had a great relationship for many years. We've known each other for a long time. And I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this — or, at least, start,” Trump told reporters as Putin beamed from a few feet away.

    They later were joined by Xi for a group photo before sitting down at a round wooden table with a large arrangement of pink flowers in the center.

    In a recent development, his interactions with and comments about Putin and Xi reflect Trump’s belief that his personal relationships can bend them toward U.S. interests. But that gambit clashed Thursday with his second term’s expiration date — the White House did not disclose any agreements reached during his various meetings with the two leaders, nor did Trump hold a press conference following the three-way session.

    It has been revealed that both Putin and Xi are adept at playing the geopolitical long game. The 26 months left in Trump’s term is a relatively short amount of time compared to the duo that has been in power for a combined 56 years and will remain in place for the foreseeable future.

    Indeed, even Trump acknowledged the first-ever meeting might not immediately yield much progress on its ostensible goal: paring each powers’ nuclear weapons arsenals.

    According to recent reports, “I must say, it's, quite frankly, a very hard thing to do, because once you have the nuclear weapons, it's very hard to not have them. It's very hard to give them up as the leader of a country,” Trump remarked as Putin and Xi looked on. “Something that's very difficult to say, because … it's the way life works.

    “You know, you have thousands of weapons and you're supposed to give them up, and yet you have countries in addition to us, in much smaller numbers, but they have nuclear weapons, also,” he added. “So it's not an easy thing to do and give them up.”.

    Trump, who was convicted by a Fresh York jury in a business records case and who saw a federal election interference case against him dismissed only because of his reelection, also appeared to join Putin’s resistance to international criminal justice entities that have alleged Putin has committed war crimes in Ukraine.

    In a recent development, “In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nations’ sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction,” Trump said, a statement that would be almost unthinkable to hear from any other sitting U.S. president.

    Sources indicate that other world leaders, including democratically elected ones, at two Pacific region economic summits in which Trump participated this week did not receive the kind of cordial and personal treatment from the U.S. side that Putin and Xi enjoyed.

    And other world leaders and congressional Democrats this week expressed concern with Trump's closeness to the Russian and Chinese strongmen.

    Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., on Thursday called the unprecedented summit a “historic embarrassment.” He criticized Trump for leaving the meeting without any apparent concrete commitments from Moscow or Beijing on a number of issues, including curbing Chinese espionage inside U.S. companies and ending the Ukraine conflict.

Let's be very clear: Arms to Ukraine are purchased by Ukraine with financial support from Europe, not America. … Let's support Ukraine.”.

    Former Kansas Republican Sen. Sam Brownback tells Fox News Digital that voters rejected President Trump himself, not his policies, citing inflation and gas prices.

    Former Kansas Republican Sen. Sam Brownback, who served as an ambassador during Donald Trump's first term, blamed the president's personal leadership style for Republicans' midterm losses.

    He claims the outcome of the 2026 elections — where Democrats' sweeping victories in traditional red strongholds helped them reclaim majorities in the House and Senate — was a sign of voters rejecting Trump more than rebuking his policies.

    "I think the thing we're missing is that it was really targeted at President Trump. I don't think it was targeted at the policies so much," Brownback told Fox News Digital in an interview.

    "Pride comes before a fall and a haughty spirit before a stumble.".

    REPUBLICANS TURN ON TRUMP AFTER DEVASTATING MIDTERM LOSSES HAND DEMOCRATS CONTROL OF CONGRESS.

    The former Kansas governor argued that Republicans should not write off the midterm results as the typical losses suffered by a president’s party through history during their second term.

    Brownback, who represented Kansas in the U.S. Senate from 1996 to 2011 before serving as governor from 2011 to 2018, stated economic concerns, including inflation and gas prices, played a role in the election results.

    He suggested voters' frustrations extended beyond the economy to Trump's approach to governing.

    DEMS SEIZE ON MIDTERM ROUT TO DEMAND ICE REFORM, BUT POLLS REVEAL A TWIST IN WHO PRIORITIZED IMMIGRATION.

    The Fox News Voter Poll found that 89% of voters considered the cost of living a crucial or major factor in their congressional vote, compared with 74% who remarked the same about the war in Iran.

    The findings suggest broader economic frustrations were also a major concern among voters, although the two problems may overlap and the polling does not establish which ultimately drove Republican defections.

    The former ambassador-at-large for international religious freedom also urged Republicans to reconsider how they communicate with voters, emphasizing the importance of humility and kindness.

    "You just can't be proud. You've got to come forward humbly," Brownback stated. "And I think you have to do that with the American public.".

    Brownback called for a more measured response to voters' concerns ahead of 2028.

    Sources indicate that "We hear you, American public. We're adjusting to the message that we heard," he stated.

    REPUBLICANS NEED HISTORY LESSON ABOUT THEIR PARTY IF THEY WANT TO MOVE ON FROM DEFEAT.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that delta Air Lines flight cancellations spilled into Monday after a tech outage snarled air traffic on Sunday. Combined with bad weather, it's made for a messy start to the Thanksgiving travel rush.

    By 7:15 a.m. EST Monday, Delta had canceled at least 92 mainline flights for the day. That's about 2% of its planned schedule.

    It came after the airline canceled or delayed thousands of flights on Sunday following a problem with a key system that automates weight and balance calculations.

    The disruption led to mass delays at its Atlanta mega-hub — the world’s busiest airport — and cascaded to other airports around the country.

    According to recent reports, delta remarked it had restored its automated system by late Sunday afternoon. But the disruptions continued to climb as the carrier worked to get operations fully back on track — and Mother Nature didn't help, either.

    Delta's operations appeared to be improving on Monday, but travelers still had to deal with some residual disruptions from a messy Sunday at airports — especially on the East Coast.

    According to recent reports, around 70% of the flight disruptions were due to the tech problems, the airline had said. The rest were tied to Sunday's weather problems, and air traffic control delays that resulted.

    “We thank our customers for their patience and our people for their professionalism," Delta said in a statement to TPG.

    Travelers had other problems to contend with as the Thanksgiving rush got underway, too.

    Mother Nature also slowed air traffic at some major hubs.

    Low cloud ceilings and poor visibility fueled flight delays and led to dozens of planes getting diverted.

    New York’s LaGuardia Airport (LGA) was most heavily affected, with nearly 60% of all departing and arriving flights delayed Sunday, per FlightAware.

    42 flights headed to LGA on Sunday were diverted to other airports, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium.

    Many of those flights landed instead in Philadelphia; Albany, N.Y.; Harrisburg, PA; and Syracuse, N.Y.

    These disruptions come a week after one of the most chaotic weekends at airports in recent memory.

    Sources indicate that more than 18,000 flights were canceled last weekend after an outage on Nov. 13 to critical Federal Aviation Administration technology.

    Last week, a brief technical outage at United Airlines also fueled a host of flight delays.

    Sources indicate that what to do if you’re affected: This week, the TPG team put our heads together to offer some of our top tips for navigating a travel meltdown. Here’s what to know.

    If your flight is canceled or significantly delayed, you’re entitled to a refund under U.S. Department of Transportation policy — but only if you choose not to fly.

    If you get stranded in Sunday’s travel mess, it pays to know what the reason was for the disruption.

    If you get stuck because of Delta’s tech outage, the carrier may be willing to pay for any hotel, meal and ground transportation costs you incur — if it’s a major delay. See details at FlightRights.gov.

    The carrier on Sunday acknowledged it was providing those accommodations to passengers "when necessary.".

    If you get stuck because of bad weather, it's less likely your airline will offer any sort of compensation. But keep your receipts: If you paid for your trip with a credit card that has travel insurance, you might be able to file a claim and seek reimbursement.

    These latest travel woes also coincide, of course, with the start of the Thanksgiving travel rush — with airports expected to be very busy with holiday travelers over the next few days.

    All eyes are on next Sunday — Nov. 29 — which could be the busiest day of the year to fly.

    Industry observers note that last year, the Sunday after Thanksgiving set the record as the most crowded day ever at U.S. airports.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Retired FBI Supervisory Special Agent Jason Pack breaks down what sits inside America’s law enforcement computers, how hackers get in and how to protect your data.

    A retired FBI supervisory special agent warned Saturday that a cyber intrusion into the bureau's National Crime Information Center (NCIC) could endanger police officers during traffic stops if hackers altered records inside the database.

    Jason Pack, a former FBI supervisory special agent who worked in cybercrime and public information, told Fox News Digital that the bureau's incident response team must promptly determine whether data was manipulated inside the system, which feeds criminal records to patrol cars nationwide.

    "What they worry about is if any of this data has changed, then it might affect officers' safety on the side of the road," Pack said, noting there is no indication yet that any records were altered or that the system is experiencing an outage.

    FBI PROBES SECOND CYBERATTACK IN MONTHS AS HACKERS BREACH KEY CRIME DATABASE, SOURCES SAY.

    Sources indicate that hackers have targeted the FBI for the second time in recent months. (Kevin Lamarque/Reuters, File).

    It has been revealed that three sources familiar with the matter told Fox News that hackers breached the NCIC, marking the second cyberattack against the bureau in months. The FBI is investigating how the intruders gained entry and whether any information was compromised.

    Recent findings suggest that in an interview with Fox News' Kayleigh McEnany on Saturday morning, President Donald Trump remarked he had "just heard" about the intrusion, adding, "I will say that it’s not good. I don’t like that.".

    Pack described the NCIC as "America's computer for law enforcement," explaining that roughly 56 state terminals feed data out to hundreds of thousands of patrol car computers, so officers can check warrants, criminal histories, missing children, gang members and suspected terrorists.

    FBI SAYS SOURCE OF ITS JOBS PORTAL BREACH STILL UNKNOWN AS HACKERS ALLEGE EMPLOYEE DATA COMPROMISED.

    While the database does not hold classified intelligence or sensitive FBI investigative case files, Pack said it stores personally identifiable information, including names, dates of birth and Social Security numbers.

    Investigators will examine IP logs and metadata to determine whether attackers exploited a compromised password among the system's more than 100,000 consumers, breached a state terminal or infiltrated through a third-party vendor, Pack stated, adding that cyberattacks have accelerated to "machine speed" as criminals increasingly use artificial intelligence to probe for vulnerabilities.

    Recent findings suggest that "You have this cat and mouse game where cybersecurity experts are trying to patch the vulnerabilities that they find. They're looking for their own vulnerabilities at the same time, they have to play defense against the criminals who are out there trying to steal information or do harm to our systems. I think we're just seeing now this speed of these intrusions ramp up a lot," Pack noted.

    TECH OUTAGE CASCADE EXPOSES US VULNERABILITIES TO FOREIGN CYBER THREATS.

    It has been revealed that A cyber intrusion into the FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC) could endanger police officers during traffic stops, a retired agent claims. (Getty Images, File).

    The intrusion follows a September cyberattack in which the extortion group ShinyHunters breached an FBI job portal website and claimed to steal personal records belonging to bureau employees.

    CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP.

    The latest incident also comes as a Government Accountability Office (GAO) report found 17 of 22 government agencies were not in compliance with federal cybersecurity regulations.

    The FBI did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the NCIC breach.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (692 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., pictured at the U.S.
    • Republicans who want to accomplish as much as possible before Democrats take control of the House are confronting a latest challenge: Attendance.
    • Thirty-two members – 21 Republicans, 10 Democrats, and one independent – did not vote in Thursday morning’s session before members headed out of town a day early for Thanksgiving break.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., pictured at the U.S. Capitol on Thursday, mentioned attendance is 'a great frustration.' (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Republicans who want to accomplish as much as possible before Democrats take control of the House are confronting a latest challenge: Attendance.

    Thirty-two members – 21 Republicans, 10 Democrats, and one independent – did not vote in Thursday morning’s session before members headed out of town a day early for Thanksgiving break. This, a day after House GOP leadership pulled a procedural rule vote when it was clear the vote might fall short because of GOP no-shows – and then canceled a planned Friday voting session.

    The House has just 12 scheduled voting days left in the 119th Congress. And leaders who have at times struggled to ensure sufficient support for their agenda from the narrow majority now say they will work to make sure cases of senioritis don’t compound the problem, as both returning and nonreturning members have been part of the problem.

    "Attendance is a great frustration for me right now,” House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., told reporters Thursday. “We'll be addressing that with members.".

    “We want to run through the tape and finish strong, but we can't do that unless people are present at work, so that's our challenge,” Johnson continued.

    According to recent reports, of 13 roll call votes in the House since the midterms, all but one has had a double-digit number of no-demonstrates; for five of the 13, more than 30 members did not vote. The average number of members not voting has more than doubled since the midterm elections, compared to the final 13 roll call votes beforehand.

    Johnson has just a few more weeks before he steps out of the spotlight and Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, takes over the GOP conference as minority leader. But his members are still counting on him to get them back to Washington.

    Industry observers note that “I think there's going to be some serious conversations over the phone, behind the scenes over the weekend,” Rep. Michael Cloud, R-Texas, remarked. “We all took an oath of office. We have a sworn duty to be here. We're still being paid to be here, and you have to show up and do the job.”.

    And it's not just leadership that's frustrated with their missing colleagues this week.

    Sources indicate that “There is, no question,” Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., who narrowly won reelection, responded when asked whether there was frustration in the caucus over members' absences.

    Industry observers note that “I don't know what you do with people that don't understand the concept of duty,” Harrigan remarked. “I mean, look, you signed up for a two-year term. You execute your two-year term, no matter what happens along the way politically. You have an obligation both to your constituency and to your country to be here, so the fact that they're not self-motivated to be here, I don't think that there's really much that you can do.”.

    According to recent reports, attendance has also been a bipartisan problem. A group of House Democrats, including members of leadership, faced harsh criticism from party activists for not returning to the chamber in time for a vote related to a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

    While Republican leadership grapples with the fallout from the party’s election losses earlier this month, lawmakers still face a slew of legislative items as Congress looks ahead to the holidays and a government shutdown looms.

    Many Republicans want to see a party-line defense spending bill cross the finish line, while the NDAA remains in treacherous territory and Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act has been dark for months.

    However, the frustration does not lie solely with absent House members.

    “The Senate needs to do their job,” Rep. John McGuire, R-Va., noted. “I know we had a hard time in the midterms. History doesn't favor the party in the president's office, but we passed the Save America Act five times here. It goes over there, nothing. We've got a farm bill, nothing. We got an NDAA. We got so many things.”.

    Industry News: Caring for Aging Loved Ones Is Not an Injustice

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Saturday Night Live struck a nerve with its recent “Sister” skit, a spoof advertisement for a supposedly revolutionary elder-care service that is free, available around the clock, and conveniently happens to be your sister.
    • There’s certainly some truth to this, but there’s a difference between objecting to an unfair division of caregiving responsibilities and treating those responsibilities as inherently oppressive.
    • Heather Madden is the vice president for policy initiatives at Independent Women.

    Saturday Night Live struck a nerve with its recent “Sister” skit, a spoof advertisement for a supposedly revolutionary elder-care service that is free, available around the clock, and conveniently happens to be your sister. The skit is funny because it captures something many families recognize: When an aging parent needs help, it’s often the women who step up, while male relatives carry on with their lives largely uninterrupted.

    There’s certainly some truth to this, but there’s a difference between objecting to an unfair division of caregiving responsibilities and treating those responsibilities as inherently oppressive. The suggestion that our elder-care challenges are largely a product of sexism, or that women who take on these responsibilities have simply been conditioned to accept their own exploitation, misses the bigger issue. This interpretation not only diminishes the contributions of female caregivers but also feeds into a troubling cultural narrative: that caring for the people we love is an injustice rather than a responsibility inherent to family.

    Heather Madden is the vice president for policy initiatives at Independent Women.

    On “Caring for Aging Loved Ones Is Not an Injustice”.

    17 major federal agencies flagged over cybersecurity gaps as watchdog warns of increased attack risk

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Wright and Turner examine growing concerns over the federal government's cybersecurity preparedness, potential vulnerabilities across government agencies and the risks posed by increasingly sophisticated cyber threats.
    • A sweeping federal watchdog report found that 17 of 22 major civilian agencies failed to fully address key cybersecurity planning guidance, warning that the shortcomings could leave government systems more vulnerable to cyberattacks and operational disruptions.
    • The Government Accountability Office (GAO) released its findings this week, identifying gaps at the Departments of Homeland Security (DHS), Justice (DOJ), State, Treasury and Health and Human Services (HHS), among others.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Wright and Turner examine growing concerns over the federal government's cybersecurity preparedness, potential vulnerabilities across government agencies and the risks posed by increasingly sophisticated cyber threats.

    A sweeping federal watchdog report found that 17 of 22 major civilian agencies failed to fully address key cybersecurity planning guidance, warning that the shortcomings could leave government systems more vulnerable to cyberattacks and operational disruptions.

    The Government Accountability Office (GAO) released its findings this week, identifying gaps at the Departments of Homeland Security (DHS), Justice (DOJ), State, Treasury and Health and Human Services (HHS), among others.

    The report examined whether agencies had incorporated selected federal guidance into their intends for implementing zero trust architecture, a cybersecurity approach requiring users, devices and systems to be verified before accessing protected networks.

    RETIRED FBI AGENT WARNS NCIC BREACH COULD THREATEN POLICE SAFETY DURING TRAFFIC STOPS.

    Recent findings suggest that the GAO report discovered that 17 of 22 federal agencies did not meet cybersecurity planning standards. (Getty Images).

    Only five of the 22 agencies fully addressed the selected guidance as of August 2026, prompting GAO to issue 40 recommendations to the remaining 17.

    "Agencies would therefore be at increased risk of cyberattacks that could interrupt operations or otherwise compromise agency resources," GAO warned.

    HHS received six recommendations, the most of any agency reviewed, after investigators found that it lacked a documented enterprise-wide zero trust implementation plan covering all its information systems.

    Although individual divisions were pursuing cybersecurity improvements, GAO warned that the absence of a unified strategy could prevent department leadership from maintaining a coherent view of its security modernization efforts.

    HHS agreed with the recommendations and said it planned to develop an actionable department-wide strategy by the second quarter of fiscal year 2027.

    CHINESE HACKERS TARGET NASA AND KEY US AGENCIES, DOJ ALLEGES.

    The Department of Commerce received four recommendations after investigators identified shortcomings in its cybersecurity planning documentation.

    Commerce officials told GAO that staffing losses had significantly constrained the department's zero trust working group, limiting its ability to coordinate improvements and maintain comprehensive documentation.

    At DHS, investigators found that the department had not fully documented cybersecurity maturity levels across all its high-value assets and high-impact systems. Officials attributed the incomplete assessments partly to lengthy government shutdowns during the preceding fiscal year.

    DHS INVESTIGATES MASSIVE DATA BREACH EXPOSING 40,000 EMPLOYEES, INCLUDING ICE AND BORDER PATROL AGENTS.

    GAO attributed many of the incomplete reports to the prior fiscal year's government shutdown. (iStock).

    DOJ similarly cited resource constraints for incomplete assessments of critical systems, while State and Treasury were among the agencies that had only partially documented cybersecurity maturity levels.

    GAO warned that incomplete assessments could leave agency leadership without the visibility necessary to determine where additional cybersecurity resources are needed.

    Investigators also found that 11 agencies had only partially documented procedures for identifying actors within their IT environments, including certain non-person entities such as software applications and service accounts.

    The watchdog warned that incomplete identification procedures could hinder efforts to ensure only authorized users and systems access government resources.

    TRUMP’S NATIONAL CYBER DIRECTOR SEAN CAIRNCROSS FIRED AMID WIDESPREAD TECH OUTAGES.

    The report found that 11 agencies had only partially documented cybersecurity procedures. (Thomas Trutschel/Photothek via Getty Images).

    The findings come years after the Biden administration directed federal agencies to adopt zero trust cybersecurity principles through a 2021 executive order, followed by additional guidance in 2022 and 2024. Despite those directives, GAO found that 17 of 22 agencies still had not fully addressed selected cybersecurity planning requirements and guidance as of August 2026.

    In a recent development, thirteen agencies agreed with GAO's 40 recommendations, while four neither agreed nor disagreed. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission, one of the four, provided documentation demonstrating that it had already addressed both recommendations, which GAO verified.

    CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP.

    Fox News Digital reached out to the White House and all 17 agencies identified in the report for comment.

    "Absent a full implementation of ZTA requirements and guidance, agencies will lack an appropriate roadmap to fully incorporate and maintain an effective zero trust architecture," GAO concluded.

    Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

    Apex predator at center of farmers vs environmentalists fight as Trump weighs major move: 'Out of control'

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1834 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foxnews

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Fox News Digital spoke to farmers grappling with devastating livestock losses from gray wolves and experts weighing in on Trump’s push to reconsider federal protections for the apex predator.
    • A powerful apex predator has reignited a fierce battle between farmers demanding greater control over gray wolves killing their livestock and environmentalists fighting to keep them shielded — a decision the Trump administration must now weigh that could shape the future of wildlife management.
    • One longtime Minnesota farmer has spent years grappling with the loss of several of his calves killed by gray wolves, also known as timber wolves, roaming around his property in the middle of the night.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Fox News Digital spoke to farmers grappling with devastating livestock losses from gray wolves and experts weighing in on Trump’s push to reconsider federal protections for the apex predator.

    A powerful apex predator has reignited a fierce battle between farmers demanding greater control over gray wolves killing their livestock and environmentalists fighting to keep them shielded — a decision the Trump administration must now weigh that could shape the future of wildlife management.

    One longtime Minnesota farmer has spent years grappling with the loss of several of his calves killed by gray wolves, also known as timber wolves, roaming around his property in the middle of the night.

    "We can walk right outside of our door and hear the howling of these timber wolves, and it'll send shivers down your spine because you have seen what they can do, and they're the top-of-the-line predator," Shayne Isane told Fox News Digital.

    In a recent development, "There's nothing that hunts them. No other animals they are afraid of.".

    ARCTIC WOLF ATTACKS CHILD DURING ZOOKEEPER EVENT, GIRL AIRLIFTED TO HOSPITAL.

    Recent findings suggest that farmers across the Great Lakes region are grappling with gray wolves killing their livestock, reigniting a fierce debate over wildlife management. (Courtesy of Jonathan Miller and Shayne Isane).

    It has been revealed that isane, who has farmed for nearly four decades, noted he is one of many farmers struggling to defend his livestock from gray wolves. Despite losing thousands of dollars and fearing for the safety of his nearly 300 cattle, Isane said he is unable to handle the threat himself.

    Recent findings suggest that "Even if we see them attacking our livestock, we can't shoot or try to help out our animals," he said. "It's just against the law. We can't do it, only in the case of the threat of human life, which is a tough sell for us, because when you see them very close to your livelihood, your families and your livestock, it's a huge concern.".

    As President Donald Trump moves to reconsider federal protections, Isane mentioned he is one of many farmers hoping to gain more control over the growing threat. The plan could affect states across the country, including Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, California and Colorado.

    In a recent development, the Interior Department has until Dec. 3 to determine whether gray wolves and their subspecies, Mexican wolves, have met the recovery criteria under the Endangered Species Act. If the criteria are met, the department must begin the process of removing or reducing federal protections.

    In a statement to Fox News Digital, a department spokesperson mentioned the department had no updates on that decision but "recognizes the importance of effective wildlife management and the challenges wolf depredation can pose for livestock producers.".

    NATIONAL PARK SERVICE DIRECTOR CALLS YELLOWSTONE'S WILD BISON RECOVERY AN 'INCREDIBLE CONSERVATION STORY'.

    According to recent reports, environmentalists have long opposed delisting gray wolves, arguing it could lead to culling, trapping and trophy hunting and threaten their recovery. (iStock).

    One of Isane's largest losses came when three of his young calves were killed in a single night. He said the wolves often drag away or dispose of the carcasses themselves, making it difficult to confirm the attack to state investigators.

    In Minnesota, a farmer must have the carcass of their livestock in order to confirm a suspected wolf attack and report the loss within 48 hours to receive reimbursement.

    "To lose one animal or two animals is $3,000 a piece, and so that really can affect our bottom line," he stated.

    A Minnesota Department of Agriculture spokesperson told Fox News Digital its program "provides 100% reimbursement of verified losses at full market value" and pointed to its Wolf Livestock Depredation Grant.

    "While we can assist farmers with livestock prevention and loss, wolf management does not fall under the work of the Minnesota Department of Agriculture," the spokesperson wrote.

    According to recent reports, but Isane mentioned keeping the livestock alive is only part of the "constant battle." He said wolves can cause "added stress" to the herd. "They're constantly being harassed by the wolves," he said. "We see it in weights. They lose weight, they are constantly on edge, and it affects their overall health.".

    Isane said many deterrent methods suggested by the state have proven unsuccessful, saying wolves are able to "outsmart" them.

    "They just don't work," he stated.

    Isane emphasized that environmentalists aren’t seeing the full picture. He remarked the wolf population had spiraled "out of control.".

    Industry observers note that "The first 30 years of my life, I hardly saw a timber wolf, and now I've seen multiple ones, 50 to 100, probably in the last 25 years," Isane remarked. "It's gotten increasingly worse.".

    OREGON BALLOT MEASURE THAT WOULD HAVE CRIMINALIZED HUNTING AND FISHING FAILS TO QUALIFY FOR VOTE.

    Sources indicate that president Donald Trump is moving to reconsider federal protections for gray wolves as farmers push for greater control over the apex predator. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images).

    According to the Minnesota DNR, there were about 2,400 gray wolves in Minnesota in 2026, with no statistically significant change from last year.

    "The Minnesota DNR is very confident in our wolf research and population estimates, which indicate a stable population, not one of unconstrained or rapid population growth," a spokesperson noted in a statement to Fox News Digital.

    Isane noted he welcomes Trump's efforts to fix a problem that has "no method of controlling.".

    White House deputy press secretary Taylor Rogers told Fox News Digital the Biden administration’s "radical environmental policies" left ranchers defenseless as "predators wiped out their livestock.".

    Recent findings suggest that "As a result, the national cattle herd reached a 75-year low, driving up prices for consumers," Rogers wrote. "As promised, President Trump is reversing these harmful policies and is fighting for America’s ranchers.".

    Shawn Regan, C3 Journal editor and Manhattan Institute senior fellow, said states can effectively manage recovered wolf populations without them being listed under the Endangered Species Act.

    "It's not the best tool for continuing to manage recovered populations into the future," Regan said. "There's a reason why the act has a delisting process to allow for transition of those species to state management.".

    Delisting gray wolves has long been part of Trump's agenda.

    It has been revealed that during his first term, the administration removed federal protections for the species across most states. Six environmental groups, represented by environmental law group Earthjustice, sued the Trump administration in 2021 over the decision.

    According to recent reports, A federal judge overturned the decision in 2022, restoring protections across most states except in the Northern Rockies, where states still have control. The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals is currently weighing whether that ruling should be upheld.

    Some environmental groups involved in the lawsuit told Fox News Digital Trump’s executive order could reverse years of recovery efforts and urged the administration to focus on other issues facing farmers.

    "The administration is offering up wolves as a bargaining chip while failing to address the real economic pressures burdening American farmers and ranchers," Sara Amundson, president of Humane World Action Fund, mentioned.

    Eric Clewis, senior Northern Rockies representative for Defenders of Wildlife, echoed this, saying, "Framing wolves as the villain distracts from policies actually squeezing the ranching industry, particularly because wolves account for less than 1% of total livestock loss.".

    Collette Adkins, a senior attorney and director of the Center for Biological Diversity’s carnivore program, worries the implications could stretch even further, saying removing federal protections could "erase decades of recovery work.".

    WASHINGTON'S GRIZZLY BEAR POWER GRAB IS FINALLY COMING TO A LONG-OVERDUE END.

    Recent findings suggest that cows on Minnesota farmer Shayne Isane's farm, where he has lost several calves to gray wolf attacks over the years. (Courtesy of Shayne Isane).

    She added that the "tiny fraction of livestock operators" who have conflicts with wolves can help by doing "a better job" learning to live with them peacefully.

    Environmentalists have advocated for years against delisting, arguing it could lead to culling, trapping and trophy hunting and reduce populations they believe have not fully recovered.

    Independent Women’s Forum Center for Energy and Conservation Director Gabriella Hoffman told Fox News Digital there is a possibility that the move to delist gray wolves may only be a short-term solution once it heads to Congress.

    It has been revealed that "Do we have to worry about lawsuits potentially blocking this from going into effect?" Hoffman, who also recently investigated wolf attacks in Wisconsin for a conservation documentary, remarked. "Congress not following through with their duty to codify this permanently and ensure this doesn't go back and forth?".

    Hoffman remarked delisting could actually prevent the species from becoming endangered again.

    "Leaning too much on emotions would undermine the science and also I think put the wolf in further danger and make it even more imperiled than it is if you have a management system in place," she said.

    She added that wolf attacks on livestock are a sign of thriving conservation efforts.

    "While it is problematic that wolf depredation or attacks by wolves is increasing, that's actually a positive sign, as counterintuitive as it sounds, of their status as a species," she remarked.

    Jonathan Miller, a Michigan dairy farmer since the 1970s who switched to raising a herd of roughly 100 cattle, mentioned protective fencing has created a "balance" with wolves.

    "It's very effective to keep them away," he said.

    He said the attacks haven’t hurt his business financially, but managing the fencing has added some extra challenges.

    "It's a lot of extra work management trying to move the fence, keep it electrified so that it's effective," he said.

    Earlier this month, Miller found the carcasses of two of his healthy sheep, which he blamed on his "lack of management" in putting up the barrier.

    "You hate to see a wolf take one of your animals, but we lose animals, and it's just another factor," he noted.

    CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP.

    When the family lost their first calf to a wolf in the early 2000s, Miller said it "kind of changed things.".

    It was the first time he laid eyes on the predator that "probably only weighed about 60 pounds, but was substantial enough to drag a calf across the yard.".

    Sources indicate that miller said wolf sightings in people's yards have become less common since locals began handling the matter themselves. However, he supports Trump's push for state management rather than "local people illegally controlling the numbers of the wolves.".

    He hopes the move can help farmers and wolves finally coexist.

    Industry observers note that "I don't want to eliminate the wolves," he stated. "I love to see wolves. I try to get pictures, but there has to be control.".

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., is seen on Capitol Hill last December. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    According to recent reports, rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., faced a setback Thursday in her effort to ditch charges tied to a scuffle during an oversight visit at an immigration detention facility last year, as a federal appeals court declined to reconsider its decision to let the case move forward.

    Recent findings suggest that the decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit leaves in place a 2-1 opinion from August which held that McIver was not immune from the charges, which stemmed from a confrontation between visiting members of Congress and federal agents while at the Delaney Hall facility in Newark. McIver has challenged the charges, arguing that her visit fell under the “speech or debate” immunity she has as a member of Congress because she was there to inspect detention conditions.

    In a statement McIver said she and her attorneys were looking at “every possible option” in response to the appeals court ruling. Her statement invoked the Trump administration’s threats to treat oversight efforts as criminal conduct and said “we are all one step closer to a world in which the president of the United States can try to imprison people simply because he does not like what they stand for.”.

    In a recent development, “Donald Trump continues to send warning shots to Democrats in Congress and in all levels of power — but their case against me right now, in broad daylight, goes well beyond a warning. Because of a weaponized Department of Justice and because I dared to do my job and conduct oversight of ICE, I am facing 17 years in prison,” McIver said in her statement.

    Following Thursday’s decision on rehearing, McIver could next ask the Supreme Court to weigh in on the case.

    The August majority opinion from Judge Cindy Chung, which Thursday’s decision leaves in place, said that two of the three charges against McIver did not fall under the immunity, which is limited to legislative acts. The majority sent the third charge back to the lower court for another ruling.

    “We have considered the ‘nature’ of the charged conduct and concluded it is unambiguously non-legislative,” the judge wrote.

    According to recent reports, separately, Judge Thomas Ambro partially dissented to offer a different approach to the case. Ambro would have required the trial judge to more closely examine the exact conduct McIver was charged with, as well as to examine whether the Trump administration targeted her because of her political views.

    “I would allow her discovery into the truth of the matter — not only for her own sake but to safeguard the independence of our legislative bodies,” Ambro wrote.

    Ambro did not vote on whether the full 3rd Circuit should rehear the case. Three judges voted to have the full 3rd Circuit hear McIver’s case, and Judge Emil Bove, a former Trump administration official and former personal attorney for the president, did not participate in the vote.

    The criminal case started shortly after the Delaney Hall visit in May 2025, as prosecutors alleged that McIver assaulted federal agents during a scuffle around Newark Mayor Ras Baraka. Officials arrested Baraka that day and charged him with trespassing, but later dropped those charges.

    Court filings in the case alleged that McIver struck agents during the confrontation. McIver has argued that she was effectively being charged for doing her job and federal agents were interfering with her attempts to inspect the facility.

    Sources indicate that earlier this year, Judge Jamel K. Semper of the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey disagreed and ruled that the case could move forward.

    Tech Report: $275M Obama-era solar fraud case could net taxpayers $1B, but Trump's DOJ backs Biden dismissal

    ⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Pat Hogan, CEO of CMB Regional Centers, alleges fraud in a $275 million Treasury grant obtained by Crescent Dunes’ former owner and companies linked to Spanish construction giant Cobra.
    • Sources indicate that this article is Part 2 of a Fox News Digital exclusive series investigating the Crescent Dunes solar power plant in Nevada.
    • The Trump administration has made fighting fraud and rooting out government waste a top priority, even offering cash rewards to Americans who expose wrongdoing.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Pat Hogan, CEO of CMB Regional Centers, alleges fraud in a $275 million Treasury grant obtained by Crescent Dunes’ former owner and companies linked to Spanish construction giant Cobra.

    Sources indicate that this article is Part 2 of a Fox News Digital exclusive series investigating the Crescent Dunes solar power plant in Nevada. You can read Part 1 here.

    The Trump administration has made fighting fraud and rooting out government waste a top priority, even offering cash rewards to Americans who expose wrongdoing.

    Yet investors in a failed Obama-era solar plant are questioning why President Donald Trump's own Justice Department is fighting to squash their fraud lawsuit over a $275 million federal grant — a case they say could recover up to $1 billion for taxpayers.

    The investors allege that Spanish construction giant ACS and companies to tied its former subsidiary Cobra, misled federal officials into approving the grant by claiming the troubled solar plant was ready for use, even though it had suffered major construction problems and was shut down for months following a molten-salt-tank failure.

    The lawsuit centers on the beleaguered Crescent Dunes solar plant, a billion-dollar, government-backed project that began operating in Nevada in 2015 but was later plagued by engineering failures, repeated shutdowns and two bankruptcies before being sold for just $7 million in July.

    HOW A $1B OBAMA-ERA SOLAR PLANT WENT BANKRUPT TWICE, LEAVING TAXPAYERS WITH THE TAB.

    Sources indicate that an aerial view of the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada, shows thousands of mirrors concentrating sunlight onto the central tower in footage published in 2018. The billion-dollar solar plant later went through two bankruptcies before being sold for $7 million in 2026. (ferrantraite/iStock via Getty Images).

    The plant was built around an emerging solar technology that used thousands of mirrors to concentrate sunlight onto a towering receiver, heating molten salt that could be stored and used to generate electricity even after sunset.

    In 2020, a group of private investors who had put $90 million into the project and suffered substantial losses filed a whistleblower lawsuit, alleging the companies had misled the federal government to secure the enormous grant.

    But in November 2024, just two days after Trump's re-election, Biden's Justice Department moved to shut down the lawsuit, arguing that pursuing the case would burden federal agencies.

    WHITE HOUSE DEBUTS INTERACTIVE MAP TRACKING BILLIONS IN SUSPECTED FRAUD.

    Recent findings suggest that solarReserve, ACS Group/Cobra and Banco Santander were original project participants in Crescent Dunes, which received a $737 million Department of Energy loan guarantee and approximately $275.6 million in Treasury grant awards. CMB investors also provided $90 million in private financing. (Fox News).

    DOJ UNVEILS NATIONWIDE TAX FRAUD CRACKDOWN INVOLVING 76 DEFENDANTS, NEARLY $500M IN ALLEGED LOSSES.

    It has been revealed that the incoming Trump administration could have reconsidered that position in early 2025. Instead, its Justice Department defended the Biden-era dismissal in an April filing with a federal appeals court.

    CMB, an investment group headed by Pat Hogan, is appealing the dismissal. Hogan is also urging Trump’s Justice Department to ask the court to reopen the case.

    "It makes no sense," Hogan told Fox News Digital in a video interview.

    Hogan remarked he had contacted Trump's Justice Department seeking help reviving the case but had received no commitment.

    According to recent reports, "The real problem here is, why isn't the government asking for this?" he said. "All in all, I would say this has just been a fleecing of the federal government by a foreign entity. And we have the opportunity to fix it, and they're doing nothing.".

    Hogan argues that allowing the lawsuit to proceed could potentially net hundreds of millions of dollars for taxpayers.

    Under the False Claims Act, which CMB used to bring its lawsuit, companies found liable can face damages of up to three times the government's proven losses, plus additional penalties.

    "This could be a billion dollars," Hogan mentioned.

    Sources indicate that tonopah Solar Energy, the plant's former owner and one of the defendants, has rejected CMB's allegations as baseless in court filings. Other companies named in the lawsuit have also backed the Justice Department's effort to dismiss the case.

    Sources indicate that in an April 2026 court filing, Trump's Justice Department defended the Biden administration's decision, making the same argument that continuing the lawsuit would drain government resources and that federal law gave it broad authority to shut down the case. In court filings reviewed by Fox News Digital, neither administration put a dollar figure on the cost of continuing the lawsuit.

    The decision has left Hogan and his investors questioning why the government shut down the case — and what Treasury officials knew about the plant's serious problems when they approved the $275 million grant.

    It has been revealed that pat Hogan, CEO of CMB Regional Centers, whose investors provided $90 million in financing for the Crescent Dunes solar project, is challenging the dismissal of a federal whistleblower lawsuit alleging fraud involving a $275 million Treasury grant. (Provided).

    The Crescent Dunes solar plant in Tonopah, Nevada, left, received approximately $275.6 million in Treasury grant awards. Private investors allege the plant's former owner and companies involved in its construction fraudulently obtained the funding. The allegations remain disputed, and a federal judge dismissed the whistleblower lawsuit at the Justice Department's request. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital; Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images).

    At the heart of the lawsuit is a dispute over whether Crescent Dunes was properly completed — and whether its owner, Tonopah Solar Energy, was entitled to collect the $275 million Treasury grant.

    The grant was part of a $26 billion program within the Obama administration's broader $90 billion green-energy push, debuted under the 2009 economic stimulus package to create jobs and turbocharge its green energy agenda.

    Known as Section 1603, the program paid developers about 30% of their qualifying construction costs once their facilities were "placed in service" — meaning ready and available for their intended use. Treasury considered several factors in determining whether a plant met that standard, including whether it had passed critical tests, begun generating electricity and come under its owner's control.

    Crescent Dunes began generating electricity in 2015, but CMB alleges it had produced no more than 32% of its expected output through June 2016.

    Then, in October 2016, a failure involving the plant's hot molten-salt storage tank shut it down for months.

    A diagram displayed at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada, illustrates how thousands of mirrors concentrate sunlight onto a central receiver, heating molten salt that is stored in tanks and used to generate electricity. The diagram bears the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy logo. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

    In December, while Crescent Dunes was still shut down, its builder, Cobra Thermosolar Plants, formally handed the plant over to its owner, Tonopah Solar Energy, under an arrangement known as "provisional acceptance.".

    But first, they changed the construction contract to allow the handover despite major defects and unfinished repairs.

    That agreement came just days before the year-end deadline for solar plants to be ready for use to qualify for the Treasury grants.

    Sources indicate that in a later court filing, CMB alleged that more than 9,000 defects had been identified and grouped into roughly 500 outstanding construction items, including seven major deficiencies. The investors argue the problems revealed the plant was not ready to be handed over.

    The December agreement itself acknowledged that repairs to the failed hot molten-salt storage tank were still needed. The tank was central to the plant's operation, storing heat from the sun so electricity could be generated even after sunset.

    CMB alleges the companies used the revised agreement to make Crescent Dunes appear ready for use and secure the Treasury grant, even though major problems remained unresolved.

    Electrical equipment and transmission infrastructure at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

    In a recent development, turbines used in the electricity-generation process sit atop steel infrastructure at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada. The plant uses heat stored in molten salt to produce steam, which drives turbines connected to generators. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

    Heliostats track the Nevada sun at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah. The mirrors concentrate sunlight onto the receiver atop the tower, visible in the distance. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

    Records reviewed by Fox News Digital show Treasury had questioned whether Crescent Dunes was ready for use months before approving the grant payment.

    In September 2016, Treasury questioned a claim by Tonopah Solar Energy that Crescent Dunes had been ready for use since February of that year. The agency pointed to a July commissioning report suggesting the builder, Cobra Thermosolar Plants, had not yet formally handed control of the facility over to Tonopah.

    In a Sept. 21 response to Treasury's questions, Tonopah Solar Energy defended its claim, arguing that the plant had passed key tests and was capable of generating electricity. It also acknowledged an earlier extended shutdown caused by problems with the plant's salt-piping system.

    The following month, the plant's hot molten-salt storage tank failed, forcing the plant offline for months.

    Despite that breakdown, Tonopah and Cobra went ahead with the revised handover agreement in December.

    On March 7, 2017, just weeks into the first Trump administration, Treasury approved a $243.7 million grant payment — even though Crescent Dunes remained shut down nearly five months after the tank failure.

    The plant would not resume generating electricity until July 2017.

    A timeline demonstrates how Crescent Dunes faced questions over its readiness for operation, suffered a major molten-salt tank failure in October 2016 and remained shut down when Treasury approved a $243.7 million grant payment in March 2017. An additional $31.9 million was approved in February 2018, bringing total grant awards to approximately $275.6 million. The approvals are central to disputed fraud allegations brought by private investors. (Fox News).

    Sources indicate that the hot molten-salt storage tank at Crescent Dunes in Nevada. Repeated leaks involving the plant's molten-salt storage system contributed to lengthy shutdowns and financial troubles. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

    In a recent development, A network of pipes and industrial equipment forms part of the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada. The concentrated solar plant uses molten salt to capture and store heat before using it to generate steam and electricity. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

    Industry observers note that rows of heliostats converge toward the base of the receiver tower at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada. More than 10,000 heliostats surround the tower across the sprawling desert facility. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

    Sources indicate that the receiver atop the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project's tower glows as thousands of computer-controlled heliostats concentrate sunlight onto it near Tonopah, Nevada. (Michael Dorgan).

    A view looking up at the receiver tower at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada, while the receiver is not being illuminated by concentrated sunlight. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

    The approval letter said Treasury was still reviewing some of the project's claimed costs before deciding whether to release additional money.

    In February 2018, Treasury approved an additional $31.9 million, bringing the total grant awards to approximately $275.6 million, according to newly obtained federal records. The additional payment was scheduled for disbursement within seven business days.

    But Treasury was not the only federal agency involved.

    It has been revealed that the Department of Energy, which had backed Crescent Dunes with a $737 million federal loan guarantee, also had a say in major construction decisions. DOE approved the revised December handover despite unfinished repairs. It also waived certain missed deadlines, allowing the plant to be formally recognized as operational under its loan agreement.

    That approval did not automatically qualify Crescent Dunes for the separate Treasury grant.

    A separate December 2016 financing agreement involving Tonopah Solar Energy and DOE required the Treasury grant money to go first toward repaying the project’s short-term federal borrowing, including principal and accrued interest.

    Documents obtained by Fox News Digital show that Tonopah Solar Energy made a $218.9 million payment toward a federal loan in March 2017, shortly after Treasury approved its initial grant award.

    According to recent reports, "So in a sense, the federal government just paid themselves, right? So they're still out the money, right," Hogan told Fox News Digital.

    On April 12, 2017, while Crescent Dunes was still offline, DOE published an article celebrating the plant as a breakthrough in solar technology without mentioning that it had been shut down for months.

    What remains unclear is whether Treasury officials knew about the October breakdown, unfinished repairs and December contract changes when they authorized the initial grant payment — information that could have affected whether the plant qualified for the grant.

    Fox News Digital has asked DOE and Treasury about the grant's approval process, the plant's condition and taxpayer losses, but neither agency has provided a full accounting.

    In a statement, the Trump administration's Department of Energy criticized previous administrations' handling of the project, saying it had resolved its financial interests in Crescent Dunes in 2020.

    According to recent reports, "It is unfortunate that previous administrations irresponsibly managed taxpayer dollars in their support of the Green Fresh Scam," a DOE spokesperson stated. "Since 2020, DOE has had no ownership, operational, or financial interest in the Obama-era project.".

    Fox News Digital has also filed Freedom of Information Act requests seeking grant payment records, loan accounting and communications between the agencies.

    Sources indicate that the Crescent Dunes solar plant near Tonopah, Nevada, features a central tower surrounded by more than 10,000 mirrors that direct sunlight toward a receiver to generate electricity. The Obama-era project, backed by more than $1 billion in federal support, went bankrupt twice before selling for $7 million in July 2026. (Getty Images).

    In January 2020, Hogan's investment group, CMB, which had lent $90 million to a organization tied to Crescent Dunes developer SolarReserve, sued Tonopah Solar Energy and companies tied to Spanish construction giant ACS, accusing them of defrauding the federal government.

    The lawsuit was filed under the False Claims Act, which allows private whistleblowers to sue on the government's behalf and receive a share of any money recovered. Known as "qui tam" cases, the lawsuits can be taken over or dismissed by the Justice Department.

    After investigating CMB's allegations for more than three years, Biden's Justice Department declined to take over the lawsuit in June 2023, leaving CMB to pursue it alone.

    Recent findings suggest that on Nov. 7, 2024, just two days after Trump's election victory, Biden's Justice Department moved to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that continuing the case would burden the Treasury, Energy and Justice departments.

    CMB challenged the move, arguing that Biden's DOJ had failed to explain what had changed since it allowed the investors to proceed.

    Then, in July 2025, six months into Trump's second term, a federal judge granted DOJ's request and dismissed the lawsuit without deciding whether the fraud allegations were true.

    CMB appealed to the Ninth Circuit, where Trump's Justice Department defended the dismissal in an April 2026 court filing.

    Matt Dunn, an attorney at Covington & Burling who specializes in False Claims Act litigation, described DOJ's decision to intervene after initially allowing the case to proceed as "unusual, but not extraordinary.".

    Dunn remarked the government may have its own assessment of a lawsuit's potential value that differs from the whistleblower's.

    "The government might privately have a different view of the merits of the case or the potential value of the case that it doesn't necessarily share publicly," Dunn said.

    Dunn said the Supreme Court has given the government substantial discretion to dismiss such cases, describing the legal hurdle for whistleblowers seeking to overturn a dismissal as "an extraordinarily high bar for a relator to overcome.".

    Hogan, meanwhile, has a financial stake in the outcome. He states his investors lost the $90 million they lent to the SolarReserve-linked organization.

    If the lawsuit is revived and CMB ultimately succeeds, the government theoretically could recover up to three times its proven damages under the False Claims Act, and CMB could receive a share, potentially offsetting its investors' losses.

    "That's my job for my investors to leave no stone unturned to try to make sure that, in fact, I get their money back," Hogan stated.

    The Ninth Circuit must now decide whether the lawsuit can move forward — potentially opening the door for the government to recover hundreds of millions of dollars in disputed funds — or whether DOJ's decision to shut it down will stand.

    The Justice Department's handling of the case has also drawn scrutiny on Capitol Hill.

    Recent findings suggest that in February 2025, Reps. Lance Gooden, R-Texas, and Carol Miller, R-W.Va., urged Attorney General Pam Bondi to investigate why the Biden administration moved to shut down the lawsuit.

    Gooden later urged Secretary of War Pete Hegseth to consider suspending federal contracts with companies tied to Spanish construction giant ACS, whose subsidiary Cobra built the plant and held a stake in Tonopah Solar Energy. He also called for an investigation into ACS and Banco Santander's roles in the project's financing and bankruptcy amid the allegations of fraud involving federal funds.

    "When taxpayers are defrauded to a scale this massive, our government has a responsibility to get the facts and hold those responsible to account," Gooden told Fox News Digital. "That is why I have asked Secretary Hegseth to pause contracts with ACS-affiliated entities until these allegations are fully reviewed and every avenue to recover taxpayer money has been pursued.".

    In February 2025, Reps. Lance Gooden, R-Texas, and Carol Miller, R-W.Va., urged Attorney General Pam Bondi to investigate why the Biden administration moved to shut down the lawsuit. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images).

    Rep. Carol Miller, R-W.Va., leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 29, 2023. Miller has questioned the collapse of the federally backed Crescent Dunes solar plant and the potential loss of taxpayer money. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images).

    Recent findings suggest that one such contract involves a $2.84 billion Navy dry dock project at Pearl Harbor awarded to a joint venture involving ACS subsidiary Dragados. The project completion date has been delayed from September 2027 to March 2029, according to the Government Accountability Office. Dragados is not accused of fraud in the Crescent Dunes lawsuit.

    Miller, meanwhile, also questioned how a project backed by nearly $1 billion in federal financing could end up selling for $7 million.

    "That's not good math," Miller told Fox News Digital. She suggested another congressional letter could be warranted, saying that "if we can recover any of that taxpayer money, that would be wonderful.".

    In April 2026, Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, a longtime defender of whistleblowers who helped strengthen the False Claims Act in 1986, demanded answers from DOJ over its handling of fraud lawsuits, particularly cases it shut down despite whistleblowers wanting to press ahead.

    In a July 10 response obtained by Fox News Digital, DOJ revealed that Crescent Dunes was one of just 12 cases in which it moved to shut down a lawsuit after initially allowing it to proceed — fewer than 0.3% of nearly 5,000 whistleblower cases received between 2020 and 2025.

    According to recent reports, DOJ also confirmed that other federal agencies can push to have such lawsuits dismissed, including to avoid the burden of producing evidence. But it did not say whether Treasury or DOE pushed to kill the Crescent Dunes case — or what investigators found when they examined the fraud allegations.

    In April 2026, Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, a longtime defender of whistleblowers who helped strengthen the False Claims Act in 1986, demanded answers from DOJ over its handling of fraud lawsuits, particularly cases it shut down despite whistleblowers wanting to press ahead. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images).

    The companies accused of fraud have backed DOJ's effort to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that federal law gives the government broad authority to shut down whistleblower cases.

    Tonopah Solar Energy, which filed for bankruptcy in January 2026, has also fiercely rejected CMB's allegations, accusing the investors of pursuing a "scorched earth mission" through repeated legal challenges against the tech giant.

    "The reality is there is no merit to CMB's claims whatsoever," the company argued in an April 2026 bankruptcy filing.

    It has been revealed that tonopah Solar Energy made those arguments while winding down its affairs in bankruptcy, before selling the plant's assets in July. The newly introduced owners had no involvement in the alleged 2016 fraud, and the bankruptcy sale generally shielded them from the former owner's legal liabilities.

    Recent findings suggest that in a separate 2020 lawsuit, Hogan's investors sought to recover an allegedly unpaid $90 million loan, suing companies tied to Crescent Dunes after SolarReserve failed to repay much of the money. They suffered a setback in 2024 when an arbitration panel rejected five of their claims and ordered them to pay $2.44 million in legal fees and costs.

    The companies did not respond to Fox News Digital's repeated requests for comment.

    The dispute was separate from the whistleblower lawsuit alleging fraud involving the $275 million Treasury grant.

    Despite years of investigation, the Justice Department has never publicly disclosed what it uncovered.

    CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP.

    Nearly seven years after Hogan's investors filed their lawsuit, the fraud allegations have never been tested at trial. And despite President Trump's pledge to crack down on fraud and wasteful green-energy spending, his Justice Department is still defending the Biden administration's decision to shut down the case.

    "If we're wrong, the evidence will show it," Hogan said. "But don't let a Biden-era dismissal prevent the merits from ever being heard.".

    Michael Dorgan is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business.
